plain: A startup making human-shaped robots intended to help in homes as well as workplaces.
snappy: Humanoid-robot startup building Neo (home) and Eve (commercial) bipeds.
detail: 1X Technologies develops the Neo home Humanoid robot and the Eve commercial platform, emphasizing safe, soft-bodied designs for Human-robot interaction in Service & Consumer settings. The company stresses Teleoperation-assisted data collection and Imitation learning to bootstrap Manipulation skills, then refines them with a learned Policy. Its consumer focus puts a premium on Compliance and lightweight actuation so a Neo robot is safe to be around people at home.

plain: A way for a robot to map its surroundings by representing the world as a cloud of tiny soft 3D blobs that it continuously adjusts as the camera moves, producing a photo-realistic reconstruction.
snappy: A SLAM approach that builds and optimizes a map of 3D Gaussian primitives online, jointly tracking camera pose and producing a dense, differentiable scene reconstruction.
detail: 3D Gaussian SLAM replaces the sparse landmarks of classic Visual SLAM with a dense field of 3D Gaussian Splatting primitives, optimizing their position, color, and opacity through differentiable rendering while estimating the camera Pose against each new frame. Compared with Neural Radiance Fields-based mapping, the explicit Gaussian representation renders far faster and supports incremental Loop closure, making it attractive for service and consumer robots that need a high-fidelity 3D reconstruction for navigation and relocalization. It still relies on familiar SLAM machinery such as Bundle adjustment-style joint optimization and consumes input from a Depth camera or RGB Visual odometry front end.

plain: A way for a robot to capture a real 3D space from camera images as a cloud of fuzzy colored blobs, which it can redraw very fast to see the space from any viewpoint.
snappy: An explicit 3D scene representation built from posed images, used in robotics for real-time perception, mapping, and capturing real environments for simulation.
detail: 3D Gaussian Splatting represents a scene as millions of anisotropic 3D Gaussians with color and opacity, rasterized far faster than the ray-marched Neural Radiance Fields it competes with while matching their photorealism. Its real-time speed and editable geometry make it attractive for robotics 3D reconstruction, live Mapping (e.g., 3D Gaussian SLAM), and capturing real environments for Sim-to-real Sensor simulation. The representation is initialized from posed camera images via Structure from motion and is used to render synthetic training views and Digital twin environments.

plain: Finding objects and working out their real-world size, position, and which way they face, not just where they appear in a flat picture.
snappy: Detecting objects with their 3D extent, position, and orientation in metric space.
detail: 3D object detection outputs a 3D bounding box with dimensions, location, and heading, giving the metric geometry a planner needs to predict motion and keep clearance. Autonomous vehicles fuse LiDAR point clouds with camera images (Camera-lidar fusion) to produce these boxes, often projected into a Bird's-eye-view representation. It extends 2D Object detection and complements an Occupancy network for full Scene understanding.

plain: Turning sensor data into a full three-dimensional model of a scene or object that you can view from any angle.
snappy: Building a 3D geometric model of a scene or object from images, depth, or lidar data.
detail: 3D reconstruction fuses many observations into a single model that can be a Point cloud, a Mesh, a Voxel grid, or a learned representation like NeRF or Gaussian splatting. It is produced by methods such as Structure from motion, Stereo matching, or registering lidar scans, and is used to build a Map for navigation or a Digital twin of a Space asset or a Service & Consumer environment. Quality depends on accurate Camera calibration and clean Point cloud registration.

plain: Designing a robot's electrical system around 48 volts so it can deliver more power through thinner, lighter wires.
snappy: A power bus built around 48 V, which lowers current for a given power level and so shrinks wiring, losses, and heat.
detail: Because power equals voltage times current, raising the bus to 48 V (the 48V system, or high-voltage bus) lets actuators pull the same power at a quarter of the current a 12 V system would need, cutting copper weight, resistive loss, and Thermal management burden, while staying below the 60 V safety threshold for extra-low voltage. It has become the default for a Humanoid robot and high-torque Quasi-direct drive joints, where a Brushless DC motor and its Motor controller benefit from the headroom. Stepping down to logic rails still needs a DC-DC converter, and the bus is fanned out through the Power distribution board.

plain: A more detailed kind of car radar that also senses height, painting a dense 3D picture of the scene.
snappy: High-resolution automotive radar that adds elevation as a fourth dimension and outputs a dense point cloud of the scene.
detail: Where classic Automotive radar gives range, azimuth, and velocity, 4D imaging radar adds elevation and many more antenna channels to produce a Point cloud approaching the richness of LiDAR while keeping radar's all-weather and Doppler-velocity strengths. This makes it attractive for a Vision-only autonomy team wanting depth redundancy, or as a Camera-lidar fusion supplement in a Self-driving truck needing long-range Perception. It feeds 3D object detection and a Bird's-eye-view representation in the Self-driving stack.

full: Six Degrees of Freedom Grasp Detection
plain: Working out how a robot hand should grab an object from any angle in space, not just straight down from above.
snappy: Predicting full grasp poses with arbitrary approach orientation rather than constrained top-down picks.
detail: 6-DoF grasp detection outputs a complete Grasp pose, the gripper position and orientation in space, letting a robot reach sideways or under an object instead of only a top-down planar grip. It typically consumes a Point cloud from a Depth camera and is the task targeted by Contact-GraspNet and the GraspNet-1Billion benchmark. Full-pose grasping is essential for clutter, shelves, and Bin picking where a constrained approach would collide or fail.

plain: Working out not just where an object is in space but also which way it is turned, giving its full position and tilt so a robot can grab it correctly.
snappy: Estimating an object's full six-degree-of-freedom position and orientation in 3D from camera, depth, or point-cloud data.
detail: 6D Pose Estimation recovers an object's translation and rotation (a Pose in the Special Euclidean group SE(3)), typically by matching detected features or learned correspondences to a known model and solving with Perspective-n-Point or Iterative closest point. It usually follows Object detection and Keypoint Detection, and is the perception step that lets a Bin picking or Pick and place cell compute a valid Grasp pose. Depth from a Stereo camera or Depth camera improves robustness, and foundation pose models now estimate it for novel objects; accuracy directly limits assembly tasks like Peg-in-hole.

plain: A method for finding the shortest route through a network of connected points by always heading toward the goal while keeping track of distance already travelled.
snappy: A best-first graph search that expands nodes by path cost plus an admissible heuristic estimate of remaining cost.
detail: A* search ranks candidate nodes by the sum of the known cost so far and a Heuristic function estimating the cost to the goal, which lets it find an optimal path while exploring far fewer cells than uninformed search. It is the workhorse Global planner for grid-based mobile robots, running over an Occupancy grid or Cost map, and is a special case of Graph search that reduces to Dijkstra's algorithm when the heuristic is zero. Variants tailored to vehicles include Hybrid A*, which respects nonholonomic turning limits, and D* algorithm for efficient Replanning.

plain: The robotics arm of the engineering company ABB, which makes factory robot arms and automation gear.
snappy: Industrial-robot division of ABB making articulated arms, cobots, and factory automation systems.
detail: ABB Robotics is one of the 'big four' Industrial robotics suppliers, building the Industrial robot arm for Manufacturing and Logistics & Warehouse applications plus a Cobot line such as YuMi for Collaborative robot tasks. Its portfolio spans Robotic welding, Pick and place, and Palletizing, paired with the RobotStudio offline programming and Robot simulator environment. ABB integrates its arms with a Robot controller, vision, and broader Industrial automation systems.

plain: A position sensor that always knows exactly where a joint is pointing, even right after power-up, without having to move first.
snappy: An encoder that reports unique absolute position and retains it across power cycles, needing no homing.
detail: An absolute encoder assigns every shaft angle a unique code, so a robot knows its true Joint position immediately on startup. This contrasts with an Incremental encoder, which only counts relative motion and must perform a homing move to find a reference. Absolute encoders are favored on a Servomotor or Joint of an Industrial robot arm where unexpected power loss must not lose track of Pose; alternatives include the Resolver.

plain: A score for how far a robot's estimated path strayed from the true path it actually took.
snappy: A SLAM accuracy metric measuring the global discrepancy between an estimated trajectory and ground truth after best-fit alignment.
detail: Absolute Trajectory Error (ATE) aligns an estimated trajectory to Ground truth with a single rigid transform, then reports the root-mean-square position difference, summarizing global drift in one number. It is the headline metric for comparing SLAM and Visual-inertial odometry systems on benchmarks like the EuRoC MAV Dataset and KITTI Dataset, complementing relative-error measures that capture local Sensor drift. Lower ATE indicates a Localization estimate that stays globally consistent over the whole run.

plain: A software toolkit that automatically writes very fast, custom code for robots to plan their motions in real time.
snappy: An embedded optimal-control toolkit that code-generates fast real-time NMPC and OCP solvers with tailored QP backends.
detail: acados generates C code for optimal-control problems using efficient SQP and real-time iteration schemes, with high-performance linear algebra (BLASFEO) and pluggable QP solvers, making it a go-to for deploying Nonlinear MPC on embedded hardware. It is widely used for Model predictive control on a Humanoid robot, drone, and Autonomous vehicle, where solve times must fit a tight Control loop. It pairs with modeling front-ends like CasADi and overlaps in role with the QP-only solver OSQP.

plain: A sensor that measures how fast something is speeding up, slowing down, or being tilted by gravity.
snappy: A sensor that measures linear acceleration, including the constant pull of gravity, along its axes.
detail: An accelerometer senses linear acceleration along one or more axes; because gravity reads as a steady acceleration, a stationary accelerometer can also estimate tilt. It is one half of an Inertial measurement unit, paired with a Gyroscope, and most modern units are a MEMS sensor on a silicon chip. Robots use it for Balance control, vibration monitoring, and as one input to Sensor fusion for orientation.

plain: A powered roller conveyor that can hold items in place in separate sections so they bunch up without crashing into each other.
snappy: A zoned conveyor that buffers products in independent sections to control spacing and prevent jams and back-pressure.
detail: An accumulation conveyor divides its length into sensor-monitored zones that start and stop independently, so upstream product queues up smoothly when a downstream station is busy instead of colliding. Zero-pressure designs eliminate contact force between cartons, protecting fragile goods during Material handling. It is a workhorse of warehouse Automation, feeding a Sortation system or buffering parcels ahead of a Palletizing cell, and is coordinated in real time by the Warehouse control system.

plain: How close a robot actually gets to the exact spot it was told to reach.
snappy: The closeness between a robot's achieved pose and its commanded target pose.
detail: Accuracy measures correctness against the commanded target, so it depends on good Calibration of the robot's kinematic model and on compensating for flex and Backlash. It differs from Repeatability, which only measures consistency: a robot can repeat a wrong Pose perfectly. Accuracy matters most when a robot works from CAD coordinates or a Vision-guided robotics frame rather than being hand-taught, and it is improved by Hand-eye calibration and careful Transform chains.

plain: Car-style steering where the two front wheels turn at slightly different angles so they roll cleanly around a curve.
snappy: A steering geometry in which the inner and outer front wheels turn at different angles so all wheels share a common turn center, eliminating tire scrub.
detail: Ackermann steering is the geometry of road cars and is used by larger field and Mobility robots and a Self-driving car, where the front wheels pivot about a single instantaneous turn center while the rear wheels drive. Like Differential drive it produces Nonholonomic motion, so planners use Reeds-Shepp curves or Dubins path solutions to respect a minimum turning radius. It contrasts with Skid steering, which turns by slipping its wheels.

plain: A wheeled robot that turns the way a car does, by angling its front wheels rather than spinning wheels at different speeds.
snappy: A car-like wheeled robot using Ackermann steering geometry, with steered front wheels and driven rear wheels.
detail: An Ackermann-steered robot adopts automobile geometry in which the inner and outer front wheels turn at slightly different angles to share a common turning center, the basis of Ackermann steering. This makes it a Nonholonomic constraint platform that cannot move sideways and has a minimum turning radius, so its motion planning uses Reeds-Shepp curves or a Dubins path and tracking controllers such as the Pure Pursuit Controller or Stanley Controller. The form factor underlies most Mobility delivery rovers and the Bicycle Model used to approximate full-size Self-driving car dynamics.

plain: A method that teaches a robot to copy demonstrations by predicting short bursts of moves using a kind of neural network good at sequences.
snappy: A Transformer-based imitation policy that predicts chunked action sequences from demonstrations, popularized by low-cost bimanual teleoperation.
detail: ACT pairs Action chunking with a Transformer and a Variational autoencoder to learn smooth manipulation skills from a few dozen demonstrations, and became well known via the ALOHA Bimanual manipulation setup. It ingests Demonstration data collected by Teleoperation and outputs short action sequences, sidestepping the drift that breaks naive Behavioral cloning. ACT sits alongside Diffusion policy as a leading recipe for Contact-rich manipulation and learning from demonstration.

plain: A way to tell a robot to carry out a longer task while it keeps reporting progress and lets you cancel partway through.
snappy: A goal-oriented interface providing feedback and preemption for long-running robot tasks.
detail: An Action extends the basic Service idea for jobs that take seconds or minutes, like commanding Navigation to a Waypoint or asking MoveIt to execute a Trajectory; the client sends a goal, streams feedback, and can cancel before completion. In ROS this was the actionlib library, while ROS 2 builds actions on top of its Topic and Service primitives. They are heavily used by the Nav2 navigation stack and by motion-planning frameworks.

plain: Having a robot predict a short burst of moves at once instead of deciding each tiny step separately.
snappy: Predicting a short sequence of future actions per inference step rather than one action at a time.
detail: Action chunking reduces the compounding error and jittery, indecisive motion that plague step-by-step Imitation learning by committing to a coherent multi-step plan. It is central to ACT and to Diffusion policy approaches for Contact-rich manipulation and Bimanual manipulation, where smooth Trajectory execution matters. By cutting the number of decision points, it also improves Sample efficiency and robustness when learning from limited Demonstration data.

plain: A learning system that watches human demonstrations and then drives a robot by predicting short bursts of upcoming moves all at once, instead of one tiny step at a time.
snappy: An imitation-learning policy that uses a Transformer to predict a chunk of future actions per inference step, reducing compounding error in fine manipulation.
detail: The action chunking transformer (ACT) outputs a short sequence of future actions at once, a form of Action chunking that limits the Compounding error that plagues step-by-step Behavior cloning on long, dexterous tasks. It pairs a Transformer encoder-decoder with a Variational autoencoder latent to model multimodal human demonstrations, and is the policy that powers the ALOHA bimanual platform for fine Bimanual manipulation. ACT is a leading example of a Visuomotor Policy trained by Imitation learning, sitting alongside Diffusion policy in the modern manipulation toolkit.

plain: The choice of what form a robot's decisions take, such as motor torques, target hand positions, or text-like tokens.
snappy: How a policy encodes its outputs: joint torques, end-effector poses, velocities, or discrete action tokens.
detail: Action representation is a core design decision for any Policy: low-level Torque control offers fine authority but is hard to learn, while an end-effector Pose target or Action Tokenization abstracts away the arm's Inverse kinematics. The choice strongly affects the Embodiment gap and Cross-embodiment learning, and modern systems like a Vision-language-action model often emit tokens decoded into trajectories. Chunked outputs, as in Action chunking, are themselves a representation choice that trades reactivity for smoothness.

plain: A robot software pattern for long jobs, like driving across a room, that reports progress, can be cancelled, and returns a final result.
snappy: A ROS pattern handling long-running goals with continuous feedback, a final result, and cancellation support.
detail: An Action Server accepts a goal from an action client, streams Feedback while the task runs, allows the client to cancel, and finally returns a result, making it ideal for operations that take time. It is the natural interface for commanding Nav2 to reach a Waypoint or asking MoveIt to execute a planned Trajectory, where a one-shot Service or a fire-and-forget Topic would be inadequate. Under the hood it is built from topics and services and implemented through rclcpp or rclpy with its own Callback Group considerations.

plain: Turning a robot's smooth, continuous movements into a string of discrete symbols so a language-style AI can predict them one at a time.
snappy: Discretizing continuous robot actions into a finite vocabulary of tokens so an autoregressive transformer can predict them like words.
detail: Action Tokenization converts continuous joint or end-effector commands into discrete tokens, letting a Transformer-based Vision-language-action model predict actions autoregressively just as it predicts language tokens. The naive scheme, per-dimension binning, was used by RT-1 and RT-2, but it wastes capacity on high-frequency, correlated Action chunking sequences. This motivated compression-based schemes like the FAST Action Tokenizer, and it stands in contrast to continuous action heads such as Diffusion policy and Flow Matching Policy used by Pi-Zero.

plain: A controller that lumps everything it doesn't know about the robot and the world into one 'disturbance', estimates it live, and cancels it out.
snappy: Control that uses an extended state observer to estimate total disturbance plus unmodeled dynamics in real time and actively cancels it.
detail: ADRC augments the model with an extra state for the 'total disturbance' and uses an Extended state observer (ESO) to estimate it online, then feeds that estimate forward to cancel it, leaving a simple loop to control. Because it needs little plant knowledge it is popular in Motion control and Servo control of machines with varying friction and load, offering strong Disturbance rejection without a precise model. It generalizes the observer idea of the Luenberger observer and competes with Adaptive control and Robust control for the uncertain-plant niche.

plain: A theory that says a creature or robot acts to make the world match its predictions, reducing how surprised it is by what it senses.
snappy: A framework in which an agent selects actions to minimize prediction error, or surprise, between its internal model and sensory input.
detail: Active inference, derived from the free energy principle, casts both Perception and action as ways to reduce surprise: the robot updates its world model to match sensory input and acts to make sensations match predictions. It generalizes Predictive coding and offers a unified account that subsumes Intrinsic motivation, since expected information gain naturally drives Exploration vs exploitation. In embodied systems it is explored as an alternative to standard Reinforcement learning and Model predictive control, tying closely to Embodied cognition and the Perception-action loop, with the agent's State estimation and control falling out of one objective.

plain: When a robot deliberately moves its camera or other sensors to get a better look, rather than passively taking in whatever happens to be in view.
snappy: Purposefully controlling sensor placement and viewpoint to reduce uncertainty and gather the most informative observations.
detail: Active perception closes a loop between sensing and motion: a robot might rotate its head, reposition a Gimbal, or move its base to resolve an occlusion, treating viewpoint selection as part of the task. It is central to Next-best-view planning, robust Pose estimation, and Tactile servoing, and it complements the broader Perception-action loop. By choosing where to look, the system fights Uncertainty and Sensor noise far more effectively than a fixed Camera ever could.

plain: A way of mapping an unknown place where the robot chooses where to move next so it learns the most about its surroundings and its own position.
snappy: SLAM in which the robot actively plans its motion to minimize uncertainty in both the map it is building and its own pose estimate.
detail: Where ordinary SLAM passively builds a map from whatever the robot happens to sense, Active SLAM closes the loop by treating exploration as a planning problem, steering the robot toward viewpoints that most reduce map and localization uncertainty. Candidate moves are typically scored by Information Gain and chosen to trigger Loop closure when revisiting known regions stabilizes the Pose graph. It is common in Frontier-based exploration for an Autonomous mobile robot building an Occupancy Grid Map, balancing the cost of travel against expected uncertainty reduction.

plain: A depth-sensing camera that projects a pattern of light onto a scene so two cameras can more easily match points and judge distance, even on blank surfaces.
snappy: A stereo depth technique that projects an artificial texture or pattern so the two cameras can find correspondences on otherwise textureless surfaces.
detail: Active Stereo augments a Stereo camera with a projector that casts a random dot or infrared pattern, giving texture for Stereo matching where bare walls would otherwise defeat passive matching. Unlike pure Structured light, the projected pattern only aids correspondence, so depth still comes from triangulation between the two views, which makes it robust outdoors. Sensors like the Intel RealSense use this approach for short-range Depth map generation in manipulation and service robots.

plain: A learning setup with two parts working together: one part chooses actions and the other judges how good they were, so the chooser improves.
snappy: An RL architecture combining a policy (actor) with a value estimator (critic) that guides its updates.
detail: Actor-critic methods pair an actor, which is the Policy that selects actions, with a critic that learns a Value function to evaluate them and reduce the variance of the Policy gradient. This structure underpins many continuous-control algorithms used in robotics, including Proximal policy optimization and Soft actor-critic, which train controllers for Legged locomotion and Whole-body control. The critic accelerates learning over pure policy-gradient methods by providing low-variance feedback within a Markov decision process.

plain: Turning stored energy, such as electricity or compressed air, into the movement that makes a robot move.
snappy: The conversion of energy into the controlled motion or force that drives a robot's mechanism.
detail: Actuation is the output side of a robot, producing the motion that Sensing and computation call for. It is delivered by an Actuator, most commonly an Electric motor or Servomotor, but also a Hydraulic actuator, Pneumatic actuator, or Series elastic actuator. The choice shapes Torque density, Backdrivability, and Compliance, and it feeds through a Gearbox or Harmonic drive into each Joint to move the End-effector. Together with Sensing it completes the Perception-action loop.

plain: The part of a robot that actually creates movement or force, like a muscle in a body.
snappy: A component that converts an energy input into mechanical motion or force at a robot joint.
detail: The Actuator is what physically moves a Joint or End-effector in response to a command, turning electrical, hydraulic, or pneumatic energy into motion. Most robots use an Electric motor as the actuator, often paired with a Gearbox and a Motor controller that regulates current. Other forms include the Hydraulic actuator, the Pneumatic actuator, and compliant designs such as the Series elastic actuator used for force-controlled tasks.

plain: A controller that tunes its own settings on the fly as the machine or its load changes, so it keeps working well without a human re-tuning it.
snappy: Control that estimates and adjusts its own parameters online to track a plant whose dynamics are uncertain or time-varying.
detail: Adaptive control updates controller gains in real time using a parameter-estimation law, useful when a Manipulator picks up an unknown Payload that changes its Dynamics, or when a Quadruped robot crosses shifting terrain. Schemes include model-reference adaptive control and self-tuning regulators, and it is closely related to System identification and Gain scheduling. It contrasts with Robust control, which fixes one controller to tolerate uncertainty rather than learning it, and connects to Learning-based control at the data-driven end.

plain: Cruise control that not only holds a set speed but also automatically slows down to keep a safe gap behind the car in front.
snappy: A driver-assistance feature that maintains a set speed while automatically adjusting it to preserve a chosen following gap to the vehicle ahead.
detail: Adaptive cruise control (ACC) uses automotive radar, a camera, or 4D imaging radar to track the lead vehicle and modulate throttle and braking, often via drive-by-wire. As an SAE Level 1 advanced driver-assistance systems feature, it pairs naturally with lane keeping assist to form a hands-on highway pilot. It relies on time to collision and gap estimates and can hand off to automatic emergency braking when closing speed becomes dangerous.

plain: A robot squeezing out a precise line of glue or sealant along a path on a part.
snappy: Robotic application of a controlled bead of adhesive or sealant along a programmed path.
detail: Adhesive dispensing coordinates a metering valve with the robot's travel so bead width stays constant, which requires smooth Motion profile control and Zone blending to avoid dwells that pool material at corners. The bead path is usually built by Offline programming against the Work object frame and may use Conveyor tracking when applied to moving parts. Precise flow-versus-speed matching makes it sensitive to Following error, much like sealing and gasketing operations.

plain: A rule for re-expressing a robot's motion or force when you look at it from a different reference frame, so the numbers stay consistent across viewpoints.
snappy: The linear operator on SE(3) that transforms twists and wrenches between coordinate frames, built from a frame's rotation and translation.
detail: The Adjoint Representation is the 6x6 operator that maps a Twist (or, via its transpose-inverse, a Wrench) from one frame to another on the Special Euclidean group SE(3), making it the workhorse of frame changes in Spatial Vector Algebra and Screw theory. It appears whenever the Jacobian matrix must be referred to a new frame, when transforming the Spatial Inertia Matrix, and in the Product of Exponentials Formula for differentiating Forward kinematics. Closely tied to the Lie Algebra so(3) and SO(3), it is essential machinery in geometric controllers and in dynamics libraries like Pinocchio.

plain: Letting a robot's degree of independence be turned up or down on the fly, so a human can grant it more freedom or take more control as needed.
snappy: The capability to dynamically vary, at runtime, how much decision authority a robot holds versus its human supervisor.
detail: Adjustable autonomy (also sliding or variable autonomy) lets a system move along the Levels of autonomy during a mission rather than being fixed at one. A Planetary rover or Defense Unmanned ground vehicle may run fully autonomous over known terrain but defer to a human at a Negative obstacle or ambiguous junction, recovering bandwidth for Vigilance decrement. It is the operational machinery behind Shared autonomy and Mixed-initiative interaction, and depends on a clean Handoff problem solution and clear Intent communication so authority transfers are safe.

plain: A control style where a robot senses the push from a person or object and responds by moving, making it feel like it gives way gently.
snappy: Interaction control that measures contact force and outputs a commanded motion, the force-in, motion-out dual of impedance control.
detail: Admittance control reads a Force/torque sensor and synthesizes a velocity or position command so the robot behaves like a virtual mass-spring-damper, then a stiff Position control inner loop executes it, making it well suited to position-controlled Industrial robot arm hardware. It is the dual of Impedance control (which outputs force from motion) and a way to achieve Compliance control. It powers Hand guiding on a Cobot and Compliant manipulation tasks like Peg-in-hole and surgical tool insertion.

plain: Electronic helpers in a car that warn or briefly act to keep the driver safe, while the human stays in charge.
snappy: Driver-supervised electronic systems that assist with safety and control but keep the human responsible for the driving task.
detail: Advanced driver-assistance systems (ADAS) span Automatic emergency braking, Lane keeping assist, Adaptive cruise control, Blind spot monitoring, and Forward collision warning, sitting at L1-L2 on the SAE levels of driving automation. They lean on Automotive radar, Camera, and increasingly a Bird's-eye-view representation for Perception, and suppliers like Mobileye build them at scale. Crucially the driver must still supervise, unlike an Automated driving system, and a Driver monitoring system enforces attention.

plain: A specially designed input, like a subtly altered image, that fools a robot's learning-based vision into making a confident mistake.
snappy: A deliberately crafted input perturbation that causes a learned perception or control model to produce incorrect outputs.
detail: From the robotics angle, an adversarial attack might be a sticker on a sign that makes a self-driving Object detection model misread a stop sign, or a patch that hides a pedestrian from a detector. Unlike Sensor spoofing, which fakes the physical signal, this exploits weaknesses in the learned model itself, and it is closely related to Distribution shift and Shortcut learning since brittle features are easiest to attack. Robustness work spans adversarial training, Out-of-Distribution Detection, redundant Sensor fusion, and a Runtime assurance monitor to catch downstream unsafe behavior.

plain: A specially tweaked input, sometimes invisible to humans, that tricks a robot's vision system into being confidently wrong.
snappy: A deliberately perturbed input crafted to make a perception model produce a confident incorrect prediction.
detail: An Adversarial Example adds a small, often imperceptible perturbation that pushes a Neural network across a decision boundary, e.g. stickers that make a stop sign read as a speed limit. In robotics this is a Sensor spoofing and security concern for Defense & Security and Mobility perception, where a fooled Object detection or Semantic segmentation output can cascade into unsafe behavior. Defenses include adversarial training and pairing the model with Out-of-Distribution Detection and Sensor fusion so no single channel is a single point of failure.

plain: A method that makes a robot move naturally by rewarding it whenever its motion looks like real reference clips, judged by an automatic critic.
snappy: A learned, discriminator-based style reward that drives a control policy to produce natural motion resembling unlabeled reference clips.
detail: Adversarial Motion Priors (AMP) borrow the Generative Adversarial Imitation Learning idea to solve the naturalness problem in legged locomotion: a discriminator scores whether short motion snippets resemble a dataset of reference clips (e.g. motion capture), and that score becomes an extra style term in the Reward function alongside the task reward. This frees designers from hand-tuning gait rewards and lets a Quadruped robot or Humanoid robot learn lifelike, agile motion via Reinforcement learning in Isaac Gym. It is closely related to motion-imitation methods like DeepMimic.

plain: Deliberately searching for the rare, tricky situations most likely to make a self-driving car fail, so they can be tested and fixed.
snappy: Automatically searching the scenario space for rare, failure-inducing situations to stress-test an autonomy stack.
detail: Adversarial Scenario Mining optimizes the behavior of other agents or environmental conditions to provoke unsafe outcomes from the Ego vehicle, surfacing the Long-tail scenario that on-road miles rarely hit. It typically runs in a Driving simulator such as CARLA, perturbing an OpenSCENARIO description and measuring surrogate metrics like Post-Encroachment Time or Time to collision. The mined cases feed Scenario-based testing, regression suites, and the evidence in a UL 4600 Safety case, complementing the broader Safety of the intended functionality effort.

plain: Shooting film and video from a flying camera drone to get sweeping shots that would otherwise need a helicopter or crane.
snappy: Capturing professional film and video footage from a stabilized camera-equipped drone.
detail: Aerial cinematography mounts a high-end camera on a stabilized Gimbal beneath a Multirotor drone, using the Flight controller and smooth Trajectory tracking to fly cinematic moves like orbits and reveals. Operators rely on First-person view feeds, GPS hold, and increasingly on autonomous subject-tracking systems such as those from Skydio for hands-free follow shots. It is the most common Service & Consumer use of camera drones, governed by Visual line of sight rules unless a Beyond visual line of sight waiver is held.

plain: A laser scanner carried by a drone that fires rapid pulses at the ground to build a detailed 3D map of the terrain.
snappy: A drone-mounted laser scanner that produces dense 3D point clouds of terrain, including under vegetation.
detail: Aerial LiDAR mounts a LiDAR scanner on a UAV to capture a dense Point cloud of the ground, and because the laser penetrates gaps in foliage it can map bare-earth terrain that photography cannot. Accurate georeferencing depends on tightly fusing the scanner with RTK GNSS or Post-Processed Kinematic positioning and the inertial measurement unit so each return is placed correctly. It is used in Agriculture, forestry, and survey, often alongside Aerial photogrammetry, and the output feeds a digital surface model.

plain: Putting a robot arm or gripper on a flying drone so it can grab, carry, or work on objects in the air.
snappy: A UAV fitted with an arm or gripper that physically interacts with objects while flying or hovering.
detail: Aerial manipulation mounts a Manipulator or Gripper on a Multirotor drone so it can grasp, place, or apply forces during flight, coupling the arm's reaction torques back into the unstable flight dynamics. Controllers must coordinate Whole-body control and Force control across the flying base and the arm, often using Visual servoing and a Grasp pose computed onboard. From the embodied-robotics view it merges fixed-arm Manipulation skills with aerial flight, and rotor Downwash and Ground effect further perturb the contact task during Precision landing onto a target.

plain: Building accurate 3D models and maps of the ground by combining many overlapping photos taken from the air.
snappy: Reconstructing 3D geometry and maps from sets of overlapping aerial images with known or recovered camera positions.
detail: Aerial photogrammetry flies a Drone in a grid so successive frames overlap, then uses Structure from motion and Bundle adjustment to recover Camera intrinsics, poses, and a dense Point cloud for 3D reconstruction. The processed output is typically an Orthomosaic or a textured Mesh, and image quality is governed by Ground sample distance set by altitude and lens. It is widely used in Agriculture, surveying, and construction monitoring, often paired with RTK positioning for survey-grade accuracy.

plain: Technology that lets a machine sense how a person is feeling and adjust how it behaves in response.
snappy: Sensing, interpreting, and responding to a human's emotional state during interaction.
detail: In embodied systems, affective computing lets a robot read cues from face, voice, posture, and a Microphone array, then modulate its behavior, for example softening its approach under Proxemics when a person seems anxious. It is foundational to a Social robot and to Socially assistive robotics, where reading frustration or engagement steers coaching. It connects to Gesture recognition, Human pose estimation, and Theory of mind, and feeds Human-robot interaction loops; the robotics challenge is doing this responsively on Onboard compute in real conditions, not just on clean datasets.

plain: What an object lets you do with it, like a handle that can be grasped or a button that can be pressed.
snappy: An action possibility an object or environment offers an agent, such as graspable, pushable, or sittable.
detail: An affordance describes the actionable opportunities a Robot can exploit on an object, for example that a mug handle is graspable or a drawer is pullable. Affordance reasoning links Perception to Manipulation: an Affordance detection model proposes where and how to act, feeding Grasp planning and selecting a Grasp pose. Affordances are increasingly predicted by a Vision-language-action model so a robot can act on novel objects via Generalization.

plain: A robot working out what it can actually do with an object it sees, such as whether a handle can be grasped or a surface can be pushed.
snappy: Perceiving the action possibilities an object offers — graspable, pushable, openable — and localizing where on the object each action applies.
detail: Affordance detection maps raw perception onto what an object permits, predicting, for example, which region of a mug is a graspable handle versus its rim, so the robot can plan accordingly. It bridges Perception and Manipulation: outputs feed Grasp planning, Grasp pose selection, and Pushing or Nonprehensile manipulation in tasks like Bin picking and Pick and place. Models are usually built on a Convolutional neural network or Transformer trained on labelled Demonstration data, and the predicted affordances ground a robot's choice of Skill primitive or Tool use. In Humanoid robot and Manufacturing settings it lets a system generalize to novel objects rather than relying on fixed, pre-programmed grasp points.

plain: The idea that we perceive things in the world in terms of what we can do with them, like seeing a handle as something to grasp.
snappy: A framework that describes objects and environments by the actions they make possible for an agent rather than by their raw properties.
detail: Originating in ecological psychology, affordance theory reframes Perception as the detection of action possibilities, which directly motivates robotic Affordance detection and Grasp affordance reasoning. Instead of recovering a full geometric model, a manipulator estimates where it can push, lift, or grasp an object, feeding a Grasp planning or Manipulation pipeline. The view is closely tied to Embodied cognition and the Perception-action loop, and modern Vision-language-action model systems implicitly learn Affordance representations from Demonstration data.

plain: Anything that senses its surroundings and takes actions to reach a goal.
snappy: An entity that perceives its environment and acts upon it to pursue objectives, the basic unit of autonomous behavior.
detail: In robotics an agent is the abstraction tying Perception to action: it observes the world through a Sensor, decides, and commands an Actuator, closing a Perception-action loop. A single mobile robot is one agent, while a warehouse Fleet is many agents forming a Multi-robot system. The concept overlaps with AI, but the embodied robotics view stresses that an Embodied agent must contend with noisy sensing, physical dynamics, and real-time deadlines that a purely software agent does not.

plain: A Chinese startup building human-shaped robots and gathering huge amounts of data to teach them tasks.
snappy: Chinese humanoid startup building Yuanzheng bipeds and large-scale embodied datasets.
detail: AgiBot (Zhiyuan Robotics) develops the Yuanzheng line of humanoid robots and emphasizes collecting large embodied datasets through teleoperation to train a vision-language-action model for general manipulation. Its data-flywheel strategy mirrors the broader push toward a foundation model for robotics, pairing bipedal locomotion hardware with learned manipulation. It is among the fastest-scaling Chinese entrants alongside Unitree and UBTECH.

plain: A company that makes Digit, a two-legged robot that moves boxes and totes in warehouses.
snappy: Maker of Digit, a bipedal humanoid designed for warehouse logistics and tote handling.
detail: Agility Robotics builds Digit, a Bipedal robot optimized for Logistics & Warehouse tasks such as Goods-to-person tote moving and Material handling. Unlike many Humanoid robot projects chasing general dexterity, Agility narrows Digit to bin and conveyor work, integrating with Fleet management and warehouse Automation systems. Its Legged locomotion lets Digit navigate human-scale spaces with steps and uneven floors that block an Automated guided vehicle.

plain: A robot that helps grow crops by doing farm jobs like planting, pulling weeds, picking fruit, or checking on plants.
snappy: A field robot built for agricultural tasks such as seeding, mechanical or laser weeding, selective harvesting, and crop monitoring.
detail: An agricultural robot is a specialized Field robot that drives crop rows using RTK positioning and GPS for centimetre accuracy, then uses computer vision and object detection to tell crop from weed. Companies like John Deere deploy units for autonomous tillage and spraying, while harvesting bots add a soft gripper and grasp planning to handle delicate fruit without bruising. Aerial scouting is often done by a precision agriculture drone doing NDVI mapping, complementing the ground agbot in Agriculture workflows.

plain: A large drone that flies over fields carrying a tank of liquid to spray crops with pesticide or fertilizer.
snappy: A heavy-lift multirotor UAV that dispenses pesticide, fertilizer, or seed over farmland along automated coverage routes.
detail: An agricultural spraying drone is typically a large Multirotor drone with a Coaxial Rotor layout to maximize Payload capacity, flying low along a Lawnmower survey pattern computed by Coverage Path Planning. Onboard RTK GNSS gives the centimeter accuracy needed to follow swath lines precisely, while flow control meters chemical against ground speed. Operators often pair it with an NDVI mapping flight first, applying inputs only where a Precision agriculture drone has flagged stressed crop, and the DJI Agras family is the dominant commercial example.

plain: A specialized chip built to run artificial-intelligence calculations far faster and more efficiently than a normal processor.
snappy: A dedicated chip optimized for neural-network inference, speeding onboard robot AI within a tight power envelope.
detail: An AI accelerator, also called a neural processing unit (NPU), offloads the matrix and tensor math of a Neural network from the CPU, delivering more inference per watt for a robot's Power budget. On a Humanoid robot it runs perception and a Vision-language-action model in real time; the Tensor processing unit and many a System on a chip block are examples. Throughput is commonly measured in TOPS, and accelerators complement the Graphics processing unit in modern Onboard compute and Edge computing setups.

plain: A video-game-like virtual house where AI agents can move around and pick up objects to learn home tasks before trying them on real robots.
snappy: An interactive photorealistic 3D indoor simulator with manipulable objects for training and benchmarking embodied-AI agents.
detail: AI2-THOR (Allen Institute for AI) is a 3D household Simulation where an Embodied agent can navigate rooms, open containers, and interact with objects, supporting tasks from Semantic navigation to rearrangement. Its ProcTHOR variant procedurally generates thousands of houses for scalable training, complementing other embodied simulators like Habitat and iGibson. Agents trained here use Reinforcement learning and Imitation learning before facing the Reality gap, making it a staple platform for Vision-Language Navigation and Embodied AI research.

plain: A lighter-than-air craft, like a blimp, that floats using a buoyant gas and can stay in one spot for a very long time.
snappy: A powered lighter-than-air vehicle that derives lift from buoyant gas, enabling extreme-endurance flight and station-keeping.
detail: An airship gets most of its lift from buoyancy rather than from a Propeller or wing, letting it hover and station-keep for days with minimal power, in contrast to a Multirotor drone constrained by Endurance. This makes it attractive as a High-altitude pseudo-satellite for persistent communications and surveillance, and for slow, heavy Logistics & Warehouse cargo movement. Its huge surface area makes it sensitive to wind, so autonomy emphasizes Wind disturbance rejection and careful trajectory planning rather than agility.

plain: A realistic video-game-quality simulator for testing drones and cars safely on a computer before flying or driving them for real.
snappy: An Unreal Engine-based simulator from Microsoft that provides photorealistic environments and physically modeled sensors for drones and ground vehicles.
detail: AirSim builds on Unreal Engine to render Photorealistic rendering scenes and emit simulated camera, Depth map, LiDAR, and IMU streams, making it a popular sandbox for Sim-to-real research on an Unmanned aerial vehicle or Self-driving car. It exposes APIs compatible with PX4 and ROS so a real Flight controller can fly a virtual aircraft in Hardware-in-the-loop simulation, and its labeled imagery supports Synthetic data generation and Domain randomization for perception training. Teams use it to stress Detect and avoid logic and Reinforcement learning policies before touching physical hardware.

plain: A statistical chart that reveals how much a motion sensor's errors grow or settle over different lengths of time, used to grade how good the sensor is.
snappy: A time-domain statistical analysis that characterizes IMU bias instability and noise terms by plotting deviation against averaging interval.
detail: Allan Variance, plotted as Allan deviation versus averaging time, separates an Inertial measurement unit's noise sources, with the short-time slope revealing angle/velocity random walk and the curve's floor revealing bias instability and Sensor drift. Engineers read these parameters straight into the process-noise tuning of a Kalman filter or Extended Kalman filter used for State estimation. It is the standard bench characterization for gyroscopes and accelerometers, including the MEMS sensor and the Fiber Optic Gyroscope.

plain: A four-fingered robotic hand that is affordable enough for many labs to use when teaching robots to manipulate objects.
snappy: A four-finger, 16-DoF research hand widely used as a platform for dexterous manipulation learning.
detail: The Allegro Hand from Wonik Robotics has four fingers and 16 degrees of freedom, making it a popular and comparatively affordable Anthropomorphic hand for Dexterous manipulation and In-hand manipulation research. It is a common target for Reinforcement learning policies trained with Sim-to-real transfer, and it is frequently fitted with a DIGIT tactile sensor or other Vision-based tactile sensor for Contact-rich manipulation. It sits between the simpler LEAP Hand and the higher-DoF Shadow Dexterous Hand.

full: A Low-cost Open-source Hardware system for bimanual teleoperation
plain: A cheap, open-design pair of robot arms you puppeteer with two matching leader arms, used to record people doing delicate two-handed tasks for robots to learn from.
snappy: A low-cost open-source bimanual Teleoperation rig for collecting fine two-arm manipulation demonstrations.
detail: ALOHA uses a Leader-follower teleoperation setup of cheap arms so an operator can demonstrate delicate Bimanual manipulation, generating the Demonstration data that trains policies like the Action chunking transformer. Its follow-on Mobile ALOHA mounts the two arms on a wheeled base to extend the workspace into whole-home Mobile manipulation. ALOHA's low cost made high-quality Imitation learning data collection broadly accessible, complementing larger datasets like DROID dataset and BridgeData.

plain: Amazon's in-house team that builds the fleets of robots which move shelves and packages around its warehouses.
snappy: Amazon's warehouse-automation division operating mobile fulfillment robots, including the Kiva-derived drive units and the Proteus AMR.
detail: Born from Amazon's acquisition of Kiva Systems, Amazon Robotics runs one of the world's largest fleets of warehouse robots, using a Goods-to-person model where squat drive units ferry mobile shelving to human pickers to raise Pick rate. Newer systems include Proteus, a fully Autonomous mobile robot that navigates open floor among workers, plus robotic arms for sortation. Coordinating tens of thousands of units demands sophisticated Fleet management and Multi-agent path finding.

plain: The widely used software that lets a wheeled robot continuously track its position on a known map by matching laser scans.
snappy: The adaptive particle-filter localizer that dynamically resizes its particle set and is the default 2D localization node in ROS navigation.
detail: AMCL is the standard implementation of Monte Carlo localization in ROS and Nav2: it runs a Particle filter against a static Occupancy grid map, using the KLD-sampling rule to shrink the particle count once the robot is confident and grow it again when it is lost (the kidnapped-robot case). It fuses Wheel odometry with Lidar scan matching to maintain the map-to-odom Transform that the rest of the Navigation stack consumes. AMCL handles Localization but not Mapping, so it pairs with a map built earlier by SLAM.

plain: The set of tools that knows how to compile and package a single piece of ROS 2 robot software so other programs can build on top of it.
snappy: The ROS 2 package build system, providing CMake (ament_cmake) and Python (ament_python) tooling for compiling and exporting packages.
detail: ament defines how an individual ROS 2 package declares its build steps, dependencies, and install rules, exporting information so that downstream packages can find its headers and libraries. It replaced the ROS 1 catkin system and is invoked package-by-package by colcon during a workspace build. A typical C++ package uses ament_cmake to compile code that calls rclcpp, while a pure-Python package uses ament_python.

plain: The ability of a single robot to move over both dry land and through water without changing bodies.
snappy: Locomotion that lets one platform transition between terrestrial and aquatic modes, switching drive mechanisms as it enters or leaves the water.
detail: An amphibious robot might paddle or undulate using Swimming locomotion in water and then switch to Legged locomotion, Tracked locomotion, or Wheeled locomotion on the beach, often reusing the same actuators in both regimes. Designs frequently borrow from Bio-inspired robotics, mimicking turtles or salamanders whose limbs serve as both flippers and feet, and many are built as a Field robot for shoreline reconnaissance in Defense and Security roles. The control challenge is detecting the medium transition and reconfiguring Gait, buoyancy trim, and Terrain adaptation on the fly.

plain: A robot that can move both on dry land and through or across water.
snappy: A robot whose locomotion system lets it transition between terrestrial and aquatic environments without external help.
detail: An amphibious robot blends locomotion modes, often pairing Tracked locomotion or legs for shore crossing with fins, propellers, or Swimming locomotion for the water, and must seal its actuators against immersion. Some designs draw on Bio-inspired robotics, mimicking salamanders or turtles, while aerial-aquatic variants add a Multirotor drone stage to fly between bodies of water. They serve Defense & Security reconnaissance and environmental survey roles where a Remotely operated vehicle or Autonomous underwater vehicle alone cannot reach the beach, relying on Sensor fusion to switch control regimes at the waterline.

plain: A signal light or board on a factory line that lights up to alert everyone the moment something goes wrong.
snappy: A visual signaling system that lets any operator flag a line problem so supervisors and support staff respond immediately.
detail: Andon (Japanese for 'lamp') is a pillar of the Toyota Production System: a worker pulls a cord or presses a button and a tower light or overhead board shows the station and fault, often stopping the Production line until the issue is resolved. It is the human-triggered cousin of Jidoka, where a machine stops itself, and it feeds the same culture as Poka-yoke error-proofing. On automated cells an Andon tower is wired into the Robot controller and the Programmable logic controller so a Drive fault or a Protective stop raises the same visible alert, and the signals are aggregated by a Manufacturing execution system for line-status tracking.

plain: A robot deliberately built to look and move like a human being.
snappy: A humanlike robot whose form, face, and motion are designed to closely resemble a person.
detail: An android is a styling and human-factors choice layered on top of a Humanoid robot platform: it adds lifelike skin, facial actuation, and gestures intended to read as human. The closer the resemblance, the more designers must navigate the Uncanny valley and manage Anthropomorphism in Human-robot interaction. Androids appear in reception, telepresence, and research settings; most working bipedal machines such as Atlas or Tesla Optimus are not androids because they prioritize Bipedal locomotion and payload over cosmetic human likeness.

plain: An American defence-technology company that builds autonomous military hardware and the software that ties it all together.
snappy: Defence-tech firm building autonomous air, ground, and undersea systems unified by its Lattice command-and-control software.
detail: Anduril develops Autonomous weapon-adjacent and surveillance platforms — counter-drone interceptors, Autonomous underwater vehicle systems, and sentry towers — coordinated through its Lattice software, which fuses sensor feeds into a shared picture and tasks assets, including Drone swarm operations and Counter-UAS engagements. Its products sit squarely in the Lethal autonomous weapons system policy debate around human-in-the-loop control. The company contrasts with traditional primes by emphasising autonomy, software updates, and self-funded product development.

plain: A small autonomous reconnaissance helicopter drone that flies surveillance missions largely on its own using onboard smarts.
snappy: An autonomous reconnaissance UAS in single-rotor helicopter form factor with onboard AI for mission autonomy in contested environments.
detail: The Anduril Ghost (Ghost-X) is an Unmanned aircraft system built around a near-silent single-rotor design and onboard autonomy that can plan and adapt missions with minimal operator input. As an embodied AI platform it leans on edge Onboard compute for Object detection and navigation, and is engineered to keep flying under GPS-denied navigation through GNSS jamming or GNSS spoofing. It targets Defense & Security intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance roles, where its autonomy reduces operator workload compared with a manually piloted Quadcopter.

plain: The spinning kind of motion a robot has, which it can shuffle around its body to keep from toppling.
snappy: The rotational momentum of a robot's bodies, managed about the center of mass for balance and agile motion.
detail: Angular momentum about the Center of mass changes only when an external torque acts, so a free-flying or single-support robot must regulate it through Contact dynamics and Ground reaction force. Humanoid robots deliberately swing arms and torso to dump or generate angular momentum during recovery, and it is the rotational half of Centroidal dynamics. Conserving it during flight phases lets a Quadruped robot or gymnastic Humanoid robot re-orient mid-air, as Boston Dynamics has demonstrated with Atlas.

plain: Noticing when something in the sensor data looks unusual or out of place compared with what is normal.
snappy: Flagging observations that deviate from learned normal patterns in sensor or perception data.
detail: Anomaly detection learns what 'normal' looks like and raises a flag when an observation departs from it, useful when defects or threats are too rare or varied to label in advance. On a Manufacturing line it drives Quality inspection by catching unfamiliar product defects, and in Defense & Security it spots out-of-place objects in a scene. It overlaps with Condition monitoring and Predictive maintenance for machine health, and is one way robots cope with the Open world and Long-tail scenario cases that closed classifiers miss.

plain: A family of US safety standards covering machine tools and other industrial machinery.
snappy: The US series of safety standards for the construction, care, and use of machine tools and machinery.
detail: ANSI B11 is a series of US machinery safety standards, with B11.0 providing the overarching Risk assessment and Risk reduction framework (the US counterpart to ISO 12100) and individual parts covering specific machine types such as presses and lathes. It is applied alongside robot-specific standards like ANSI/RIA R15.06 and ANSI/RIA R15.08 and references OSHA regulations for compliance. Its risk-based approach drives the selection of safeguards such as a Light curtain, Two-Hand Control, or Lockout/Tagout, each engineered to an appropriate Performance Level.

full: Safety Standard for Driverless, Automatic Guided Industrial Vehicles
plain: The US safety rules for forklifts and warehouse vehicles that drive themselves with no operator on board.
snappy: The US safety standard specifying requirements for driverless, automatic guided industrial trucks and automated guided vehicles.
detail: ANSI/ITSDF B56.5 sets US requirements for the braking, obstacle detection, warning systems, and emergency stops of an Automated guided vehicle and driverless Autonomous forklift in shared facilities. It is the North American counterpart to the international ISO 3691-4, and its protective-stopping requirements are implemented through a Safety scanner and a Dynamic Safety Field. Warehouse integrators cite B56.5 alongside the test methods of ASTM F45 when commissioning a driverless truck fleet.

plain: The American safety standard that tells factories how to install and run industrial robots safely.
snappy: The US national industrial-robot safety standard, the American adoption of ISO 10218 Parts 1 and 2.
detail: ANSI/RIA R15.06 is the United States robot-safety standard published by the Robotic Industries Association (now A3), and it adopts the international ISO 10218 Parts 1 and 2 essentially verbatim. It guides the Robot integrator through the Risk assessment, safeguarding selection (Machine guarding, Light curtain, Safety scanner), and Collaborative robot safety modes such as Speed and separation monitoring. OSHA references it as the recognized good practice for US robot installations.

plain: The US safety standard covering robots that drive themselves around a facility, such as autonomous warehouse vehicles.
snappy: The US national safety standard for industrial mobile robots and the platforms they run on.
detail: ANSI/RIA R15.08 is the US standard addressing the safety of an Autonomous mobile robot and industrial mobile platform, including the case where a Manipulator is mounted on a mobile base (a Mobile manipulator). It complements the fixed-arm scope of ANSI/RIA R15.06 and aligns with international work like ISO 3691-4, covering navigation safety, a Safety scanner field, Speed and separation monitoring, and stopping behavior. It is widely applied to logistics fleets alongside the VDA 5050 interface and warehouse Risk assessment practices.

plain: Using two pulling actuators on opposite sides of a joint, like muscles, so the robot can set both where the joint sits and how stiff it is.
snappy: An opposing-actuator pair that independently controls joint position and mechanical stiffness.
detail: Modeled on biological agonist-antagonist muscle pairs, Antagonistic Actuation drives a joint with two opposing one-way elements (often a Tendon-driven actuation pair or a Pneumatic artificial muscle such as a McKibben Actuator) whose combined pull sets position while their co-contraction sets stiffness. It is a hardware route to Variable impedance control and safe Compliant manipulation, valued on a Humanoid robot and in Research/Frontier dexterous hands. The approach contrasts with achieving compliance electronically via Impedance control on a single Series elastic actuator.

plain: A robot hand shaped like a human hand, with fingers and a thumb that can pinch and grip.
snappy: A human-like robotic hand with fingers, an opposable thumb, and human-scale proportions.
detail: An Anthropomorphic hand is a Robotic hand deliberately patterned on human anatomy, with four fingers and an opposable thumb so it can use tools and objects designed for people. Its human-like kinematics support Precision grasp and Power grasp as well as Finger gaiting during In-hand manipulation. These hands are a hallmark of the Humanoid robot, appearing on platforms like Tesla Optimus and from companies such as Apptronik, and are usually built as a Tendon-driven hand to fit the actuators into a slim palm.

plain: Making robots look or act human-like, or people treating robots as if they were human.
snappy: The design or perception of robots with human-like form, expression, or behavior.
detail: Anthropomorphism has two sides: deliberately giving a robot a human-like body, such as an Android or Humanoid robot with an Anthropomorphic hand, and people's tendency to attribute feelings and intent to machines. Human-likeness can ease Human-robot interaction and build Trust in a Service robot, but overdoing it risks the Uncanny valley. Designers weigh it carefully, since the same face that makes a greeter robot friendly can make a near-human one unsettling.

plain: A safety system that rapidly pulses the brakes so the wheels keep turning instead of locking up and skidding during hard braking.
snappy: A system that modulates brake pressure per wheel to prevent lockup, preserving steering control and shortening stopping distance.
detail: An Anti-lock Braking System (ABS) detects impending wheel lockup from wheel-speed sensors and rapidly cycles brake pressure to keep tires in the grip region rather than sliding. It is the foundation that Electronic Stability Control and Automatic emergency braking build upon, and it interfaces with an Automated driving system through Brake-by-wire and the Controller Area Network. It manages longitudinal Wheel slip, complementing the lateral Tire Slip Angle that stability control addresses.

plain: A control method that moves a crane or hanging load quickly while keeping the swinging cargo from swaying like a pendulum.
snappy: Control that suppresses the pendulum oscillation of a suspended payload during and after crane or gantry motion.
detail: Anti-sway control shapes the command to a Gantry robot or overhead crane so the hanging load arrives without residual swing, often using Input shaping to cancel the payload's pendulum mode or model-based feedback on the cable angle. It is heavily used in Logistics and Material handling, and analogous techniques tame oscillation when a Mobile manipulator carries a long load. The underlying problem is an Underactuation challenge, since the swing is not directly actuated, and it relates to Resonance suppression and Trajectory generation.

plain: A safeguard that stops a controller from over-building a correction it cannot actually deliver, so it does not lurch when limits clear.
snappy: A technique that prevents a controller's integral term from accumulating during actuator saturation.
detail: When an Actuator hits Saturation, a PID controller's integral term keeps summing the unresolved Error signal, winding up to a huge value that then causes massive Overshoot once the actuator unclips. Anti-windup stops this by clamping or back-calculating the integrator while saturated, so the controller resumes cleanly. It is essential in robot joints and drone Flight controller loops that frequently run actuators to their limits during aggressive moves.

plain: Gripping an object by pinching two flat sides that face directly opposite each other.
snappy: A two-finger grasp made on opposing, roughly parallel surfaces of an object.
detail: An Antipodal grasp places two contacts on opposite, near-parallel faces of an object so their normals point toward each other, the natural grasp geometry for a Parallel-jaw gripper. When friction at the Contact points is sufficient (the line between them lies inside both Friction cone regions) the grasp achieves Force closure. Antipodal points are the dominant grasp representation in Bin picking and Learned grasping, because they are simple to detect from a Depth camera or Point cloud and easy to score with a Grasp quality metric.

plain: Picking grip points by finding pairs of spots on opposite sides of an object where two gripper fingers can squeeze inward and hold it.
snappy: Generating parallel-jaw grasp candidates by sampling pairs of opposing surface points whose contact normals nearly align.
detail: Antipodal sampling produces Parallel-jaw gripper grasp candidates by drawing pairs of surface points whose inward normals are roughly collinear, the geometric condition for an Antipodal grasp that resists slipping. Candidates are typically extracted from a Point cloud and then scored with a Grasp quality metric or a Force closure test before execution. It underpins many Grasp planning pipelines and serves as the candidate generator that learned rankers such as GQ-CNN, Dex-Net, and Contact-GraspNet evaluate.

plain: A Swiss company that makes a four-legged robot which walks around industrial sites taking readings and spotting problems.
snappy: Swiss developer of the ANYmal quadruped inspection robot for autonomous monitoring of industrial facilities.
detail: ANYbotics is a spin-off from ETH Zurich that builds ANYmal, a Quadruped robot designed for autonomous inspection of refineries, offshore platforms, and substations, where its Legged locomotion lets it climb stairs and traverse terrain a wheeled robot cannot. Equipped with thermal cameras, microphones, and lidar, it performs Condition monitoring and Predictive maintenance rounds, navigating via onboard SLAM and Foothold selection. It competes directly with the Spot platform from Boston Dynamics in the industrial inspection market.

plain: A computer procedure that always has an answer ready to give, getting better the longer it is allowed to think.
snappy: An algorithm that returns a valid solution whenever interrupted and improves that solution as more computation time is allowed.
detail: Anytime algorithms let a robot trade computation time for solution quality, which matters when a deadline is fixed but the planning budget is uncertain. They are the backbone of practical Motion planning under hard control loops: an Anytime Planning variant of Rapidly-exploring random tree such as Informed RRT* returns a feasible but rough path immediately, then keeps shortening it, and ARA* (Anytime Repairing A*) does the same for grid Graph search. A robot arm can begin executing the first path while the planner continues to refine the rest.

plain: A planner that gives you a usable answer almost immediately and then keeps improving it for as long as you let it think.
snappy: A planning paradigm that returns a valid (possibly suboptimal) solution quickly and refines it toward optimality given more time.
detail: Anytime Planning trades optimality for availability: it produces a feasible plan fast, then progressively tightens it as computation continues, so a deadline can be honored at any moment with the best plan found so far. This is essential for an Autonomous vehicle or Defense & Security platform that must always have an executable route, and it underlies algorithms such as ARA*, Informed RRT*, and BIT* that improve a bound as they run. It pairs naturally with Receding Horizon Planning and Replanning, where a continually refined solution is repeatedly executed and updated.

plain: Baidu's free, complete software package that other companies can use as the brain of a self-driving car.
snappy: Baidu's open autonomous-driving platform bundling perception, prediction, planning, and control modules into a full self-driving stack.
detail: Apollo (Baidu Apollo) ships a Modular pipeline spanning Perception, Trajectory Prediction, Motion planning, and vehicle control over a Drive-by-wire interface. It supports HD map ingestion, simulation, and integrates with the LGSVL Simulator for Closed-loop simulation. As one of the most complete open stacks alongside Autoware, it underpins Robotaxi pilots and is a reference Automated driving system architecture.

plain: A large free driving dataset from Baidu with detailed labels on every image pixel and matching 3D laser scans, used to teach cars to understand roads.
snappy: Baidu's large-scale driving dataset offering dense per-pixel labels and lidar point-cloud annotations for perception and 3D tasks.
detail: Part of Baidu's Apollo autonomous-driving program, ApolloScape pairs camera images with Lidar Point Cloud data and dense annotations supporting Semantic segmentation, 3D object detection, and lane parsing. It joins peer benchmarks like nuScenes, the Waymo Open Dataset, KITTI, and BDD100K in training the Sensor fusion and perception stacks of self-driving systems. Because it includes both pixel and point-cloud labels, it is well suited to developing Camera-lidar fusion models.

plain: A company that makes Apollo, a human-shaped robot for warehouse and factory jobs.
snappy: Humanoid-robot maker of Apollo, targeting logistics and manufacturing material handling.
detail: Apptronik, spun out of the University of Texas Human Centered Robotics Lab, builds Apollo, a Humanoid robot for Manufacturing and Logistics & Warehouse tasks like case handling and Palletizing. Apollo uses force-controlled, mass-producible actuators emphasizing Compliance and safe Human-robot interaction on the factory floor. The company has partnered with automakers and logistics firms for Pilot deployment of its Bipedal locomotion platform.

plain: A printed square black-and-white pattern that a camera can spot from far away to know exactly where it is and which object it is looking at.
snappy: A robust square fiducial marker encoding an ID that yields a precise 6-DoF pose from a single camera image.
detail: An AprilTag is a high-contrast square Fiducial marker whose interior bits encode an ID; detecting its four corners lets a camera recover full Pose estimation via Perspective-n-Point. Manufacturing and Logistics & Warehouse robots stick them on bins, docking stations, and end-effectors for Localization, Hand-eye calibration, and Conveyor tracking. Compared with the related ArUco Marker, AprilTags emphasize low false-positive rates and long-range robustness, and they are widely used as Ground truth in benchmarks and as cheap landmarks for Visual SLAM.

plain: A route finder that quickly returns a rough route, then keeps polishing it toward the best possible one for as long as you give it time.
snappy: An anytime variant of A* search that runs Weighted A* with a decreasing inflation factor, reusing prior expansions to tighten the solution toward optimality.
detail: ARA* (Anytime Repairing A*) is an Anytime algorithm built on A* search: it first finds a fast, suboptimal path using a large heuristic-inflation factor exactly like Weighted A*, then progressively lowers that factor and repairs the previous search instead of restarting, providing a bounded-suboptimality guarantee at every step. This is valuable for robot Path planning under tight time budgets where a usable plan is needed immediately. It is often combined with incremental methods like LPA* for anytime Replanning.

plain: A robot that joins metal by laying down a continuous welded line using an electric arc that melts the metal together.
snappy: A robot that deposits a continuous weld bead along a joint using an electric-arc process.
detail: An arc welding robot is a slender-wristed Industrial robot arm carrying a MIG or TIG torch, coordinating travel speed and weave through a precise Motion profile while a Robot positioner repositions the part. Paths are built with Offline programming and refined by Seam tracking to follow the joint despite fit-up variation. It is a major application of Robotic welding and often runs on a Seventh axis to reach long weldments.

plain: Free, open-source software that controls drones, planes, boats, and rovers automatically.
snappy: Open-source Autopilot firmware supporting many uncrewed vehicle types from a single project.
detail: ArduPilot, descended from the early APM project, runs on a Pixhawk and other flight controllers and provides flight modes including Loiter, Waypoint navigation, and Return-to-home for a Multirotor, Fixed-wing drone, Hybrid VTOL, rover, or boat. Like PX4 it uses the MAVLink protocol to talk to a Ground control station such as Mission Planner or QGroundControl. The two stacks compete for the same open-hardware ecosystem and both target Pixhawk-class boards.

plain: A large public collection of real driving data used by researchers to train and test programs that predict how vehicles move and that map roads.
snappy: An open autonomous-driving dataset providing HD maps and richly annotated motion-forecasting scenarios for benchmarking prediction models.
detail: Argoverse (and Argoverse 2) pairs LiDAR, surround camera, and HD map data with curated agent tracks for Trajectory Prediction leaderboards. It is a primary proving ground for models like VectorNet and is frequently compared against the Waymo Open Motion Dataset and nuScenes. Its bundled Lane graph and centerline priors make it popular for Behavior prediction research feeding the Self-driving stack.

plain: A fast method that predicts how a multi-jointed robot will accelerate when you apply known forces, by passing information up and down its chain of parts.
snappy: An O(n) recursive forward-dynamics algorithm that propagates articulated-body inertias along the kinematic tree to solve for joint accelerations from applied torques.
detail: The Articulated Body Algorithm (ABA) computes Forward dynamics in time linear in the joint count by performing a three-pass sweep over the Kinematic chain, propagating articulated-body inertias and bias forces so that joint accelerations follow without explicitly inverting the Mass matrix. It is the preferred integrator for simulating Floating-base dynamics in Humanoid and legged platforms and underlies the forward-dynamics routines in Pinocchio and many physics engines. Like the Recursive Newton-Euler Algorithm, ABA is most cleanly derived using Spatial Vector Algebra and is part of the Featherstone Algorithm family.

plain: A robot arm built from rigid segments connected by rotating joints, usually six of them, so it can reach almost any angle.
snappy: A serial manipulator with multiple rotary (revolute) joints, typically six axes, giving full position and orientation freedom.
detail: An articulated robot is a Serial manipulator whose Revolute joint axes give it six Degrees of freedom, letting its End-effector reach any Pose within the Workspace, which is why it is often called a Six-axis robot. Control depends on Forward kinematics and Inverse kinematics, with care taken near a Kinematic singularity. It is the workhorse of Manufacturing for Robotic welding, Assembly, and machine tending, built by FANUC, KUKA, and ABB Robotics.

plain: Extra pivoting arms wrapped in tank-style treads that a robot swings down to climb stairs and over rubble.
snappy: Auxiliary track-covered flippers that pivot at the front or rear of a tracked robot to extend its footprint over stairs and obstacles.
detail: By rotating these flipper arms a Tracked robot can reach up a stair edge, plant the flipper tread, and pull its body over, dramatically improving Terrain adaptation beyond what plain Tracked locomotion allows.
