Articulated tracks are standard on the bomb-disposal and reconnaissance platforms used in Defense and Security, where stair and debris negotiation is essential and a flip onto the back needs Self-righting. They are a mobility upgrade within wheeled-versus-tracked Locomotion, trading mechanical complexity for far greater obstacle-climbing reach.

plain: Operating things that have hinges or sliders, like opening a door, pulling out a drawer, or turning a valve, by respecting how they are allowed to move.
snappy: Manipulating jointed objects such as doors, drawers, and valves by inferring and following their kinematic constraints.
detail: Articulated-Object Manipulation requires a robot to estimate an object's hidden joint, whether a Revolute joint hinge or a Prismatic joint slider, and then apply motion along that allowed direction, often perceived as an Affordance from a Depth camera. The arm must comply with the discovered constraint using Compliance control or Cartesian impedance control so it does not fight the door or jam the drawer, and Mobile manipulation lets a Humanoid robot brace against reaction forces. Door and drawer opening are benchmark Service & Consumer tasks tackled with Imitation learning, a Vision-language-action model, or affordance-based Grasp planning.

plain: Giving a learning robot a built-in reward for finding new or surprising things, so it explores on its own.
snappy: An intrinsic-motivation technique that rewards a learning agent for visiting surprising or novel states.
detail: Artificial curiosity, or curiosity-driven exploration, is a concrete form of Intrinsic motivation: the robot earns internal Reward proportional to how surprising or poorly predicted a state is, often measured by a learned forward model's error or by Random Network Distillation. It is most valuable on a Sparse-reward task, where a Reinforcement learning agent would otherwise wander aimlessly, and it underpins Developmental robotics and Open-ended learning. Closely related to Novelty search, it improves Sample efficiency and is paired with Curriculum learning so a manipulator or mobile robot practices the most informative skills first.

plain: A printed black-and-white square barcode that a camera reads to figure out its ID and exact position in space.
snappy: A binary square fiducial marker, popularized by OpenCV, used for fast camera pose tracking and localization.
detail: An ArUco Marker encodes an ID in a black-and-white grid surrounded by a border; OpenCV detects the corners and, with the Camera intrinsics, computes a 6-DoF Pose estimation through Perspective-n-Point. Manufacturing and Mobility robots place ArUco boards for Camera calibration, Visual servoing targets, and Localization waypoints. It is closely related to the AprilTag as a Fiducial marker family, and arrays of markers (ArUco boards) improve accuracy and resilience to Sensor Occlusion of individual tags.

plain: A very simple two-wire system for connecting basic on/off switches and actuators to a controller without lots of separate cables.
snappy: A simple two-wire fieldbus connecting binary sensors and actuators at the lowest automation level.
detail: AS-Interface (AS-i) carries both data and power on one unshielded two-wire cable, addressing dozens of simple binary devices like limit switches and valves with minimal wiring. It typically sits below a higher-level Fieldbus, gatewaying its bit-level I/O up to PROFIBUS or PROFINET for the Programmable logic controller to process. As a low-cost discrete-I/O layer it occupies the device tier of the Automation pyramid, and safety variants extend it to carry interlock signals.

plain: A grade from A to D showing how serious a car's electronic safety function is, with D being the most critical, like the brakes.
snappy: The ISO 26262 risk classification (ASIL A-D, plus QM) assigned to automotive functions based on severity, exposure, and controllability.
detail: ASIL is the risk-rating scheme of ISO 26262, derived from a hazard analysis that combines severity, exposure, and controllability; ASIL D is the most stringent (e.g., steering and braking in an Autonomous vehicle). It dictates the rigor of the development process and the diagnostic coverage needed for a function in an Automated driving system. ASIL is the automotive counterpart of the Safety Integrity Level scale from IEC 61508.

plain: Putting separate parts together into a finished product, done by a robot instead of by hand.
snappy: Joining parts via robotic insertion, fastening, mating, or stacking operations.
detail: Robotic Assembly covers screwing, snapping, press-fitting, and mating tasks on a Production line, and most of it is Contact-rich manipulation where parts touch and slide under force. The hard sub-steps are insertion problems like Peg-in-hole, which demand a Force/torque sensor and Hybrid position/force control rather than pure Position control. Tight-tolerance work often relies on Fixturing, a Remote center of compliance, or Compliant manipulation, while complex products may need Bimanual manipulation to hold and join at once.

plain: A committee that writes the test and safety rules for self-driving industrial vehicles used in factories and warehouses.
snappy: The ASTM International standards committee developing test methods and terminology for driverless automatic guided industrial vehicles and mobile robots.
detail: ASTM F45 publishes standards on navigation, docking, obstacle avoidance, and performance testing for an Automated guided vehicle and Autonomous mobile robot fleet, giving buyers repeatable benchmarks rather than vendor claims. Its work sits alongside the safety requirements of ANSI/ITSDF B56.5 and the international ISO 3691-4, but focuses on measurable capability such as Localization accuracy and Collision avoidance. Warehouse integrators reference F45 methods when comparing a Goods-to-person robot from competing suppliers.

plain: NASA's cube-shaped flying robots that float around inside the space station helping astronauts.
snappy: NASA's free-flying cube robots that assist astronauts and run experiments aboard the ISS.
detail: Astrobee is a family of cube-shaped free-flying space robots that propel themselves with fans inside the International Space Station to take inventory, record video, and run guest experiments. Each robot localizes against a vision-based map, plans collision-free motion in the cabin, and can dock to recharge, demonstrating autonomous navigation in microgravity. It is an open research platform with code built on ROS.

plain: A training setup where the part being graded can peek at hidden facts about the simulation, but the part that actually runs the robot only sees what real sensors give it.
snappy: An actor-critic scheme where the critic consumes privileged simulator state while the actor is restricted to observations available at deployment.
detail: Asymmetric Actor-Critic exploits the fact that in simulation you know everything (object poses, contact forces, friction) but a deployed robot does not. The critic, used only during training, ingests this privileged state to compute accurate value estimates, while the Policy (the actor) is trained on the same partial observations it will have on hardware. This is a form of Privileged learning and underpins many Soft actor-critic and Proximal policy optimization training runs for Sim-to-real transfer; it is closely related to Teacher-Student Distillation, which goes a step further by distilling a privileged teacher into a deployable student.

plain: A company that makes the swappable connectors and force sensors that go between a robot's wrist and its tools.
snappy: A maker of robotic tool changers, force-torque sensors, and material-removal end effectors.
detail: ATI Industrial Automation specializes in the robotic Tool changer, which lets one Industrial robot arm automatically swap between a Gripper, welding torch, or sander mid-program, plus a six-axis Force/torque sensor used for assembly and force control. Its compliant material-removal tools support Robotic deburring, Robotic Grinding, and Robotic Sanding. ATI's sensors feed Force control and Hybrid position/force control loops, and the company competes with Schunk, Robotiq, and OnRobot in robot peripherals.

plain: A human-shaped robot that can walk, lift things, and balance on two legs, made by Boston Dynamics.
snappy: Boston Dynamics' bipedal humanoid robot, now an all-electric commercial platform aimed at industrial tasks.
detail: Atlas is the flagship Humanoid robot from Boston Dynamics, originally hydraulic and famous for parkour and backflip demos that showcased aggressive Dynamic walking and Whole-body control. The platform was relaunched as an all-electric robot positioned for manufacturing and Material handling rather than research stunts. Its control stack relies on Model predictive control, Zero moment point reasoning, and online Trajectory optimization to stay balanced under disturbance.

plain: A device that continuously tells a robot which way it is tilted and which direction it is facing.
snappy: A system that fuses IMU and magnetometer data to output 3D orientation in real time.
detail: An attitude and heading reference system (AHRS) extends a raw Inertial measurement unit by adding a Magnetometer and running an onboard fusion filter, such as a Kalman filter, to produce stable roll, pitch, and yaw. Unlike a bare IMU, it outputs corrected orientation rather than raw rates, countering Sensor drift. A Drone Flight controller and a Humanoid robot both rely on an AHRS for Balance control and stabilizing a Gimbal.

plain: A display, often a headset or tablet, that draws a robot's data and controls directly on top of what the operator sees in the real world.
snappy: An operator interface that overlays robot state, sensor data, or control affordances onto the user's live view of the physical scene.
detail: An augmented reality interface registers virtual graphics, planned paths, sensor readings, or safety zones, onto the operator's real-world view so a Human-machine interface no longer requires looking away at a separate screen. In Manufacturing it lets a technician see a robot's intended Trajectory and a Collaborative workspace boundary overlaid on the cell, and during Offline programming it can preview waypoints in situ before committing them. For Teleoperation and Surgical robot work it supports a Predictive display that overlays the robot's projected motion to mask Latency, and it strengthens Intent communication by making the robot's plan visible to nearby people.

plain: A company whose robot steers a flexible scope deep into the lungs to find disease.
snappy: Maker of the Monarch robotic endoscopy platform for bronchoscopy and urology.
detail: Auris Health (now part of Johnson & Johnson) built the Monarch Platform, which drives a flexible, steerable endoscope, effectively a continuum robot, through the airways via teleoperation from a controller. It fuses live camera views with preoperative imaging for navigation deep into the lung periphery, a form of catheter robot manipulation. It addresses early lung-cancer biopsy and competes with other robotic bronchoscopy surgical robot systems.

plain: A company building the self-driving system for big freight trucks on highways.
snappy: Autonomous-driving company focused on self-driving trucks via the Aurora Driver.
detail: Aurora Innovation develops the Aurora Driver, a Self-driving stack initially targeting the Self-driving truck market for highway freight in Logistics & Warehouse supply chains. It uses LiDAR (including long-range FMCW LiDAR), Radar, and Camera sensing for Level 4 automation along defined trucking lanes as its Operational design domain. Long-haul trucking is attractive because highway driving is more structured than the urban Robotaxi problem.

plain: The combined hardware and software that can drive a vehicle by itself across an entire trip.
snappy: The hardware and software collectively capable of performing the entire dynamic driving task on a sustained basis.
detail: An Automated driving system (ADS) is the L3-L5 brain of an Autonomous vehicle: it runs the full Self-driving stack, performing the entire Dynamic driving task within an Operational design domain rather than just assisting like Advanced driver-assistance systems. It must manage its own Fallback to a Minimal risk condition and is built to Functional safety standards such as ISO 26262. The ADS behind a Waymo or Aurora vehicle integrates Perception, prediction, Behavior planning, and control into one certified system.

plain: A driverless cart that hauls loads around a factory by following a fixed route, like a magnetic strip or wire taped to the floor.
snappy: A mobile transport robot that follows predefined guide paths (wire, magnetic tape, or fiducial markers) rather than planning its own routes.
detail: An AGV is the older, infrastructure-dependent cousin of the Autonomous mobile robot: it tracks a fixed guidepath and stops when something blocks it, rather than replanning around obstacles. AGVs are common in Manufacturing and Logistics & Warehouse Material handling, governed by the safety standard ISO 3691-4. Compared with an AMR, an AGV is cheaper and more deterministic but far less Flexible automation when the layout changes.

plain: A system that steers the car into a parking space for you, sometimes while you watch from outside with your phone.
snappy: A feature that autonomously maneuvers the vehicle into or out of a parking space, controlling steering and often throttle and braking.
detail: Automated parking uses ultrasonic sensors, a camera, and sometimes LiDAR to detect a free space and plan a parking maneuver, executing it through drive-by-wire. It applies path planning and trajectory tracking in a tight, low-speed envelope, leaning on Ackermann steering geometry and Reeds-Shepp curves for the forward-and-reverse arcs. It is the supervised precursor to automated valet parking, where the driver leaves the vehicle entirely.

plain: A warehouse system of computer-controlled cranes or shuttles that automatically put goods away into racks and fetch them back without people walking the aisles.
snappy: A computer-controlled arrangement of cranes, shuttles, and racking that stores and retrieves loads at fixed locations on command.
detail: An Automated storage and retrieval system (AS/RS) uses cranes or rail-guided shuttles moving in dense high-bay racking, directed by control software tied into a Warehouse management or Manufacturing execution system. It is a core piece of warehouse Material handling and often pairs with a Goods-to-person station and an Autonomous mobile robot for the last leg of transport. Because the storage map is fixed and deterministic, an AS/RS achieves high Throughput and density compared with manual picking, and vendors like Symbotic and Amazon Robotics build large-scale versions.

plain: Where you get out at the entrance and the car drives itself off to find a parking space and park, with no one inside.
snappy: Driverless parking in which the vehicle navigates and parks itself within a designated facility after the occupants have left.
detail: Automated valet parking (AVP) is an SAE Level 4 feature confined to a structured environment such as a parking garage, often using vehicle-to-infrastructure communication and fiducial markers or an HD map for localization. The car performs its own path planning, obstacle avoidance, and trajectory tracking with no safety driver aboard, treating the garage as its operational design domain. It is more autonomous than automated parking because the human is fully out of the loop within that domain.

plain: A training method that starts a robot practicing in nearly-identical pretend worlds, then automatically makes them more varied as the robot gets better.
snappy: A curriculum that widens the randomization ranges of a simulator automatically as the policy's competence on the current spread improves.
detail: Automatic Domain Randomization (ADR) removes the manual tuning from Domain randomization by treating the randomization bounds themselves as a Curriculum learning problem: whenever the policy clears a performance threshold, the sampling ranges for parameters like friction and mass expand. Famously used to train an in-hand cube reorientation policy that transferred via Sim-to-real to a real Shadow Dexterous Hand, it pairs naturally with Dynamics Randomization and massively parallel Reinforcement learning. The widening ranges keep the task perpetually at the edge of the policy's ability, closing the Reality gap without a human picking the bounds.

plain: A safety feature that slams on the brakes by itself when it senses a crash is about to happen and the driver has not reacted.
snappy: A system that autonomously applies braking to prevent or reduce the severity of an imminent collision.
detail: Automatic emergency braking (AEB) fuses automotive radar, a camera, and pedestrian detection to estimate time to collision, then commands maximum braking through brake-by-wire when impact is imminent. It is usually preceded by forward collision warning, which alerts the driver first, and is a core advanced driver-assistance systems function regulated under standards like ISO 26262. AEB extends to vulnerable road user protection, braking for cyclists and pedestrians who enter the path.

plain: Using machines to do tasks on their own so that little or no human effort is needed.
snappy: The use of machines and control systems to perform tasks with minimal human intervention.
detail: Automation spans from a single self-running machine to a whole automated plant, and robotics is one of its most flexible forms. Industrial automation organizes equipment along the Automation pyramid, from a Programmable logic controller on the floor up to a Manufacturing execution system. The field divides into Fixed automation for rigid high-volume lines and Flexible automation for changeable production, with an Industrial robot arm and Cobot deployments sitting in between.

plain: The tendency to believe a machine's answer even when your own eyes or other information say it is wrong.
snappy: The human tendency to over-trust automated recommendations and discount contradicting evidence.
detail: In robotics, automation bias shows up when an operator accepts a robot's perception or plan without independent checking, an error of commission (following a bad cue) or omission (failing to act because the system did not flag anything). It matters wherever a Human-in-the-loop reviews machine output, such as a surgeon trusting a Surgical robot's overlay or a Safety driver deferring to Autopilot. It compounds Automation complacency and is a known failure mode of Shared autonomy and Scalable oversight as systems grow more capable.

plain: The habit of trusting a machine so much that you stop watching it carefully and miss the moment it goes wrong.
snappy: Operator over-reliance on automation that reduces active monitoring and lets failures go undetected.
detail: Automation complacency grows when a system is highly but not perfectly reliable, so the operator learns that vigilance rarely pays off and tunes out. In an Autonomous vehicle, a Safety driver lulled by long error-free stretches may miss an Edge case the perception stack mishandles. It is a driver of the Out-of-the-loop performance problem and Vigilance decrement, and a core concern in any Human-in-the-loop or Supervised autonomy arrangement; it overlaps with but is distinct from Automation bias.

plain: The strange fact that the better a machine runs on its own, the harder and more important the leftover job of the human watching it becomes.
snappy: The principle that as a system automates more of a task, the human's residual supervisory role grows rarer, harder, and more safety-critical.
detail: Coined in human-factors research, the automation paradox warns that pushing Automation higher does not eliminate the operator but leaves them with only the hardest exceptions, which they now face out of practice. In a Robotaxi or on a Manufacturing line running near Lights-out manufacturing, the rare moment a Safety driver or supervisor must intervene is precisely when skills have atrophied. It is closely tied to Automation complacency, the Out-of-the-loop performance problem, and Vigilance decrement, and motivates careful Human-in-the-loop design.

plain: A diagram showing factory control as a stack of layers, from sensors at the bottom up to company-wide planning at the top.
snappy: A layered reference model of plant control, from field devices up through control, MES, and enterprise planning.
detail: The classic pyramid runs field devices and sensors at the base, then control via the Programmable logic controller and SCADA, then the Manufacturing execution system, and finally Enterprise resource planning at the apex, mirroring the ISA-95 hierarchy. Each layer abstracts and aggregates data from the one below, with cycle times getting slower toward the top. Industry 4.0 and the Industrial Internet of Things are flattening this strict pyramid as data flows directly between layers in a Smart factory.

plain: The share of tasks in a workplace that robots do instead of people.
snappy: The fraction of a process's or facility's total tasks performed by automation rather than human labor.
detail: Automation Rate is a headline KPI for tracking how far a facility has progressed from manual work toward Lights-out manufacturing, often reported per process step or per shift. In a warehouse it might describe the percentage of orders flowing through a Goods-to-person system, with the remainder handled manually because of low SKU Coverage or high Exception Handling demands. It rises as Brownfield Deployment projects mature and as Each Picking and Truck Unloading, historically labor-bound tasks, become viable. Automation Rate is closely watched alongside Robot density when assessing a plant's broader Industrial automation maturity.

plain: A self-operating machine built to move or perform actions on its own, often a historical mechanical figure that predates modern robots.
snappy: A self-acting mechanical device that follows a fixed sequence without sensing or adapting, the pre-electronic ancestor of the robot.
detail: Classic automata, like 18th-century clockwork writing figures, executed predetermined motions through cams and gears with no Feedback or Perception. They contrast sharply with a modern Robot, which closes a Perception-action loop and exhibits Autonomy and Automation under software control. The term survives in computer science (finite automata) and is echoed by the Finite state machine that still governs much robot Behavior planning today.

plain: A type of high-speed networking cable and protocol that lets the many cameras, sensors, and computers inside a car talk to each other quickly.
snappy: An in-vehicle networking standard delivering high-bandwidth, single-pair-wire data transport for sensors and compute in modern vehicles.
detail: Automotive Ethernet (variants like 100BASE-T1 and 1000BASE-T1) moves the gigabit-scale data that a camera, LiDAR, or Automotive radar produces toward the perception and planning compute of a Self-driving stack over lightweight single twisted-pair wiring. It coexists with legacy buses like the CAN Bus and FlexRay but offers far higher throughput, and is increasingly paired with Time-Sensitive Networking to give deterministic latency for safety-critical traffic. It underpins the centralized Domain controller architectures favored by an Automated driving system.

plain: A car sensor that bounces radio waves off objects to measure how far away they are and how fast they move.
snappy: A millimeter-wave radio sensor that measures range and relative velocity of road objects, robust in rain, fog, and darkness.
detail: Automotive radar uses mmWave signals (typically 77 GHz) and the Doppler effect to read closing speed directly, making it the backbone of Adaptive cruise control and Automatic emergency braking in Advanced driver-assistance systems. It complements Camera and LiDAR through Sensor fusion because it sees through weather that blinds vision, though classic radar has coarse angular resolution. Higher-resolution variants are sold as 4D imaging radar, and it feeds the AV's Perception layer.

plain: A robot driving itself back to a charging station and plugging in without a person's help.
snappy: A robot autonomously navigating to and aligning with a charging station to recharge unattended.
detail: Autonomous docking lets an Autonomous mobile robot or robot vacuum return to its charger when State of charge runs low, using Localization, a Fiducial marker, and fine Visual servoing to align contacts precisely. It closes the loop on unattended operation, and Fleet management schedules docking across a Fleet to keep enough robots working. The dock may use physical contacts or Wireless charging, and it is an alternative to a Hot-swappable battery swap when continuous human handling is undesirable.

plain: A challenge where a drone flies a race course of gates entirely on its own, as fast as a top human pilot, using only its cameras.
snappy: A research benchmark in which a UAV flies a gate course autonomously at champion-level speed using onboard vision-based control.
detail: Autonomous drone racing is a flagship Research/Frontier benchmark for agile flight, demanding perception, planning, and Trajectory tracking at the edge of the vehicle's Thrust-to-weight ratio. The robotics challenge is doing it with Onboard compute and Visual-inertial odometry rather than a Motion Capture System, since the drone must perceive gates and react within milliseconds. The Swift system famously beat human champions by combining a learned perception module with a Reinforcement learning policy, and datasets like the UZH-FPV dataset support this line of work.

plain: A forklift that drives itself, picking up and moving loaded pallets around a warehouse without a human in the seat.
snappy: A self-driving forklift that autonomously lifts, transports, and stacks palletized loads, combining AMR navigation with mast-handling control.
detail: An autonomous forklift extends the Automated guided vehicle into vertical material handling, using LiDAR and Natural feature navigation to drive aisles and Pose estimation to align its forks with pallet pockets and racking. As a heavier sibling of the Pallet jack robot, it must satisfy ISO 3691-4 safety for driverless industrial trucks, slowing or stopping via a Safety scanner when people enter its path. It works alongside Palletizing and Truck Unloading operations and is coordinated by the same Fleet management software that runs a warehouse's AMR fleet.

plain: A wheeled robot that drives itself around a building, figuring out its own path instead of following a painted line or buried wire.
snappy: A self-navigating mobile robot that builds a map, localizes within it, and plans collision-free routes on the fly.
detail: An AMR uses onboard Localization and Mapping (often SLAM with a LiDAR or cameras) plus a Navigation stack to reach goals while avoiding people and changing obstacles, unlike an Automated guided vehicle that needs fixed infrastructure. AMRs dominate Logistics & Warehouse Goods-to-person picking, with vendors like Locus Robotics and Amazon Robotics deploying large fleets coordinated by Fleet management software. Most run ROS 2 with Nav2 for Path planning and Obstacle avoidance.

plain: A powered pallet truck that drives itself, moving loaded pallets around a warehouse without a human operator.
snappy: A driverless powered pallet truck that transports palletized loads autonomously along warehouse routes.
detail: An autonomous pallet jack is a self-driving version of the familiar powered pallet truck, a class of Autonomous mobile robot (and a form of Autonomous forklift) that picks up and moves pallets for Material handling. It navigates with LiDAR and SLAM or follows mapped routes, performs Collision avoidance around people, and obeys ISO 3691-4 safety requirements for driverless industrial trucks. Coordinated by a fleet manager and the Warehouse management system, it competes with offerings from OTTO Motors and Mobile Industrial Robots for pallet transport.

plain: A small, slow, driverless bus that ferries passengers along set routes.
snappy: A low-speed, driverless passenger vehicle operating fixed or semi-flexible routes, typically in geofenced campuses or city zones.
detail: An Autonomous shuttle is a boxy, often bidirectional Level 4 automation vehicle running under 25 mph within a tightly bounded Operational design domain, using LiDAR and Camera Perception plus Map-relative localization against an HD map. Because routes are fixed and speeds low, it is a relatively tractable deployment compared with a general Robotaxi, and it falls back to a Minimal risk condition by stopping in lane. Operators frequently keep a Remote operation center for Teleoperation oversight.

plain: An untethered robot submarine that navigates and runs its mission underwater on its own, with no cable to the surface.
snappy: A self-navigating, untethered submersible robot that executes preprogrammed or autonomous underwater missions.
detail: An AUV carries its own power and runs missions without a tether, unlike the cable-connected Remotely operated vehicle, navigating by Dead reckoning, an Inertial measurement unit, and acoustic positioning since GPS does not penetrate water (GPS-denied navigation). It is used in Research/Frontier oceanography, seabed mapping, and Defense & Security mine countermeasures. AUVs require careful State estimation and Sensor fusion because surfacing to fix position is costly.

plain: A car or vehicle that drives itself by sensing the world around it, without a person steering.
snappy: A vehicle that perceives its environment and performs the driving task itself without continuous human control.
detail: An Autonomous vehicle (AV) runs a Self-driving stack that fuses LiDAR, Camera, and Automotive radar through Perception, then Behavior planning and control, often localizing against an HD map. Degree of capability is graded by the SAE levels of driving automation, with a true driverless Robotaxi like those from Waymo or Zoox sitting at Level 4 automation within a fixed Operational design domain. The car must always be able to fall back to a Minimal risk condition when automation fails.

plain: A weapon system that can choose and attack targets on its own, without a person directly controlling each engagement.
snappy: A weapon system that can select and engage targets without direct human control of each engagement.
detail: An autonomous weapon, often termed a lethal autonomous weapon system (LAWS), uses onboard Perception and decision-making to find and engage targets without a human approving each shot. The category overlaps with a Loitering munition and armed Drone swarm concepts, and it sits at the center of Robot ethics debates over meaningful human control. Policy discussion stresses keeping a Human-in-the-loop and applying strict Verification and validation before any field use.

plain: A robot's ability to do its job by itself, without a person controlling it the whole time.
snappy: The capacity of a robot to sense, decide, and act toward a goal without continuous human control.
detail: Autonomy ranges from none, where a person drives every motion via Teleoperation, up to a fully self-directed Autonomous mobile robot or Autonomous vehicle. Achieving it requires Perception, Localization, Navigation, and decision-making that close the loop without an operator. Because full independence is rare in practice, designers describe systems along Levels of autonomy and often deploy intermediate schemes such as Shared autonomy and Supervised autonomy.

plain: The share of a robot's work it completes entirely on its own, without a human stepping in to help.
snappy: The fraction of operation a robot completes without any human intervention, a key operational autonomy metric.
detail: Autonomy rate measures how often a robot finishes a job with no human help, the complement of how frequently an Intervention or Remote Assistance is needed. For a Self-driving car it relates to Miles per intervention and Disengagement counts; for warehouse fleets it tracks against the Operator-to-Robot Ratio that drives labor economics. It is a headline indicator of Field reliability during a Pilot deployment and a direct lever on Total cost of ownership.

plain: The system that flies a drone or aircraft automatically along a set route, without the operator steering by hand.
snappy: The hardware-and-software stack that stabilizes a vehicle and flies programmed routes autonomously.
detail: A drone autopilot runs on a Flight controller such as a Pixhawk and fuses an Inertial measurement unit with GPS to hold attitude and execute Waypoint navigation, Loiter, and Return-to-home. The two dominant open-source autopilot stacks are PX4 and ArduPilot, both of which speak MAVLink to a Ground control station. The term is used identically for ground and marine vehicles, where the same Sense-plan-act loop applies.

plain: A shared software framework that lets carmakers and suppliers build the programs running inside a vehicle's computers in a standard, reusable way.
snappy: A standardized layered software architecture for automotive electronic control units, separating application logic from hardware to enable supplier interoperability.
detail: AUTOSAR Classic targets deeply embedded, real-time control over buses like the CAN Bus and FlexRay, while AUTOSAR Adaptive targets the high-performance compute that runs an Automated driving system, often communicating over Automotive Ethernet. Its hardware-abstraction layers map cleanly onto Functional safety processes required by ISO 26262, letting safety-relevant components reach a target Automotive Safety Integrity Level. The framework gives a vehicle's Self-driving stack a portable foundation across suppliers.

plain: A warehouse system where robots crawl on top of a giant grid of stacked bins, digging out the one needed for each order.
snappy: A cube-storage system with grid-running robots that retrieve densely stacked bins for goods-to-person picking.
detail: AutoStore packs inventory into bins stacked in an aluminum grid; battery-powered robots travel across the grid top, lift the target bin, and deliver it to a workstation, a dense form of Automated storage and retrieval system. It is a classic Goods-to-person setup, eliminating aisle travel and maximizing storage per square foot. The robot fleet is coordinated by a Warehouse control system that talks to the Warehouse management system, and AutoStore competes with Ocado, Exotec, and Symbotic in cube and grid storage.

plain: A free, open software stack that turns a car into a self-driving vehicle, built on common robotics tools.
snappy: An open-source, ROS-based self-driving software stack covering localization, perception, planning, and control.
detail: Autoware (Autoware.Auto, Autoware Universe) is built on ROS 2 and bundles Localization via Normal Distributions Transform scan matching, Perception, Trajectory Prediction, and Motion planning into a deployable Self-driving stack. It consumes HD map data in the Lanelet format and is commonly validated against the LGSVL Simulator and CARLA Simulator. Maintained by the Autoware Foundation, it is a leading open alternative to Apollo for research and small-scale Robotaxi or Autonomous shuttle deployments.

plain: A robot that a person controls from far away to be present somewhere else, seeing, hearing, and acting through the machine as if they were there.
snappy: A remotely embodied robot, often humanoid, that lets an operator sense and physically act in a distant location in real time.
detail: An avatar robot (or telexistence robot) extends Telepresence beyond a moving camera-on-wheels into full physical agency: the operator's hand motions drive the robot's Manipulator and the robot streams back vision, audio, and Haptic feedback so it feels like being there. It builds directly on Teleoperation and Bilateral teleoperation, frequently using Wave variable encoding to stay stable over delayed links, and on Shared autonomy so the local robot can handle balance and fine grasping without low-level operator input. Applications range from a remote caregiver embodied in a Service robot to a specialist operating through a Surgical robot, and competitions like the ANA Avatar XPRIZE have pushed the genre beyond a simple Telepresence robot toward dexterous, sensation-rich remote presence.

plain: A flat, disc-shaped electric motor whose magnetic pull runs along its axle, giving lots of turning force for its weight.
snappy: A motor with magnetic flux directed axially across a disc-shaped air gap, yielding high torque-to-weight density.
detail: In an Axial Flux Motor (pancake or disc motor) the magnetic flux crosses the air gap parallel to the shaft rather than radially, producing a short, large-diameter machine with outstanding Torque density. That geometry suits direct or near-direct wheel and joint drives where packaging is flat - electric-vehicle Hub Motor designs and the compact joints of some Humanoid robot platforms. Like other Permanent magnet synchronous motor types it runs under Field-oriented control, and its high pole count gives smooth low-speed motion akin to a Gimbal Motor.

plain: Describing how a body is turned by naming a single line to spin around and how far to spin it.
snappy: Orientation expressed as a rotation angle about a single unit axis.
detail: By Euler's rotation theorem any 3D orientation equals one rotation by some angle about one fixed axis, and the axis-angle form states exactly that pair. Scaling the axis by the angle gives the rotation vector used in Screw theory and in the exponential map onto the Special orthogonal group SO(3). It converts directly to a Quaternion or Rotation matrix and avoids the Gimbal lock that troubles Euler angles.

plain: A smooth robot path built from a handful of control points, where nudging one point only changes a nearby section of the path.
snappy: A trajectory parameterized by B-spline basis functions over control points, giving smoothness and local support for efficient editing.
detail: A B-spline Trajectory represents motion as a weighted sum of basis functions over control points, so it is inherently smooth and, unlike a global Polynomial Trajectory, has local support: moving one control point only reshapes a nearby segment. This local-edit property makes it the backbone of gradient-based quadrotor planners such as EGO-Planner and of Spline Optimization, where the control points are adjusted against smoothness and clearance costs. Its convex-hull property also bounds the curve inside its control polygon, which simplifies Collision avoidance checks during Receding Horizon Planning.

plain: The voltage a spinning electric motor pushes back against its own power supply, which grows as the motor turns faster.
snappy: The speed-proportional counter-voltage a rotating motor generates that opposes the applied drive voltage.
detail: As any motor spins, its windings act like a generator and produce Back-EMF proportional to speed, set by the Back-EMF Constant; this voltage subtracts from the supply and ultimately limits top speed at a given bus voltage. A Brushless DC Motor Controller measures or estimates it for Sensorless Commutation, and Field Weakening exists precisely to push speed beyond the point where back-EMF would otherwise stall the drive. Back-EMF also enables Regenerative Braking, returning energy to the battery when a mobile robot decelerates.

plain: A number describing how much voltage a motor generates for each unit of speed it spins at.
snappy: The constant (Ke, inverse of KV rating) relating motor angular speed to the back-EMF voltage it generates.
detail: The Back-EMF Constant Ke quantifies how many volts of Back-EMF a motor produces per unit speed; its inverse, expressed in RPM-per-volt, is the familiar KV rating used to spec drone and robot motors. In consistent SI units Ke equals the Motor Torque Constant Kt, so a low-KV Gimbal Motor that holds position smoothly is also a high-torque-per-amp device. Drive engineers use Ke to predict the no-load speed at a given bus voltage and to plan Field Weakening when higher speeds are needed.

plain: How easily you can push or move a robot's joint by hand from the outside, without the robot resisting you.
snappy: The ease with which a joint can be moved by an external force applied at its output.
detail: A backdrivable joint transmits force smoothly in both directions, so a person pushing on the limb feels little resistance and the motor itself can sense the contact. High backdrivability is central to safe physical interaction and underpins approaches like Series elastic actuator and Quasi-direct drive designs in a Humanoid robot or Legged robot. It is the opposite of a high-ratio Harmonic drive or Cycloidal drive, whose large Gear reduction makes the output very hard to backdrive.

plain: A motor-and-gear unit so low in friction that you can push the robot's joint by hand and the motor spins backward, letting the robot feel outside forces.
snappy: An actuator with low reflected inertia and friction that external loads can move, enabling transparent force sensing and gentle contact control.
detail: A backdrivable actuator exhibits low Backdrivability resistance, so a person or the environment can move the joint without fighting a stiff gearbox, which is essential for Force control and Compliance control. Designs achieve this with Direct drive, Quasi-direct drive, or a Series elastic actuator rather than high-ratio worm or harmonic gearing that locks up. Legged platforms such as the MIT Cheetah and torque-controlled arms like the Franka Emika Panda use backdrivable actuators so they can estimate contact and perform Kinesthetic teaching without a dedicated Force/torque sensor.

plain: The tiny bit of slack or play between gears or parts, so when you reverse direction nothing moves for a moment until the gap closes.
snappy: Lost motion caused by clearance between mating parts such as gear teeth, felt as dead motion when the drive reverses direction.
detail: Backlash is the small free play between meshing teeth in a Gearbox or Gear reduction; on direction reversal the input moves before the output responds, hurting Repeatability and Accuracy. It is a key reason a Harmonic drive or Cycloidal drive is favored in an Industrial robot arm, since both offer near-zero backlash, and why Direct drive and Quasi-direct drive joints avoid geartrains entirely. Backlash shows up as Deadband in a Servo control loop and is often confused with mechanical Hysteresis.

plain: A control design method that stabilizes a chain of connected subsystems by tackling them one layer at a time, from the goal outward.
snappy: A recursive Lyapunov-based nonlinear design that stabilizes cascaded subsystems by treating each stage's state as a virtual control for the next.
detail: Backstepping builds a controller and a Control Lyapunov function together, recursively: it stabilizes the outer loop, treats that loop's required input as a setpoint for the next inner loop, and repeats inward, guaranteeing Lyapunov stability of the cascade. It is common in Nonlinear control of strict-feedback systems such as drone attitude-then-rate loops and electrically driven joints, and is often combined with Adaptive control to handle unknown parameters. It contrasts with Sliding mode control and Feedback linearization as a constructive nonlinear-design route.

plain: The system that keeps a walking robot from tipping over by constantly adjusting how it stands and steps.
snappy: Control that keeps a legged or wheeled-inverted robot upright by regulating its center of mass and foot forces.
detail: Balance control regulates the Center of mass relative to the Support polygon, keeping the Zero moment point inside it, often using the Linear inverted pendulum model and the Capture point to decide where to step. It is implemented with Model predictive control or Whole-body control commanding ground forces through Torque control, and it draws on Center of pressure and Ground reaction force feedback. It is what lets a Humanoid robot like Atlas recover from a shove via Disturbance rejection.

plain: A threaded rod that uses tiny rolling balls to convert spinning into smooth straight-line motion with very little friction.
snappy: A low-friction power screw that recirculates ball bearings between screw and nut to convert rotation to linear motion.
detail: A Ball screw replaces the sliding contact of a Lead screw with recirculating balls, slashing friction and enabling high efficiency, speed, and back-driving precision for a Prismatic joint or Linear actuator. It is standard on CNC machine tools and high-accuracy Cartesian robot axes, usually riding a Linear guide and driven by a Servomotor. The low friction improves positioning Accuracy and Repeatability over a lead screw.

plain: A tall robot that balances and rolls on top of a single large ball, like an upside-down version of riding a basketball.
snappy: A dynamically balancing mobile robot that drives omnidirectionally by actuating a single spherical wheel beneath its body.
detail: A ballbot is the omnidirectional cousin of the Two-wheeled inverted pendulum: it must continuously balance an inverted body while a set of rollers spin the ball, giving true Holonomic motion in any direction without reorienting. CMU's original Ballbot demonstrated graceful Human-robot interaction because its compliant, always-balancing base yields softly when pushed, an inherent form of Push recovery. Control combines an inner balance loop, like Balance control on a Spherical robot, with an outer Trajectory tracking layer, and it competes with Omnidirectional drive bases on Mecanum wheel or Omni wheel hardware.

plain: How fast a control system can keep up with changing demands before it starts lagging behind.
snappy: The frequency range over which a control system responds effectively to commands or disturbances.
detail: Bandwidth measures how quickly a controller can react: a high-bandwidth joint can track fast, jerky Trajectory commands, while a low-bandwidth one smooths them out and falls behind. It is limited by the Control rate, actuator dynamics, Sensor latency, and the need to avoid Overshoot or instability. In Force control and Impedance control, bandwidth determines how crisply a robot can respond to contact before the loop becomes sluggish or unstable.

plain: Control that only ever turns the actuator fully on or fully off, with nothing in between, like a basic thermostat.
snappy: A control scheme that switches the actuator between full-on and full-off rather than proportioning the command.
detail: Bang-bang control applies maximum effort in one direction until the Error signal flips sign, then maximum effort the other way, producing a limit-cycle oscillation around the Setpoint. It is simple and time-optimal for some systems but causes chatter, so practical versions add Hysteresis or a Deadband to slow switching. Robotics uses it for simple gripper opening, cooling fans, and as the bang-bang phase of time-optimal Trajectory optimization where actuators run at Saturation.

plain: Finding and reading the striped or square codes on products so a robot knows exactly what item it is handling.
snappy: Locating and decoding 1D and 2D codes in an image to identify items and retrieve their data.
detail: Barcode Detection scans a camera frame for the characteristic patterns of linear barcodes or 2D codes (QR code detection), localizes them despite rotation and perspective, and decodes the embedded payload. It is fundamental to Logistics & Warehouse robots performing Bin picking, Pick and place, and Sortation system routing, and to Manufacturing for part identification. It often shares a Smart camera pipeline with Optical Character Recognition as a fallback, and OpenCV plus dedicated decoders handle the heavy lifting; reliable lighting and minimizing Sensor Occlusion are key to read rates.

plain: A sensor that estimates how high a flying robot is by measuring air pressure, which falls steadily the higher you go.
snappy: A sensor that infers altitude from ambient air-pressure measurement, providing vertical-position feedback independent of satellite signals.
detail: A Barometric Altimeter is a staple on a Drone and other Multirotor drone platforms, giving fast relative-altitude updates for vertical position hold even during GPS-denied navigation or GNSS jamming. Because absolute pressure drifts with weather, it is usually fused with GPS, an Inertial measurement unit, and downward Optical flow in a Complementary Filter or Extended Kalman filter rather than trusted alone, and prop wash near the airframe must be shielded to limit Sensor noise. It is a small MEMS sensor on the Flight controller board, so it adds Altitude to Sensor fusion at negligible weight.

plain: Evening out the charge in every cell of a battery pack so no single cell is over- or under-filled, which keeps the whole pack healthy.
snappy: Equalizing per-cell voltage across a series battery pack so the weakest cell does not limit usable capacity or cycle life.
detail: A Battery Pack wires many cells in series, but tiny manufacturing differences mean they drift apart in charge; Battery Cell Balancing bleeds off or shuttles energy so they stay matched, protecting both State of charge accuracy and Battery Cycle Life. It is a core function of the Battery management system in any Lithium-ion battery or Lithium iron phosphate battery robot, from a Humanoid robot to an Automated guided vehicle. Passive balancing dumps excess charge as heat while active balancing moves it between cells, the latter preserving more usable capacity and limiting Depth of Discharge stress.

plain: How many times a battery can be charged and drained before it no longer holds enough charge to be useful.
snappy: The number of full charge-discharge cycles a cell sustains before capacity falls below a defined fraction of its original rating.
detail: Battery Cycle Life is the count of charge-discharge cycles before a cell degrades to a threshold, often 80 percent of rated capacity, and it depends strongly on chemistry, C-Rate, Depth of Discharge, and temperature. For a fleet operator it drives total cost of ownership: a Lithium iron phosphate battery typically outlasts a standard Lithium-ion battery, while a Sodium-Ion Battery and Nickel-Metal Hydride Battery occupy other points on the curve. A Battery management system limits Depth of Discharge and performs Battery Cell Balancing to extend cycle life, and degradation shows up as a falling State of Health.

plain: Electronics that watch over a robot's battery to keep it safe and working well.
snappy: Electronics that monitor, balance, and protect a battery pack while estimating its charge and health.
detail: A Battery management system (BMS) measures cell voltages, current, and temperature, balances cells, and enforces safe limits to protect a Lithium-ion battery or Lithium iron phosphate battery from over-charge, over-discharge, and thermal runaway. It computes State of charge and state of health, feeding the robot's Power budget decisions and Thermal management, and is itself an Embedded system on a Microcontroller. On a Humanoid robot or AMR the BMS also coordinates a Hot-swappable battery swap and reports status during Autonomous docking.

plain: A robot's complete power source: many battery cells wired together inside a case with electronics that watch over them.
snappy: An integrated assembly of series-parallel cells with a BMS, enclosure, thermal path, and connectors that powers the robot.
detail: A Battery Pack groups individual cells in series to raise the Bus Voltage and in parallel to raise capacity, wrapping them in a case with connectors, a thermal path, and a Battery management system that handles Battery Cell Balancing and protection. The pack defines a robot's Power budget, endurance, and weight, and many mobile robots use a Hot-swappable battery design or a Battery Swapping Station to avoid downtime. Its downstream electronics include a Power distribution board and a Buck-Boost Converter, while health is tracked through State of charge, State of Health, and Coulomb Counting.

plain: A station that quickly pulls a robot's drained battery and slots in a fresh one, so the robot can get back to work without waiting to recharge.
snappy: Infrastructure that automatically exchanges a robot's depleted pack for a charged one, eliminating recharge dwell time on a fleet.
detail: A Battery Swapping Station lets a robot trade a spent Battery Pack for a charged one in seconds rather than idling for an hour of recharge, keeping fleet Uptime and Utilization Rate high. It pairs with a Hot-swappable battery design and is managed by Fleet management software that routes robots to swap when State of charge runs low, an alternative to Charging Infrastructure with passive Charging Contacts. Such stations are common in Logistics & Warehouse operations and Agriculture, where continuous coverage by an Autonomous mobile robot fleet matters more than per-unit cost.

plain: A grid of tiny red, green, and blue color filters laid over a camera chip's pixels, which is how a single sensor captures a color image.
snappy: A mosaic color filter array over image-sensor pixels, typically in an RGGB pattern, that lets a monochrome sensor record color via demosaicing.
detail: A Bayer Filter places one red, blue, or green filter over each pixel of a CMOS Image Sensor in a repeating 2x2 RGGB color filter array, so each pixel records only one channel and a demosaicing algorithm interpolates full RGB. The green-heavy pattern matches human luminance sensitivity, but demosaicing introduces artifacts that can hurt precise Feature matching and color-based machine vision inspection. Robots needing raw spectral fidelity instead use a Hyperspectral Camera or a monochrome global-shutter sensor.

plain: A large free collection of 100,000 driving video clips, labeled so computers can learn to spot cars, lanes, and road objects in many weather and lighting conditions.
snappy: A large, diverse driving video dataset with detection, segmentation, and lane annotations spanning varied weather, time of day, and cities.
detail: Released by UC Berkeley, BDD100K is a benchmark for training and evaluating perception models on tasks like Object detection, Semantic segmentation, and Lane detection, with deliberate diversity to stress-test against Distribution Shift in Driving. It sits alongside other driving datasets such as nuScenes, the Waymo Open Dataset, KITTI, Cityscapes, and ApolloScape in the autonomous-driving research ecosystem. Its scale makes it a common pretraining source for the Computer vision components of a Self-driving stack.

plain: A company that makes Servi, a robot that carries food and dishes between the kitchen and tables in restaurants.
snappy: Maker of Servi food-running robots for restaurants and hospitality.
detail: Servi is a tray-carrying Service robot that uses a SLAM map and a Navigation stack to shuttle dishes between kitchen and tables, handling the food-running task in busy restaurants. As an indoor Autonomous mobile robot it relies on depth sensing and Obstacle avoidance to weave around diners and staff in an Unstructured environment. Bear targets the hospitality labor shortage and ties units into a small Fleet management console.

plain: A component that lets parts move smoothly against each other while reducing friction.
snappy: A machine element that constrains relative motion to a desired type while minimizing friction.
detail: A Bearing supports a Joint or shaft so it rotates or slides cleanly, carrying radial and axial loads while keeping a Link rigidly located; its quality directly affects a robot's Backlash, Accuracy, and Repeatability. Robotics uses specialized types such as the Crossed roller bearing in compact joints and the Slew bearing under a rotating base. Bearings pair with Gearbox elements and Linear guide rails throughout a manipulator's drivetrain.

plain: A German company known for running factory machines from regular PCs instead of traditional controllers.
snappy: A maker of PC-based control, the EtherCAT fieldbus, and the TwinCAT automation software platform.
detail: Beckhoff pioneered PC-based control, where the TwinCAT software turns an Industrial PC into a soft Programmable logic controller and Motion controller running multiple axes deterministically. The company created EtherCAT, the high-speed Industrial Ethernet fieldbus widely used to drive a Servo drive at tight Control loop rates. Beckhoff competes with Siemens, Rockwell Automation, and Bosch Rexroth, and its open platform suits Industry 4.0 lines and synchronized multi-axis motion such as Electronic gearing.

plain: A standardized test set of everyday household chores that virtual robots must complete in simulation, used to compare how capable they are.
snappy: A large benchmark (BEHAVIOR-1K) of long-horizon everyday household activities for evaluating embodied agents in realistic simulation.
detail: The BEHAVIOR Benchmark defines hundreds of human-relevant Long-horizon task activities (cleaning, tidying, cooking) with semantic success conditions, running in the iGibson/OmniGibson simulation environments to test Embodied AI agents. It stresses Mobile manipulation, Task and motion planning, and Generalization across Procedural Scene Generation rather than single skills, complementing manipulation-focused suites like ManiSkill, robosuite, and RoboCasa. Researchers use it to measure whether a Generalist policy or Robot foundation model can chain skills across realistic homes.

plain: Teaching a robot a skill by showing it many recordings of the task being done correctly and having it copy the input-to-action mapping.
snappy: Learning a manipulation policy by supervised regression from observations to the demonstrated actions in expert data.
detail: Behavior cloning (BC) is the simplest form of Imitation learning: it treats Learning from demonstration as supervised regression from each observation to the expert action, using Demonstration data collected by Teleoperation or Kinesthetic teaching. Its core weakness is Distribution shift, where small errors push the robot into states absent from training and cause Compounding error; remedies include DAgger and richer action models such as the Action chunking transformer and Diffusion policy. BC underlies many modern Visuomotor Policy systems and is the fine-tuning step for generalist policies like Octo policy.

plain: The part of a self-driving car's brain that makes the everyday driving choices, like whether to change lanes, yield, or wait at a junction.
snappy: The decision-making layer that selects high-level maneuvers such as lane change, yield, or proceed before detailed trajectory generation.
detail: Behavior planning sits above the local planner and motion planning in a self-driving stack, turning the outputs of behavior prediction and the route from route planning into discrete tactical decisions. It commonly uses a finite state machine, behavior tree, or learned policy to resolve situations like an unprotected left turn or a cut-in. Its chosen maneuver is then handed to trajectory optimization and trajectory tracking for execution within the safety envelope.

plain: Guessing what the cars, cyclists, and pedestrians around a self-driving vehicle are about to do next, so it can plan ahead safely.
snappy: Forecasting the future trajectories and intentions of surrounding road agents so the planner can react in advance.
detail: Behavior prediction takes tracked objects from multi-object tracking and an HD map and outputs likely future paths for each road agent, often as multiple weighted trajectories. In a self-driving stack it sits between perception and behavior planning, letting the car anticipate a cut-in or an unprotected left turn rather than merely reacting. Modern systems use a transformer or other neural network trained on datasets like nuScenes and the Waymo Open Dataset, and feed the resulting forecasts into time to collision and safety envelope checks.

plain: A diagram, shaped like a branching tree, that lays out the if-this-then-that logic a robot follows to decide what to do next.
snappy: A modular, hierarchical structure that sequences and selects a robot's tasks by ticking nodes in priority order.
detail: A Behavior tree organizes decision logic into reusable nodes such as sequences, fallbacks, and condition checks, evaluated by a periodic tick that flows down from the root. It has largely replaced the flat Finite state machine for complex robot autonomy because subtrees compose and reorder cleanly, which is why the Nav2 navigation stack uses BehaviorTree.CPP to orchestrate recovery behaviors like backing up and clearing the Cost map. Behavior trees pair naturally with Task planning and a Behavior planning layer that supplies high-level goals to the underlying Motion planning system.

plain: Building a robot's smarts out of many small, simple behaviors that all run at once instead of one big planning program.
snappy: A control paradigm that composes intelligence from a set of parallel, reactive behaviors rather than a single deliberative reasoner.
detail: Behavior-based robotics, pioneered by Rodney Brooks, rejects the slow Sense-plan-act pipeline in favor of many tightly-coupled sensing-to-action modules running concurrently. Each behavior, such as avoid-obstacle or follow-wall, maps stimuli to motor commands, so the robot stays responsive without maintaining a heavy world model. The best-known instance is the Subsumption architecture, and the style sits firmly in the Reactive control tradition, often blended with planning in a Hybrid architecture for tasks needing foresight.

plain: The simplest way to copy a demonstration: train the robot to output the same move the expert made in each situation it saw.
snappy: Supervised imitation that directly maps observations to demonstrated actions.
detail: Behavioral cloning treats Imitation learning as plain supervised learning, fitting a Policy that reproduces the Action an expert took for each observed state. It is fast and simple but suffers from compounding errors when the Robot drifts into states absent from the Demonstration data, a problem DAgger addresses by querying the expert on visited states. In manipulation, behavioral cloning is often improved with a Diffusion policy and Action chunking to handle multimodal, long-horizon behavior.

plain: A software library that lets a robot follow a flowchart of tasks, reacting and retrying when steps fail.
snappy: A C++ library for authoring and executing modular, reactive behavior trees that orchestrate robot tasks.
detail: BehaviorTree.CPP turns a Behavior tree into running code, ticking nodes that sequence, fall back, and retry actions while reacting to changing conditions, an approach often preferred over a rigid Finite state machine for complex tasks. It is the task-orchestration engine inside Nav2, where it coordinates Recovery Policy behaviors during Navigation. It competes conceptually with SMACH and the Hierarchical task network for high-level Task planning.

plain: Planning a robot's moves while accounting for the fact that it is never quite sure where it or the world really is, so it picks actions that work even with that uncertainty.
snappy: Planning over probability distributions of state rather than single estimates, so actions account for sensing and motion uncertainty.
detail: Instead of planning over exact configurations, Belief Space Planning reasons over the full probability distribution of the robot's state, which makes it the practical machinery behind solving a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process. It is closely tied to the Markov decision process formalism and to filters like the Kalman filter or Particle filter that propagate the belief forward. Robots use it to choose information-gathering detours, for example a Mobile manipulator that deliberately re-localizes before a delicate grasp, and it underpins Active SLAM and Chance-Constrained Planning where uncertainty must be bounded explicitly.

plain: A way to send power between two spinning shafts using a flexible loop of belt over pulleys.
snappy: A power-transmission element using a flexible belt over pulleys to couple rotating shafts.
detail: A Belt drive (often a toothed timing belt) transmits torque and motion between pulleys, letting a Servomotor sit away from the Joint it drives, much like a Cable-driven mechanism but for rotary transmission. SCARA robot and Cartesian robot axes commonly use timing belts, sometimes with a Gearbox or Gear reduction, while the belt's slight stretch can add compliance and Backlash. Belts are quiet, low-cost, and tolerant of misalignment compared with a rigid geartrain.

plain: A standard test and scoring rule used so that different robot systems can be compared fairly on the same task.
snappy: A standardized task and metric used to compare the performance of robot systems.
detail: A benchmark fixes the task, the data, and the metric so results from different teams are comparable rather than anecdotal. In autonomous driving, the Waymo Open Dataset and nuScenes serve as benchmarks for 3D object detection and tracking, scored against Ground truth labels. In manipulation, Open X-Embodiment provides shared data and tasks so a Generalist policy can be compared across labs, and simulators like Isaac Lab host standardized Gym environment benchmarks.

plain: A company that builds robots which pick items off shelves and sort packages in big shipping warehouses.
snappy: Supplier of robotic pick-and-pack and sortation systems for e-commerce fulfillment centers.
detail: Berkshire Grey integrates vision-guided robotics arms with conveyors to perform piece-picking, bin picking, and parcel sortation in fulfillment centers. Its pick cells combine 6-DoF grasp detection and a suction gripper or parallel-jaw gripper with object detection to handle mixed SKUs, a hard case of bin picking. It competes with RightHand Robotics and other order-fulfillment automation suppliers.

plain: A gripper that holds a flat part by blowing air fast across it, creating suction-like lift without actually touching it.
snappy: A non-contact gripper that lifts flat parts using the low pressure created by high-velocity airflow.
detail: A Bernoulli gripper directs a high-speed jet of air radially across a flat workpiece; by the Bernoulli principle the fast-moving air drops pressure and lifts the part, holding it with a small gap and no surface marring. Because it is non-contact, it suits delicate or contamination-sensitive items like silicon wafers, solar cells, and fabric, where a Suction gripper or Parallel-jaw gripper would damage or mark them. It is used as specialized End-of-arm tooling in semiconductor and electronics handling.

plain: Free software that runs inside a racing drone's electronics to keep it stable and responsive to the pilot's sticks.
snappy: Open-source flight-controller firmware optimized for the low-latency, high-rate control loops of FPV racing and freestyle drones.
detail: Betaflight is the dominant firmware for the FPV racing drone community, running on a Flight controller to read the Gyroscope and Accelerometer of an inertial measurement unit and drive each Electronic speed controller hundreds of times per second. Its tightly tuned PID controller loops prioritize crisp manual response over the autonomous waypoint features found in PX4 or ArduPilot. Pilots flash it to small acro quads and tune rates, filtering, and motor output to chase the lowest possible control Latency.

plain: A cone-shaped gear that lets two shafts meeting at an angle, usually a right angle, turn each other.
snappy: A conical-toothed gear that transmits rotation between intersecting shaft axes, most often at 90 degrees.
detail: A Bevel Gear redirects motion around a corner, so it appears in robot wrists and drivetrains wherever a turning axis must change direction within a Gear Train. A matched pair of equal-size bevels (a Miter gear) changes direction without changing speed, while unequal sizes also provide Gear reduction. It is mechanically distinct from a Worm Gear or Helical Gear because the shaft axes intersect rather than run parallel or skew, and a Differential Gear is built from a set of bevels.

plain: A self-driving software component that takes pictures from several cameras around a car and merges them into one map-like view seen from directly above.
snappy: A Transformer model that builds a unified bird's-eye-view representation from multi-camera images using spatial and temporal attention.
detail: BEVFormer queries learnable grid cells in a bird's-eye plane against features from surround-view cameras, fusing them over time to handle occlusion and motion. It is a workhorse of camera-only perception in the modern Self-driving stack, feeding 3D object detection and Semantic Occupancy Prediction without LiDAR. Built on the Transformer and Vision Transformer lineage, it underpins Bird's-Eye-View Perception used by Waymo-class autonomy and research benchmarks like nuScenes.

plain: A method that blends camera pictures and laser scans into one flat overhead map so a self-driving system sees everything in one place.
snappy: A multi-sensor fusion architecture that projects camera and lidar features into a shared bird's-eye-view grid before detection.
detail: BEVFusion lifts image features into 3D and rasterizes both camera and LiDAR data into a common Bird's-eye view feature map, where 3D object detection and Semantic segmentation heads operate jointly. Unlike Object-Level Fusion that merges late, it performs Camera-lidar fusion at the feature level, retaining geometry from lidar and semantics from cameras. It powers Research/Frontier autonomous Mobility stacks, builds on encoders like PointPillars and Lift-Splat-Shoot, and is benchmarked on the nuScenes dataset; accurate Lidar-Camera Extrinsic Calibration is a prerequisite for the projection to align.

plain: Flying a drone so far away that the operator can no longer see it with their own eyes.
snappy: Drone operation conducted beyond the operator's direct unaided sight, requiring extra safety systems and approvals.
detail: BVLOS unlocks long-range Drone delivery, pipeline inspection, and Agriculture surveys, but because the pilot cannot see traffic the operation must add Detect and avoid, reliable command links over MAVLink, Remote ID, and often participation in Unmanned traffic management. Regulators like the FAA grant BVLOS approvals as waivers or under emerging rules beyond standard Part 107. It is the operational opposite of Visual line of sight flight.

plain: A simplified picture of a car that pretends each axle has just one wheel on the centerline, making its steering and motion easy to compute.
snappy: A single-track vehicle kinematics model that lumps each axle into one wheel to relate steering angle and speed to vehicle motion.
detail: The Bicycle Model (single-track or kinematic bicycle model) collapses a four-wheeled vehicle's two front and two rear wheels into one steerable front wheel and one fixed rear wheel, giving a compact relation between steering angle, speed, and the resulting path curvature. It is the standard model for Ackermann steering vehicles and underlies path trackers such as the Pure Pursuit Controller and the Stanley Controller in a Self-driving car stack. Like other wheeled models it obeys a Nonholonomic constraint, and its turning geometry is described by the Instantaneous Center of Rotation; a dynamic version adds Tire Slip Angle for higher speeds.

plain: Remotely controlling a robot in a way that lets the operator feel the forces the robot is pushing against, like touch sent back over the link.
snappy: Teleoperation in which forces sensed at the remote robot are reflected back to the operator, closing a two-way force loop.
detail: Bilateral teleoperation sends commands one way and reflects contact forces the other, so a surgeon controlling a Surgical robot feels tissue resistance through Haptic feedback. It relies on a Force/torque sensor at the follower and careful control to stay stable, since communication Latency can make the force loop oscillate; Wave variable methods and a Smith predictor are used to tame this. It is the force-reflecting upgrade to plain Teleoperation and is closely tied to Teleoperation transparency and Leader-follower teleoperation.

plain: A complete itemized list of every part needed to build a product, along with quantities and costs.
snappy: A structured, itemized list of all components, quantities, and costs required to manufacture a robot or assembly.
detail: The bill of materials (BOM) is the backbone of robot manufacturing: every Actuator, Gearbox, motor controller, and fastener is enumerated so cost, sourcing, and assembly can be planned. It feeds the Total cost of ownership and Return on investment math that decides whether a design survives the Valley of death, and Vertical integration is often pursued to cut BOM cost. In production it links to the Enterprise resource planning and Manufacturing execution system that track parts through the line.

plain: Using two robot arms or hands together to handle something neither could manage alone.
snappy: Coordinating two arms or hands to manipulate an object cooperatively.
detail: Bimanual manipulation lets a robot hold a part with one arm while working on it with the other, as when folding cloth, threading a cable, or stabilizing a box during Assembly. Coordinating two arms creates a Closed kinematic chain and tight constraints, so it needs Whole-body control and careful Collision avoidance between the limbs. It is central to the Humanoid robot agenda and to Dual-arm robot platforms, and is a common testbed for Imitation learning and Teleoperation data collection.

plain: A robot reaching into a box of jumbled-up parts and pulling out one item at a time.
snappy: Grasping individual parts from a cluttered, randomly piled bin or container.
detail: Bin picking is a classic warehouse and factory challenge because parts overlap at unpredictable angles, so the robot must run Pose estimation on each item before computing a Grasp pose. A 3D vision system such as a Depth camera or Structured light scanner feeds an Object detection and Grasp planning pipeline, often paired with a Suction gripper or Parallel-jaw gripper on an Industrial robot arm. Modern systems increasingly use Learned grasping and Synthetic data to handle the long tail of part shapes and lighting conditions.

plain: Taking a jumbled heap of items in a bin and separating them into a single, one-at-a-time stream a robot can handle.
snappy: Separating a cluttered pile of items into an ordered, one-at-a-time stream for picking or sorting.
detail: Bin singulation is the perception-and-manipulation problem of converting overlapping, touching parcels or parts into individual items presented one at a time to a downstream pick or Sortation system. It relies on Machine vision and 6D Pose Estimation to choose a graspable item, then a robot performs Bin picking with a Suction gripper to extract it. Although it leans on AI for segmentation, in the warehouse bin singulation is an embodied loop of Grasp planning and Pick and place, and 'parcel singulation' often runs on a conveyor feeding a Truck Unloading or sortation line.

plain: A robot designed to copy how a real animal or living thing is built and moves.
snappy: A robot whose morphology, materials, or control are modeled on a biological organism to gain its mechanical or behavioral advantages.
detail: A bio-inspired robot borrows a solution that evolution already refined, such as a Snake robot using snake locomotion to slither through rubble or a Legged robot copying animal gaits for terrain adaptation. The approach leans on bio-inspired robotics and morphological computation, where bio-inspired structure offloads work from the controller to the body itself, often built with soft robotics or a tensegrity structure. It overlaps with swarm robotics for collective insect-like behavior and is a major Research/Frontier theme distinct from rigid factory machinery.

plain: Designing robots by copying clever ideas from animals and plants.
snappy: Designing robot structure, materials, and behavior by drawing on principles observed in biological organisms.
detail: Bio-inspired robotics borrows solutions evolution already found: gecko-foot adhesion, fish undulation, or insect Hexapod locomotion, often realized with a Bio-inspired structure. It overlaps heavily with Soft robotics for compliant bodies and with Morphological computation, where the body's mechanics do part of the control job. Examples include a Snake robot for confined spaces and the collective coordination of Swarm robotics modeled on ant colonies and bird flocks.

plain: A robot body designed by copying how living things are built, like legs based on insects or a spine based on a fish.
snappy: A robot structure whose form and mechanics are modeled on biological organisms to capture their efficiency, agility, or robustness.
detail: A bio-inspired structure borrows morphology from nature, such as a tendon-and-muscle layout, a segmented spine, or a gecko-like foot, and pairs with Bio-inspired robotics design methods. Examples include a Hexapod robot patterned on insects, a Snake robot mimicking serpentine motion, and a Tendon-driven hand copying human anatomy; many lean on Morphological computation so the body itself simplifies control. Such structures frequently use Soft robotics structure materials and Tensegrity structure principles, and are a staple of Research/Frontier robotics.

plain: Published limits on how hard a robot may press or hit each part of the human body without causing injury.
snappy: The tabulated maximum pressures and forces a collaborative robot may apply to specific body regions, drawn from ISO/TS 15066.
detail: Biomechanical Limit Values are the pain-and-injury thresholds in ISO/TS 15066 that bound how much force or pressure a Cobot may exert on each body region during Power and force limiting operation. Designers compare a robot's contact loads against these limits separately for Quasi-Static Contact and Transient Contact, since a clamped body part tolerates less than one that can recoil. A Collaborative robot cell is validated by pressing a Pressure Distribution Sensor against the moving arm and confirming readings stay below the table values, supporting compliance with ISO 10218.

plain: An underwater robot that swims by wiggling a fish-like body or tail instead of using a propeller.
snappy: An underwater robot that swims by undulating a fish-like body or oscillating fins, mimicking biological propulsion.
detail: A Biomimetic fish robot generates thrust through body or fin undulation rather than a propeller, an example of Undulatory locomotion that offers quiet, efficient, and highly maneuverable swimming valued for unobtrusive marine observation. Its flexible body draws on Soft robotics and often a Central pattern generator to coordinate the swimming gait, contrasting with the buoyancy-only Underwater glider and propeller-driven Autonomous underwater vehicle. The form is a Research/Frontier and Defense & Security interest for ecological monitoring, covert sensing, and studying real fish behavior up close.
