plain: A method that finds the best whole motion for a robot by repeatedly improving a guess using simple local approximations of the physics and goal.
snappy: A trajectory optimizer that builds local quadratic models of dynamics and cost and applies Bellman backward passes to refine a control sequence.
detail: DDP performs a backward pass that solves a local Riccati equation-like recursion to compute feedforward and feedback gains, then a forward rollout, iterating to a locally optimal trajectory. It underpins much modern Trajectory optimization for a Humanoid robot and Legged robot, and its Gauss-Newton simplification is Iterative LQR. As an Optimal control method it scales linearly in horizon, which is why it feeds warm-starts into Nonlinear MPC and Contact-implicit trajectory optimization.

plain: A handy property of drones that lets you work out every motor command just from the desired flight path, without solving the hard physics step by step.
snappy: A system property letting a quadrotor's full state and inputs be expressed algebraically from a few flat outputs (position and yaw) and their derivatives.
detail: A Quadcopter is differentially flat in its three position coordinates and yaw, so once a Minimum-snap trajectory specifies those flat outputs over time, the required attitude, angular rates and rotor thrusts follow by differentiation rather than by integrating the Equations of motion. This is why flatness-based planning pairs so naturally with Geometric tracking control and Trajectory optimization, and it makes real-time replanning feasible on the limited Onboard compute of a Multirotor drone. The concept is foundational to Learned quadrotor control and aggressive flight research.

plain: A clever gear set that lets two driven wheels turn at different speeds while still sharing engine power, such as when a vehicle rounds a corner.
snappy: A gear arrangement that splits input torque between two output shafts while allowing them to rotate at different speeds.
detail: A Differential Gear splits mechanical torque evenly between two output shafts yet lets them spin at different rates, which is essential for a Wheeled robot turning a corner where the outer wheel must travel farther than the inner one. It complements rather than replaces a Differential drive scheme, and Ackermann steering vehicles rely on it to avoid Wheel slip during turns. Some manipulators and a Tendon-driven hand use miniature differentials as an Underactuated Mechanism so one Actuator can drive several Joint motions that share load passively.

plain: The study of how the speed of a robot's hand relates to the speeds of its joints.
snappy: Relating joint velocities to end-effector velocities through the Jacobian.
detail: Differential (or velocity) kinematics is the velocity-level counterpart to Forward kinematics: the Jacobian matrix maps Joint space velocities to the End-effector Twist. Inverting that relation with the Jacobian pseudoinverse yields resolved-rate Inverse kinematics, the standard way to track a Cartesian path. It also exposes a Kinematic singularity, where the velocity map degenerates, and defines Manipulability.

plain: A robot with two powered wheels side by side that turns by spinning one wheel faster than the other, like a wheelchair.
snappy: A mobile base with two independently driven wheels that steers by varying their relative speeds.
detail: Differential drive is the simplest steerable configuration: equal wheel speeds drive straight, opposite speeds spin in place, and a speed difference arcs a turn. It is a Nonholonomic system (it cannot slide sideways), so its motion planning uses Wheel odometry and Dead reckoning for pose tracking. Countless Service robot and Logistics & Warehouse platforms, from vacuum robots to the Autonomous mobile robot, use the Differential drive scheme.

plain: An AI technique that starts from random noise and gradually cleans it up into a useful result, like a sharp motion plan or image.
snappy: A generative model that learns to reverse a noising process, denoising random samples into structured outputs such as action trajectories.
detail: In robotics a diffusion model most often appears as a Diffusion policy: rather than generating pictures, it denoises noise into a short Trajectory of future actions, which makes it good at multimodal, Contact-rich manipulation where several valid motions exist. It is trained from Demonstration data via Imitation learning and frequently combined with Action chunking, and it competes with a Transformer-based Vision-language-action model as a control backbone. Diffusion is also used in Generative simulation to synthesize varied scenes and Synthetic data.

plain: A robot control method that turns random noise into a smooth sequence of moves, the same denoising trick image generators use, but applied to actions.
snappy: A visuomotor policy that generates action trajectories by iteratively denoising, using a diffusion model.
detail: A diffusion policy frames action selection as a Diffusion model: starting from noise, it iteratively denoises into a coherent short trajectory of robot actions, which handles the multimodal, long-horizon nature of Manipulation better than naive Behavioral cloning. Trained from Demonstration data via Imitation learning, it pairs naturally with Action chunking and excels at Contact-rich manipulation tasks like Peg-in-hole. It has become a default Policy class for learned manipulation on parallel-jaw and dexterous Grippers.

plain: A small, low-cost fingertip sensor that uses a tiny camera to see the dimples and shapes that objects press into a soft rubber pad.
snappy: Compact, low-cost vision-based fingertip Tactile sensor from Meta that images deformations of an elastomer gel for in-hand sensing.
detail: DIGIT is an open, inexpensive Vision-based tactile sensor in which a small internal camera watches a soft illuminated gel deform under contact, recovering fine surface texture and Contact point geometry much like GelSight but in a fingertip-sized package. It supports Tactile sensing for Dexterous manipulation, Slip detection, and Tactile pose estimation on robotic hands and Humanoid robot fingers. Because each touch produces an image, it integrates naturally with learned perception and Tactile Representation Learning pipelines.

plain: A small, cheap fingertip sensor that uses a built-in camera to see how its soft surface deforms when touching things.
snappy: A compact, low-cost vision-based tactile fingertip sensor from Meta AI for dexterous manipulation research.
detail: The DIGIT tactile sensor is a small, inexpensive Vision-based tactile sensor that, like GelSight, images an internal elastomer pad to capture contact geometry, but in a form factor that mounts on the fingertips of an Allegro Hand or similar Robotic hand. Its low cost and open design made dense Visuotactile sensing practical for Dexterous manipulation and In-hand manipulation learning. It feeds Slip detection and Tactile servoing pipelines in Contact-rich manipulation research.

plain: A rough simulated stand-in for a real scene that captures the gist but does not have to match it exactly.
snappy: An approximate simulated analog of a real environment, looser and cheaper to build than a one-to-one Digital twin.
detail: Where a Digital twin mirrors a specific system precisely, a digital cousin swaps in similar-but-not-identical assets (a generic chair for the exact chair) to generate cheap, varied training data. It pairs naturally with Domain randomization and Synthetic data, trading Real-to-sim fidelity for scalability, and is generated inside simulators like NVIDIA Isaac. The bet is that training across many cousins improves Generalization more than overfitting one twin.

plain: A processor designed to crunch streams of sensor numbers, like audio or motor signals, very fast and on a strict schedule.
snappy: A processor with hardware tuned for real-time signal filtering, transforms, and tight control-loop arithmetic on robots.
detail: A Digital Signal Processor (DSP) has single-cycle multiply-accumulate units and deterministic timing built for streaming math, making it ideal for the inner Current loop and Field-oriented control of a Motor controller or the Microphone array processing on a Service robot. Its predictable, low-Latency execution suits Real-time control loops that a general CPU handles less reliably, so it appears in a Servo drive, a Medical & Surgical instrument, and Sensor fusion front-ends. DSP cores are also embedded inside SoCs like the Qualcomm Robotics RB5, contributing to Heterogeneous Compute and Hardware Accelerator Offload.

plain: A digital map of heights that records the top of everything in a scene, including buildings and trees, not just the bare ground.
snappy: An elevation raster derived from aerial imagery that captures terrain plus all objects on it, such as vegetation and structures.
detail: A digital surface model is reconstructed from overlapping drone photos during Aerial photogrammetry, often alongside an Orthomosaic, using the camera geometry recovered by Structure from motion. Unlike a bare-earth model, it includes canopy and rooftops, which makes it useful for volume measurement, line-of-sight analysis, and crop-height monitoring. Its accuracy depends on the Ground sample distance, photogrammetric overlap, and the Ground control point network or RTK GNSS used to georeference the flight.

plain: A constantly updated virtual copy of a real machine or factory that mirrors what the physical one is doing right now.
snappy: A live, synchronized virtual replica of a physical robot, cell, or system fed by real sensor data.
detail: Unlike a one-off Simulation, a digital twin stays continuously linked to its physical counterpart, ingesting telemetry to reflect current state and predict wear or failures, which makes it central to Predictive maintenance and Industry 4.0 lines. Platforms such as NVIDIA Isaac and Isaac Sim build photorealistic twins using the USD scene format. A factory digital twin can replay a Smart factory layout to test Fleet management changes before touching hardware.

plain: A method for finding the shortest routes from one starting point to every other point in a network, exploring outward evenly in all directions.
snappy: An uninformed graph search that computes shortest paths from a source by expanding nodes in order of accumulated cost.
detail: Dijkstra's algorithm grows a shortest-path tree outward from the start, always expanding the cheapest-so-far node, and is guaranteed optimal on graphs with non-negative edge costs. In robotics it serves as a Global planner over a Cost map or Occupancy grid and is the foundation that A* search extends by adding a goal-directed Heuristic function to prune the search. Because it has no goal bias, Dijkstra explores more nodes than A*, but it naturally yields distances to many destinations at once, useful for Route planning across a facility.

plain: A company that makes Moxi, a hospital robot that fetches and delivers supplies so nurses can focus on patients.
snappy: Maker of Moxi, a hospital service robot that autonomously fetches and delivers supplies.
detail: Moxi is a Service robot and Mobile manipulator that navigates hospital corridors and uses an arm to fetch lab samples, medications, and supplies, freeing clinical staff from fetch-and-carry errands. It combines a SLAM-based Navigation stack with social navigation behaviors so it shares elevators and hallways safely under standards like ISO 13482 for personal-care robots. Diligent emphasizes socially appropriate Human-robot interaction so the robot is accepted by staff and patients.

plain: A vision model trained without any human labels that learns rich, reusable features from raw images, giving other systems a strong head start on understanding pictures.
snappy: A self-supervised Vision Transformer that produces general-purpose dense visual features transferable across many downstream perception tasks.
detail: DINOv2 uses Self-supervised learning (self-distillation with no labels) over a Vision Transformer to yield patch-level features that encode semantics and correspondence without task-specific training. Its dense embeddings serve as a frozen Foundation model backbone for Semantic segmentation, Keypoint Detection, depth, and correspondence, and they pair naturally with the language alignment of CLIP. In robotics, DINOv2 features improve Place recognition, object correspondence for 6D Pose Estimation, and visual policies, often outperforming hand-engineered descriptors like SIFT or ORB features for matching across viewpoints.

plain: Connecting a motor straight to the thing it moves, with no gears in between.
snappy: Coupling a load directly to a motor without gearing, eliminating backlash and transmission losses.
detail: In a direct-drive joint the motor's output connects straight to the load, so there is no Gearbox to introduce Backlash, friction, or compliance, giving clean Torque control and excellent Backdrivability. The cost is that the motor itself must supply the full joint torque, demanding a large, high Torque density Permanent magnet synchronous motor or Frameless motor. Direct drive appears in high-precision rotary tables, a Linear motor, and the Voice coil actuator.

plain: Automating the making of separate, countable things like car parts, phones, or bottles, one item at a time down a line.
snappy: Automation of operations that produce distinct, countable items, as opposed to continuous flows of fluids or bulk material.
detail: Discrete automation handles part-by-part manufacturing: an Industrial robot arm performing Assembly, a Pick and place machine, Robotic welding, or Conveyor tracking on a Production line. It is the natural home of the Programmable logic controller, Ladder logic, and event-driven sequencing, measured by Cycle time, Takt time, and Overall equipment effectiveness. The contrast is Process automation, which regulates continuous flows; discrete plants instead coordinate countable steps, often through a Robot integrator who builds the Robot cell.

plain: The moment a self-driving system gives up control and a human has to take over.
snappy: An event in which an automated driving system hands control back to a safety driver, usually because it cannot proceed safely.
detail: During public-road testing, a Safety driver records each Disengagement, and regulators like California's DMV require an annual disengagement report; companies such as Waymo and Cruise publish miles-between-disengagement as a maturity proxy. It is closely tied to Takeover request and Intervention, and metrics like Miles per intervention or Interventions per mile normalize it across fleets. A high disengagement rate often points to recurring Edge case failures in the Self-driving stack.

plain: A robot that drives through rooms by itself and kills germs on surfaces using strong ultraviolet light or a sanitizing spray.
snappy: A mobile Service robot that autonomously sterilizes indoor spaces by emitting germicidal UV light or dispensing disinfectant.
detail: A disinfection robot is a Service robotics platform built on an Autonomous mobile robot base that navigates hospital rooms or transit hubs and dwells at locations long enough to deliver a germicidal UV-C dose. It maps and routes using SLAM and Coverage path planning so no surface is missed, while Human-robot interaction safeguards and Obstacle detection shut off the lamp if a person enters, since UV exposure is hazardous. Closely related to the Cleaning robot, it surged in healthcare and Service & Consumer deployments and pairs Localization with timed exposure models to certify each space.

plain: A network of controllers spread across a large plant that work together to run a continuous process like a refinery or chemical plant.
snappy: A control architecture using networked, distributed controllers to coordinate large continuous-process plants.
detail: A DCS distributes control across many controllers tied to a central engineering and operations layer, contrasting with a single Programmable logic controller running a discrete machine. It excels at continuous Process automation such as refining, power generation, and chemicals, where thousands of loops run a Function block diagram for regulation. A DCS overlaps with SCADA and a Human-machine interface for operator supervision, communicates over a Fieldbus like PROFIBUS or Industrial Ethernet, and increasingly exchanges data via OPC UA within the Automation pyramid.

plain: Spreading many small electric motors and propellers across an aircraft instead of using one or two big engines.
snappy: An airframe powertrain that splits thrust across many small electric motors distributed along the structure.
detail: Distributed electric propulsion (DEP) replaces a few large engines with many small Brushless motor units and propellers spread across the wing and airframe, improving redundancy, control, and efficiency. Because each motor can be commanded independently, the aircraft gains fine yaw and lift control useful for the vertical phases of an eVTOL or Tiltrotor, managed through Control allocation. DEP is foundational to Urban air mobility designs and to large multirotor cargo drones, and depends on a high-voltage Battery management system and accurate Field-oriented control of each Electronic speed controller.

plain: When the situations a robot meets in the real world differ from the examples it learned from, so its skills quietly stop working well.
snappy: A mismatch between deployment-time input or state distributions and those seen during training, degrading a learned policy's reliability.
detail: Distribution shift (dataset or covariate shift) is a central reason a Behavior cloning policy or perception net that excelled in training falters in the field, for instance an Autonomous vehicle meeting weather, lighting, or road markings absent from its data. It is tightly linked to the Reality gap in Sim-to-real transfer, to Compounding error in rollouts, and to Generalization limits. Mitigations include Domain randomization, Domain Adaptation, Out-of-Distribution Detection, the Data flywheel of field collection, and conservative Offline reinforcement learning.

plain: When a self-driving car performs worse in the real world because the roads, weather, or traffic it meets differ from the examples it learned on.
snappy: Degraded driving performance caused by deployment data diverging from the training data distribution.
detail: A core challenge for any learned Self-driving stack and a road-specific case of generic Distribution shift, it is especially acute for Imitation learning and Behavior cloning, where small steering errors compound into states never seen in demonstrations. This compounding-error problem motivated DAgger, which iteratively adds expert corrections on the policy's own visited states. Practitioners fight it with Domain randomization, broad datasets like BDD100K, Out-of-Distribution Detection to trigger a fallback, and by tracking the Operational design domain so the car knows when it has left familiar conditions.

plain: A learning method where the robot estimates the full range of possible future outcomes for an action, not just the average, giving it a richer picture of risk.
snappy: Reinforcement learning that models the entire probability distribution of returns rather than only their expected value.
detail: Instead of learning a single expected Value function, distributional RL (e.g. C51 and QR-DQN) learns the whole return distribution, which improves stability and enables risk-aware control such as avoiding low-probability catastrophic outcomes in Mobility tasks. The richer signal often boosts performance even when only the mean is ultimately used and integrates with Deep Q-Network style agents. It connects to Uncertainty estimation and risk-sensitive variants of Constrained Reinforcement Learning.

plain: How well a controller fights off unexpected pushes, loads, and noise to keep the machine doing what it should.
snappy: A controller's ability to suppress the effect of unmodeled external forces and disturbances on the output.
detail: Disturbance rejection is measured by how quickly a controller returns to its Setpoint after a shove, and it can be boosted with high loop Gain, integral action, feedforward, or an explicit disturbance observer that estimates and cancels the unknown force. It is what lets a Humanoid robot survive a push during Balance control or a Drone hold position in wind. It is a core goal of Robust control and Sliding mode control and is traded against Sensor noise amplification.

plain: The runaway part of a walking robot's motion that, left alone, would make it tip over, isolated so the controller can deal with it directly.
snappy: The unstable mode of center-of-mass dynamics, equal to the position plus a scaled velocity, that walking controllers track and stabilize.
detail: Splitting the Linear inverted pendulum model dynamics into stable and unstable parts yields the divergent component of motion, mathematically identical to the Capture point: where the robot must step to stop. Humanoid controllers plan a DCM reference and regulate it via the Center of pressure or Zero moment point, keeping the Center of mass well-behaved. DCM tracking underpins Footstep planning, Stepping strategy, and Push recovery on robots such as Atlas.

plain: The dominant maker of camera drones, a Chinese company whose flying machines are used by hobbyists, filmmakers, and businesses worldwide.
snappy: Market-leading Chinese manufacturer of consumer and commercial multirotor drones with integrated cameras, gimbals, and flight controllers.
detail: DJI builds the bulk of the world's small camera-equipped Drone fleet, from consumer Quadcopter models to enterprise platforms used for Aerial photogrammetry, inspection, and Precision agriculture drone work. Its aircraft pair a stabilising Gimbal with onboard Obstacle avoidance, GPS hold, and Return-to-home behaviours, and integrate Remote ID for regulatory compliance. The company's dominance has made it a focus of Counter-UAS and supply-chain security debates in defence markets.

plain: Techniques that help a robot trained in one setting work in a different setting by lining up what the two settings look like to its perception.
snappy: Aligning the feature distributions of a source domain (often simulation) and a target domain (the real world) so a learned model transfers.
detail: Domain Adaptation tackles the Domain Shift between where a model is trained and where it is used, for example a perception net trained on Synthetic data that must run on real camera frames. Methods align intermediate feature distributions, often adversarially, so the two domains become indistinguishable to the network while preserving task-relevant content. In robotics it complements Domain randomization and is a common lever for Sim-to-real transfer and Transfer learning, helping a Grasping or driving model bridge the Reality gap without re-collecting labels.

plain: A single powerful computer inside a car that runs most of the self-driving software instead of spreading it across many small chips.
snappy: A centralized high-performance compute unit that consolidates an autonomous or assisted-driving software stack onto one platform.
detail: As vehicles move from dozens of distributed microcontrollers toward zonal architectures, the domain controller becomes the brain that fuses radar, camera, and LiDAR streams and runs perception, behavior planning, and motion planning. It typically hosts an AI accelerator or system on a chip such as NVIDIA Jetson-class silicon, and must meet the relevant Automotive Safety Integrity Level for the functions it controls. Tesla's Autopilot computer and Mobileye's EyeQ platforms are well-known examples of this autonomy compute consolidation.

plain: Deliberately scrambling lots of details in a simulation so a robot learns a skill robust enough to survive the messiness of the real world.
snappy: Randomizing simulation parameters (masses, friction, lighting, delays) during training so a policy generalizes to reality.
detail: Rather than building one perfect simulator, domain randomization trains across many imperfect ones, forcing a Policy to treat the real world as just another sampled variation, which is a key tool for crossing the Sim-to-real gap and shrinking the Reality gap. It powers GPU-scale training in Isaac Lab and MuJoCo for both Learned locomotion and dexterous Manipulation. Visual randomization (textures, lights) helps a vision Policy generalize, while dynamics randomization aids Reinforcement learning of control.

plain: When a robot trained in one setting suddenly does worse because the real world looks different from its training data.
snappy: A drop in model performance caused by deployment data differing statistically from the training data.
detail: Domain Shift (distribution shift, domain gap) occurs when conditions at deployment, such as new weather, lighting, geographies, or sensors, diverge from training, degrading Object detection and Semantic segmentation. It is the practical face of the Reality gap that also plagues Sim-to-real transfer. Mobility perception teams counter it with Domain Adaptation, Domain randomization, broader datasets, and continuous Online adaptation, while Out-of-Distribution Detection flags inputs that have shifted too far to trust during a Long-tail scenario.

plain: A Korean company that makes safe robot arms able to sense how hard they are pushing, for working near people.
snappy: Korean collaborative-robot maker of force-sensing cobot arms.
detail: Doosan Robotics builds a Collaborative robot lineup featuring torque sensors at every joint, enabling sensitive Force control and Compliance for safe Human-robot interaction. Its cobots target Machine tending, Pick and place, and even food-service applications, programmed via Hand guiding and a graphical Teach pendant. The force sensing supports Power and force limiting under ISO/TS 15066, letting the arm stop on contact.

plain: The change in a wave's pitch or frequency when its source or reflector is moving toward or away from you, like a passing siren rising then falling.
snappy: The frequency shift of a reflected wave caused by a target's radial velocity relative to the sensor.
detail: The Doppler effect lets a sensor read how fast a target is approaching or receding directly from the returned signal's frequency shift. Radar and Imaging radar exploit it to report instant velocity, and FMCW LiDAR recovers the same per-point motion cue optically. This velocity channel strengthens Perception, Multi-object tracking, and Behavior prediction in Mobility and Autonomous vehicle systems.

plain: Working out how fast something is moving toward or away from a sensor by measuring how its reflected signal changes pitch.
snappy: Recovering a target's radial (line-of-sight) velocity from the frequency shift in reflected radar or lidar returns.
detail: Doppler Velocity Estimation exploits the Doppler effect: a moving target shifts the frequency of the reflected wave in proportion to its radial speed, which Radar and FMCW LiDAR measure directly per return. Unlike position-only sensors, this gives instantaneous velocity without differentiating positions, sharpening Multi-object tracking and ego-motion compensation. Mobility and Defense & Security platforms feed it into Sensor fusion and Kalman filter trackers, and richer modulation gives rise to the Micro-Doppler Signature used for target classification.

plain: Figuring out how fast something is moving toward or away from you by measuring how a reflected signal's frequency shifts.
snappy: Deriving a target's radial (line-of-sight) velocity from the frequency shift in returned radar or lidar signals.
detail: Doppler Velocity Measurement exploits the Doppler effect: a moving target shifts the frequency of the reflected beam in proportion to its closing speed, giving instantaneous Radial velocity without tracking across frames. Automotive radar relies on it heavily, and FMCW LiDAR brings the same per-point velocity to a Lidar Point Cloud. It is a key cue for Multi-object tracking and Behavior prediction, and the fine structure of this signal is exploited in Radar Micro-Doppler.

plain: A pair of stacked four-sided jointed frames arranged so a tool always pivots around one fixed point in the air.
snappy: Two coupled parallelogram four-bar linkages stacked to enforce a fixed remote pivot point purely mechanically.
detail: A Double Parallelogram Linkage is the classic hardware way to create a Remote Center of Motion, holding the pivot at a patient's incision in a Surgical robot without active control. Built from coupled instances of the Four-bar linkage, it keeps the tool shaft passing through a fixed point even as the arm reconfigures, removing the burden of enforcing that constraint through Inverse kinematics. Its rigid, passive geometry gives predictable motion and is a recurring motif in Medical & Surgical mechanism design.

plain: The brief moment in walking when both of the robot's feet are touching the ground at the same time.
snappy: The walking interval during which both feet are in ground contact simultaneously, between successive single-support phases.
detail: In a Gait cycle, double support is the overlap between one foot's Heel strike and the other's Toe-off, when the Support polygon is largest and weight transfers between legs. Controllers exploit this widened polygon for the most stable Zero moment point trajectory and for re-planning Footstep planning, and its duration relative to the Single support phase sets the Duty factor of the walk. It shrinks toward zero as a Bipedal robot transitions from walking to Running and a Flight phase appears.

plain: The fast column of air a drone's rotors push downward, which can disturb the ground, crops, or its own cargo.
snappy: The high-velocity air column accelerated downward by rotors, affecting payloads, nearby surfaces, and flight stability.
detail: Downwash (prop wash) is the accelerated air a rotor pushes down to make lift, and on an agricultural spraying drone it both carries the spray into the canopy and risks blowing light crops, while near surfaces it drives Ground effect and turbulence. It complicates close-formation flight in a Drone swarm and disturbs slung loads in Aerial manipulation. Excessive downwash recirculation during fast descent is what triggers Vortex ring state.

plain: A research software toolbox for designing, simulating, and mathematically optimizing how robots move.
snappy: A C++/Python toolbox for model-based design, multibody simulation, and trajectory/control optimization of robots.
detail: Drake, originated at MIT and now maintained by Toyota Research Institute, pairs a high-accuracy multibody Physics engine with rich optimization tooling, making it a favorite for Trajectory optimization, Optimal control, and Model predictive control research. It excels at Contact-rich manipulation problems where precise Contact dynamics matter more than rendering speed. Researchers use it alongside Pinocchio and MuJoCo to prototype controllers before Sim-to-real transfer onto hardware.

plain: A robot-learning method that builds an imagined model of how the world works, then practices and improves inside that imagination instead of always acting for real.
snappy: A model-based RL agent that learns a latent world model and optimizes behavior by imagining rollouts entirely within it.
detail: Dreamer (and DreamerV3) is a leading Model-based reinforcement learning agent: it learns a compact latent World model of the environment from experience, then trains its actor and critic on thousands of imagined trajectories rolled out in that latent space, which dramatically improves Sample efficiency. Because it learns from imagination, it suits robots where real interaction is costly, and DreamerV3 has been shown to learn diverse control tasks with fixed hyperparameters. It contrasts with Model-free reinforcement learning methods like Soft actor-critic and with ensemble planners like Probabilistic Ensembles with Trajectory Sampling.

plain: The slow build-up of error in a robot's guess of where it is, so its estimated position gradually wanders away from the true one.
snappy: Accumulating error in an estimated pose or sensor reading that grows over time without correction.
detail: Drift is the steady divergence of an estimate from ground truth as small errors compound, most visibly in Dead reckoning and Wheel odometry where each step adds uncertainty. Visual odometry and Inertial measurement unit integration drift without correction, which is why Loop closure and Localization against a Map are used to bound it. Sensor drift specifically refers to a sensor's reading slowly biasing away even when the true quantity is constant.

plain: An error state where a motor's power controller shuts down because something exceeded safe electrical or thermal limits.
snappy: A fault condition where a servo drive trips on overcurrent, overvoltage, or overtemperature and disables the axis.
detail: A drive fault is raised by the Servo drive when current, bus voltage, or temperature crosses a protective threshold, often from a jam, a Robot crash detection event, or a Following error growing too large. The drive opens its output, the axis coasts or brakes, and a fault code surfaces on the Teach pendant or the Robot controller HMI. On networked motion systems the fault propagates over EtherCAT or PROFINET to the Programmable logic controller, raises an Andon alert, and is logged for Predictive maintenance trending.

plain: Controlling a car's steering, brakes, and accelerator through electronic signals and motors instead of mechanical cables or rods.
snappy: Electronic actuation of steering, braking, and throttle via signals and motors, removing direct mechanical linkage between control and mechanism.
detail: Drive-by-wire replaces mechanical linkages with electronic actuation (steer-by-wire, brake-by-wire, throttle-by-wire), giving the self-driving stack a direct command interface to the chassis. It is the actuation layer that executes outputs from trajectory tracking and behavior planning, and it enables automatic emergency braking, lane keeping assist, and automated parking. Because it controls safety-critical motion, drive-by-wire demands fail-operational and fault tolerance design under ISO 26262 and a high ASIL rating.

plain: An in-car camera that checks whether the driver is paying attention and awake, ready to take over if needed.
snappy: A camera-based system that monitors driver gaze, head pose, and alertness to confirm readiness to resume control.
detail: A driver monitoring system (DMS) uses an inward-facing camera with human pose estimation and gaze tracking to detect drowsiness, distraction, or hands-off-wheel states. It is mandatory for SAE Level 2 to 3 features like a highway pilot, because it gates whether the system may continue and how urgently to issue a takeover request. If the driver fails to respond, the vehicle escalates to a minimal risk condition.

plain: Running self-driving vehicles on real roads with nobody behind the wheel as a backup.
snappy: The commercial milestone of operating autonomous vehicles with no onboard safety driver, relying only on remote support.
detail: Driver-Out Operations (driverless or rider-only operations) is the threshold where a Robotaxi or Self-driving truck removes the in-vehicle Safety driver, eliminating the cost that dominates early Cost per Mile. Reaching it requires a high Recovery Rate, low Disengagement and intervention frequency, and a Teleoperation Center able to provide Remote Assistance at a sustainable Operator-to-Robot Ratio. It is typically launched first inside a tightly Geofenced Deployment area and within a proven Operational design domain before Operational Design Domain Expansion broadens coverage. Driver-out status, supported by a documented Safety case, is the inflection point that turns a pilot into a commercial service.

plain: A computer-generated world where engineers can develop and test self-driving cars without using a real vehicle on real roads.
snappy: A virtual environment that renders sensors, vehicle dynamics, and traffic for developing and validating autonomous driving software.
detail: A driving simulator provides sensor simulation for camera, radar, and LiDAR plus a physics engine for vehicle motion, letting teams run millions of miles safely and cheaply. It underpins both closed-loop simulation and scenario generation, and can drive sim-to-real transfer of learned policies. Open platforms like CARLA, along with NVIDIA Isaac Sim and Gazebo, are widely used AV simulator tools for the self-driving stack.

plain: An AI that learns how driving scenes unfold over time, letting it imagine likely futures the way a person pictures what might happen next.
snappy: A generative model that predicts future driving observations, enabling imagined rollouts for planning and scenario generation.
detail: A Driving World Model such as GAIA-1 learns the dynamics of driving scenes and can roll out plausible future video conditioned on the Ego vehicle's actions, supporting Model-based reinforcement learning, Behavior prediction, and synthetic Scenario generation. It is the autonomous-driving instance of the general World model concept and overlaps with Neural Radiance Fields for Driving for sensor-realistic rollouts. Such models feed Adversarial Scenario Mining and reduce reliance on real miles for validating a Self-driving stack.

plain: A very large shared collection of robot-arm recordings, gathered by many labs in many real settings, used to teach robots how to handle objects.
snappy: A large-scale, crowd-collected manipulation dataset spanning diverse real-world scenes for training generalist robot policies.
detail: DROID is a Demonstration data corpus assembled by dozens of institutions teleoperating Franka Emika Panda arms across hundreds of everyday scenes, deliberately maximizing visual and task diversity to improve Generalization. It is a cornerstone resource for Imitation learning and for training a Generalist policy, and it feeds into broader Cross-embodiment dataset efforts like Open X-Embodiment. Models such as OpenVLA and Pi-Zero draw on DROID to learn robust Manipulation behavior that transfers beyond the lab bench.

plain: A very large collection of robot-arm task recordings gathered in messy real-world settings across many labs, not just one tidy lab bench.
snappy: A large in-the-wild manipulation dataset collected with a common hardware setup across many institutions and scenes.
detail: The DROID dataset standardizes a Franka Emika Panda plus camera rig across dozens of institutions to capture manipulation episodes in diverse, uncontrolled real environments, deliberately maximizing scene and task variety. This in-the-wild diversity targets Generalization and robustness for a Robot foundation model, and it is a major source within Open X-Embodiment for training policies like Octo policy and OpenVLA. It complements narrower lab sets such as BridgeData and ALOHA-collected Demonstration data.

plain: An aircraft with no human pilot on board, flown either by remote control or by flying itself.
snappy: An uncrewed aircraft operated remotely or flown autonomously.
detail: A drone is an uncrewed aircraft, formally an unmanned aerial vehicle, ranging from a small Quadcopter to a fixed-wing or Hybrid VTOL platform. It is controlled by a Flight controller running firmware like PX4 or ArduPilot, and in the US its operation is regulated by the FAA under Part 107 and Remote ID rules. Drones span Drone delivery, Aerial photogrammetry, and defense uses, and many fly Beyond visual line of sight under a Ground control station.

plain: Using small flying robots to carry packages directly to customers instead of sending them by truck.
snappy: Autonomous aerial transport of parcels over the final leg of a route, typically by a multirotor or hybrid VTOL drone.
detail: Drone delivery handles Last-mile delivery by flying small payloads from a depot to a doorstep, exemplified by operators such as Zipline carrying medical supplies. The aircraft is usually a Multirotor drone or Hybrid VTOL that lowers a Payload by winch, navigating with GPS and Waypoint navigation while respecting Geofencing and UAS traffic management rules. Regulators treat longer routes as Beyond visual line of sight operations, which raises the bar for Detect and avoid and reliability.

plain: A large group of small flying robots that coordinate with each other to act together as a single team.
snappy: Many drones that communicate and cooperate so the group behaves as one distributed collective rather than independent aircraft.
detail: A drone swarm applies Swarm robotics principles to aerial vehicles, with each Drone following simple local rules that produce coordinated formations, search patterns, or saturating attacks as Emergent behavior. As a Multi-robot system it must handle Collision avoidance between members, shared mapping, and resilient communication when individuals are lost. Swarms appear in Defense & Security saturation tactics and in research light shows, and are a key Counter-UAS challenge because defenses must engage many targets at once.

plain: A camera-based navigation method that tracks motion by directly comparing pixel brightness between frames, rather than first detecting corner features.
snappy: A direct, sparse visual odometry method that jointly optimizes photometric error and inverse depth over selected high-gradient pixels.
detail: DSO performs Visual odometry without explicit Feature matching: instead of tracking corners like ORB-SLAM, it minimizes the photometric (brightness) error of a set of sparse high-gradient pixels while jointly estimating their depth and the camera trajectory, similar in spirit to LSD-SLAM. This direct formulation can track in low-texture scenes where the FAST Corner Detector finds few features, and it models photometric calibration explicitly. It outputs a semi-dense Point cloud and a camera trajectory useful for Mobility navigation, though as pure odometry it lacks the Loop closure that full Visual SLAM systems add.

plain: A robot with two arms that work together to handle objects the way a person uses both hands.
snappy: A platform with two coordinated manipulators enabling bimanual manipulation of objects too large or awkward for one arm.
detail: A dual-arm robot coordinates two manipulators for Bimanual manipulation, letting one arm hold a workpiece while the other operates on it, or sharing a load between them. This is central to the Humanoid robot upper body and to assembly cells needing handoffs and Contact-rich manipulation. Coordinated control treats both arms as a single Whole-body control problem, often planned in MoveIt for Manufacturing tasks.

plain: The shortest possible route for something that can only drive forwards and can't turn tighter than a certain circle.
snappy: The provably shortest forward-only path between two oriented poses for a vehicle with a fixed minimum turning radius.
detail: A Dubins path is composed of at most three segments drawn from turning at the minimum radius (left/right) and going straight, giving six canonical word types like RSL or LSR. It models the Nonholonomic constraint of Fixed-wing drone flight and car-like Ackermann steering vehicles that cannot reverse. Planners use Dubins curves to connect Waypoint goals and as the steering function inside a Rapidly-exploring random tree; allowing reverse motion generalizes them to Reeds-Shepp curves.

plain: A drone rotor enclosed in a ring or tube, which makes it push more air and shields the spinning blades.
snappy: A rotor surrounded by a shroud that increases static thrust efficiency and protects the blades from contact.
detail: A ducted fan (EDF) wraps a Propeller in a close-fitting shroud that reduces tip losses, raising static Thrust-to-weight ratio for a given diameter while guarding the blades during contact, which suits Perching and confined-space inspection. The duct adds weight and aerodynamic complexity, especially during Transition flight on a Hybrid VTOL, but improves safety around people. Electric ducted fans are common on small jets and some Urban air mobility lift configurations.

plain: A shorthand for the kinds of unpleasant or risky jobs that are good candidates to hand off to robots.
snappy: The classic three-category rationale (dull, dirty, dangerous) for deploying robots on tasks people would rather not do.
detail: The phrase frames the value case for automation: dull tasks like Palletizing suit a tireless Industrial robot arm, dirty tasks like sewer inspection suit a Field robot, and dangerous tasks like bomb disposal suit a remotely driven Unmanned ground vehicle. It is frequently invoked alongside the Labor shortage argument and Return on investment analysis when justifying a deployment. Some practitioners add a fourth D (dear, meaning expensive) to capture cost-driven Automation.

plain: A company whose small floor robot prints building blueprints directly onto a job-site floor.
snappy: Maker of the FieldPrinter robot that prints full construction layouts directly onto building floors.
detail: Dusty Robotics' FieldPrinter is a small differential-drive robot that drives across a slab and inkjet-prints architectural layout lines from a digital model, replacing manual chalk-line work. It relies on a total-station-grade localization reference for millimeter accuracy and follows a coverage path planning route across the floor. It is a marquee construction robot that automates the layout step of building.

plain: How much of the time a robot or motor can run before it has to rest or cool down.
snappy: The fraction of time a system can operate at a given load before thermal or wear limits force a rest period.
detail: Duty cycle bounds sustainable operation: a motor rated at 30 percent duty cycle can run a third of the time before overheating, set by Thermal management and the gap between Peak torque and continuous torque. It shapes how long an Industrial robot arm can weld before pausing and is distinct from but related to Uptime and how a Hot-swappable battery extends working hours. Pushing past it triggers protective derating or shutdown to avoid damage.

plain: The share of each step a leg spends on the ground rather than in the air.
snappy: The fraction of the gait cycle that a given leg spends in stance contact with the ground.
detail: Duty factor crisply distinguishes gaits: a value above 0.5 means each leg is grounded more than half the cycle, characteristic of a walking Crawl gait with good Static stability, while values below 0.5 imply a flight-prone running Gait such as a Gallop. It is computed as the Stance phase duration divided by the full Gait cycle. Dropping the duty factor is the route from walking into Running and Dynamic stability.

plain: Everything involved in actually driving moment-to-moment: steering, braking, watching the road, and reacting.
snappy: The real-time operational and tactical functions of driving, including steering, acceleration, braking, monitoring, and maneuver execution.
detail: The Dynamic driving task (DDT) excludes strategic choices like destination but covers lateral and longitudinal control plus the Perception and Behavior planning needed to react in traffic. In the SAE levels of driving automation, who performs the DDT and its Fallback defines each level: an Automated driving system performs the whole DDT at Level 4 automation, while Advanced driver-assistance systems handle only parts of it. When the system cannot continue, the DDT Fallback returns control to the user or reaches a Minimal risk condition.

plain: Using motion and momentum, like throwing or flicking an object, to do things a robot could not do by slowly carrying it.
snappy: Manipulation that exploits momentum, impacts, and inertial dynamics, such as throwing or tossing, rather than slow quasi-static motion.
detail: Dynamic Manipulation deliberately uses inertia, impacts, and release timing, contrasting with Quasi-Static Contact assumptions, so a robot can throw, toss, or swing objects beyond its static reach. Throwing extends an arm's effective Workspace and boosts Throughput in Logistics & Warehouse picking, but it demands accurate dynamics models or learned residuals because release velocity and air drag are hard to predict. It overlaps with Nonprehensile manipulation and is exemplified by learned systems like TossingBot that pair Grasping with Reinforcement learning to place items in distant bins.

plain: A compact mathematical recipe for a movement that can be stretched, sped up, or aimed at a new goal while keeping the same overall shape.
snappy: A dynamical-system encoding of a trajectory whose attractor goal and timing can be re-targeted while preserving learned shape.
detail: Dynamic movement primitives (DMP) represent a motion as a stable second-order dynamical system plus a learnable forcing term, so a single demonstrated reach or strike can be re-aimed at a new Pose or rescaled in time without replanning. They are a popular Action representation for Learning from demonstration and Kinesthetic teaching because one recorded trajectory generalizes to nearby goals. DMPs are often combined with Reinforcement learning for refinement and are related to the Probabilistic Movement Primitives family used in Trajectory generation.

plain: A protective bubble around a moving vehicle that grows when it goes faster and shrinks when it slows.
snappy: A protective field whose size and shape scale with a mobile vehicle's speed and direction to maintain safe stopping distance.
detail: A Dynamic Safety Field is the speed-dependent version of Safe Workspace Zoning, where a Safety scanner enlarges the protective field as an Automated guided vehicle accelerates so there is always room to stop before contact. The field is computed from current velocity and steering so a turning Autonomous mobile robot widens its field toward the turn, supporting compliance with ISO 3691-4 and ANSI/ITSDF B56.5. This lets a warehouse vehicle drive faster in clear aisles while still guaranteeing a timely Protective stop.

plain: Staying balanced while moving, the way a person stays upright by stepping rather than standing still.
snappy: Balance maintained through ongoing motion and active control rather than by keeping the center of mass over a fixed support base.
detail: A dynamically stable robot can have its Center of mass momentarily outside the Support polygon as long as it steps or accelerates to recover, which is what enables fast Bipedal locomotion and Running. Controllers reason about it using the Zero moment point and Capture point, and a fall is prevented by Balance control reacting to the Ground reaction force. It contrasts with Static stability, where the robot is stable even when frozen mid-motion.

plain: Energy-efficient walking that lets the legs swing naturally like pendulums instead of forcing every motion.
snappy: Walking that exploits the natural pendulum dynamics of the legs for efficiency, rather than tightly tracking a stiff reference posture.
detail: Dynamic walking builds on the insight of Passive dynamic walking by adding just enough actuation to keep an otherwise gravity-driven Gait going on level ground, yielding a low Cost of transport. It relies on Dynamic stability rather than always keeping the Center of mass over the feet, so it tolerates the body falling and catching itself each step. It is the efficiency target for modern Bipedal locomotion and informs the Linear inverted pendulum model.

plain: A way for a moving robot to pick its next steering and speed by quickly testing which of its reachable speeds keep it safe and on course.
snappy: A reactive local planner that samples admissible velocity pairs within the robot's dynamic limits and scores them.
detail: The Dynamic Window Approach restricts its search to the velocities the robot can actually reach in the next control cycle given its acceleration limits, then scores each candidate on progress to the goal, clearance from obstacles, and speed. It is a classic Local planner in the ROS navigation stack, performing Obstacle avoidance on a Differential drive base by directly emitting velocity commands against the current Cost map. DWA is simple and fast but myopic, so it pairs with a Global planner; richer alternatives include the Timed Elastic Band.

plain: The study of how forces and torques make things move, speed up, and slow down.
snappy: The study of robot motion as produced by forces and torques, including mass, inertia, and acceleration.
detail: Dynamics relates the forces and torques on a robot to its motion through the Equations of motion, accounting for the Mass matrix, Coriolis and centrifugal forces, and gravity. It is essential for fast or heavy motion, for Force control, and for balancing a Bipedal robot, and it is computed via Forward dynamics and Inverse dynamics, often formulated with Lagrangian dynamics or Newton-Euler dynamics. Unlike Kinematics, which ignores forces, dynamics is what Computed torque control and Model predictive control exploit.

plain: A training trick where a robot is practiced in many slightly-different pretend physics worlds so it can cope when the real one does not match.
snappy: Randomizing physical parameters like mass, friction, and inertia in simulation so a learned control policy stays robust on the real robot.
detail: Dynamics Randomization is a flavor of Domain randomization that perturbs the physics rather than the visuals: link masses, joint friction, motor gains, and the inertia tensor are sampled randomly each training episode in simulators like Isaac Gym or MuJoCo. By forcing a policy to succeed across the resulting spread of dynamics, it learns a controller that survives the Reality gap, which is central to any Sim-to-real transfer pipeline for a Quadruped robot or manipulator. It is a staple of Reinforcement learning approaches to learned locomotion where exact system identification is impractical.

plain: An all-in-one smart motor module that bundles the motor, gears, controller, and position sensing into one networked unit you can chain together.
snappy: Robotis' networked smart servo integrating motor, gearbox, controller, and feedback in a single daisy-chainable module.
detail: A Dynamixel packages a small DC motor or Brushless DC motor, a gear train, a Motor controller, and an Absolute encoder into one unit that speaks a digital bus protocol, so dozens can be daisy-chained and addressed individually. This lets builders assemble a robot arm, gripper, or small Humanoid robot without designing custom drive electronics, exposing Position control, Velocity control, and current-based Torque control over the bus. Robotis' smart servos are ubiquitous in education and research, and integrate cleanly with ROS for rapid prototyping.

plain: Picking out single individual items, not whole boxes or pallets, which is the hardest thing for a robot to do.
snappy: Retrieving individual units (eaches) rather than cases or pallets, the most varied and hardest-to-automate fulfillment task.
detail: Each Picking (piece picking) is the frontier of warehouse automation because every order touches a different mix of shapes, weights, and packaging, demanding robust Bin picking, 6-DoF grasp detection, and a versatile gripper. Its difficulty is captured by SKU Coverage (how many catalog items the robot can reliably handle) and by the Exception Handling rate when items fall outside that envelope. It contrasts with case- or pallet-level work like Depalletizing and Palletizing, which face less variety. Because labor for eaches is expensive and scarce, lowering its Cost per Pick is one of the highest-value goals in a Goods-to-person fulfillment operation.

plain: Mixing the raw data from different sensors together before any of them have decided what they see.
snappy: A fusion strategy that combines raw or low-level sensor data before feature extraction or detection.
detail: Early Fusion (Raw-data fusion) merges, for example, a Lidar Point Cloud with camera pixels at the input stage so a single network reasons jointly, preserving cross-modal cues that Late Fusion loses. Architectures such as BEVFusion and Pseudo-Lidar embody this idea, projecting modalities into a shared Bird's-Eye-View Perception representation. It demands tight Sensor Calibration and Temporal Calibration because misaligned inputs corrupt every downstream 3D object detection.

plain: A rare, tricky situation that a system rarely sees and may handle badly.
snappy: An uncommon, hard scenario at the boundary of normal operation that stresses a robot's perception or decision-making.
detail: For an Autonomous vehicle, an Edge case might be a couch in the middle of a highway or a person in a chicken costume crossing the road, situations a Self-driving stack rarely encounters in training data. The accumulation of these rare events is called the Long tail, and surfacing them drives Scenario-based testing and Scenario generation in simulators like CARLA. Robust Perception and Behavior planning must degrade gracefully here, often triggering a Minimal risk condition rather than guessing.

plain: Doing the robot's thinking on the machine itself instead of sending data to distant servers.
snappy: Running perception, planning, and control on or near the robot rather than in a remote data center.
detail: Edge computing keeps the Perception-action loop local so a robot stays responsive even with poor connectivity, cutting the Latency and network risk of Cloud robotics. A self-driving car or a Humanoid robot typically runs neural inference on Onboard compute such as an NVIDIA Jetson or an AI accelerator, reserving the cloud for map updates and fleet learning. Edge inference is often paired with model compression so a large Foundation model or Vision-language-action model fits within the robot's Power budget.

plain: Finding the outlines in a picture by spotting where brightness suddenly jumps, which usually marks the border of an object.
snappy: Identifying intensity discontinuities in an image that mark object boundaries and surface contours.
detail: Edge Detection locates pixels where image intensity changes sharply, using gradient operators like the Sobel operator or the multi-stage Canny edge detection that adds noise smoothing and hysteresis thresholding. The resulting edge maps feed classic Computer vision steps such as the Hough Transform for line fitting, Feature extraction, and contour-based Object recognition. Manufacturing inspection and Mobility lane-finding pipelines rely on it, and it is one of the most-used primitives in OpenCV, often a precursor to model-based Pose estimation.

plain: How heavy a robot's tool effectively feels when it bumps something in a given direction, which sets how hard the impact is.
snappy: The apparent inertia the end-effector presents along a chosen direction, derived from the robot's mass matrix and used to bound impact forces.
detail: Effective mass is the directional inertia a robot's End-effector exhibits in collision, computed from the joint-space Mass matrix mapped through the Jacobian matrix into Cartesian directions, and captured compactly by the Task-Space Inertia Matrix. A low effective mass means lighter impacts, which is central to Collaborative robot safety and the contact limits in ISO/TS 15066, and it informs how a Surgical robot may safely contact tissue. Configurations and Cartesian impedance control are chosen to reduce effective mass in likely collision directions, trading off against Manipulability.

plain: The self-driving car you are talking about from its own point of view, treated as the center of the world that everything else is measured against.
snappy: The autonomous vehicle under control, used as the origin of the coordinate frame for perception and planning.
detail: In a self-driving stack, the ego vehicle is the reference frame against which every detected object, pedestrian, and lane is positioned, so a bird's-eye view or occupancy grid is centered on it. Ego-motion estimation tracks how the ego vehicle moves between sensor frames, while behavior prediction forecasts how other road agents will act relative to it. Datasets like nuScenes and the Waymo Open Dataset annotate scenes from the ego vehicle's perspective.

plain: Working out how a moving machine is itself traveling, just by watching how its own sensor views change over time.
snappy: Estimating the vehicle's own motion (translation and rotation) from onboard sensor streams such as cameras, lidar, or inertial data.
detail: Ego-motion estimation underpins localization for the ego vehicle, computing how far and which way it has moved between frames. Techniques include visual odometry, wheel odometry, and visual-inertial odometry, often fused with an inertial measurement unit via a Kalman filter or extended Kalman filter. It feeds the SLAM and state estimation pipeline so the vehicle can register new LiDAR scans or images against its prior map.

full: ESDF-free Gradient-based Local Planner for Quadrotors
plain: A fast onboard planner that lets a flying drone weave smoothly through cluttered space without first building a heavy distance map of obstacles.
snappy: An ESDF-free gradient-based quadrotor planner that generates smooth trajectories directly from local collision information without a full distance field.
detail: EGO-Planner generates smooth quadrotor trajectories by optimizing a B-spline Trajectory with gradients computed only near detected collisions, avoiding the cost of maintaining a full ESDF, which makes it lightweight enough for onboard use. It runs in a Receding Horizon Planning loop, replanning continuously from incoming Point cloud data to dodge obstacles during aggressive flight on a Quadcopter. Its EGO-Swarm extension coordinates multiple vehicles for Drone swarm flight, making it a popular choice for fast autonomous flight that needs aggressive Trajectory optimization with minimal compute.

plain: A widely used building-block of code that lets robot programs do fast math with vectors and matrices.
snappy: A header-only C++ template library for linear algebra that underpins much of modern robotics software.
detail: Almost every C++ robotics stack leans on Eigen for the matrix and vector math behind a Rotation matrix, a Homogeneous transformation matrix, or a Jacobian matrix. It is a core dependency of Pinocchio, Ceres Solver, and many ROS packages, providing expression templates that compile down to efficient code for State estimation and Optimal control. Its fixed-size types are popular in real-time loops because they avoid heap allocation.

plain: A company that makes wearable robotic suits that help injured people walk and support factory workers.
snappy: Maker of powered lower-limb and upper-body exoskeletons for rehabilitation and industrial support.
detail: Ekso Bionics builds a powered exoskeleton worn over the legs that drives the hips and knees to retrain gait in stroke and spinal-cord patients during rehabilitation. The wearable robot senses the user's intent and provides assist-as-needed torque, a clinical use of human-robot interaction and powered prosthesis-style actuation. Ekso also makes passive upper-body suits that reduce strain for overhead industrial work.

plain: A pose where a robot arm is stretched out almost straight, sitting right at the edge of how far it can reach.
snappy: A boundary singularity occurring when an arm is fully extended and the wrist center reaches the edge of its reachable workspace.
detail: An elbow singularity arises when an arm straightens until its wrist center sits on the outer boundary of the Workspace, so the manipulator cannot accelerate outward any further. At this Kinematic singularity the Jacobian matrix drops rank and the Inverse kinematics returns ill-conditioned joint velocities, a problem mitigated with Damped Least Squares or by keeping motions inside a dexterous reach margin. It is the boundary member of the three Robot singularity families, the others being the Wrist Singularity and Shoulder Singularity, and it limits the practical Reach of any Six-axis robot.

plain: A device that turns electricity into spinning motion, used to power most robots.
snappy: A machine that converts electrical energy into rotary mechanical motion to drive a robot.
detail: The Electric motor is the dominant Actuator in modern robotics because it is clean, controllable, and pairs naturally with electronics. Variants include the DC motor, the Brushless DC motor, the Permanent magnet synchronous motor, the Stepper motor, and the Induction motor, each driven by a Motor controller that manages current and Commutation. In a robot arm the motor usually feeds a Gearbox or Harmonic drive to trade speed for torque before reaching the Joint.

plain: A plastic that changes shape when you apply electricity, acting like a soft, lightweight artificial muscle.
snappy: A polymer that mechanically deforms under an electric field, used as a lightweight artificial-muscle actuator.
detail: An Electroactive Polymer (EAP) bends, stretches, or contracts in response to an applied voltage, with the dominant dielectric type behaving like the Dielectric elastomer actuator used in Soft robotics, while ionic types include the Ionic Polymer-Metal Composite. Its muscle-like, high-strain, low-mass behavior makes it appealing for Soft robot grippers, Research/Frontier artificial muscles, and Service & Consumer haptics. As an actuator it competes with the Shape memory alloy actuator and the Piezoelectric actuator, trading high voltage and modest force for large, compliant motion.

plain: Sticking to a surface using static electricity, the same force that makes a balloon cling to a wall after you rub it.
snappy: Surface attachment generated by applying high voltage across electrode pads, inducing electrostatic forces that hold the robot to nearly any material.
detail: Electroadhesion works on conductive and insulating surfaces alike, draws little holding power once charged, and engages or releases in milliseconds, which makes it attractive for a lightweight Climbing robot and for the Electroadhesion gripper used to handle flexible or fragile sheets. Holding force per area is modest, so it is often combined with Gecko-inspired adhesion or Microspine gripping to boost capacity for Climbing locomotion. Among adhesion schemes it is the most material-agnostic, contrasting with metal-only Magnetic adhesion and the power-hungry Vortex adhesion.

plain: A gripper that sticks to objects using a static-electricity cling, like a balloon stuck to a wall.
snappy: Gripper that holds objects via electrostatic adhesion from charged electrode pads.
detail: An electroadhesion gripper applies high voltage to electrode pads on a flat surface, inducing opposite charges in the target so electrostatic attraction holds it, then releases by switching the field off. As a Soft gripper variant it handles delicate, porous, or non-flat items, such as fabric, paper, and packaging, that defeat a Suction gripper, making it useful for Logistics & Warehouse picking and Bin picking of mixed goods. It is still largely a Research/Frontier technology, valued for low power draw and gentle, residue-free grip.

plain: A soft pouch of liquid that an electric charge squeezes to push the fluid around, making the pouch flex like a muscle without any pump.
snappy: A soft actuator that uses electrostatic force to displace an enclosed dielectric liquid, combining hydraulic output with electrical drive.
detail: An electrohydraulic actuator such as a HASEL pouch places electrodes on a fluid-filled flexible shell; charging them pulls the electrodes together and forces the liquid to bulge the rest of the pouch, producing fast, self-sensing motion. It blends the force of a Hydraulic actuator with the clean electrical drive of a Dielectric elastomer actuator, and is a leading muscle for the next generation of Soft robotics. Researchers pair it with a Soft robot and Pneumatic artificial muscle designs, contrasting it with the slower Shape memory alloy actuator for high Torque density artificial muscle.

plain: A self-contained unit that combines an electric motor, a small pump, and a hydraulic cylinder into one package, getting hydraulic strength from an electric input.
snappy: A self-contained actuator pairing a motor-driven bidirectional pump with a local hydraulic cylinder, eliminating central hydraulics.
detail: An Electrohydrostatic Actuator (EHA) replaces a plumbed hydraulic system and its Hydraulic Servovalve with a closed loop in which a Brushless DC motor drives a small pump that directly pressurizes a local Hydraulic actuator, so force is controlled by motor current rather than valve metering. This 'power-by-wire' approach delivers high force density with the cleanliness and efficiency of electric drive, which is why it is used in aircraft flight surfaces, Space mechanisms, and high-force robot legs. It blends hydraulic Torque density with electric Backdrivability when the motor is operated in Torque Control Mode.

plain: A spring-loaded brake that grabs and holds a joint the instant power is lost, so a robot arm won't fall.
snappy: A spring-engaged, electrically-released brake that holds a joint safely when power is removed.
detail: A power-off Electromagnetic Brake uses a spring to clamp the rotor and an energizing coil to release it, so cutting power automatically locks the joint, making it a Fail-safe holding device on a Humanoid robot or Industrial robot arm. It is essential where a non-backdrivable reducer is absent and gravity would otherwise drop the limb, complementing Gravity Compensation during normal operation and Safe Torque Off during a Protective stop. Unlike Regenerative Braking it does not modulate motion, only holds it, and is sized against the joint's Holding torque.

plain: A software table that makes a follower motor move through a custom, repeating motion pattern locked to a driving motor's position.
snappy: A programmable position table coupling a follower axis to a master through an arbitrary cam profile.
detail: Electronic camming replaces a physical Cam Mechanism with a lookup table that maps master position to follower position, executed by a Servo drive under a Motion controller. It generalizes Electronic gearing from a fixed ratio to any smooth Motion profile, letting packaging and printing machines accelerate and dwell a follower axis in step with a master. Cam profiles are often combined with Registration mark sensing and S-curve acceleration to limit jerk.

plain: A software trick that makes one motor automatically follow another at a fixed speed ratio, like meshed gears but with no physical teeth.
snappy: A firmware-locked ratio slaving a follower servo axis to a master axis's position.
detail: Electronic gearing reads a master Encoder and commands a follower Servo drive to track it at a programmed ratio, replacing mechanical Gear Train linkages with reconfigurable software. It is a core Motion control function used to keep paired rolls or conveyors synchronized in web lines, and it underlies Tension control and Registration mark correction. Unlike Electronic camming, the relationship is a constant ratio rather than an arbitrary profile.

plain: A small electronic part that takes the flight computer's commands and tells a motor exactly how fast to spin.
snappy: A circuit that regulates Brushless motor speed by switching power in response to Flight controller commands.
detail: Each motor on a Multirotor has its own ESC, which performs Commutation of a Brushless DC motor and adjusts speed using Pulse-width modulation signals from the Flight controller. Fast, accurate ESC response is what lets a Quadcopter hold attitude, since the Autopilot stabilizes the craft purely by varying the four motor speeds. Modern ESCs may report current and RPM telemetry back to the flight controller for tighter control and fault detection.

plain: A safety system that automatically brakes individual wheels to stop a car from skidding or spinning out during a sharp turn.
snappy: An active chassis system that brakes individual wheels and trims engine torque to counter oversteer, understeer, and skidding.
detail: Electronic Stability Control (ESC, ESP) compares the driver's intended yaw, inferred from steering and speed, against the measured yaw rate from an Inertial measurement unit, then applies targeted braking to correct a skid. It builds on the wheel-speed sensing of an Anti-lock Braking System and reacts to excessive Tire Slip Angle. As foundational Advanced driver-assistance systems hardware, it is a low-level actuator that an Automated driving system commands over the Controller Area Network.

plain: A terrain map that records the ground height at each spot on a grid, so a walking or rolling robot knows where the bumps and dips are.
snappy: A 2.5D terrain representation storing a single ground-height value per grid cell to support traversability assessment and foothold planning.
detail: An Elevation Map stores one height value per cell of a 2D grid, a compact 2.5D alternative to a full Point cloud or OctoMap that is cheap to update from a Depth camera or LiDAR as the robot moves. Legged systems use it for Foothold selection and traversability scoring, while wheeled field robots use it to detect slopes and a Negative obstacle. It is a staple of Perceptive locomotion for the Quadruped robot and for agricultural ground vehicles.

plain: A small computer built into a device to make it do one specific thing reliably.
snappy: A dedicated, purpose-built computer integrated into a robot to perform a specific control or sensing function.
detail: An embedded system combines a processor (often a Microcontroller, System on a chip, or FPGA), firmware, and I/O tailored to one job, and forms the building blocks of a robot's electronics. Examples include a drone Flight controller, a motor Motor controller, and a Battery management system, each running deterministic code close to the hardware. Embedded systems prioritize Real-time computing, low power within the Power budget, and reliability over general-purpose flexibility.

plain: An artificial intelligence that controls a real or simulated physical body and learns by acting in the world rather than just processing text or images.
snappy: An AI agent whose decisions drive a physical or simulated body, closing the loop between perception, action, and consequence.
detail: Unlike a chatbot, an embodied agent senses through cameras and a Force/torque sensor and acts through an Actuator, so it must respect physics, latency, and contact. Research on Embodied AI and Embodied intelligence trains these agents in a Gym environment or Isaac Sim before Sim-to-real transfer onto hardware like a Humanoid robot. A Vision-language-action model such as RT-2 is a concrete embodied agent: it maps language and camera input directly to robot Action via a learned Policy.

plain: Artificial intelligence that lives in a body, learning and acting by sensing and moving in the world rather than only processing text or images.
snappy: AI that perceives and acts through a physical or simulated body, closing the perception-action loop.
detail: Embodied AI studies agents whose intelligence emerges from sensing and acting in an environment, whether a real Robot or a simulated Embodied agent in Isaac Sim or MuJoCo. It draws on the principle of Embodiment and the Perception-action loop, and increasingly uses a Robot foundation model and Vision-language-action model for control. The field spans learned Manipulation, Legged locomotion, and navigation, with Sim-to-real transfer the bridge from training to real-world deployment.

plain: The view that being smart is not just about the brain, but grows out of having a body that senses and acts in the world.
snappy: The thesis that intelligence arises from and is shaped by an agent's body and its physical interaction with the environment.
detail: Embodied (or situated) cognition argues that intelligence cannot be separated from the body, the Perception-action loop, and the environment, a stance that grounds modern Embodied AI and Embodied intelligence research. It motivates Morphological computation, where the body's mechanics handle work a controller would otherwise do, and it informs Developmental robotics and Affordance theory, which treat perception as action-oriented. The view sharpens the Symbol grounding problem and the Frame problem, since meaning and relevance must come from real sensorimotor experience rather than from disembodied symbols.

plain: The idea that real intelligence comes from having a body that moves through and interacts with the physical world, not just from thinking.
snappy: Intelligence that arises from a physical agent sensing and acting in its environment rather than from disembodied computation.
detail: Embodied intelligence holds that a body, its sensors, and its interaction with the environment are part of cognition itself, so a Robot learns about the world by acting in it through the Perception-action loop. In modern robotics this framing drives Embodied AI and the Robot foundation model, where a Vision-language-action model maps camera and language input directly to motor commands on a Humanoid robot. It contrasts with treating intelligence as pure symbol manipulation, and underlies Moravec's paradox, the observation that physical dexterity is harder for machines than abstract reasoning.

plain: Having a physical body, so a machine learns and acts by actually moving and sensing in the real world rather than just thinking about it.
snappy: The principle that intelligence is grounded in a physical body interacting with its environment, rather than abstract computation alone.
detail: Embodiment is the idea that a Robot's perception, learning, and behavior are shaped by having an actual body that senses and acts in the world. A Humanoid robot with arms, legs, and Tactile sensing learns very different skills than a disembodied model because it must contend with gravity, contact, and Proprioception. The concept underpins Embodied AI and motivates research into Sim-to-real transfer, since a body trained in Simulation must eventually move real Actuators.

plain: The drop in performance you get when you take skills learned on one robot body and try to run them on a differently shaped robot.
snappy: Degradation when a policy trained for one robot morphology is transferred to another with different kinematics, dynamics, or sensors.
detail: Because a policy bakes in assumptions about joint counts, link lengths, and Actuator behavior, moving it from, say, a Franka Emika arm to a different Manipulator breaks it; this is the embodiment gap. It is the central obstacle for Cross-embodiment learning and Generalist policy efforts like Open X-Embodiment, and is related to but distinct from the Sim-to-real Reality gap. Mitigations include action-space alignment via Action representation and morphology-conditioned networks.

plain: The big red button that instantly cuts a machine's dangerous movement when someone hits it in an emergency.
snappy: A manually actuated function that immediately initiates a stop and removes hazardous motion or power, overriding all other controls.
detail: The Emergency stop (E-stop) is a mandatory, prominently colored manual control on virtually every robot and machine, required by ISO 10218 and the Machinery Directive.
