snappy: The running-gait interval with zero ground contact, during which the body follows a ballistic trajectory.
detail: A flight phase is what distinguishes Running from walking: the absence of a Double support phase means a Duty factor below 0.5 and a fully airborne body governed by the Spring-loaded inverted pendulum model. It appears in the Pronking, Bounding gait, and Gallop of quadrupeds and in the run cycle of bipeds like Cassie, where Raibert heuristic foot placement sets up the next landing. Because there is no Ground reaction force to correct attitude mid-flight, controllers rely on Angular momentum conservation and pre-planned Footstep planning.

plain: An onboard emergency device that deliberately stops a drone's flight, often by popping a parachute, when the aircraft can no longer be controlled, to keep it from flying off or crashing dangerously.
snappy: An independent onboard system that forcibly ends a flight, commonly via parachute deployment or motor cutoff, on detected loss of control or command.
detail: A Flight Termination System (FTS) is a last-resort mitigation distinct from a routine Return-to-home, triggering when the aircraft enters an unrecoverable state or experiences a Flyaway and the Flight controller can no longer guarantee safe flight. By bringing the Unmanned aircraft system down within a known area, it shrinks the required Ground Risk Buffer and supports the safety argument in a Specific Operations Risk Assessment. It is mandatory for many higher-risk Beyond visual line of sight operations and is weighed when assigning a Specific Assurance and Integrity Level and granting an Operational Authorization.

plain: The physics of a robot that is not bolted down, so its whole body can drift, tip, and rotate freely in space.
snappy: The dynamics of a robot whose root link is unconstrained, adding six unactuated base coordinates to the model.
detail: Unlike a bolted-down Industrial robot arm, a Humanoid robot, Quadruped robot, or Drone has a free-floating base, so its Equations of motion include six extra unactuated degrees of freedom for base translation and rotation. The robot can only influence those coordinates indirectly through Contact dynamics and Ground reaction force, which is the central challenge of Whole-body control and Legged locomotion. Floating-base formulations underpin Centroidal dynamics and the dynamics models used by Pinocchio and modern Physics engine simulators.

plain: The coordinated group motion of birds or robots that arises from each member just trying to stay near, aligned with, and not crashing into its neighbors.
snappy: Coordinated group movement that emerges from simple per-agent rules of alignment, cohesion, and separation, with no leader.
detail: Flocking, formalized in the classic Boids model, shows how three local rules, alignment, cohesion, and separation, produce coherent group motion as Emergent behavior. It is a canonical demonstration of Self-organization and Decentralized control in Swarm robotics, and the velocity-matching rule is effectively a Consensus algorithm. Aerial Drone swarm and Formation control systems build on flocking, layering in Collision avoidance such as a Velocity obstacle so a defense or surveillance swarm holds cohesion while avoiding obstacles.

plain: A robot control method that learns to gradually transform random noise into a smooth sequence of movements by following a learned flow.
snappy: An action-generation technique that trains a network to predict velocity fields transporting noise samples into action samples, integrated at inference to produce trajectories.
detail: A Flow Matching Policy learns a continuous velocity field that deterministically transports random noise into action samples, an alternative to the iterative denoising of a Diffusion policy that often needs fewer integration steps at inference. It produces smooth, multimodal Action chunking outputs well suited to Dexterous manipulation and high-frequency Visuomotor Policy control. Flow matching is the action head used by the Pi-Zero Vision-language-action model and is closely related to the broader Diffusion model family, trading sampling speed against the same expressiveness over continuous action distributions.

plain: A soft rubbery part with hollow chambers that bends or stretches when air or liquid is pumped into it.
snappy: A monolithic elastomer actuator whose embedded chambers bend or elongate the body when pressurized with air or fluid.
detail: A Fluidic Elastomer Actuator, often built as a PneuNet, is a cornerstone of Soft robotics: pressurizing asymmetric chambers makes a finger curl, giving a Soft gripper that conforms safely to delicate objects. As a Pneumatic actuator with no rigid joints, it sidesteps the kinematics of linkages and gears, trading precision for inherent Compliance and human-safe contact. It is one of several soft-robotics structure options alongside the McKibben Actuator and Dielectric elastomer actuator, and its robotics-specific form is also indexed as PneuNet Actuator.

plain: When a drone stops obeying its pilot and flies off on its own, out of control.
snappy: A failure mode in which a UAV departs uncommanded from operator control, often due to lost link, navigation error, or firmware fault.
detail: A flyaway occurs when a drone ignores operator input and drifts or accelerates away, typically triggered by Compass interference, GNSS spoofing, a corrupted state estimate, or loss of the Radio control link. Well-designed autopilots like PX4 mitigate it with failsafes such as Return-to-home, Geofencing, and as a last resort a Flight Termination System. Flyaways are a major Defense & Security and safety concern, which is why robust state estimation and Software-in-the-loop simulation testing are emphasized before flight.

plain: A cutter that slices material to length while it keeps moving, by briefly racing alongside it at the same speed.
snappy: A servo-synchronized mechanism that cuts continuously moving stock without stopping the line.
detail: A flying shear accelerates a knife carriage to match line speed using Electronic gearing, cuts during the synchronized window, then decelerates and returns under an S-curve acceleration profile before the next part. The Motion controller phases the cut to a Registration mark or a length count, coordinating the Servo drive that carries the blade. It is a continuous-process cousin of Conveyor tracking and depends on tight Following error control to keep cut length accurate.

plain: A tailless aircraft that is essentially one smooth wing, with its steering surfaces built into the back of the wing itself.
snappy: A tailless fixed-wing UAV airframe that blends fuselage into the wing and uses elevons on the trailing edge for control.
detail: A flying wing is a Fixed-wing drone with no separate tail, using combined elevon control surfaces on the wing to handle both pitch and roll, which lowers drag and radar signature for long-endurance and Defense & Security missions. The low drag boosts Endurance but reduces natural pitch stability, so the flight controller's stabilization is essential. Such airframes often launch by Catapult launch and recover by Net recovery since they lack landing gear and a runway.

plain: A laser sensor that smoothly sweeps its light's frequency so it can measure both how far away a target is and how fast it is moving.
snappy: A LiDAR that uses a chirped continuous laser and coherent detection to recover per-point range and radial velocity simultaneously.
detail: FMCW LiDAR continuously sweeps (chirps) the laser frequency and mixes the return with the outgoing beam, reading range from the beat frequency and velocity from the Doppler effect, much as Radar does. This per-point velocity gives Perception and Behavior prediction an instant motion cue that pulsed LiDAR lacks, valuable in Mobility and Autonomous vehicle stacks. It also rejects interference and sunlight better, at the cost of more complex optics than a standard Solid-state LiDAR.

plain: A structured checklist that asks, part by part, how each piece of a machine could fail and what would happen if it did.
snappy: A bottom-up reliability method that tabulates each component's failure modes and traces their effects on system safety and function.
detail: FMEA works upward from individual components, listing how each could fail, the resulting effect, and a risk priority so designers fix the worst cases first. In robotics it complements top-down Fault Tree Analysis and feeds the Risk assessment required by ISO 12100 and ISO 10218. Its quantitative extension FMEDA adds failure rates and Diagnostic Coverage for Safety Integrity Level and Performance Level claims, and FMEA findings often inform a HAZOP review of the wider process.

full: Failure Modes, Effects and Diagnostic Analysis
plain: A numbers-based version of failure analysis that calculates how often a part fails and how well the system catches that failure.
snappy: A quantitative FMEA extension that computes component failure rates and diagnostic coverage to substantiate safety-integrity claims.
detail: FMEDA augments FMEA with quantitative failure rates split into safe and dangerous, detected and undetected, yielding metrics like Diagnostic Coverage and Probability of Dangerous Failure per Hour. These numbers are the evidence behind a Safety Integrity Level claim under IEC 61508 and a Performance Level claim under ISO 13849 for a robot's safety functions. A safety engineer runs FMEDA on a Safe Torque Off circuit or Safety PLC to prove the design's hardware fault tolerance and meet Mean Time to Dangerous Failure targets.

plain: A route planner that lays down all its random points first, then grows a single tree outward in cost order like a wave spreading across the space.
snappy: An asymptotically optimal sampling planner that performs a single dynamic-programming 'marching' pass over a fixed batch of samples, lazily expanding the lowest-cost-to-come frontier.
detail: FMT* (Fast Marching Tree) samples a fixed set of points up front, then builds an optimal tree in one outward sweep that always expands the unconnected node with the lowest cost-to-come, conceptually borrowing the wavefront idea from the fast-marching method and the Wavefront Planner. By performing lazy Collision detection only on the edges it actually keeps, it is often faster than RRT* for the same Sampling-based planning problem and is provided in OMPL for Motion planning. It sits in the same optimal-planner family as BIT* and Informed RRT*.

plain: The small gap between where a motor was told to be and where it actually is at any instant; too big a gap signals a problem.
snappy: The instantaneous difference between commanded and actual servo position; large values trigger a fault.
detail: Following error (also called position lag) is the Error signal inside a Servo drive's Position control loop, and a configurable threshold trips a Drive fault to protect the machine when the axis can't keep up. It grows when load, friction (Stiction), or an aggressive Motion profile exceeds the drive's authority. Tuning Feedforward and Gain tuning reduces steady following error, while a sudden spike often reveals a Collision detection event on an Industrial robot arm.

plain: Deciding exactly where to put each foot when walking over rough or uneven ground.
snappy: Choosing safe and effective foot placement locations on terrain to maintain balance and make forward progress.
detail: Foothold selection turns a perceived terrain map into specific footstep targets, avoiding holes, edges, and slippery patches while keeping the next Support polygon valid. It is informed by Perception and a Terrain adaptation pipeline, and feeds the Swing phase trajectory of each leg in Legged locomotion. A Quadruped robot or Bipedal robot crossing stairs uses it together with Balance control and the Zero moment point to stay upright.

plain: Deciding exactly where a walking robot should place each foot across uneven ground so it stays balanced and reaches its goal.
snappy: Selecting discrete, kinematically and dynamically feasible foot placements over terrain to keep a legged robot balanced en route to a goal.
detail: Footstep planning chooses a sequence of footholds that are reachable, on safe terrain, and consistent with balance, often as a discrete search layered above a continuous Reduced-order model control balance layer. It draws on Perceptive locomotion to read terrain via an Elevation Map and is tightly coupled to Foothold selection, Capture point control, and Zero moment point control. Quadrupeds like ANYmal and bipedal humanoids both rely on it, and the resulting plan feeds Whole-body control for execution.

plain: A robot team task of searching an area, collecting items, and carrying them back to a home base, like ants gathering food.
snappy: A swarm task in which robots search for, collect, and transport resources back to a designated base or nest.
detail: Foraging is a benchmark task in Swarm robotics that combines exploration, retrieval, and Task allocation: robots disperse, locate resources, and return them while balancing the Exploration vs exploitation tradeoff. It is often coordinated through Stigmergy, where successful foragers lay trails that recruit others, an instance of Self-organization under Decentralized control. Applied versions appear in Agriculture (collecting fruit or samples) and Logistics & Warehouse picking, and the round-trip structure connects to Coverage problem search and Multi-robot path finding.

plain: A grip strong and well-placed enough that the object can't be pushed or twisted out of the robot's grasp.
snappy: A grasp in which the finger contact forces can resist any external wrench applied to the object.
detail: Force closure is the gold-standard stability condition for a grasp: through friction at the Contact points, the fingers can generate forces that counter any external Wrench, holding the object firmly against gravity, pushes, or twists. It depends on having enough contacts within their Friction cone, a property checked using the Grasp matrix and predicted by a Grasp quality metric. Unlike Form closure, force closure relies on friction, so a two-fingered Antipodal grasp can achieve it with fewer contacts.

plain: Telling a robot how hard to push or press on something, instead of just telling it where to move.
snappy: A control scheme that regulates the contact force a robot applies rather than its position.
detail: Force control closes the loop on a measured contact force, typically read from a Force/torque sensor or estimated via Torque control, so the robot presses with a target Wrench regardless of small position errors. It is essential for tasks like Peg-in-hole assembly, deburring, and Medical & Surgical procedures where pushing to a fixed position would jam or damage parts. It is often blended with position control as Hybrid position/force control, or generalized into Impedance control.

plain: A sensor, usually at a robot's wrist, that measures how hard it is pushing and twisting in every direction.
snappy: A six-axis sensor measuring the three forces and three torques acting at a robot's wrist or tool.
detail: A force/torque sensor (F/T sensor) measures the full Wrench, that is three force and three torque components, typically mounted between the Robot wrist and the End-effector. It is essential for Force control, Impedance control, Admittance control, and Compliant manipulation, enabling tasks like Peg-in-hole assembly. Most designs read deformation with a Strain gauge bridge, and the data also supports Collision detection on a Cobot.

plain: Holding an object so completely caged by the fingers that it can't move at all, even if it were perfectly slippery.
snappy: A grasp that fully immobilizes an object through contact geometry alone, without relying on friction.
detail: Form closure constrains every possible motion of an object purely through the geometry of the Contact points, so the grasp holds even if friction were zero, unlike Force closure which depends on the Friction cone. Achieving it generally requires more contacts (at least seven for a 3D object), making it the basis of secure Fixturing and caging grasps in Assembly. It is analyzed with the same Grasp matrix machinery used for grasp stability and is a foundational concept in Manipulation theory.

plain: A company that offers software for watching, controlling, and managing groups of robots over the internet.
snappy: Maker of a cloud platform for teleoperating, observing, and managing robot fleets.
detail: Formant provides a Cloud robotics dashboard for Fleet management that streams Telemetry radio data, video, and logs from deployed robots and lets operators run Teleoperation or issue Remote Assistance when a robot gets stuck. It is data-source agnostic and commonly ingests from ROS topics, giving observability and Predictive maintenance insight across mixed fleets. Operators use it to track Uptime and intervene on an Autonomous mobile robot from a Remote operation center.

plain: Keeping a group of robots in a fixed geometric pattern, like a V or a line, even while they all move.
snappy: Control that maintains a desired geometric arrangement among multiple robots as the group moves through space.
detail: Formation control keeps a Multi-robot system in a prescribed shape, using either a Leader-follower control scheme, where followers hold offsets from a leader, or a distributed Consensus algorithm on relative positions. It is essential for satellite Formation flying in Space and for coordinated defense Drone swarm maneuvers, and it layers Collision avoidance on top so the formation deforms safely around obstacles. Formation maintenance is a structured cousin of Flocking, trading emergent cohesion for an explicit target geometry under Decentralized control.

plain: An alert that warns the driver with a sound or light when the car is closing in too fast on whatever is ahead.
snappy: A driver-assistance alert that notifies the driver of an impending frontal collision so they can react.
detail: Forward collision warning (FCW) uses automotive radar and a camera to compute time to collision with the vehicle or pedestrian ahead and issues an audible or visual warning when it drops below a threshold. It is the alerting tier that precedes automatic emergency braking: warn first, brake if the driver does not respond. As an advanced driver-assistance systems feature it pairs with pedestrian detection and a driver monitoring system to ensure the warning reaches an attentive driver.

plain: Working out how a robot will move when you push or twist its joints with known forces.
snappy: Computing the accelerations a robot's joints produce given the torques applied to them.
detail: Forward dynamics maps applied joint torques to the resulting joint accelerations, which are then integrated to predict motion over time. It is the computation at the heart of any Physics engine or Robot simulator such as MuJoCo, Gazebo, or PyBullet, where the Equations of motion are solved every step to advance the simulated robot. It depends on the configuration-dependent Mass matrix plus Coriolis and centrifugal forces and gravity, and is the inverse problem to Inverse dynamics.

plain: Working out exactly where a robot arm's hand ends up once you know how far each joint has turned.
snappy: Computing end-effector pose from known joint angles.
detail: Forward kinematics (FK) chains together the per-link transforms, often built from Denavit-Hartenberg parameters, to map a point in Joint space to an End-effector Pose in Task space. It is deterministic and always has a unique answer, which is why it is far simpler than Inverse kinematics. Robot controllers compute FK continuously to know where the tool actually is, and the result feeds straight into the Jacobian matrix.

plain: A very large AI model trained on huge amounts of data that can be adapted to many different robot jobs.
snappy: A large, broadly pretrained model that serves as a reusable base, fine-tuned or prompted for many downstream robot tasks.
detail: In robotics a foundation model is pretrained on web-scale text, images, or cross-robot Demonstration data, then adapted instead of being built per-task. A Robot foundation model such as a Vision-language-action model maps camera images and language goals to actions, with families like RT-2 and OpenVLA trained on Open X-Embodiment data to enable Cross-embodiment learning. The promise is a Generalist robot that handles open-ended tasks, though Grounding actions in real physics and closing the Reality gap remain hard.

plain: A single very large AI model trained on huge amounts of data that gives a robot broad, reusable abilities to perceive and act, instead of training a fresh model for every new task.
snappy: A large pretrained model offering broad, transferable robot capabilities that can be adapted to many downstream perception, planning, or control tasks.
detail: Analogous to large language models, a robotics foundation model is trained at scale, often on a Cross-embodiment dataset like Open X-Embodiment, to produce a Generalist policy that can be adapted via Foundation Policy Fine-Tuning. Concrete examples include the Vision-language-action model family such as RT-2, OpenVLA, and pi0, as well as GR00T for humanoids. It promises to mitigate Robot data scarcity by amortizing learning across embodiments and tasks, and is a central Research/Frontier theme in Embodied AI.

plain: Taking a big, general robot brain that already knows many tasks and giving it a short extra training session so it does one specific new job really well.
snappy: Efficiently adapting a pretrained generalist robot policy to a target task or embodiment, often with parameter-efficient methods like LoRA.
detail: Rather than training from scratch, a pretrained Generalist policy or Foundation Model for Robotics, such as OpenVLA or pi0, is adapted to a new task with a small dataset, frequently using parameter-efficient LoRA to avoid Catastrophic forgetting. This is the practical deployment path for Vision-language-action model systems and complements Residual Reinforcement Learning as a way to specialize a strong prior. It directly attacks Robot data scarcity by reusing broad pretraining, and pairs naturally with Cross-embodiment learning when the target robot differs from those in the pretraining mix.

plain: A general-purpose vision system that can figure out the exact 3D position and rotation of an object it has never seen before, without being trained on that specific object.
snappy: A generalist neural model that estimates the 6-DoF pose of arbitrary, previously unseen objects from a CAD model or a few reference images, with no per-object retraining.
detail: Unlike classic 6D Pose Estimation pipelines that train one network per known part, a Foundation Pose Model generalizes across novel objects by combining a learned visual Foundation model backbone with render-and-compare refinement against an RGB or Depth camera stream. In a manufacturing Bin picking cell, it lets a robot localize a freshly introduced component the moment its mesh is loaded, feeding the resulting Pose directly into Grasp Pose Detection and Pick and place. It is closely tied to Object recognition and is increasingly paired with Open-vocabulary perception so the system can both find and orient items it was never explicitly programmed to handle.

plain: A loop of four rigid bars hinged together that produces a fixed, repeatable motion path.
snappy: A four-link closed loop that generates constrained, coupled planar motion from one input.
detail: The Four-bar linkage is the simplest useful Closed kinematic chain: with one Revolute joint driven, the remaining bars trace a determined path, which designers exploit for grippers, leg mechanisms, and self-aligning structures. It underlies many a Legged robot knee and Parallel manipulator limb, and is a textbook example of a Linkage. Because the loop constrains motion, only one of its Degrees of freedom is actuated.

plain: A Chinese company that makes both a walking human-shaped robot and machines that help patients rehabilitate.
snappy: Chinese maker of the GR-1 humanoid and rehabilitation robotics for medical use.
detail: Fourier Intelligence began in rehabilitation and Exoskeleton products for Medical & Surgical recovery before launching the GR-1, a full-size Humanoid robot. Its rehab heritage gives it expertise in Compliance control, Force control, and safe Human-robot interaction with patients. The GR-1 uses high-torque actuators and Whole-body control for Bipedal locomotion, positioned for both research and assistive applications.

plain: A visual dashboard that lets engineers see and play back what a robot's sensors and software are doing.
snappy: A web-based visualization and debugging tool for live and recorded robotics data across multiple message formats.
detail: Foxglove (formerly Foxglove Studio) renders robot data, 3D point clouds, camera frames, transforms, and plots, from a live connection or a recorded log, serving a similar role to RViz but in the browser and across frameworks. It reads the MCAP and rosbag formats, making it the standard tool for inspecting what went wrong after a run via Log replay. Teams use it to debug Sensor fusion, the transform tree (tf), and navigation behavior during field testing.

plain: An app that turns the flood of data coming off a robot into charts and 3D views so engineers can see what it is doing.
snappy: A web and desktop visualization tool for inspecting live and recorded robotics data streams across multiple panels.
detail: Foxglove Studio reads live ROS 2 topics or recorded logs in MCAP and rosbag2 format and renders them as plots, 3D scenes, image views, and Transform tree displays for debugging. It plays a role similar to RViz and PlotJuggler but works in a browser and across the web, easing remote inspection of a deployed Fleet. Engineers use it to diagnose problems like Message Drop, Sensor latency, or bad State estimation after the fact.

plain: A small, fast camera drone flown by a pilot wearing goggles that show a live view from the drone, as if sitting inside it.
snappy: An agile camera-equipped quadcopter flown manually through goggles showing a low-latency first-person video feed.
detail: An FPV racing drone is a high-thrust Quadcopter built for agility, streaming a live camera feed to the pilot's goggles so they fly from the aircraft's First-person view rather than line of sight. Extreme thrust-to-weight ratios and a tuned flight controller let it perform aggressive aerobatics, making the platform a benchmark for autonomous-flight research such as Autonomous drone racing and aggressive Minimum-snap trajectory control. Beyond Service & Consumer sport racing, the agile, low-cost airframe has been adopted for Defense & Security roles, and it contrasts with the stability-first Multirotor drone used for cinematography.

plain: The difficulty of figuring out which facts about the world stay the same after an action, without having to recheck everything.
snappy: The challenge of efficiently representing what does not change in the world when an agent performs an action.
detail: First posed in symbolic AI, the frame problem is the difficulty of specifying which facts remain unchanged after an action, since explicitly listing every non-effect is intractable; it matters whenever a robot reasons about action consequences in Task planning or Task and motion planning. A manipulator that moves one object should not have to reverify the pose of every other object, yet keeping its World model consistent and current is exactly the hard part. The problem is deeply linked to the Symbol grounding problem and Embodied cognition, and Common sense reasoning and modern World model approaches are partly attempts to sidestep it.

plain: A motor sold as just its two core working parts so it can be built straight into a robot's joint, saving space and weight.
snappy: A motor supplied as only a rotor and stator for direct integration into a robot joint housing.
detail: A frameless (or frameless torque) motor ships without a housing, shaft, or bearings, letting the designer mount the rotor and stator directly into the structure of a robot Joint or Robot wrist. This integration removes couplings and shrinks the actuator, which is why it appears in collaborative arms and a Humanoid robot. Frameless units are typically Brushless DC motor or Permanent magnet synchronous motor types paired with a Harmonic drive and an Absolute encoder.

plain: A German maker of a sensitive, touch-aware robot arm widely used in research labs.
snappy: German maker of the Panda torque-controlled research robot arm popular in academia.
detail: Franka Emika builds the Panda (and later Franka Research) arm, a torque-controlled Industrial robot arm prized in Research/Frontier labs for its joint torque sensors and easy Impedance control. Its sensitivity makes it a standard platform for Contact-rich manipulation, Peg-in-hole, and Learning from demonstration experiments. The arm integrates tightly with ROS and MoveIt, making it a go-to for manipulation research and Imitation learning datasets.

plain: A popular lightweight robot arm with seven joints and built-in force sensing, widely used in university labs to study how robots touch and handle objects.
snappy: A seven-axis torque-sensing collaborative manipulator from Franka Emika that became a de facto standard platform for manipulation research.
detail: The Franka Emika Panda is a Seven-axis robot built by Franka Emika with a Joint Torque Sensor in every joint, giving it strong Backdrivability and native Cartesian impedance control for safe Contact-rich manipulation. Its Kinematic redundancy lets researchers exploit the Null space while the arm runs Force control or Compliance control, and it is a common test bed for Imitation learning, Diffusion policy, and Peg-in-hole studies. ROS and MoveIt drivers plus a real-time control interface make it a default Collaborative robot for benchmarking against the KUKA LBR iiwa.

plain: The open area around a robot where it can move without hitting anything.
snappy: The region of the environment a robot can occupy or traverse without collision.
detail: Free space is the obstacle-free portion of the world (or of Configuration space) that planning can route through, the complement of occupied cells in an Occupancy grid. Detecting it, called free space detection, is a core Perception task for an Autonomous vehicle deciding where it may drive and is closely tied to Ground segmentation. A planner searches free space to produce a collision-free Trajectory.

plain: Figuring out which part of the road ahead is open and safe for the vehicle to drive into.
snappy: Perception that segments the navigable, unobstructed drivable surface ahead, distinct from obstacles and non-road areas.
detail: Free space detection answers 'where can I go?' by classifying drivable surface versus curbs, vehicles, and Vulnerable road user, often as a polygon or mask in a Bird's-eye-view representation. It complements Object detection (which finds discrete things) and feeds Behavior planning and Motion planning, and on a Sidewalk delivery robot it identifies walkable pavement. It is closely tied to Semantic segmentation, Ground segmentation, and Occupancy grid mapping in the Self-driving stack.

plain: A small robot that floats and propels itself freely inside or around a spacecraft, where there is no gravity to hold it down.
snappy: A self-propelled robot that maneuvers in six degrees of freedom in microgravity, using thrusters or fans to fly around or inside a spacecraft.
detail: A free-flying space robot moves untethered in microgravity, like NASA's Astrobee, which uses a Ducted fan system to hover and translate inside the ISS as a mobile sensor and assistant. Lacking a floor to push against, it must actively control all six Degrees of freedom via thrust, demanding precise State estimation and Pose estimation from vision and an Inertial measurement unit, plus careful Collision avoidance near astronauts and structure. It differs from the surface-bound Planetary rover and from the larger Orbital servicing robot, performing inspection, inventory, and Human-robot interaction tasks aboard crewed vehicles.

plain: A way of planning a car's motion using coordinates that follow the road, measuring how far along the lane and how far sideways it is rather than using fixed map directions.
snappy: Trajectory generation in a road-aligned coordinate frame parameterized by arc-length-along-the-path and lateral offset, decoupling longitudinal and lateral motion for lane driving.
detail: Frenet Frame Planning reparameterizes the world into coordinates attached to a reference Lane graph or centerline, using a longitudinal coordinate s along the road and a lateral coordinate d across it, so a planner can independently shape speed profiles and lane-change offsets and then convert the result back to Cartesian. It is a backbone of Autonomous vehicle behavior and Trajectory generation, letting a Self-driving stack sample many candidate curves and score them for comfort and safety. It is frequently paired with a Lattice Planner that enumerates Frenet trajectories.

plain: Adding extra motor force to overcome the sticking and dragging inside a joint, so it moves smoothly even very slowly.
snappy: Feedforward torque countering Coulomb, viscous, and Stribeck friction in a joint or drive.
detail: Friction Compensation models the joint's Coulomb friction model, viscous drag, and the velocity-dependent Stribeck and Stiction effects, then injects offsetting Feedforward torque to linearize the actuator's response. It is critical for smooth slow motion and accurate Torque Control Mode where uncompensated Backlash and stick-slip would otherwise dominate, and it often pairs with cogging compensation to fight Cogging torque and Torque Ripple. Combined with Gravity Compensation it makes a Manufacturing arm or Humanoid robot joint feel nearly ideal to higher-level Force control.

plain: The range of directions a robot finger can push without the object sliding away, shaped like a cone.
snappy: The set of contact forces a finger can apply without slipping, geometrically a cone around the surface normal.
detail: The Friction cone describes all contact forces that stay within the limits of static friction at a Contact point: any force whose angle from the surface normal exceeds the friction angle would cause slipping. It is the linchpin of grasp analysis, deciding whether contacts can combine into Force closure and feeding the Grasp matrix and Grasp quality metric. Because exact cones are nonlinear, planners often approximate them as polyhedral cones, and real grippers monitor their friction limits through Slip detection and Grip force control.

plain: A way for a robot to explore on its own by always heading for the edge of what it has mapped so far, until nothing unknown is left.
snappy: An autonomous exploration strategy that repeatedly drives the robot to the boundary between known-free and unknown space to grow its map.
detail: Frontiers are the cells where Free space in the Occupancy grid map borders unmapped 'unknown' regions; frontier-based exploration detects these boundaries, picks the best one (by distance, information gain, or cost), and sends the robot there via the Navigation stack, repeating until no frontiers remain. It turns Mapping and SLAM into an active, goal-driven process for Defense & Security search-and-rescue and Space planetary rovers operating without prior maps. The frontier selection is a form of Active perception balancing exploration cost against expected map gain.

plain: A single number that compares speed and size to tell whether two different-sized legged things move in a similar way.
snappy: A dimensionless ratio of speed to the square root of leg length times gravity that predicts dynamic similarity and gait transitions in legged systems.
detail: The Froude number lets engineers and biologists compare a tiny robot, a human, and a horse on equal footing, predicting roughly the same value at which each transitions, say, from walking to a Trot. In Legged locomotion it guides Froude scaling so a controller tuned on one Legged robot can be transferred to a larger one, and it relates speed to the natural dynamics captured by the Linear inverted pendulum model and Spring-loaded inverted pendulum. It is a foundational analysis tool for Gait selection and helps explain why a Quadruped robot picks particular speeds for each Gait cycle.

plain: A way to send safety signals like emergency stops over a normal EtherCAT factory network instead of separate safety wires.
snappy: A safety protocol transmitting certified fail-safe control data over standard EtherCAT networks.
detail: FSoE (Safety over EtherCAT) wraps safety data in a protected container with sequence numbers, watchdogs, and CRCs so it can traverse an ordinary EtherCAT network as a Black Channel without compromising integrity. It connects safety I/O and a Safety PLC to actuators that support Safe Torque Off and Safe Operating Stop, meeting Functional safety requirements. FSoE is the EtherCAT-family counterpart of PROFIsafe and CIP Safety, widely used to safeguard Servo drive axes and Collaborative robot cells.

plain: A device that makes electricity from hydrogen, letting a robot run far longer than on a battery.
snappy: An electrochemical device generating electricity from hydrogen fuel to give robots extended endurance.
detail: A fuel cell converts hydrogen and oxygen into electricity and water, offering far higher effective Energy density than a Lithium-ion battery for long-Endurance missions, which is why defense and inspection drones and field robots explore it. It refuels in minutes rather than recharging, but adds tank weight, lower Power density, and Thermal management complexity, so it is often hybridized with a battery or Supercapacitor for peaks. Sizing it is a major input to a robot's Power budget.

plain: A way of programming factory controllers by wiring together reusable boxes, like building a circuit out of pre-made parts.
snappy: A graphical PLC language that connects reusable function blocks with signal wires to express control logic.
detail: A function block diagram (FBD) is one of the five IEC 61131-3 languages, representing logic as boxes (timers, counters, PID, arithmetic) joined by lines carrying data and signals. It suits continuous and process control where signal flow is natural, complementing Ladder logic for discrete logic and Structured text for algorithms. FBD is common in a Distributed control system and on a Programmable logic controller handling closed-loop tasks like a PID controller regulating temperature or flow.

plain: The engineering discipline of making sure that when something breaks, it breaks in a safe way.
snappy: The branch of safety engineering ensuring electronic and software systems detect faults and fail in predictable, non-hazardous ways.
detail: Functional safety (FuSa) governs how an Autonomous vehicle handles a sensor dropout or compute crash, demanding Redundancy and Fail-operational designs so the car can still reach a Minimal risk condition. In automotive it is codified by ISO 26262, which assigns each hazard an ASIL rating, while industrial robots follow IEC 61508 and ISO 13849. It complements Safety of the intended functionality, which covers hazards arising even when nothing has technically failed.

plain: A specialized robot chip designed to catch its own errors so a malfunction can't cause a dangerous failure.
snappy: A controller, often dual-core lockstep with built-in diagnostics, designed to meet automotive or industrial functional-safety integrity levels.
detail: A Functional Safety Processor runs critical control redundantly, typically in lockstep where two cores execute the same instructions and compare results, plus self-tests and error-correcting memory to reach a target Safety Integrity Level or ASIL under IEC 61508 and ISO 26262. In a Mobility platform it supervises Drive-by-wire and braking; in Manufacturing it backs a Safety PLC and Safe Torque Off in a Robot controller. It is a cornerstone of Functional safety architecture, paired with Diagnostic Coverage analysis and FMEDA to bound the Probability of Dangerous Failure per Hour.

plain: A compact rule that links two photos of the same scene, telling you that a point in one image must lie along a specific line in the other.
snappy: A 3x3 matrix encoding the epipolar constraint between corresponding points in two uncalibrated camera views.
detail: The fundamental matrix maps a point in one image to its epipolar line in another, formalizing Epipolar Geometry for uncalibrated cameras; its calibrated counterpart, the essential matrix, additionally uses the Camera intrinsics to recover relative Pose up to scale. It is typically estimated from Feature matching correspondences (e.g. SIFT or ORB features) inside RANSAC, and underlies Structure from motion, Visual odometry, and the initialization of Visual SLAM systems like ORB-SLAM. Robotics teams use it to verify two-view geometry before triangulating a Point cloud in Multi-View Stereo.

plain: A pre-computed collection of safe motion 'tubes' that a robot strings together, each one guaranteeing it stays inside a region even with disturbances.
snappy: A precomputed set of verified region-of-attraction funnels sequenced to compose robust feedback motion plans.
detail: A Funnel Library precomputes, offline, a set of motion primitives each wrapped by a verified funnel: a shrinking region of attraction guaranteed by a stabilizing feedback controller such as a Linear quadratic regulator, so that any state inside the funnel mouth is driven to the goal region despite disturbances. At runtime the planner composes feasible funnels like puzzle pieces (the LQR-Trees idea) to build a robust plan with formal guarantees. It is used for agile Mobility and Space systems where Robust control matters, and is conceptually related to a Control Lyapunov function and Tube MPC.

plain: The simple text language of numbered commands that tells a CNC machine where to move and how fast.
snappy: The numerical-control programming language specifying tool paths, speeds, and motions for CNC machines.
detail: G-code is a line-by-line language where commands like G01 (linear move) and G02 (arc) plus coordinates and feed rates direct a Computer numerical control machine along its tool path, usually generated by CAM software from a 3D model. Each block specifies a motion, spindle, or coolant action, and the machine's Motion controller interpolates the axes accordingly. It is the lingua franca of machining and 3D printing, and contrasts with the taught point-to-point programs of a Six-axis robot driven from a Teach pendant.

plain: A dial that sets how strongly a controller reacts to being off-target, more aggressive or more gentle.
snappy: A multiplier that scales how strongly a controller responds to the error signal.
detail: Gain converts the Error signal into a command: high gain reacts hard and fast but risks Overshoot and instability, while low gain is sluggish and leaves Steady-state error. A PID controller has separate proportional, integral, and derivative gains set during Gain tuning. When operating conditions change, the gain itself can be varied via Gain scheduling, and excessive gain can drive an Actuator into Saturation.

plain: Swapping in different controller settings depending on the situation, the way a car shifts gears for different speeds.
snappy: A technique that switches or interpolates controller gains across operating regimes to maintain consistent performance.
detail: Gain scheduling pre-computes sets of Gain values for different operating points, say a robot arm carrying different payloads or a drone at different airspeeds, and blends between them as a measured variable changes. It is a pragmatic way to control a nonlinear plant with linear tools, sitting between fixed Gain tuning and full Adaptive control. Aircraft Flight controller and Manufacturing temperature loops use it to keep Bandwidth and Stability consistent across the envelope.

plain: Adjusting a controller's settings until the machine responds quickly without overshooting or wobbling.
snappy: The process of adjusting controller parameters to balance response speed, stability, and overshoot.
detail: Gain tuning sets the proportional, integral, and derivative Gain values of a PID controller to trade off Settling time, Overshoot, and Steady-state error. It can be done by hand, by heuristic recipes like the Ziegler-Nichols method, or by model-based and auto-tuning algorithms. Tuning a robot joint too aggressively excites resonances and instability; too softly leaves it sluggish with poor Bandwidth and weak Disturbance rejection.

plain: The repeating pattern of leg movements a walking robot uses to get around.
snappy: A coordinated, repeating sequence of limb lifts and placements that produces legged locomotion.
detail: A gait specifies the timing and order in which legs leave and meet the ground, and switching gaits lets a robot trade speed for stability. A Quadruped robot might use a Crawl gait at low speed and a Trot or Gallop at high speed, each defined by its Duty factor and Gait cycle. Gait generation can be hand-tuned, derived from a model like the Spring-loaded inverted pendulum, or produced by Learned locomotion.

plain: One complete repetition of a walking pattern, from a foot touching down to that same foot touching down again.
snappy: A single full period of a gait, measured from one footfall of a given leg to the next footfall of the same leg.
detail: The gait cycle is the basic clock of legged locomotion, splitting each leg's motion into a Stance phase on the ground and a Swing phase in the air. The Duty factor is the fraction of the cycle spent in stance, and the relative phase of different legs distinguishes a Trot from a Gallop. Controllers index foot trajectories and Foothold selection against position within the gait cycle.

plain: A Chinese startup that builds part-human-shaped robots on rolling wheeled bases designed to fetch and handle items in shops and other everyday settings.
snappy: Beijing-based humanoid-robotics startup developing wheeled-base mobile manipulators aimed at retail, logistics, and service tasks.
detail: Galbot pursues a wheeled-base body plan rather than legs: a Humanoid robot torso and arms mounted on a Mobile manipulator chassis, trading Bipedal locomotion for the stability and battery efficiency of Wheeled locomotion while keeping a human-height reach envelope for shelves and counters. Its target workloads are Service robot and Service robotics duties such as Pick and place, Bin picking, and store restocking, where the arms perform Mobile manipulation against partially Unstructured environment clutter. Like peers AgiBot, Unitree, Figure AI, and 1X Technologies, Galbot frames learned control around a Vision-language-action model and broader Foundation model for Robotics methods, positioning the platform within the Embodied AI push toward a Generalist robot.

plain: A new kind of electronic switch made from a special crystal that handles power faster and with less wasted heat than traditional silicon.
snappy: A wide-bandgap GaN power switch that conducts and switches faster than silicon, enabling compact, high-efficiency robot power converters.
detail: A Gallium Nitride Transistor (GaN FET) switches far faster than a silicon part, so a DC-DC converter or Brushless DC Motor Controller built around it can be smaller, lighter, and cooler. This matters for a Humanoid robot or drone where Power density and Payload-to-weight ratio are tight, and it pairs well with a 48-volt architecture. Like the Silicon Carbide MOSFET it is a wide-bandgap device, but GaN targets lower voltages and the highest switching frequencies, improving Energy efficiency in onboard chargers and motor inverters.

plain: The fastest four-legged gait, where the animal or robot briefly leaves the ground entirely.
snappy: A high-speed quadruped gait with asymmetric leg timing and an aerial phase where no foot touches the ground.
detail: The gallop sacrifices the steady support of a Trot for raw speed, using an airborne flight phase and a low Duty factor that demands strong Dynamic stability and energy storage. It is the quadruped analogue of Running and is often modelled with the Spring-loaded inverted pendulum to capture the bouncing leg dynamics. Galloping is a research frontier for fast Quadrupedal locomotion and Legged robot agility.

plain: A way of passing signals or power between two circuits without letting electricity flow directly between them, so a fault on one side cannot harm the other.
snappy: Separating two power or signal domains so no direct conductive path exists, blocking fault currents and breaking ground loops.
detail: Galvanic Isolation uses optocouplers, transformers, or capacitive barriers to transfer energy or data across a gap, so a high-voltage motor fault cannot reach low-voltage logic and ground loops do not corrupt signals. In robotics it protects the Onboard compute and a CAN Bus link from the noisy high-current side of a Servo drive or Brushless DC Motor Controller, and it is mandatory in a Medical & Surgical robot or Surgical robot for patient safety. It also appears in the gate drivers of an Insulated-Gate Bipolar Transistor stage and in isolated DC-DC converter designs feeding sensitive rails.

plain: Planning a car's moves while predicting how other drivers will react to those moves, like reasoning in a negotiation.
snappy: Motion planning that models the coupled, reactive responses of other agents to the ego vehicle's own actions.
detail: Unlike planners that treat predicted trajectories as fixed obstacles, Game-Theoretic Planning (Interactive planning) solves for an equilibrium in which the Ego vehicle's plan and other agents' Behavior prediction influence each other, which is essential for an Unprotected left turn, merges, and a Cut-in. It addresses the freezing-robot problem that decoupled Motion planning suffers in dense traffic and overlaps with multi-agent reinforcement-learning research. It is evaluated on closed-loop benchmarks like nuPlan.

plain: A machine that moves a tool back and forth along an overhead bridge frame, like an overhead crane that can pick and place things precisely.
snappy: A Cartesian manipulator mounted on an overhead bridge structure that slides along rails to cover a large rectangular workspace.
detail: A Gantry robot is a large-footprint variant of the Cartesian robot in which the linear axes are carried on an elevated bridge rather than a tabletop, so the working volume can span an entire production line or warehouse aisle. Because motion is purely prismatic, its forward kinematics and inverse kinematics are trivial and its repeatability is high, making it favored for heavy Pick and place, machine tending, and large-part welding cells. Unlike an Articulated robot, the gantry keeps its Payload suspended over the work area, freeing floor space and supporting very high payload-to-weight ratios.

plain: A single piece of robot-control AI from DeepMind that learned to operate many different machines and tasks with one shared brain, instead of training a separate program for each robot.
snappy: A single transformer policy trained across many embodiments that controls real and simulated robot tasks from one shared network, alongside other token-sequence tasks.
detail: Gato, from DeepMind, is an early Generalist policy that tokenizes robot observations and actions, joint commands, gripper signals, and camera images, into one sequence so a single transformer can drive many embodiments. Trained across stacking and Manipulation tasks on a real robot arm plus simulated control (with non-control tasks folded into the same sequence as a side demonstration of generality), it argued that one set of weights could span robot bodies and tasks, foreshadowing the Robot foundation model and Vision-language-action model wave that includes RoboCat, RT-1, and the Octo policy. It is a touchstone for Cross-embodiment learning and the Scaling hypothesis applied to embodied control.

plain: A method that represents a real-world scene as millions of tiny coloured fuzzy blobs, which can be drawn together extremely quickly to show the scene from any viewpoint.
snappy: An explicit 3D scene representation made of many oriented, coloured Gaussians that rasterize in real time to produce photorealistic novel views.
detail: Gaussian splatting stores a scene as a cloud of 3D Gaussians, each with position, shape, colour, and opacity, then rasterizes them far faster than a NeRF can ray-march, making it practical for real-time robot perception. It is used for live 3D reconstruction, building Photorealistic rendering assets for Sensor simulation, and creating navigable maps that pair naturally with a Point cloud or Mesh. The Gaussians are typically initialized from Structure from motion output and refined against captured images, so accurate Camera calibration and Pose estimation drive the result quality. Because it renders quickly on a Graphics processing unit, it suits Digital twin construction and on-robot scene reconstruction.

plain: A free 3D simulator where you can test a robot in a virtual world, complete with physics and fake sensors, before building it.
snappy: An open-source robot simulator providing physics, sensor models, and tight ROS integration.
detail: Gazebo simulates a robot described in SDF (or a converted URDF) inside a physical world, generating synthetic Camera, LiDAR, and Inertial measurement unit data for an entire ROS or ROS 2 stack to consume. It is a default open-source choice for testing Navigation and Manipulation, complementing heavier tools like Isaac Sim and lighter ones like PyBullet. The modern rewrite was branded Ignition Gazebo and later Gazebo Sim.

plain: The original version of a popular free simulator where engineers test robots in a virtual world with realistic physics.
snappy: The original generation of the Gazebo simulator (through Gazebo 11), now superseded by the rearchitected Gazebo Sim.
detail: Gazebo Classic is the long-standing 3D Robot simulator that pairs a Physics engine (such as Open Dynamics Engine, Bullet, or DART) with sensor and rendering plugins and tight ROS integration. It loads robots from a URDF or SDF and was the default for years of ROS tutorials and Software-in-the-Loop testing. It reached end of life with Gazebo 11, with development moving to Gazebo Sim; teams also compare it with Webots, CoppeliaSim, and NVIDIA Isaac.

plain: The modern, rebuilt version of the popular free robot simulator, designed to be more flexible than the original.
snappy: The modern, modular successor to Gazebo Classic, built on a new component-based architecture (formerly Ignition Gazebo).
detail: Gazebo Sim (formerly Ignition Gazebo, invoked as gz sim) re-architects the simulator around an entity-component system and swappable libraries for physics, rendering, and transport. It loads models from SDF, supports multiple Physics engine backends including DART and Bullet, and integrates with ROS 2 for closed-loop Simulation. It competes with NVIDIA Isaac Sim, Webots, and Unreal Engine-based simulators for high-fidelity sensor and Domain randomization workflows.

plain: The tiny bit of free play in a gearbox, where the gears can move slightly before they actually push on each other when direction reverses.
snappy: Lost motion arising from the clearance between meshing gear teeth, manifesting as positional dead zone on reversal.
detail: Gear Backlash is the unavoidable clearance left between meshing teeth in a Gear Train so they do not jam; on direction reversal the output does not move until the slack is taken up, creating a Deadband that degrades Repeatability and Accuracy. It is the main reason precision joints favor a Harmonic drive or Cycloidal drive, which achieve near-zero backlash, over a simple Spur Gear set. Excess backlash also limits control Bandwidth and can cause limit-cycle oscillation in a tightly tuned Position control loop.

plain: A number comparing how fast a gear's input spins to how fast its output spins, showing the trade between speed and turning strength.
snappy: The ratio of input to output rotational speed in a gear set, inversely trading angular velocity for torque.
detail: The Gear Ratio is the headline number of any Gear reduction: a 100:1 ratio turns a fast, weak motor into a slow, strong output, multiplying torque while dividing speed (minus losses). It is set by the tooth counts across a Gear Train and determines the Reflected Inertia and resolution a Joint sees at the load. Choosing it balances the available motor torque against required joint speed, and very high ratios from a Worm Gear or Harmonic drive can sacrifice Backdrivability.

plain: Using gears to make a motor turn slower but with much more turning strength.
snappy: Trading motor speed for proportionally higher torque through meshed gears in a drivetrain.
detail: Gear reduction (or gear ratio) lets a small, fast Electric motor drive a slow, high-torque Joint by multiplying torque and dividing speed by the same factor. A high ratio gives strength and holding power but adds Backlash, reduces Backdrivability, and lowers efficiency, which is why a Harmonic drive, Cycloidal drive, or Planetary gear is chosen to suit the task. A low ratio is the basis of Quasi-direct drive, while a ratio of one is Direct drive.

plain: A row of meshing gears working together to pass power along while changing how fast or how strongly things turn.
snappy: A series of meshing gears that transmits power while modifying speed, torque, or direction between input and output.
detail: A Gear Train chains multiple meshes so the overall Gear Ratio is the product of each stage, letting designers reach large reductions a single Spur Gear pair cannot. The arrangement also redirects motion, for example inserting a Bevel Gear to turn a corner or a Helical Gear stage for smoothness, and a compact form is the Planetary Gearbox. Every meshing interface adds friction and Gear Backlash, so the train's design directly shapes the efficiency, accuracy, and Backdrivability of a robot Joint.

plain: A sealed box of gears that turns a motor's fast, weak spin into slower, stronger motion.
snappy: A geared assembly that reduces speed and multiplies torque between a motor and the driven joint.
detail: A gearbox (or reducer) packages the gear train that applies Gear reduction between an Electric motor and the load, setting the actuator's torque, speed, and stiffness. Robotics relies on specialized types such as the Harmonic drive and Cycloidal drive for zero-backlash precision and the Planetary gear for compact, high-torque drives. Key selection factors include Backlash, efficiency, and Backdrivability, all of which shape how the Joint behaves.

plain: Sticking to smooth surfaces using millions of tiny synthetic hairs, copying how a gecko climbs glass.
snappy: Dry adhesion that relies on van der Waals forces from arrays of synthetic micro-fibrillar setae to grip smooth surfaces without glue or suction.
detail: Gecko-inspired adhesion engages and releases by shear loading, leaves no residue, and consumes no power while attached, which suits a Climbing robot working on glass, solar panels, or spacecraft skins, and underlies the Gecko-Inspired Adhesive used in some grippers. It performs best on smooth surfaces, the inverse of Microspine gripping, which needs roughness, so the two are complementary tools in the Climbing locomotion toolkit. It is a flagship example of Bio-inspired robotics and is compared against Electroadhesion, Vortex adhesion, and Magnetic adhesion when selecting an attachment strategy.

plain: A dry, sticky material covered in tiny hairs that grips smooth surfaces using the same weak molecular attraction a gecko's feet use.
snappy: A microstructured dry adhesive that grips surfaces via van der Waals forces, engaging and releasing under controlled shear.
detail: A Gecko-Inspired Adhesive lets a Climbing robot cling to glass or solar panels and a Free-flying space robot grab smooth orbital debris, attaching without suction, magnets, or residue. The fibrillar microstructure activates under shear load and releases when peeled, enabling repeatable grip ideal for a gripper in vacuum where Electroadhesion or a Suction gripper may fail. It is one of several bio-inspired attachment strategies alongside the Microspine gripper and Magnetic adhesion, and is indexed as Gecko-inspired adhesion.

plain: A Chinese company that makes the wheeled robots which carry shelves of goods to warehouse workers.
snappy: A Chinese maker of goods-to-person mobile robots and fulfillment automation systems.
detail: Geek+ builds an Autonomous mobile robot fleet for warehouses, including shelf-lifting Goods-to-person robot units (the Kiva-style model), tote-handling robots, and sorting and Palletizing robots. Its robots navigate via floor markers or natural features and are coordinated by a Warehouse control system layered over the Warehouse management system. A leader in the Chinese fulfillment market, Geek+ competes with Hai Robotics, Exotec, Locus Robotics, and Amazon Robotics in mobile-robot-based picking.

plain: A fingertip sensor that uses a tiny camera to photograph how a soft rubber pad squishes against whatever it touches.
snappy: A vision-based tactile sensor that images the deformation of an elastomer gel surface with an internal camera.
detail: GelSight is a Vision-based tactile sensor in which an internal camera photographs a coated elastomer pad as it presses against an object, recovering high-resolution surface geometry, texture, and local force. As a leading example of Visuotactile sensing, it supports Slip detection, fine Contact-rich manipulation, and Tactile pose estimation for tasks like Peg-in-hole. It inspired more compact designs such as the DIGIT tactile sensor used on a Robotic hand.

plain: One learned robot controller that can handle lots of different tasks, objects, or even different robots, rather than just one job.
snappy: A single learned policy that performs many tasks, objects, or embodiments instead of being specialized to one.
detail: A generalist policy is the goal behind RT-X, OpenVLA, and modern Robot foundation model efforts, trained via Multitask learning on broad Demonstration data such as Open X-Embodiment. Rather than a separate controller per skill, one network handles picking, placing, opening, and pushing, ideally with Zero-shot generalization to new objects. It relies on Representation learning and Transfer learning so shared structure across tasks reduces data needs.

plain: A robot that can handle lots of different jobs rather than being built for just one.
snappy: A robot able to perform a wide range of tasks across varied settings rather than a single fixed function.
detail: A generalist robot aims for breadth: one platform, often a Humanoid robot or Mobile manipulator, that can fold laundry, load a dishwasher, and tend a machine without retooling. This contrasts with the single-purpose Industrial robot arm and is enabled by a Foundation model or Generalist policy trained on diverse data, frequently via Open X-Embodiment. The hard part is robust Generalization to the Open world, where unseen objects and a Long-tail scenario break narrowly trained systems.

plain: A robot's ability to handle new situations it never practiced on, not just the exact ones it was trained for.
snappy: The capacity of a learned model or policy to perform well on inputs and conditions unseen during training.
detail: Generalization measures whether a learned Policy transfers to new objects, scenes, or tasks beyond its training distribution, the key bottleneck for deploying robots in an Unstructured environment. It is pushed by larger and more diverse datasets, a Robot foundation model, and techniques like Domain randomization, and an extreme form is Zero-shot generalization where the system handles tasks with no task-specific data. Poor generalization is a major cause of the Long-tail scenario failures seen in real deployments.

plain: A way of estimating how much better a robot's chosen action was than average, balancing between quick noisy guesses and slow accurate ones.
snappy: An exponentially-weighted estimator of the advantage function that trades bias against variance via a lambda parameter.
detail: Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE) computes the advantage used in Policy gradient updates by blending multi-step Temporal Difference Learning errors with a decay parameter lambda, smoothly interpolating between low-variance/high-bias and high-variance/low-bias estimates. It is a standard component of Proximal policy optimization and Trust Region Policy Optimization, and is what makes large-scale On-policy learning robot training in Isaac Gym stable. Tuning lambda and the discount factor directly affects convergence on legged locomotion and manipulation tasks.

plain: An improved way to line up two 3D scans of the same scene by accounting for how the measured surfaces are locally shaped, not just where individual dots fall.
snappy: An ICP variant that models the local surface covariance of each point so registration behaves like plane-to-plane matching, improving robustness to sampling differences.
detail: Generalized ICP extends classic Iterative closest point by attaching a local covariance, derived from each point's neighborhood normal, so the alignment cost favors matching surfaces rather than exact point pairs. This plane-to-plane formulation makes Point cloud registration far more robust when two LiDAR scans sample the same surface differently. It is a common front-end for LiDAR Odometry pipelines and for registering scans against a prior Map.

plain: A robot learns to act like an expert by repeatedly trying behaviors while a judge tries to tell the robot's behavior apart from the expert's, pushing the robot to fool the judge.
snappy: Imitation learning that trains a policy via a GAN-style discriminator matching the policy's and expert's state-action distributions.
detail: Generative Adversarial Imitation Learning (GAIL) casts Imitation learning as a game: a discriminator learns to distinguish expert demonstrations from policy-generated behavior, and the policy is trained with Reinforcement learning to maximize a reward that is the discriminator's confusion. This matches the occupancy (state-action) distribution of the expert without the compounding errors of plain Behavior cloning and without explicitly recovering a reward as in Inverse reinforcement learning. It is the conceptual parent of Adversarial Motion Priors for legged and humanoid motion.

plain: Using AI to automatically invent practice worlds and tasks for robots to train in, instead of having engineers build each one by hand.
snappy: Using generative models to author training environments, tasks, assets, and scenarios at scale for robot learning.
detail: Generative simulation turns large models into authors of training content: a language model or Diffusion model proposes new objects, layouts, and reward goals, which are instantiated in a Physics engine and Robot simulator like Isaac Sim or MuJoCo. Combined with Massively parallel simulation and Domain randomization, it widens the data distribution to improve Generalization and ease Sim-to-real transfer. It is closely tied to Curriculum learning, since generated tasks can be ordered from easy to hard, and to producing Synthetic data for an Embodied AI Foundation model.

plain: A fast physics simulator that runs on graphics cards and can also tell you how to tweak a robot's actions to improve them.
snappy: A GPU-accelerated, differentiable physics platform built for very fast and large-scale robotics and embodied-AI simulation.
detail: Genesis runs rigid, soft, and fluid Physics engine dynamics on the GPU at high throughput and exposes gradients for Differentiable Simulation, so it can drive both Massively parallel reinforcement learning and gradient-based Trajectory optimization. It competes with platforms like MuJoCo XLA, Brax, and Isaac Lab for training Manipulation and Legged locomotion policies, and emphasizes Generative simulation of varied scenes to attack the Sim-to-real transfer problem. Its speed targets the data-hungry training loops behind modern embodied-AI and Robot foundation model work.

plain: A fast physics simulator that can model rigid robots, soft materials, cloth, and fluids together to train and test robots.
snappy: A GPU-accelerated generative physics platform unifying rigid-body, soft-body, fluid, and other material simulation for robotics.
detail: Genesis is a physics platform that unifies multiple solvers, rigid bodies, deformables, cloth, and fluids, under one fast GPU-accelerated engine, aiming at both robot learning and generative scene creation. It supports GPU-Accelerated Simulation for Massively parallel reinforcement learning and Sim-to-real workflows, positioning it against Isaac Gym, MuJoCo Playground, and engines like MuJoCo and PhysX. Its broad material support targets Soft-body simulation and Deformable object manipulation that rigid-only engines handle poorly, with an emphasis on Generative simulation of training scenes.

plain: A mechanism that turns a steady spin into a stop-start motion, advancing one step and then pausing, over and over.
snappy: An intermittent indexing mechanism that converts continuous input rotation into precise stepped output rotation with dwell.
detail: A Geneva Mechanism (Maltese cross) advances a turntable one fixed station per drive revolution and then dwells, ideal for an Indexing table that must pause for an operation before stepping to the next position. The dwell phase locks the output rigidly, giving repeatable positioning without feedback, a purely mechanical alternative to a servo-driven index. It contrasts with a Cam Mechanism by producing discrete stepped rotation rather than a continuous follower profile, and underpins many fixed-automation Assembly stations.

plain: An AI system from DeepMind that builds an interactive, playable virtual world from a single picture or instruction, giving a robot or agent a place to practice moving and acting.
snappy: A DeepMind interactive World model that generates controllable, playable environments from images or text for training embodied agents.
detail: Genie is a generative World model that turns an image or prompt into a frame-by-frame environment whose dynamics respond to control inputs, learning physics and affordances without explicit labels. For robotics this gives an Embodied agent a place to rehearse skills, much as it would inside Isaac Lab or any Physics engine, complementing Domain randomization and Sim-to-real transfer pipelines. Genie 3 extends this toward longer, more consistent rollouts, aligning it with World Model Pretraining and Generative simulation approaches for embodied learning.

plain: Limiting where a robot fleet can go to a specific mapped area that has been approved.
snappy: Restricting an autonomous fleet's operation to a pre-mapped, validated geographic zone using Geofencing.
detail: A Geofenced Deployment uses Geofencing to keep a Robotaxi or Sidewalk delivery robot fleet inside an area that has been mapped with an HD map and validated within the vehicle's Operational design domain. Confining operations bounds the Long-tail scenario problem and is the standard way to launch Driver-Out Operations safely before broadening via Operational Design Domain Expansion. The size of the service area is an economic lever: a larger zone spreads Depot Operations and Charging Infrastructure costs over more revenue, lowering Cost per Mile. Crossing a geofence boundary typically triggers a Minimal Risk Maneuver or hands control to a Teleoperation Center.

plain: Limiting where a robot or self-driving vehicle is allowed to operate by drawing an invisible boundary on the map.
snappy: Constraining autonomous operation to a predefined geographic area using map boundaries and positioning.
detail: Geofencing defines the spatial part of an operational design domain, so a robotaxi or autonomous shuttle only drives in mapped, validated zones, and a delivery robot or drone stays inside approved airspace or sidewalks. It pairs with GNSS positioning and an HD map to enforce limits, and crossing the geofence can trigger a minimal risk condition or return-to-home. Waymo's robotaxi service and many drone delivery deployments rely on tightly geofenced operation.

plain: A precise math-based way to steer a drone through sharp aerobatic moves by describing its tilt on the curved space of all possible orientations instead of with simple angles.
snappy: A quadrotor controller formulated directly on the rotation group SO(3) and SE(3), avoiding angle singularities so it tracks aggressive trajectories.
detail: Geometric tracking control defines attitude error directly on the Special orthogonal group SO(3) and the Special Euclidean group SE(3) rather than with Euler angles, eliminating the Gimbal lock singularity and letting a Quadcopter follow loops and flips. It is a form of Nonlinear control closely tied to Differential flatness and Minimum-snap trajectory generation, since the planner supplies position and yaw references the controller tracks almost globally. The approach underpins much of the aggressive Autonomous drone racing and Learned quadrotor control literature.

plain: Technology that lets a robot understand hand or body movements as commands, so a person can point, wave, or signal instead of pressing buttons.
snappy: Interpreting a human's hand or body movements as discrete commands or continuous control inputs for a robot.
detail: Gesture recognition uses Computer vision and often Human pose estimation to classify movements like a pointing hand or a raised palm into robot commands, forming a natural channel for Human-robot interaction on a factory floor or in the home. A Cobot or Collaborative robot may pause when an operator raises a flat hand, or a Service robot may follow a beckoning gesture, replacing a Teach pendant or Human-machine interface for quick on-the-fly direction. Robust systems must reject ambiguous motions and handle occlusion, which is why depth data from a Depth camera or Stereo camera is commonly fused in to improve reliability over plain RGB input.

plain: A company that makes tough four-legged robots used by militaries for patrols and security.
snappy: Maker of rugged quadruped robots like Vision 60 for defense and security missions.
detail: Ghost Robotics builds the Vision 60, a Quadruped robot designed for harsh outdoor Legged locomotion in defense, perimeter security, and inspection roles. Its limbs use a Quasi-direct drive actuator approach for robust, low-maintenance Quadrupedal locomotion over rubble and stairs, and the platform can carry sensor or other mission payloads. It competes in the rugged-legged space with the Unmanned ground vehicle offerings of Boston Dynamics and similar firms.

plain: A fake blip on radar that looks like a real object but is not, caused by signals bouncing in odd ways.
snappy: A spurious radar detection, often from multipath or interference, that appears as a nonexistent object.
detail: Ghost targets come from Multipath Error, reflections off guardrails or large vehicles, or radar interference, and the Radar processing chain uses techniques like Constant False Alarm Rate thresholding to suppress them. They are the radar counterpart of the camera/lidar Phantom obstacle and, if not filtered, can cause Phantom braking or corrupt Multi-object tracking. In Defense & Security, ghost targets may also be induced deliberately as a form of Sensor spoofing.

plain: A motorized mount that keeps a camera pointed steadily even while the drone tilts and shakes.
snappy: A motorized multi-axis mount that stabilizes a camera or payload against vehicle motion.
detail: A drone Gimbal uses an Inertial measurement unit and brushless motors to counter-rotate on two or three axes, so footage stays level regardless of how the Multirotor pitches and rolls, which is essential for Aerial cinematography. It is a common Payload on camera drones and can also carry thermal or zoom sensors for inspection. The same mechanical concept and the failure mode called Gimbal lock appear in spacecraft and Attitude and heading reference system designs.

plain: A glitch where a rotation system suddenly loses the ability to turn in one direction because two of its axes line up.
snappy: Loss of one rotational degree of freedom when two axes of an Euler-angle system align.
detail: Gimbal lock strikes Euler angles when the middle rotation reaches 90 degrees and the first and third axes coincide, leaving you unable to rotate cleanly about one direction. It plagued real mechanical gimbals on the Apollo guidance platform and still bites naive attitude code on drones and humanoids. The standard fix is to represent orientation with a Quaternion or a Rotation matrix, both of which live smoothly on the Special orthogonal group SO(3).

plain: A motor designed to hold and aim something steadily and smoothly at low speed, like keeping a camera level.
snappy: A high-pole-count, low-KV brushless motor optimized for smooth low-speed, high-resolution position holding.
detail: A Gimbal Motor is a Brushless DC motor wound with many poles and a low KV rating so it produces high torque at very low speed with minimal Cogging torque, ideal for smoothly aiming a camera Gimbal or sensor turret. The same low-speed, high-torque character makes gimbal motors a popular building block for a Quasi-direct drive joint, where T-Motor antigravity types are driven by an ODrive or Moteus Controller under Field-oriented control. Their smoothness comes at the cost of a low top speed.

plain: A network of orbiting satellites that lets a receiver work out exactly where it is on Earth, plus the precise time.
snappy: A constellation-based positioning system (GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, BeiDou) providing a receiver's global position, velocity, and time.
detail: GNSS is the umbrella term covering GPS and other satellite constellations that an outdoor robot uses for absolute Localization across Mobility and Agriculture. Raw GNSS is accurate to a few meters, so Real-time kinematic positioning adds carrier-phase corrections for centimeter precision, and Sensor fusion blends it with an Inertial measurement unit and Wheel odometry. Where signals are blocked, robots fall back to GPS-denied navigation.

plain: The part of a robot's navigation that plots the whole route to the destination using its map, before it starts moving.
snappy: A planner that computes a complete route to the goal over the known map, abstracting away short-term reactions.
detail: The Global planner consumes a Cost map built from the robot's Map and searches it end to end, typically with A* search, Dijkstra's algorithm, or Hybrid A*, to produce a route to the goal. It works in tandem with a Local planner, which tracks that global route while handling immediate Obstacle avoidance and the robot's kinematics. In the Nav2 stack the global planner replans when the path becomes blocked, a process known as Replanning, and feeds a Waypoint sequence to the controller.

plain: A camera setting that snaps every pixel of the image at the exact same instant, so fast-moving things are not smeared or skewed.
