snappy: A camera readout mode that exposes all pixels simultaneously, avoiding motion-induced distortion.
detail: A global shutter exposes the entire sensor at once, freezing motion cleanly so straight edges stay straight even when the robot or scene moves fast. This contrasts with a Rolling shutter, which scans rows in sequence and skews fast subjects. Global shutter is preferred for Visual odometry, Visual SLAM, Fiducial marker tracking, and Visual servoing where geometric accuracy matters more than cost.

plain: A common file format for sharing 3D models and scenes between programs, like a JPEG but for 3D objects.
snappy: An open, runtime-efficient transmission format (with binary variant GLB) for 3D scenes, meshes, materials, and animations.
detail: glTF packages a Mesh with materials, textures, and skeletal animation in a compact, ready-to-render form, making it a common way to bring visual robot and environment assets into simulators and viewers like Foxglove or web tools served via rosbridge. In robotics pipelines it complements engineering formats such as URDF and the scene-composition framework OpenUSD, often supplying the visual geometry while collision geometry is built via Convex Decomposition. Its GLB binary variant is favored for streaming assets into Photorealistic rendering and AR interfaces.

plain: A classic, widely used program that turns a robot's spinning laser scans into a flat floor-plan map as it explores.
snappy: A Rao-Blackwellized particle-filter SLAM package that builds 2D occupancy grid maps from laser range data and odometry.
detail: GMapping maintains a set of map hypotheses with a Particle filter, where each particle carries its own trajectory and Occupancy grid, and uses laser Scan Matching to keep the proposal distribution sharp so few particles are needed. Distributed as the slam_gmapping package in ROS, it was for years the default 2D SLAM for differential-drive Logistics & Warehouse and indoor Mobility robots feeding the Navigation stack. Its filtering approach contrasts with graph-optimization mappers like Cartographer and GraphSLAM, and unlike them it does not perform explicit global Loop closure.

plain: Flooding the airwaves with noise so a drone can no longer hear the faint satellite signals it needs to know where it is.
snappy: Overpowering satellite frequencies with RF noise to deny a UAV any usable positioning fix.
detail: GNSS jamming radiates broadband or tone interference on the satellite bands so the receiver loses lock on the Global Navigation Satellite System, leaving the drone without GPS; unlike GNSS spoofing it simply denies service rather than faking a position. It is a core Counter-UAS technique and forces resilient autonomy onto GPS-denied navigation using the inertial measurement unit, an Optical flow sensor, and Visual-inertial odometry. Sustained jamming can also disrupt the Telemetry radio and Radio control link if they share nearby spectrum.

plain: An attack that tricks a drone with fake satellite signals so it believes it is somewhere it is not.
snappy: Broadcasting counterfeit satellite signals to feed a UAV a false, attacker-controlled position estimate.
detail: GNSS spoofing transmits forged signals stronger than the genuine Global Navigation Satellite System constellation so a drone's receiver locks onto them, corrupting its position and potentially commanding it off course or down. It is a form of Sensor spoofing central to Counter-UAS work and is harder to detect than GNSS jamming because the receiver still reports a healthy fix. Defenses include cross-checking against the inertial measurement unit, Optical flow sensor velocity, and Visual-inertial odometry, and falling back to GPS-denied navigation when an anomaly is flagged.

full: Global Navigation Satellite System / Inertial Navigation System
plain: Combining satellite positioning with motion sensors so a vehicle always knows where it is, even when the satellite signal briefly drops out.
snappy: Fusing satellite positioning with inertial sensors so localization stays continuous and accurate through GNSS dropouts.
detail: GNSS/INS Integration blends a Global Navigation Satellite System fix with an Inertial Navigation System using an Extended Kalman filter, bridging outages from tunnels or urban canyons by Dead reckoning on the Inertial measurement unit. Tightly coupled designs fuse raw satellite observables for robustness against GNSS spoofing and Multipath Error, often combined with RTK GNSS for centimeter accuracy. It provides the global-frame backbone of Localization in a Self-driving stack, complementing LiDAR-based Lidar Odometry and Mapping.

plain: A robot controller you can steer by handing it a target, so the same controller can chase many different goals.
snappy: A policy that takes a goal as input and produces behavior to reach that specified goal.
detail: Instead of one Policy per task, a goal-conditioned policy accepts a goal, often a target Pose, image, or position, and acts to achieve it, so a single Manipulation network can place objects at many requested locations. Goals can be specified by an image, a coordinate, or, in Language-conditioned manipulation, a sentence. It is a natural way to build a Generalist policy and pairs well with Hierarchical reinforcement learning, where a high level emits goals for a low-level controller.

plain: Once you turn a measurement into the goal everyone chases, people and machines start gaming it, and it stops being a good measurement.
snappy: The principle that when a proxy metric becomes an optimization target, it ceases to track the underlying objective it was meant to measure.
detail: In robot learning, Goodhart's law underlies Reward hacking: a Reinforcement learning agent maximizes its Reward function literally and finds a degenerate Policy that scores high while ignoring the designer's intent, such as a locomotion agent exploiting a Physics engine glitch instead of walking. It motivates careful Reward shaping, held-out Verification and validation, Preference learning to capture intent, and Value alignment more broadly. The same trap appears when a single throughput KPI on a Manufacturing line distorts real productivity.

plain: A warehouse setup where robots fetch the shelves or bins and bring them to a worker who stays in one spot, instead of the worker walking the aisles.
snappy: A fulfillment model in which mobile robots bring inventory to stationary human pickers, eliminating walking.
detail: Goods-to-person (G2P) flips traditional order picking: rather than a worker traversing miles of aisles, an Autonomous mobile robot or shelf-lifting drive unit ferries the relevant inventory pod to a fixed pick station, dramatically raising Pick rate. Amazon Robotics popularized the model and it is the backbone of a Micro-fulfillment center. G2P depends heavily on Fleet management to route hundreds of robots without gridlock and is judged on overall Throughput.

plain: A warehouse robot that picks up an entire shelf of products and carries it to a worker standing at a station, instead of the worker walking to the shelf.
snappy: A warehouse AMR that lifts and ferries movable shelving racks to stationary pick stations, implementing the goods-to-person fulfillment model.
detail: A goods-to-person robot is the hardware behind the Goods-to-person fulfillment model popularized by Amazon Robotics: a low Autonomous mobile robot slides under a portable rack, lifts it, and drives it to a human picker. A central Fleet management system coordinates hundreds of units using Multi-agent path finding to prevent gridlock on the grid floor, optimizing Pick rate and Slotting Optimization. It contrasts with the Pallet jack robot and Autonomous forklift, which move pallets rather than shelving, and depends on dense AprilTag or floor-marker Localization.

plain: A tiny add-on chip that runs compact AI models very fast and efficiently right on a small device.
snappy: A compact, low-power accelerator running quantized neural networks efficiently at the edge for on-robot inference.
detail: The Google Coral Edge TPU is a small ASIC that executes 8-bit integer neural networks far more efficiently than a CPU, requiring Model Quantization to fit its fixed-point datapath. As Edge computing hardware it gives a low-cost robot real-time Object detection or Semantic segmentation without a full GPU System-on-Module, sipping power within a tight Power budget. It is popular for an Agriculture or Service robot doing on-device Computer vision, and it embodies Hardware Accelerator Offload by moving the neural workload off the host CPU, much like a Hailo Accelerator or Vision Processing Unit.

plain: Configurable pins on a robot's controller board that can either read a simple on/off signal or switch something on and off.
snappy: Software-controllable digital pins that can be set as inputs to read logic levels or as outputs to drive loads.
detail: GPIO pins are configured in firmware as inputs to read a Limit Switch, a Bumper Sensor, or a button, or as outputs to drive an LED, a relay, or a motor-driver enable line on a robot. On boards like NVIDIA Jetson or a Microcontroller they also multiplex into peripheral functions, exposing an I2C Bus, Serial Peripheral Interface, UART, or Pulse-width modulation channel on the same physical header. They are the lowest-level electrical hooks an Embedded system uses to sense and actuate the physical world.

plain: A method that plans a robot arm's smooth path by treating the whole motion as a statistical best-guess curve and refining it to avoid collisions.
snappy: A trajectory optimizer that casts continuous-time motion planning as Gaussian-process inference solved on a factor graph.
detail: GPMP2 represents a continuous-time trajectory as a sample from a Gaussian process and formulates planning as probabilistic inference on a Factor graph, where smoothness and collision-avoidance costs become factors solved efficiently with GTSAM. Because the Gaussian process interpolates between sparse support states, it produces smooth motion for a Manipulator while keeping the optimization sparse and fast. It belongs to the family of optimization-based planners alongside CHOMP, STOMP, and TrajOpt, and like them it is typically warm-started and refined rather than searched, complementing sampling planners in OMPL.

plain: The familiar satellite service that tells a device where it is on Earth, used in phones, cars, and outdoor robots.
snappy: The U.S. satellite positioning constellation; the most widely known instance of a GNSS providing global position and time.
detail: GPS is the original and most recognized Global Navigation Satellite System, giving an outdoor robot a few-meters absolute fix for Localization in Mobility and Agriculture. For precision work it is augmented to centimeter accuracy by Real-time kinematic positioning, and indoors or in urban canyons robots switch to GPS-denied navigation or Ultra-wideband. It is routinely fused with an Inertial measurement unit and Wheel odometry for smooth State estimation.

plain: Finding your way through the air when satellite signals are blocked, jammed, or unavailable, by relying on cameras and motion sensors instead.
snappy: Estimating a drone's position and motion without satellite signals, using onboard vision and inertial sensing rather than GPS.
detail: When a drone flies indoors, in urban canyons, or in contested areas where signals are jammed, it cannot rely on GPS or GNSS positioning, so it falls back on Visual-inertial odometry, Visual SLAM, and its Inertial measurement unit to track where it is. This is essential for Defense & Security missions and for any Beyond visual line of sight flight near tall structures. Techniques like Visual odometry and Loop closure keep drift bounded over long flights.

plain: A small plug-in board carrying a powerful graphics-capable computer chip, so a robot maker can drop AI computing into a product easily.
snappy: A compact pluggable module integrating a GPU/SoC and memory for AI compute, designed to slot into a robot's carrier board.
detail: A GPU System-on-Module (GPU SoM) puts the processor, GPU, and memory on one connectorized board that mates with a custom carrier supplying power, the Bus Voltage rails, and I/O, letting a robotics team upgrade compute without redesigning the whole system. The NVIDIA Jetson family is the canonical example, providing the Onboard compute that runs Perception, SLAM, and a Vision-language-action model on a Humanoid robot or Autonomous mobile robot. A Power Management Integrated Circuit on the carrier feeds it, and Thermal management plus Heterogeneous Compute partitioning keep its accelerators fed during real-time control.

plain: Running thousands of copies of a robot physics world at the same time on a graphics card so an AI can gather huge amounts of practice quickly.
snappy: Running many physics environments in parallel on GPU hardware to massively increase the data throughput of robot policy training.
detail: GPU-Accelerated Simulation runs thousands of physics environments concurrently on the GPU, keeping data on-device to feed Massively parallel reinforcement learning without CPU bottlenecks. It is the enabling technology behind fast Sim-to-real transfer pipelines, usually combined with Domain randomization and Automatic Domain Randomization to bridge the Reality gap. Platforms such as Isaac Gym, MuJoCo Playground (via MuJoCo XLA), NVIDIA Warp, and the Genesis Simulator implement it, turning weeks of Legged locomotion training into hours.

plain: A neural network that looks at a depth picture and scores how likely each candidate grip is to hold the object.
snappy: A convolutional network that scores candidate grasps from depth images, trained on Dex-Net labels.
detail: A GQ-CNN is a Convolutional neural network that takes an aligned depth patch around a candidate Grasp pose and outputs a probability that the grip will succeed, the predictive core of the Dex-Net system. Candidates are sampled via Antipodal sampling from a Depth camera image and ranked, with the top grasp executed by a Parallel-jaw gripper or Suction gripper. It is a foundational example of Learned grasping for reliable Bin picking.

plain: An AI vision network that looks at a depth photo of objects and instantly draws where a two-finger gripper should grab, marking the best spot for every pixel.
snappy: A fully-convolutional network that predicts pixelwise antipodal grasp quality, angle, and width maps from a depth image in real time.
detail: GR-ConvNet (Generative Residual Convolutional Network) regresses dense Antipodal grasp maps, outputting grasp quality, angle, and gripper width at every pixel of a Depth camera image for fast Grasp Pose Detection. Its single-shot inference suits closed-loop Visual servoing and high-Throughput Bin picking with a Parallel-jaw gripper, contrasting with sampling-and-ranking approaches like GQ-CNN and Dex-Net. The original network (Kumra et al., 2019) was trained and evaluated on the Cornell and Jacquard planar grasping datasets, placing it in the learned-grasping line of Grasp Detection research.

plain: NVIDIA's platform and AI model designed to give humanoid robots a shared, general set of skills they can learn from human videos and simulation.
snappy: NVIDIA's open foundation-model platform and architecture for humanoid robots, trained on human video, teleoperation, and synthetic simulation data.
detail: GR00T (NVIDIA, 2024) is a Foundation Model for Robotics aimed at Humanoid robot control, learning a Generalist policy from a blend of internet human video, Teleoperation demonstrations, and synthetic data generated in NVIDIA Isaac and Isaac Sim. The released NVIDIA Isaac GR00T N1 model is a Vision-language-action model with a slow reasoning path and a fast Diffusion policy-style action path, and it is trained with heavy use of GPU-Accelerated Simulation for Sim-to-real transfer. It competes in the same space as Pi-Zero and Helix and is meant to be fine-tuned onto specific humanoid hardware.

plain: Designing a system so that when part of it breaks, it keeps doing a reduced version of its job instead of failing completely.
snappy: A fault-tolerance property where partial failures cause a controlled drop to reduced functionality rather than total collapse.
detail: Graceful degradation is a cornerstone of Fault tolerance: if one motor on an Octocopter fails, the Flight controller redistributes thrust to keep flying, and a Fail-operational autonomous vehicle reaches a Minimal risk condition instead of stopping dead in traffic. It complements a Fail-safe design and Redundancy, and is often the difference between a controlled stop and a crash. Engineers verify it through Verification and validation and tie it to a Safety case and a Fallback strategy.

plain: Finding a route by treating the world as a network of connected points and systematically working outward until you reach the destination.
snappy: Finding a path over a graph of nodes and edges that represents discretized configuration or workspace, expanding nodes by cost until the goal is reached.
detail: Graph search is the discrete foundation of most Path planning: the world is reduced to nodes (grid cells, a Probabilistic roadmap, or a State lattice) and weighted edges, then algorithms expand nodes by accumulated cost. Dijkstra's algorithm explores uniformly while A* search adds a Heuristic function to expand toward the goal; D* algorithm repairs the search during Replanning. It operates over a Cost map derived from an Occupancy grid map, and contrasts with continuous Sampling-based planning. Though shared with AI, here edges encode drivable Free space and traversal cost.

plain: A chip with thousands of small cores that crunch many calculations at once, great for robot vision and AI.
snappy: A massively parallel processor that accelerates perception, neural inference, and simulation on robots.
detail: A Graphics processing unit (GPU) excels at the parallel math behind Computer vision, Neural network inference, and Convolutional neural network workloads, making it central to a robot's Onboard compute. On a Humanoid robot the GPU runs perception and a Vision-language-action model in real time, while in the lab GPUs power Massively parallel simulation in Isaac Sim for Reinforcement learning. The NVIDIA Jetson packages a mobile GPU with a CPU on a System on a chip; its throughput is often quoted in TOPS and bounded by the Power budget.

plain: A mapping approach that records the robot's path as a web of connected positions and constraints, then adjusts the whole web at once to make the map consistent.
snappy: A SLAM formulation that represents the problem as a pose-constraint graph and solves it by nonlinear least-squares optimization.
detail: GraphSLAM models each robot Pose as a node and each odometry or sensor measurement as an edge constraint, forming a Pose graph (a special Factor graph) that is solved as a single sparse nonlinear least-squares problem. This back-end optimization, distinct from filtering approaches like the Extended Kalman filter or a Particle filter, is what makes a Loop Closure Constraint propagate corrections across the entire trajectory. It is the conceptual basis of modern SLAM and Visual SLAM systems and is implemented atop solvers such as Ceres Solver and GTSAM; Cartographer and RTAB-Map are practical graph-based realizations.

plain: The part of an object a robot learns it can usefully grab, like the handle of a mug rather than its rim.
snappy: A learned region of an object that indicates where and how it affords being grasped.
detail: A grasp affordance is a specialization of the broader Affordance concept: instead of all actions an object permits, it marks the surface regions that support a stable grip, such as a tool's shaft or a cup's handle. Predicting it is a form of Affordance detection often run on a Point cloud or image, and it constrains downstream Grasp planning and Grasp Pose Detection so the robot grasps in a task-meaningful way. It supports Language-conditioned manipulation by linking what to do with where to hold.

plain: Working out where and how a robot hand should grab an object just from looking at it with a camera or depth sensor.
snappy: Predicting stable gripper poses on objects directly from visual or depth input.
detail: Grasp Detection (grasp pose detection, GPD) maps an image or Point cloud to candidate gripper Pose estimation results ranked by predicted stability, bypassing full Object recognition. Networks like GQ-CNN, GR-ConvNet, and Contact-GraspNet learn this from datasets such as Dex-Net and GraspNet-1Billion. Manufacturing and Logistics & Warehouse robots use it for Bin picking and Pick and place, feeding the chosen grasp into Grasp planning and Force closure checks; 6-DoF grasp detection extends it from top-down picks to arbitrary approach directions.

plain: A table of numbers that converts the pushes from each finger into the overall force and twist felt by the object.
snappy: A linear map relating the forces at all contact points to the net wrench applied to the grasped object.
detail: The Grasp matrix (or grasp map) is a linear operator that sums the individual Contact point forces, each constrained by its Contact model and Friction cone, into the total Wrench acting on the object. Its rank and span determine whether a grasp achieves Force closure, and it underpins most analytical Grasp quality metric computations. It is the central algebraic object of Grasp planning and Manipulation analysis, paired with the contact Jacobian to relate finger motions to object motion.

plain: Working out the best place and angle for a robot to grab an object so it won't slip.
snappy: Computing where and how to place a gripper's fingers to achieve a stable grasp of an object.
detail: Grasp planning, also called grasp synthesis, takes a model or sensor view of an object and outputs a candidate Grasp pose plus finger placements, scored by a Grasp quality metric for stability under a Friction cone and Force closure. Classical methods reason geometrically over Contact points using the Grasp matrix, while modern systems use Learned grasping from a Point cloud or Depth camera, sometimes a Diffusion policy. It runs upstream of nearly every Bin picking and Pick and place pipeline and is often executed through MoveIt.

plain: Exactly where and at what angle a robot's gripper should be to grab a particular object.
snappy: The full 6-DoF position and orientation of the gripper relative to the object it will grasp.
detail: A Grasp pose specifies the gripper's 6-DoF Pose, three translations and three rotations, with respect to the target object, defining the precise approach and finger placement. It is the principal output of Grasp planning and the input that Inverse kinematics and Motion planning convert into joint angles the Manipulator can reach. In Bin picking, a perception system proposes many candidate grasp poses from a Point cloud, ranks them by a Grasp quality metric, and sends the best reachable one to the Robot controller.

plain: Software that looks at an object and figures out exactly how a robot gripper should be positioned and oriented to pick it up successfully.
snappy: Predicting feasible 6-DoF gripper poses from sensed object geometry, typically point clouds or depth images.
detail: Grasp Pose Detection (GPD) predicts candidate 6-DoF grasp detection poses, gripper position and orientation, directly from a Point cloud or depth image, scoring each for stability before execution. It underpins Bin picking and warehouse Pick and place, and relates to learned methods like Dex-Net, GQ-CNN, and Contact-GraspNet that estimate a Grasp quality metric. The detected Grasp pose feeds Motion planning and Visual servoing to align the End-effector, making GPD a core perception building block for Manipulation in Logistics & Warehouse settings.

plain: A number that estimates how good a planned grip is, so the robot can choose the most reliable one.
snappy: A numeric score predicting how stable or robust a candidate grasp will be before it is attempted.
detail: A Grasp quality metric scores a candidate Grasp pose so a planner can rank many options and pick the most reliable, capturing how well finger forces resist disturbance. Classical metrics derive from the Grasp matrix and Friction cone, measuring the largest external Wrench the grasp can resist while maintaining Force closure. Learning-based pipelines instead train a network to predict grasp success directly from images or a Point cloud, a key component of Learned grasping for Bin picking.

plain: The full set of pushes, pulls, and twists a robot's grip can withstand without the object slipping or being knocked loose.
snappy: The set of all wrenches a grasp can resist through its contacts, whose geometry yields grasp quality metrics.
detail: Built from the forces and torques each Contact point can apply within its Friction cone, the grasp wrench space is the set of every Wrench the grip can counter. Its convex hull is the basis for a Grasp quality metric: if the origin lies inside the hull the grasp achieves Force closure, and the larger the enclosed region, the more disturbance it tolerates. Grasp planning systems compute it for candidate grips on a Robotic hand or Parallel-jaw gripper before committing to an approach.

plain: Getting a firm hold of an object so a robot can pick it up without dropping it.
snappy: Securing an object by closing a gripper or hand around it so it can be held and moved.
detail: Grasping is the act of establishing a stable hold on an object, the entry point to almost all Manipulation. A robot first identifies a viable Grasp pose via Grasp planning, then closes a Gripper or Robotic hand to form Contact points that ideally achieve Force closure. In warehouse Bin picking, a Suction gripper or Parallel-jaw gripper grasps items off a conveyor, and increasingly the grasp itself comes from Learned grasping trained on large datasets.

plain: A classic computer simulator that lets researchers test how a robot hand would grip a virtual object and scores how good each grip is.
snappy: An early grasp-planning simulator that models articulated hands contacting objects and computes analytic grasp quality metrics.
detail: GraspIt! is a long-standing Grasp planning simulator that imports hand and object models, simulates finger contacts, and evaluates analytic Grasp quality metric measures such as the Ferrari-Canny metric and Force closure. Researchers use it to compare grippers from a simple Parallel-jaw gripper to a multi-finger Robotic hand like the Shadow Hand, and to seed Antipodal sampling or Superquadric grasping pipelines. It predates learned approaches like Dex-Net and GQ-CNN but remains a reference for analytic Grasp Detection.

plain: A huge labeled dataset of real cluttered scenes showing where and how a robot hand could grab each object from any angle.
snappy: A large-scale benchmark of dense 6-DoF grasp annotations on real cluttered RGB-D scenes.
detail: GraspNet-1Billion provides over a billion grasp labels across thousands of real Point cloud scenes captured with a Depth camera, supplying dense 6-DoF grasp detection ground truth for training and ranking. Each annotated Grasp pose carries a quality score so models learn to favor stable grips in clutter, the way Contact-GraspNet does. It has become a standard benchmark for Learned grasping and Grasp Pose Detection on the YCB object set and similar everyday items.

plain: Feeding a robot arm just enough motor force to cancel its own weight, so it hangs weightlessly in the air.
snappy: Feedforward torque that cancels gravitational load so joints float at rest.
detail: Gravity Compensation computes the gravity term of the manipulator's Equations of motion from Inverse dynamics and the link masses, then applies it as Feedforward torque so the arm neither sags nor needs a holding current. It is what lets a clinician hand-guide a Surgical robot or a teacher perform Kinesthetic teaching on a Humanoid robot with almost no effort, and it underpins Impedance control and Torque Control Mode. Accurate compensation depends on good Inertial Parameter Identification of the links.

plain: Building a brand-new facility designed from the start around robots.
snappy: Constructing a new, purpose-built facility whose layout, power, and workflows are designed around automation from day one.
detail: A Greenfield Deployment lets designers optimize aisle widths, Charging Infrastructure, and a dense Automated storage and retrieval system or Shuttle system layout for maximum Throughput per Square Foot, unconstrained by legacy equipment. It usually achieves higher Automation Rate and lower long-run Cost per Pick than a Brownfield Deployment, at the cost of much larger upfront Capital Expenditure and longer Commissioning. Purpose-built fulfillment centers built around Goods-to-person robots are the canonical example. Greenfield economics depend on sustained demand to keep Utilization Rate high enough to repay the build.

plain: A company that supplies warehouse robots and the software that tells them where to go.
snappy: Warehouse-automation vendor of Ranger fulfillment robots plus AI-driven orchestration software.
detail: GreyOrange supplies Ranger goods-to-person robots together with orchestration software that decides which order to pick next and routes each autonomous mobile robot, treating fulfillment as a multi-agent path finding and task allocation problem. The software layer sits between the warehouse management system and the robot fleet, optimizing throughput. It competes with Locus Robotics and similar fulfillment-automation vendors.

plain: Controlling exactly how hard a robot grips so it neither drops nor smashes what it's holding.
snappy: Regulating the force a gripper's fingers apply to hold an object securely without crushing or dropping it.
detail: Grip force control adjusts finger force in real time to keep a held object stable, applying just enough force to stay inside the Friction cone without damaging fragile items. It draws on Force control and feedback from a Force/torque sensor or Tactile sensor, and reacts to Slip detection by increasing grip when sliding begins. It is essential whenever a Gripper or Robotic hand handles variable or delicate objects, and pairs naturally with a Precision grasp and Compliance control.

plain: The hand-like tool at the end of a robot arm that opens and closes to hold things.
snappy: An end effector that grasps and holds objects between movable fingers, jaws, or via suction.
detail: A Gripper is the most common type of End-effector, attached to the Tool flange of a Manipulator to perform Grasping. Designs range from the simple Parallel-jaw gripper and Suction gripper used in Logistics & Warehouse to the Soft gripper and Underactuated gripper that conform to irregular shapes. Selecting and switching grippers (sometimes via a Tool changer) is central to End-of-arm tooling, and grip strength is regulated by Grip force control.

plain: A precisely surveyed marker placed on the ground so that a map made from drone photos lines up correctly with real-world locations.
snappy: A surveyed reference marker visible in aerial imagery, used to georeference and improve the accuracy of photogrammetric maps.
detail: Ground control points are physical targets whose true coordinates are measured with survey-grade equipment, then matched to their appearance in overlapping drone photos during Aerial photogrammetry. Tying the imagery to these known points anchors the resulting Orthomosaic and Digital surface model to real-world coordinates, correcting drift and scale error. They remain important even on missions flown with RTK GNSS, where a few checkpoints verify that the Ground sample distance and positional accuracy meet survey tolerances.

plain: The computer or tablet on the ground that an operator uses to plan a drone's flight and watch what it is doing.
snappy: The operator interface for planning, monitoring, and commanding a drone, part of the full Unmanned aircraft system.
detail: A GCS such as QGroundControl or Mission Planner displays live telemetry, lets the operator draw a Waypoint navigation route, and sends commands like Loiter or Return-to-home over MAVLink to a PX4 or ArduPilot Autopilot. It is the human-facing half of the Unmanned aircraft system and the place where Geofencing limits and failsafes are configured before flight. For Beyond visual line of sight operations the GCS may also display Detect and avoid traffic and Remote ID feeds.

plain: The extra lift and easier hovering a drone gets when it flies very close to the ground.
snappy: The increase in lift and reduction in induced power that occurs when rotors operate within roughly one rotor diameter of a surface.
detail: Ground effect (in-ground effect, IGE) arises when the cushion of air beneath the rotors is constrained by a nearby surface, increasing lift and reducing the power a Multirotor drone needs to hover close to the ground. It complicates Precision landing and Perching because thrust changes nonlinearly near touchdown, so controllers must compensate during the final descent. It is the benign counterpart to the hazardous Vortex ring state and interacts with rotor Downwash.

plain: The push the ground gives back to a foot whenever the foot presses down on it.
snappy: The contact force the ground exerts on a foot during stance, equal and opposite to the force the foot applies.
detail: Ground reaction force (GRF) is what actually supports, propels, and steers a walking robot, and its point of application is the Center of pressure. Legged controllers regulate GRF through the Stance phase, often via Force control or whole-body optimization, to keep the Zero moment point inside the foot and preserve balance. It is measured with a Force/torque sensor or load cells in the feet and is central to Dynamic stability.

plain: A control method for legged robots that decides how hard each foot should push on the ground to make the whole body move as intended.
snappy: Legged control that distributes desired contact forces across the feet to realize commanded body motion and balance.
detail: Ground reaction force control (GRF control) takes a desired body wrench and solves for the per-foot Ground reaction force that produces it, respecting each foot's Friction cone so the feet do not slip. It is the core of many quadruped controllers, often formulated as Quadratic programming control or Convex MPC, and connects directly to Centroidal momentum control and Whole-body control. Robots like Spot and the MIT Cheetah use force-distribution schemes of this kind for robust Quadrupedal locomotion.

plain: An extra ring of ground around a drone's planned flying area, set aside in case the drone loses control and drifts off course, so planners know how far it could fall and who might be underneath.
snappy: A safety margin added around the intended flight geography to contain where a drone could end up on the ground after a loss of control or flyaway.
detail: In a Specific Operations Risk Assessment the operator defines the intended flight geography, a contingency volume, and then a Ground Risk Buffer covering the worst-case ground footprint if the aircraft exits controlled flight in a Flyaway. Its size depends on altitude, speed, and mitigations such as Geofencing or a Flight Termination System that limit how far an out-of-control Unmanned aircraft system can travel. The buffer underpins the ground-risk class and the resulting Specific Assurance and Integrity Level, and it is a core consideration when seeking an Operational Authorization for Beyond visual line of sight flights.

plain: How much real-world ground one pixel of an aerial photo covers, which tells you how much detail the image can show.
snappy: The real-world ground distance represented by one pixel in aerial or satellite imagery, set by altitude, sensor, and lens.
detail: Ground sample distance (GSD) determines whether a 2 cm leaf lesion or only a 10 cm clump is resolvable, and it scales linearly with flight altitude and inversely with focal length and sensor resolution. Mission planners choose a target GSD before a flight to guarantee the detail needed for NDVI mapping, an Orthomosaic, or a 3D reconstruction. It is a core quality metric in Aerial photogrammetry and Agriculture surveying, trading against coverage area and Endurance per battery.

plain: Sorting which parts of a 3D scan are flat floor or road and which are things standing on it.
snappy: Separating ground or road surface points from non-ground points in a point cloud or depth image.
detail: Ground segmentation labels the floor or road plane so the remaining points can be treated as potential obstacles, dramatically simplifying Obstacle detection. It typically fits a ground plane to a LiDAR Point cloud, often with RANSAC, then removes those points before clustering the rest. In a Mobility robot it is an early step that feeds Free space detection and a Cost map, and it complements semantic methods like Semantic segmentation.

plain: The known, correct answer used to check how accurate a robot's measurements or guesses are.
snappy: Verified reference data treated as correct, used to evaluate or train a robot's estimates.
detail: Ground truth is the trusted baseline against which a system's outputs are scored, often captured with higher-accuracy equipment than the system under test. A localization stack is graded by comparing its estimated Pose against RTK positioning ground truth, and an Object detection model is trained on labeled images whose Bounding box annotations are the ground truth. Datasets such as the Waymo Open Dataset and nuScenes ship ground-truth labels so a Benchmark can measure Accuracy fairly.

plain: The perfect, known answers a simulator can hand you for free, like exactly which pixels are an object or how far away it is.
snappy: Exact, simulator-emitted labels (segmentation, depth, bounding boxes, pose) used to train and evaluate perception models.
detail: Because a simulator knows the true state of every object, it can emit pixel-perfect Semantic segmentation, Instance segmentation, Depth map, Bounding box, and 6D Pose Estimation labels with no human labeling cost. Tools like Replicator in NVIDIA Isaac and Omniverse generate this Synthetic data at scale, combining it with Domain randomization to train perception that survives Sim-to-real transfer. Ground-Truth Annotation also provides the reference against which a deployed Object detection or Mapping system's accuracy is measured.

plain: Connecting the words a robot is told to the actual objects, places, and actions it can see and do in the real world.
snappy: Linking language symbols (words and instructions) to the specific perceived objects, locations, and motor actions a robot can act on.
detail: Grounding is the bridge between a natural-language instruction like 'pick up the red mug near the sink' and the pixels, Point cloud, and Grasp pose a robot must produce to carry it out. It is central to Language-conditioned manipulation and to a Vision-language-action model, which must map words onto detected objects via Object detection and Affordance detection before issuing an Action. Poor grounding is a common failure mode in Embodied AI, where a Foundation model parses a sentence linguistically but cannot tie it to the right object.

plain: A system that reads a text phrase and then points to exactly where that thing is in a picture, even for objects it was never trained to recognize by name.
snappy: A text-prompted open-set detector that grounds free-form language phrases to image regions, fusing language and vision features.
detail: Grounding DINO marries the transformer detector lineage (DETR-style queries built on a Vision Transformer) with language Grounding, cross-attending text tokens to image features so any phrase yields a Bounding box. It is a practical Open-Vocabulary Detection engine and a workhorse for Open-set recognition; paired with the Segment Anything Model it produces precise masks for arbitrary prompts. Robotics pipelines use it to let a natural-language instruction localize a target before Grasp Detection or 6D Pose Estimation, giving a Service robot Zero-shot generalization to novel objects without retraining like YOLO would require.

plain: A counting rule that tells you how many independent ways a linkage of bars and joints can move.
snappy: A mobility formula computing a mechanism's degrees of freedom from its link and joint counts and each joint's freedoms.
detail: The Grubler Formula, also called the Kutzbach criterion, sums each joint's freedoms and subtracts the constraints imposed by the links and ground to predict a mechanism's total Degrees of freedom. It tells a designer whether a Linkage is rigid, mobile, or overconstrained before any Forward kinematics is attempted, and it is the standard check when sizing a Closed kinematic chain such as a Four-bar linkage or a Parallel robot. The count can mislead at special geometries, where a Loop Closure Constraint degenerates and the true mobility differs from the formula's prediction.

plain: A library that models a robot's sensor measurements as a network of factors and efficiently keeps the best estimate up to date as new data streams in.
snappy: A factor-graph optimization library for smoothing and mapping, with incremental solvers (iSAM2) for online SLAM and state estimation.
detail: GTSAM represents estimation as a Factor graph, where variables (poses, landmarks, biases) connect to factors (measurements), and solves it via sparse nonlinear least-squares; its iSAM2 algorithm updates the solution incrementally as new measurements arrive instead of re-solving from scratch. This makes it ideal for online Visual SLAM, GraphSLAM, and Sensor fusion such as Visual-inertial odometry, handling Loop Closure Constraint updates and Inertial measurement unit preintegration cleanly. It is the factor-graph counterpart to the more general Ceres Solver and underpins many Mobility state-estimation stacks.

plain: A method that first uses precise math to plan good robot motions, then trains a neural network to copy those motions so it can run fast on its own.
snappy: Trajectory-optimization-guided supervised learning of neural manipulation policies, alternating between local optimal control and policy fitting.
detail: Guided Policy Search (GPS) sidesteps the high variance of raw Policy gradient by using Trajectory optimization (often iterative LQR / differential dynamic programming) to produce locally optimal trajectories, then training a neural network policy to imitate them under a constraint that keeps the two consistent. It was an early route to learning visuomotor manipulation end-to-end on real arms, and is conceptually a bridge between Optimal control and Imitation learning, related to later Privileged learning and Teacher-Student Distillation schemes.

plain: A standard software wrapper that turns a robot task into a game an AI can practice on by trying actions and getting scores.
snappy: A standard reset/step API exposing a simulated robot task as a reinforcement-learning problem with observations, actions, and rewards.
detail: A Gym environment (the Gymnasium and OpenAI Gym interface) standardizes how a learning agent interacts with a simulated task: call reset, then step with an Action to receive an observation and a Reward. This shared contract lets the same Reinforcement learning algorithm, such as Proximal policy optimization or Soft actor-critic, train a Policy on locomotion or manipulation without custom plumbing. Robotics environments wrap simulators like MuJoCo, PyBullet, or Isaac Lab, often with Parallel simulation for throughput.

plain: A standard software interface that lets reinforcement-learning programs talk to many different simulated tasks in the same simple way.
snappy: The maintained successor to OpenAI Gym providing a standard step/reset API and environment library for reinforcement-learning agents.
detail: Gymnasium is the community-maintained continuation of OpenAI Gym, defining the de-facto standard API (reset, step, observation/action spaces) that Reinforcement learning agents use to interact with a Gym environment. Its uniform interface lets algorithms like Proximal policy optimization and Soft actor-critic be tested across many tasks, and robotics suites such as MuJoCo Playground, ManiSkill, and robosuite expose Gymnasium-compatible wrappers. It underpins much of the tooling around the Markov decision process formulation used throughout learned control.

plain: A sensor that measures how fast something is spinning or rotating.
snappy: A sensor that measures angular velocity about one or more of its axes.
detail: A gyroscope reports rotation rate, which integrates to give change in heading or attitude, though that integration accumulates Sensor drift over time. Combined with an Accelerometer it forms an Inertial measurement unit, and most are a MEMS sensor. Robots use the gyroscope for Balance control, stabilizing a Gimbal on a Drone, and feeding an Attitude and heading reference system through Sensor fusion.

plain: A circuit of four switches that lets you send current through a motor in either direction, so it can spin forwards or backwards.
snappy: A four-switch topology that reverses the current direction across a load to drive a motor bidirectionally.
detail: An H-Bridge arranges four transistors so that closing one diagonal pair drives current one way and the other pair reverses it, giving forward and reverse control of a DC motor; adding Pulse-width modulation sets the speed. It is the core of most small Motor controller boards and the building block scaled up into the three-phase bridge of a Brushless DC Motor Controller. In robotics it drives the wheels of a Differential drive robot, gripper fingers, and pan-tilt mechanisms, and it is widely used with a Microcontroller in hobby and Service robot designs.

plain: A fast, photo-realistic computer simulation of indoor spaces used to train and test robots that need to find their way around homes and buildings.
snappy: A high-performance photorealistic 3D simulator and benchmark suite for embodied indoor navigation and household tasks.
detail: Habitat (and its Habitat-Sim engine) renders scanned indoor scenes at thousands of frames per second so an Embodied agent can be trained and benchmarked on tasks like point-goal and object-goal navigation entirely in simulation. It sits alongside AI2-THOR and iGibson as a standard platform for Embodied AI research, and is a common training ground for Vision-Language Navigation and Semantic navigation policies before any Sim-to-real transfer. Because it emphasizes speed, it enables large-scale Reinforcement learning of navigation behaviors that would be impractical on physical hardware.

plain: A company that makes warehouse robots which reach up tall shelves to fetch storage bins.
snappy: Maker of HaiPick autonomous case-handling robots for dense, high-bay tote storage.
detail: Hai Robotics' HaiPick is an autonomous mobile robot with a telescoping mast that retrieves and replaces totes on tall racks, a goods-to-person scheme that triples storage density versus human-reachable shelving. The robots navigate the floor with onboard localization and coordinate through fleet management software in a warehouse management system. It competes with shuttle systems and other case-handling automation.

plain: A low-power chip that runs AI vision models efficiently on small devices by streaming data through it in a special flow-based design.
snappy: A low-power dataflow neural-network accelerator optimized for embedded computer-vision inference on robots and edge devices.
detail: A Hailo Accelerator (Hailo-8) uses a dataflow architecture that maps a neural network's layers spatially onto the chip, achieving high throughput per watt for embedded inference. As Edge computing silicon it accelerates Object detection, Semantic segmentation, and other Perception tasks on a Mobility or Defense & Security robot where the Power budget rules out a large GPU System-on-Module. Like the Google Coral Edge TPU and Vision Processing Unit it relies on Model Quantization and performs Hardware Accelerator Offload, freeing the host CPU and Onboard compute for control and planning.

plain: A small sensor that detects a nearby magnet's field and outputs a signal, used to tell where a spinning motor's magnets are.
snappy: A solid-state magnetic sensor that detects rotor magnet position to time brushless motor commutation.
detail: A Hall effect sensor produces a voltage proportional to magnetic field strength, so three of them spaced around a Brushless DC motor reveal which winding to energize next during Commutation. It gives coarse position cheaply, making it the default low-cost alternative to an Encoder or Resolver in hobby and consumer drives, including the Electronic speed controller on a Drone. Beyond motors, Hall sensors act as a Proximity sensor or current sensor and feed the Motor controller the rotor data it needs for smooth startup.

plain: An equation that describes the best possible future cost a system can achieve from any situation, and from it the ideal control choice at every moment.
snappy: A partial differential equation whose solution is the optimal cost-to-go (value) function, from which the optimal control law follows.
detail: The Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation is the continuous-time statement of Bellman's principle of optimality; its solution is the value function that an Optimal control policy greedily exploits. For embodied robots it is the bridge between control and learning: the discrete analogue is the Bellman equation that grounds Reinforcement learning, Q-learning, and the Value function used to train walking or grasping policies. Because solving HJB exactly is intractable in high dimensions, robotics relies on approximations like Differential dynamic programming, Iterative LQR, or learned value functions, and on its specialization the Riccati equation.

plain: A way of teaching or moving a robot by simply grabbing it and pushing it where you want it to go.
snappy: A collaborative operation mode in which an operator manually moves the robot using a hand-operated, safety-rated guiding device.
detail: Hand guiding lets an operator physically push or lead the Industrial robot arm through positions, often to teach a path without a Teach pendant. As one of the four collaboration modes in ISO 10218 and ISO/TS 15066, it requires a Safety-rated monitored stop before the operator takes hold, plus safety-rated speed monitoring and an enabling device. It pairs naturally with Compliance control and backdrivable joints so the motion feels light.

plain: Working out exactly how a camera is mounted relative to a robot arm's gripper so the arm can move precisely to what the camera sees.
snappy: Estimating the transform between a camera frame and a robot arm's end-effector (or base) frame.
detail: Hand-eye calibration solves for the fixed Transform linking a Camera to a robot arm's End-effector (eye-in-hand) or base frame, so a detected Grasp pose can be reached accurately. It underpins Vision-guided robotics and Visual servoing in Manufacturing bin picking and Medical & Surgical procedures. The classic method moves the Manipulator to known poses and solves the resulting equation set, a specialized cousin of Extrinsic calibration.

plain: The challenge of safely passing control back and forth between a machine and a person, especially when there is very little time to do it.
snappy: The difficulty of safely transferring control authority between automation and a human within a limited time budget.
detail: The handoff problem is acute in conditional automation, where an Autonomous vehicle may issue a Takeover request giving the driver only seconds to regain Situational awareness. It is worsened by the Out-of-the-loop performance problem and Automation complacency, since the human re-enters cold. Robust handoffs rely on early Intent communication, Predictive display, and a Minimal risk condition or Minimal Risk Maneuver fallback when the human fails to respond, and they shape the design of Shared control and Adjustable autonomy systems.

plain: Touch and force sensations sent back to a person so they can feel what a device or robot is touching.
snappy: Tactile and kinesthetic force sensations relayed to an operator to convey a robot's physical contact with its environment.
detail: Haptic feedback gives a teleoperator a sense of touch: a surgeon at a Surgical robot console feels suture tension, and a worker doing Bilateral teleoperation feels a part seating into place. It is generated from a Force/torque sensor or estimated contact and rendered through motors in the leader device, and its fidelity is exactly what Teleoperation transparency measures. Closely related to Haptics and Kinesthetic teaching, it improves dexterity and safety in delicate Leader-follower teleoperation.

plain: Technology that lets a person feel touch, force, or vibration through a device, so a machine can convey a sense of physical contact.
snappy: The conveyance of touch and force feedback to a human operator through a controlled interface.
detail: Haptics closes the loop between a human and a remote or virtual robot, rendering contact forces so the operator feels what the machine touches. It is central to Teleoperation and Telerobotics, where a surgeon driving a Surgical robot from Intuitive Surgical feels tissue resistance through the console. Haptic rendering depends on accurate Force/torque sensor data and tight Force control so the felt forces match what Tactile sensing detects at the end-effector.

plain: A software middle layer that hides the messy details of specific hardware so the rest of the program does not have to care which device it is talking to.
snappy: A software interface that decouples robot logic from device-specific drivers behind a uniform API.
detail: A hardware abstraction layer (HAL) presents generic operations like read encoder or set motor command, while a Device driver underneath translates them for a particular Microcontroller, bus, or chip. This lets the same control code target different robots by swapping drivers rather than rewriting logic, a separation that ros2_control formalizes for actuators and sensors. It is a staple of any Embedded system and of Middleware that must run portably across hardware revisions.

plain: Handing demanding jobs, like image recognition, off the main processor onto a dedicated chip built to do them faster and more efficiently.
snappy: Moving perception or control kernels onto dedicated silicon to free the host CPU and improve throughput and efficiency.
detail: Hardware Accelerator Offload routes heavy, repetitive workloads, neural-network inference, image preprocessing, or signal filtering, onto a GPU, Vision Processing Unit, Digital Signal Processor, or an AI accelerator like the Hailo Accelerator or Google Coral Edge TPU, leaving the CPU free for planning and the Real-time control loop. It is the practical mechanism behind Heterogeneous Compute on a GPU System-on-Module, and it cuts both Latency and the Power budget when paired with Model Quantization. On an Autonomous mobile robot this lets a modest host run Perception, SLAM, and navigation concurrently without stalling the control thread.

plain: A plug-in piece of software that connects the control system to a specific robot's motors and sensors so it can command and read them.
snappy: A ros2_control plugin (SystemInterface) exposing a robot's actuators and sensors to the control framework via a common API.
detail: A Hardware Interface implements the read and write methods that ros2_control calls every control cycle, translating between the framework's command/state interfaces and a real robot's drivers or a simulator. It abstracts an Actuator and sensor so that the same controller code runs on different machines or in Gazebo by swapping the plugin. The Controller Manager loads it and exchanges joint commands and feedback through it, often using values published by robot_state_publisher and the robot's URDF.

plain: The idea that an approach often wins not because it is best, but because it happens to run well on whatever computer chips are popular at the time.
snappy: The notion that research ideas succeed partly because they fit prevailing hardware, not solely because of inherent merit.
detail: The hardware lottery explains why GPU-friendly deep Neural network methods eclipsed alternatives once the Graphics processing unit made them cheap to train, a dynamic now repeating with the Tensor processing unit and AI accelerator chips. In robotics it shapes which controllers ship: a Massively parallel simulation pipeline like Isaac Gym thrives on GPUs, while equally valid model-based methods that suit a different Onboard compute target may lose out. It frames the Bitter lesson and the Scaling hypothesis as partly contingent on the silicon that won, and it influences Hardware-software co-design choices on real robots.

plain: Testing a robot's real controller by tricking it with a computer that pretends to be the robot's body in real time.
snappy: A test method where real controller hardware runs against a real-time simulation of the plant's sensors and actuators.
detail: Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL) connects the actual Robot controller or Electronic control unit to a real-time Simulation that emulates motors, sensors, and dynamics, so control firmware is exercised at full Control Loop Frequency without risking real mechanics. It is heavily used in Mobility and Manufacturing to validate edge cases, fault handling, and a Functional Safety Processor before Commissioning, complementing Software-in-the-loop simulation and the broader Verification and validation workflow. Because the simulated plant must respond within microseconds, HIL rigs rely on deterministic real-time computers and buses such as CAN Bus or EtherCAT.

plain: Testing a drone by running its real control electronics while feeding them fake sensor data and movement, so the actual hardware is exercised without flying.
snappy: Connecting a physical flight controller to a real-time simulator that supplies synthetic sensor inputs and consumes its actuator commands.
detail: Hardware-in-the-loop simulation plugs a genuine Flight controller such as a Pixhawk into a Physics engine running in Real-time, so the board's processor, timing, and IO are exercised against simulated dynamics. Unlike Software-in-the-loop simulation, it validates the actual embedded execution path, exposing driver, Latency, and Jitter issues that pure-software testing misses. It is a key step in qualifying an autopilot for safe flight and complements the firmware models built in Gazebo.

plain: Designing a robot's physical body and its control programs together, so each shapes the other, instead of building the body first and writing the software afterward.
snappy: Jointly optimizing a robot's mechanical morphology and its control software so the two are tuned to each other.
detail: Hardware-software co-design recognizes that a clever body simplifies control, an idea formalized as Morphological computation: a Compliant actuator or Series elastic actuator can absorb impacts that software would otherwise have to manage. Designers iterate on Morphology, actuator placement, and the controller together, often inside a Physics engine before committing to metal, as with a Soft robot or an optimized Quadruped robot. The approach is contrasted with treating Mechatronics and the Robot controller as separate, sequential design phases.

plain: A compact gear unit that gives a robot arm a lot of strength with no looseness, using a flexible toothed ring that wobbles inside a rigid one.
snappy: A compact, zero-backlash, high-ratio reducer using a flexible spline; standard in precision robot arms.
detail: A harmonic drive (strain wave gear) achieves very high Gear reduction in a thin, lightweight package by flexing an elliptical spline so its teeth engage a slightly larger rigid ring, producing essentially zero Backlash. This precision and compactness made it the default Gearbox for an Industrial robot arm, a Cobot, and many Humanoid robot joints, usually paired with a Frameless motor and Harmonic-drive-friendly Servo control. Its drawbacks are limited efficiency, flexspline compliance, and high cost compared with a Planetary gear.

plain: The company that commercialized a special compact gear system that lets robot joints move precisely with almost no wobble.
snappy: Manufacturer that pioneered and commercializes the strain-wave (harmonic) gearing used throughout precision robot joints.
detail: Harmonic Drive LLC produces the Harmonic drive strain-wave reducer, whose core components are the Wave Generator and a flexible Strain Wave Flexspline that meshes against a rigid circular spline to give very high Gear reduction in a thin, lightweight package with near-zero Gear Backlash. These reducers dominate the joints of the Industrial robot arm and many a Humanoid robot, where compact size and high Torque density are essential. They commonly sit downstream of a Brushless DC motor in a Servo drive train.

plain: A clever trick that sends extra digital information on top of the standard analog signal wires that process sensors already use, without replacing them.
snappy: A hybrid protocol overlaying digital data on legacy analog 4-20mA process instrument loops.
detail: HART superimposes a frequency-shift digital signal on the existing 4-20mA current loop, so a process transmitter keeps sending its primary measurement as an analog signal while also exposing configuration, multiple variables, and diagnostics digitally. This lets plants add device intelligence and Condition monitoring without rewiring legacy instrumentation, a major advantage in Process automation. HART data is read by a Distributed control system or asset-management tool and feeds the OT historian, and it underpins device-level data for Predictive maintenance.

plain: A team meeting that walks through a process step by step using prompt words like more, less, or reverse to imagine what could go wrong.
snappy: A structured, guideword-driven team study that systematically identifies deviations and hazards in a process or robotic operation.
detail: HAZOP applies guidewords such as no, more, less, and reverse to each part of a process to surface deviations and their consequences, originally for chemical plants and now for robotic cells and automated lines. It is more process-oriented than the component-level FMEA and the top-down Fault Tree Analysis, and its outputs feed the Risk assessment mandated by ISO 12100. For a robotic process, a HAZOP team might examine what happens if a conveyor runs in reverse or a Robot controller commands more speed than intended.

plain: An extremely precise, pre-made map of roads, accurate to a few centimeters, that a self-driving car carries to know exactly where everything is.
snappy: A centimeter-accurate prior map of road geometry, lanes, and features used by autonomous vehicles.
detail: An HD map, or High-Definition map, stores lane geometry, signs, traffic lights, and curbs to centimeter accuracy as a prior the vehicle reads before its sensors even confirm them, often encoded with a Lane graph or Lanelet. By matching live perception to the map, a self-driving stack performs Map-relative localization to place the Ego vehicle precisely in its lane. It supplements Lane detection and Traffic sign recognition, and the Mapless driving approach deliberately reduces reliance on it because HD maps are costly to build and keep current.

plain: Running a simulation with the graphics turned off so the computer can crunch through it much faster.
snappy: Running a simulator without on-screen rendering to maximize speed and enable large-scale, parallel data collection.
detail: By skipping the visualization window, headless simulation frees the GPU and CPU to advance physics as fast as possible, which is essential when training a Policy needs millions of steps. It is the standard mode for Reinforcement learning on a server or cluster and pairs naturally with Parallel simulation to run thousands of Gym environment instances at once. Tools like Isaac Lab, MuJoCo, and Gazebo all offer a headless mode for data collection and Sim-to-real transfer.

plain: A company selling snap-together robot building blocks that let researchers assemble a custom robot quickly.
snappy: Maker of modular X-Series series-elastic actuators for rapidly building custom research robots.
detail: HEBI Robotics sells X-Series smart modules that combine a motor, gearbox, encoder, and a series elastic actuator in one networked unit, so a researcher can bolt together an articulated robot or a legged robot without designing custom drivetrains. The built-in compliance supports force control and impedance control, and the modules expose forward kinematics and inverse kinematics APIs. They are common in academic mobile manipulation prototypes.

plain: The instant a robot's foot first hits the ground at the start of a step.
snappy: The gait event marking initial foot-ground contact at the onset of Stance phase.
detail: Heel strike is the discrete impact that ends Swing phase and begins the Double support phase, producing a sudden Ground reaction force spike that energy-loss models and Hybrid zero dynamics treat as the reset map of the walking Limit cycle. Robots use Force/torque sensor data or estimated Contact point timing to detect it for state-machine gait switching and Push recovery. In running, heel strike and the subsequent Toe-off bracket the contact period that separates two Flight phase intervals.

plain: A gear whose teeth are cut at a slant so they engage gradually, making the gear run more smoothly and quietly than straight-toothed ones.
snappy: A gear with angled (helical) teeth that mesh gradually for smoother, quieter running and higher load capacity than spur gears.
detail: A Helical Gear engages each tooth progressively rather than all at once, so it runs quieter and carries more load than an equivalent Spur Gear, at the cost of an axial thrust the bearings must absorb. This makes it common in higher-torque robot drivetrains and in the stages of a precision Gearbox where smoothness matters. It still establishes its Gear Ratio by tooth counts within a Gear Train and exhibits Backlash that must be controlled for accurate positioning.

plain: Figure AI's robot brain that lets a humanoid understand spoken requests and use its arms and hands to handle everyday objects.
snappy: Figure AI's vision-language-action model that controls full upper-body humanoid manipulation, including coordinated bimanual and hand movements, at high rate.
detail: Helix (Figure AI, 2025) is a Vision-language-action model that runs a dual-system architecture: a slower vision-language reasoning model sets intent while a fast network outputs high-rate control of the Humanoid robot's torso, arms, and multi-fingered hands for Bimanual manipulation. It targets Service robot scenarios like putting away groceries, emphasizing Zero-shot generalization to unseen household items. Helix belongs to the same Robot foundation model wave as Pi-Zero, GR00T, and RDT-1B, and relies on large-scale Teleoperation data plus onboard compute for real-time Visuomotor Policy execution.

plain: A company that makes Stretch, a slim mobile robot with a lifting arm for research and helping people at home.
snappy: Maker of the Stretch mobile manipulator for research and assistive use.
detail: Hello Robot's Stretch is a lightweight, affordable Mobile manipulator with a telescoping arm on a slim mobile base, designed to bring Mobile manipulation research and in-home assistance within reach of smaller labs. It is fully ROS-native with a published URDF and works with the Navigation stack and MoveIt for combined navigation and grasping. Its low cost and safety make it a popular platform for Learning from demonstration and assistive Human-robot interaction studies.

plain: Using several different kinds of processors together in one machine, each handling the work it is best at.
snappy: Combining CPUs, GPUs, and specialized accelerators in one system to partition robot workloads onto the best-suited engine.
detail: Heterogeneous Compute means a robot's Onboard compute mixes a CPU for control logic, a GPU for parallel Perception, and accelerators like a Vision Processing Unit, Digital Signal Processor, or AI accelerator for specific kernels, each chosen for efficiency. A GPU System-on-Module such as a NVIDIA Jetson or the Qualcomm Robotics RB5 embodies this, running a SLAM thread, a neural Object detection network, and a Real-time control loop concurrently. The challenge is partitioning work and moving data without bottlenecks, which is why Hardware Accelerator Offload and careful Power budget management are central to a Humanoid robot's compute design.

plain: A quick rule-of-thumb guess of how far is still left to go, used to steer a route search so it doesn't waste effort exploring backwards.
snappy: A cheap estimate of remaining cost-to-go from a state to the goal, used to focus an informed search like A* toward promising directions.
detail: In robotics path search a heuristic function h(n) estimates the cost from node n to the goal and lets A* search expand far fewer nodes than blind Dijkstra's algorithm. If the heuristic never overestimates (an admissible heuristic, such as straight-line distance ignoring obstacles) the search remains optimal; Euclidean and obstacle-aware distance fields are common choices over an Occupancy grid map. The same idea drives Hybrid A* and State lattice planners for car-like Mobility platforms. Note the overlap with AI search, but here the cost-to-go reflects physical Free space.

plain: A drone with six propellers, used when you need to lift more weight or keep flying if a motor fails.
snappy: A six-rotor Multirotor offering greater Payload and motor-failure redundancy than a Quadcopter.
detail: The extra rotors of a Hexacopter let the Flight controller redistribute thrust through Control allocation if one motor or Electronic speed controller fails, allowing a controlled Return-to-home instead of a crash. The added Thrust-to-weight ratio headroom suits cinematography rigs carrying heavy Gimbal-mounted cameras and survey payloads. For the most demanding heavy-lift or high-redundancy missions operators step up again to an Octocopter.

plain: Moving on six legs the way many insects do.
snappy: Legged locomotion on six legs, giving strong static stability through redundant ground contacts.
detail: With six legs a robot can keep three down at all times in a tripod gait, granting Static stability while the other three swing forward, which makes Hexapod locomotion robust on rough ground. It is a hallmark of Bio-inspired robotics and the Hexapod robot, and is studied alongside the Gait cycle, Stance phase, and Swing phase concepts. The redundancy also means the robot can keep walking even if one leg fails.

plain: A six-legged robot, like a mechanical insect, that stays very steady because it can always keep several feet on the ground.
snappy: A six-legged robot using Hexapod locomotion for high static stability over uneven terrain.
detail: With six legs a hexapod can keep a tripod of feet planted at all times, giving excellent Static stability and a large Support polygon even on rubble. This Bio-inspired robot draws on insect morphology and is used in Research/Frontier inspection and search tasks where a Quadruped robot or Bipedal robot might topple. Gait generation coordinates leg phases through the Gait cycle to maintain balance during Legged locomotion.

plain: A way to give a robot a ranked to-do list of motions and solve them so that lower-priority goals never disturb the most important ones.
snappy: Solving a strictly prioritized stack of whole-body tasks as a sequence of nested constrained quadratic programs.
detail: Hierarchical Quadratic Programming (HQP), or the stack of tasks, enforces strict task priorities by solving each level's quadratic program within the Null space of all higher-priority tasks, so balance and contact constraints dominate posture or reaching goals. It is the engine behind much modern Whole-body control and Whole-Body Inverse Kinematics on Humanoid robots, handling Unilateral Contact Constraint and joint limits as inequalities. Built atop the Operational Space Formulation and the Jacobian matrix, HQP is the prioritized cousin of single-level Quadratic programming control and is implemented in solvers like OSQP.

plain: Splitting a robot's learning into a planner that picks big-picture steps and a controller that carries each one out.
snappy: Reinforcement learning that decomposes a task into a high-level policy choosing subgoals and low-level policies executing them.
detail: HRL tackles long-horizon, Sparse reward tasks by having a high-level Policy issue subgoals to low-level controllers, much as a Humanoid robot might decide walk-then-open-then-grasp while sub-policies handle each motion. The low level often reuses a Skill primitive library, and the high level resembles a Goal-conditioned policy. By structuring exploration, HRL improves Sample efficiency on tasks too long for flat Reinforcement learning.

plain: A planning method that solves a big job by repeatedly breaking it into smaller ordered steps until each step is something the robot can directly do.
snappy: A planning formalism that recursively decomposes abstract tasks into ordered subtasks using predefined decomposition methods.
detail: HTN planning encodes human know-how as decomposition rules ('assemble' becomes 'fetch', then 'align', then 'fasten'), making it a structured alternative to flat search like PDDL. It is widely used in Task planning and Task and motion planning for manufacturing cells, and its decomposed leaves map onto entries in a Skill library executed via Skill chaining. HTN sits in the Deliberative control half of a Hybrid architecture, providing the high-level plan that lower-level Motion planning realizes.

plain: A camera technique that captures both very bright and very dark parts of a scene in one image, so neither is washed out or lost in shadow.
snappy: Combining or capturing exposures across a wide brightness range so a single image preserves detail in both highlights and deep shadows.
detail: High Dynamic Range Imaging lets a robot's Camera handle scenes where bright sunlight and dark shadow appear together, such as a Self-driving car exiting a tunnel or a delivery robot facing direct sun. Because a standard CMOS Image Sensor clips highlights or buries shadows, HDR is critical upstream of Object detection and Lane detection, where missing a pedestrian in a backlit doorway is a safety failure. It is often implemented in the Image Sensor itself or by fusing multiple exposures, and pairs with careful Camera calibration to keep colors and geometry stable.

plain: A solar-powered aircraft that flies very high for months at a time, doing the job of a satellite without leaving the atmosphere.
snappy: An ultra-long-endurance solar UAV that loiters in the stratosphere to provide persistent communications or imaging coverage.
detail: A high-altitude pseudo-satellite (HAPS) flies above weather and most air traffic, around 20 km, using daytime solar charging and lightweight Distributed electric propulsion to achieve months of Endurance from a single launch. It delivers satellite-like services such as connectivity and persistent imaging at far lower cost and latency, bridging Defense & Security surveillance and Space applications. Like any long-flight Drone it depends on robust autonomy and station-keeping, with Loiter patterns managed by the onboard Flight controller.

plain: A super-precise digital map for self-driving cars that pinpoints every lane line, sign, and curb to within a few centimeters.
snappy: A centimeter-accurate prior map encoding lane geometry, signs, and road features that an autonomous vehicle uses for localization and planning.
detail: An HD map gives a Self-driving stack a precise prior so the car can perform Map-relative localization, knowing exactly which lane it occupies before its sensors even confirm it. Lane topology is often encoded in formats like Lanelet and OpenDRIVE, and the map is built by a Mobile Mapping System and refreshed against live perception. HD maps reduce the perception burden but raise maintenance cost, which is why some teams pursue Mapless driving; they pair naturally with RTK GNSS and GNSS/INS Integration for global positioning.

plain: A feature that can handle most of the driving on a motorway or in a traffic jam by itself, while the person stays ready to take back control.
snappy: A conditional automation feature that sustains lane keeping and speed control on highways or in congestion within a defined operational design domain.
detail: A highway pilot combines adaptive cruise control and lane keeping assist into sustained SAE Level 2 to 3 driving within a bounded operational design domain such as a divided highway. At Level 3 the driver may disengage but must respond to a takeover request, so it depends on a driver monitoring system. A traffic jam pilot is the low-speed congested variant, and the feature relies on an HD map, behavior prediction, and a minimal risk condition fallback if the operational design domain is exited.

plain: A method that teaches a real robot tricky hands-on skills in under an hour by letting a person step in and correct it whenever it starts to go wrong.
snappy: A Real-world reinforcement learning system that masters dexterous tasks quickly by blending human corrective interventions with online learning.
detail: HIL-SERL is a Real-world reinforcement learning recipe that reaches near-perfect success on contact-rich skills—like Peg-in-hole insertion or Dexterous manipulation—within about an hour by keeping a Human-in-the-loop who supplies corrective takeovers, echoing the DAgger style of interactive Imitation learning. Those interventions seed a Replay Buffer and shape the Reward function, dramatically improving Sample efficiency over pure trial-and-error and avoiding unsafe exploration on a real Manipulator. It is frequently demonstrated on Franka Emika Panda hardware and contrasts with Offline reinforcement learning by learning directly on the physical robot.

plain: A learning trick where a robot that failed to reach a goal pretends the place it actually ended up was the goal, so even failures teach it something.
snappy: An off-policy RL method that relabels failed episodes with achieved goals to learn efficiently from sparse rewards.
detail: Hindsight experience replay (HER) attacks the Sparse reward problem in goal-conditioned manipulation by storing each failed trajectory in the Replay Buffer twice, once with the intended goal and once relabeled with the state actually reached, so every rollout yields useful signal. It is an Off-policy learning augmentation typically paired with Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient or Soft actor-critic for tasks like Pick and place and Peg-in-hole. HER greatly improves Sample efficiency on a Goal-conditioned policy where naive Reinforcement learning rarely sees success.

plain: The turning force a motor can resist while staying perfectly still, like how hard it can grip a load without moving.
snappy: The maximum torque an actuator can sustain while stationary against an external load.
