It is the performance counterpart to the safety-focused ISO 13482 for a personal-care robot, and its test methods are echoed in the North American UL 3300 listing process. A maker of an Autonomous mobile robot or cleaning robot runs ISO 18646 test courses to publish credible performance numbers.

plain: A companion standard that tells you exactly how to test whether a personal-care robot meets its safety rules.
snappy: The ISO standard providing concrete test methods and application guidance for verifying ISO 13482 safety requirements on personal care robots.
detail: ISO 23482 turns the safety requirements of ISO 13482 into repeatable test procedures for a personal-care Service robot such as a mobile servant, physical-assistant exoskeleton, or person-carrier robot. It defines how to measure hazards like collision force, stability, and Effective Mass during contact, complementing the performance methods of ISO 18646. A Humanoid robot or assistive-mobility robot vendor uses ISO 23482 to demonstrate compliance through documented, reproducible Verification and validation tests.

full: Tractors and Machinery for Agriculture and Forestry - Safety-Related Parts of Control Systems
plain: The safety rulebook for the control systems on farm and forestry machines, including self-driving tractors.
snappy: The functional-safety standard for safety-related parts of control systems on agricultural and forestry machinery, defining Agricultural Performance Levels.
detail: ISO 25119 adapts functional-safety principles to agricultural and forestry equipment, defining Agricultural Performance Levels (AgPL) much as ISO 13849 defines a Performance Level for general machinery and IEC 61508 defines a Safety Integrity Level. It governs the safety logic of an autonomous tractor or Agricultural robot, covering hazards from steering, implement control, and unexpected motion. A self-driving John Deere or Monarch Tractor platform documents its safety-related control architecture against ISO 25119 to claim the required AgPL for each function.

plain: The safety rulebook for the electronics and software inside cars, making sure things like braking computers do not fail dangerously.
snappy: The functional-safety standard for electrical and electronic systems in road vehicles, derived from IEC 61508.
detail: ISO 26262 adapts the IEC 61508 Functional safety framework specifically to road vehicles, governing the electronics behind an Automated driving system, steering, and braking. It introduces the ASIL risk-classification scheme and a full safety lifecycle from hazard analysis to verification, and is central to certifying an Autonomous vehicle alongside Safety of the intended functionality (ISO 21448). Where ISO 26262 addresses failures of components, SOTIF addresses hazards from the system's intended-but-insufficient behavior.

plain: The safety standard for self-driving warehouse trucks and carts that move around without a human driver.
snappy: The safety standard for driverless industrial trucks, covering automated guided vehicles and autonomous mobile robots and their systems.
detail: ISO 3691-4 sets the safety requirements for driverless industrial trucks, the standard that governs a warehouse Automated guided vehicle and Autonomous mobile robot fleet. It mandates personnel-detection means such as a Safety scanner, defined Safety-rated stop behavior tied to speed, and rules for shared traffic areas and load handling. It complements ISO 10218 (which covers fixed robot arms) for the mobile side of Logistics & Warehouse automation.

plain: An early-stage international document on keeping automated driving safe even when no part is broken, just outmatched by the situation.
snappy: The publicly available specification predecessor of ISO 21448 addressing hazards from performance limits absent any component fault.
detail: ISO/PAS 21448 was the publicly available specification that introduced SOTIF, the discipline of managing hazards from performance limitations rather than faults, later formalized as the full ISO 21448 standard. It addresses cases like a Perception model misclassifying an object at the edge of the Operational design domain in an Autonomous vehicle, complementing the fault-driven ISO 26262. Practitioners expand the validated scenario space through Scenario-based testing and often combine it with STPA to surface unsafe control actions.

plain: The rulebook for protecting cars and self-driving vehicles from hacking throughout their whole life.
snappy: The joint ISO/SAE standard governing cybersecurity engineering and threat management across a road vehicle's entire lifecycle.
detail: ISO/SAE 21434 defines a process for threat analysis, risk assessment, secure development, and incident response so an Autonomous vehicle's electronics resist tampering and remote attack from design through decommissioning. It is the security companion to the safety-focused ISO 26262, and a compromised system can defeat both that standard and SOTIF by causing hazards in an otherwise fault-free vehicle. It draws on industrial security practice like IEC 62443 and addresses risks such as GNSS spoofing or Sensor spoofing against the perception stack.

plain: A technical guide giving the exact force and pressure limits a robot may apply to a person so that sharing a workspace with a machine stays safe.
snappy: The technical specification that defines biomechanical force and pressure thresholds for collaborative robot operation, supplementing ISO 10218.
detail: ISO/TS 15066 quantifies the human-body pain and injury thresholds a Collaborative robot must respect, providing per-body-part force and pressure limits that underpin the Power and force limiting collaboration mode. It is the technical companion to ISO 10218 and is essential when a Cobot or Humanoid robot shares a Collaborative workspace with people without fences. Integrators use its tables together with a Risk assessment to validate Collaborative robot safety.

plain: A method that lines up two 3D scans by repeatedly pairing nearest points and nudging one scan toward the other.
snappy: An algorithm that aligns point clouds by iteratively matching nearest-neighbor points and minimizing their distance.
detail: Iterative closest point (ICP) alternates between associating each point with its closest neighbor in the other cloud and solving for the transform that minimizes those distances, repeating until convergence. It is the standard engine of Point cloud registration for LiDAR, underpinning lidar Odometry and SLAM. It needs a decent initial guess to avoid local minima and is often combined with RANSAC or a Voxel grid downsampling step for speed and robustness.

plain: A method that lets a robot get better at a repeated motion by remembering and correcting the exact errors it made last time.
snappy: Control that improves tracking of a fixed, repeated trajectory by updating the command using the error recorded on previous executions.
detail: ILC exploits the fact that an Industrial robot arm or Servo drive often repeats the identical Trajectory many times: it stores the tracking error from each run and adds a learned feedforward correction to the next, converging to near-perfect Trajectory tracking despite repeatable disturbances. It is heavily used in Pick and place, Robotic welding, and precision Motion control where Following error must shrink cycle over cycle. Conceptually it is a repetition-domain cousin of Feedforward control and overlaps with Learning-based control.

plain: A method that finds a good robot motion by repeatedly straightening the problem into a simple form and solving that simple form over and over.
snappy: A nonlinear trajectory optimizer that repeatedly linearizes the dynamics and applies an LQR solve around the current trajectory until convergence.
detail: iLQR is the Gauss-Newton variant of Differential dynamic programming, dropping the second-order dynamics term so each iteration is a Linear quadratic regulator solve around the latest rollout. It is a standard backbone for real-time Trajectory optimization and Model predictive control on a Quadruped robot or manipulator, and frequently provides the warm-start for Nonlinear MPC. Practitioners reach for it when Optimal control over smooth dynamics is needed but full DDP is too expensive.

plain: A table that tells you how fast the robot's hand moves for a given speed of each joint.
snappy: The matrix mapping joint velocities to end-effector velocities.
detail: The robot Jacobian linearly relates Joint space velocities to the End-effector Twist in Task space, and its transpose maps a Wrench to joint torques. It is the heart of Differential kinematics and of iterative Inverse kinematics via the Jacobian pseudoinverse. When the Jacobian loses rank the arm hits a Kinematic singularity, and its shape defines the Manipulability ellipsoid that quantifies how freely the arm can move.

plain: A best-fit way to undo the hand-versus-joint-speed table when it can't be reversed exactly.
snappy: A least-squares (Moore-Penrose) inverse used to solve velocity-level inverse kinematics.
detail: When the Jacobian matrix is not square, as on a Kinematic redundancy arm, it has no ordinary inverse, so the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse gives the least-squares joint velocities that best achieve a desired end-effector Twist. This is the standard engine for iterative Inverse kinematics and resolved-rate Differential kinematics. Near a Kinematic singularity the solution blows up, so damped variants are used, and the Null space term lets a redundant arm pursue secondary goals.

plain: A simple way to make a robot arm push or pull with a desired force by converting that force into motor twists at each joint.
snappy: Mapping a desired Cartesian force to joint torques by multiplying it through the transpose of the Jacobian.
detail: Jacobian transpose control exploits the fact that the transpose of the Jacobian matrix maps an end-effector Wrench to the joint torques that produce it, so a robot can apply or regulate a tip force without inverting the Jacobian. Unlike the Jacobian pseudoinverse, it stays well-behaved near a Kinematic singularity, which makes it a stable backbone for Force control and Impedance control. It is widely used to drive the End-effector toward a target by treating error as a virtual spring force.

plain: A gripper with a soft bag of grains that wraps around an object then hardens to hold it tight.
snappy: Gripper using granular jamming to mold around an object and stiffen on command.
detail: A jamming gripper presses a flexible membrane full of granular media (like coffee grounds) onto an object, then a vacuum jams the grains so the bag locks into the object's shape, gripping it without a custom finger design. As a kind of Soft gripper and Universal gripper it shines at Bin picking of varied, irregular parts where a Parallel-jaw gripper or Suction gripper would struggle. It is a popular Research/Frontier example of Morphological computation, since the hardware itself handles shape adaptation that would otherwise demand complex control.

plain: A motion plan that limits how abruptly the robot can change its acceleration, giving gentle, vibration-free moves.
snappy: A motion profile that bounds jerk, the rate of change of acceleration, to produce smooth, low-vibration moves.
detail: By capping jerk, this profile rounds the corners of the acceleration curve, reducing the high-frequency content that excites a structure's Resonance and causes overshoot, which is why it is also called an S-curve profile. It is the standard output of Trajectory generation on a CNC machine tending cell or Industrial robot arm, smoothing the references a Servo control loop must track and reducing wear and Following error. Where structural modes persist beyond what jerk limiting handles, it is supplemented by Input shaping or a Notch filter; libraries like Ruckig compute it online.

plain: The idea that a machine should stop itself automatically the moment it makes or detects a faulty part.
snappy: Autonomation: building machines that halt on detecting an abnormality so defects are never passed downstream.
detail: Jidoka, or 'automation with a human touch,' lets equipment run unattended yet stop and signal the instant quality deviates, freeing operators from babysitting and enabling Lights-out manufacturing. It pairs naturally with an Andon alert and with Poka-yoke devices that supply the detection logic. On a robotic line, Jidoka is realized through Robot crash detection, a Drive fault trip, or a vision-based Quality inspection check wired into the Robot controller and Programmable logic controller, with events logged by the Manufacturing execution system.

plain: Small wobbles in the timing of events that are supposed to happen at perfectly even intervals.
snappy: Variability in the timing of periodic events such as control updates or sensor samples around their nominal period.
detail: Jitter is the spread around the intended period of a Control loop: a controller meant to run every millisecond that sometimes fires at 0.9 or 1.2 ms exhibits jitter, which injects noise into Real-time control and degrades Trajectory tracking. It arises from scheduling contention, Clock skew, and bus delays, and is minimized with a Real-time operating system, PREEMPT_RT, and bounded Worst-case execution time. In sensing it appears as Sampling jitter, smearing the effective timestamp of measurements feeding Sensor fusion.

plain: A company building electric air taxis with tilting propellers that take off straight up and carry passengers like a small, quiet aircraft.
snappy: An eVTOL air-taxi developer building a piloted, tilt-propeller passenger aircraft for urban air mobility.
detail: Joby Aviation is a leading developer in the eVTOL sector, building a piloted aircraft with Distributed electric propulsion whose tilting rotors enable vertical takeoff before transitioning to wing-borne Cruise. The company is pursuing FAA Type Certification to fly passengers between Vertiport sites as part of the emerging Urban air mobility ecosystem, competing with the autonomous-focused Wisk Aero. Its piloted approach contrasts with fully autonomous concepts, though shared challenges include Wind disturbance rejection and certifying Transition flight.

plain: A long-established farm-equipment maker that now builds tractors and machines able to drive and work fields by themselves.
snappy: Agricultural-equipment manufacturer deploying autonomous tractors, GPS-guided machinery, and computer-vision farm robotics.
detail: John Deere has evolved from tractor maker into an agriculture-robotics company, fielding a fully autonomous tractor that plows without an operator using stereo cameras and onboard Perception. Its machines pair RTK positioning and GPS for centimetre-accurate guidance with computer-vision systems like See & Spray that target weeds individually, making it a flagship example of the Agricultural robot and Precision agriculture drone ecosystem. The shift reflects acute farm Labor shortage pressures and a move toward data-driven, sensor-rich field equipment.

plain: The movable connection between two parts of a robot that lets them move relative to each other.
snappy: A connection between two links that permits constrained relative motion.
detail: Each Joint in a Kinematic chain connects two Link members and allows a specific motion: a Revolute joint rotates, a Prismatic joint slides, and a Spherical joint pivots in three rotations. The number and type of joints set a robot's Degrees of freedom and define its Joint space. Most joints are powered by an Actuator with an Encoder for feedback, and their software description lives in the URDF.

plain: A task that a person and a robot carry out together, each doing part of it toward the same shared goal.
snappy: A coordinated activity in which a human and robot act jointly and interdependently toward a common goal.
detail: Joint action (human-robot collaboration) requires mutual prediction, shared timing, and complementary roles, such as a Cobot holding a panel while a worker fastens it, or two-agent assembly on a Manufacturing line. It depends on Intent communication, Legibility, and the robot maintaining a model of the partner, linking it to Theory of mind and Mixed-initiative interaction. Safe physical joint action is governed by Speed and separation monitoring and Power and force limiting under collaborative-robot safety standards.

plain: A way of training a robot's perception system so it forecasts an abstract summary of what its cameras and sensors will show next, focusing on what matters for acting and ignoring unpredictable visual noise.
snappy: A self-supervised architecture (JEPA) that learns robot-usable visual features by predicting future or masked content in a latent embedding space rather than reconstructing raw pixels.
detail: For an embodied agent, JEPA and its video variant V-JEPA train an encoder and predictor so the embedding of a masked or future camera region is predicted from context in latent space, giving a manipulation or locomotion robot compact state features without the wasted effort of pixel-level reconstruction used by Masked Visual Pretraining. Because the learned representations are abstract and predictable, they serve as a scalable backbone for a World model and for the Representation learning that feeds a Visuomotor Policy. It builds on Self-supervised learning and the predictive principle of Contrastive Predictive Coding, and supports World Model Pretraining for embodied control.

plain: A way of controlling a robot so each of its joints behaves like its own soft spring-and-shock-absorber, gently resisting being pushed out of place.
snappy: Impedance control that renders a virtual spring-damper behavior independently at each joint rather than at the end-effector.
detail: Joint impedance control sets a target stiffness and damping for every joint, making each one back-drivable and compliant, which is valuable on robots with a Series elastic actuator or a Joint Torque Sensor such as the KUKA LBR iiwa. It contrasts with Cartesian impedance control, which regulates compliance in Task space at the End-effector; joint-space rendering is simpler but couples tip stiffness to arm posture. It is a building block for Compliance control, Gravity Compensation, and safe Human-robot interaction.

plain: The description of a robot arm purely by the angle or extension of each of its joints.
snappy: The coordinate space defined by a robot's individual joint variables.
detail: Joint space lists one variable per joint, for example the angle of each Revolute joint or the extension of each Prismatic joint, and a point in it fully fixes the arm's configuration. Forward kinematics maps from joint space to Task space, while Inverse kinematics goes the other way. Planning directly in joint space avoids Kinematic singularity issues but makes it harder to reason about the End-effector path.

plain: A sensor built right into a robot joint that measures how hard the joint is twisting, so the robot can feel the forces it applies.
snappy: An in-joint sensor measuring actual output torque to close a force or torque feedback loop.
detail: A Joint Torque Sensor typically uses a Strain gauge bridge on a compliant spoke at the joint output, giving a direct reading downstream of the Gearbox where motor current alone cannot account for friction and Reflected Inertia. This enables high-fidelity Torque control, Impedance control, and Joint impedance control on collaborative arms such as the KUKA LBR iiwa or Franka Emika Panda. It is the alternative to inferring torque from current in Torque Control Mode, and to mechanical compliance approaches like a Series elastic actuator.

plain: A grid route finder that skips over long stretches of empty equal-cost cells, jumping straight to the points where a decision actually matters.
snappy: An optimal speedup of A* search on uniform-cost grids that prunes symmetric paths by 'jumping' over intermediate nodes to identify only the decision points.
detail: Jump Point Search (JPS) accelerates grid A* search without losing optimality by recognizing that on a uniform-cost Occupancy grid many paths are symmetric; it scans ahead along straight lines and diagonals, generating successors only at 'jump points' where an obstacle forces a turn. This can be an order of magnitude faster than ordinary A* search for Path planning in games and warehouse grids. Unlike Theta* it still produces grid-aligned paths, so any-angle smoothing may follow.

plain: Getting around by springing into the air in discrete leaps to clear obstacles instead of walking smoothly.
snappy: Ballistic locomotion that stores energy in springs or legs and releases it in a single impulsive push to launch the robot over obstacles.
detail: Jumping locomotion exploits energy storage (springs, elastic tendons, or a Series elastic actuator) charged slowly and released rapidly, so a small motor can produce a leap many times the robot's body height. It overlaps closely with Hopping and the Spring-loaded inverted pendulum model used to analyze repeated leaps, and many jumpers also need Self-righting to recover after an uncontrolled landing. The approach lets tiny robots clear barriers that would defeat Wheeled locomotion or Legged locomotion, at the cost of poor controllability mid-flight during the Flight phase.

plain: A method that keeps a running best guess of something by blending each new measurement with what it already expected.
snappy: A recursive estimator that optimally fuses model predictions with noisy measurements for linear-Gaussian systems.
detail: The Kalman filter alternates a predict step (advancing the state via a motion model) with an update step (correcting using a measurement), tracking both the estimate and its Uncertainty as a covariance. It is a cornerstone of State estimation, Localization, and Sensor fusion, for example merging Wheel odometry with an Inertial measurement unit. For the nonlinear models common in robotics it is extended into the Extended Kalman filter, and it contrasts with the sampling-based Particle filter.

plain: The robot-making division of Kawasaki, one of the first companies ever to sell industrial robot arms.
snappy: Japanese industrial-robot arm maker and one of the earliest commercial robot suppliers.
detail: Kawasaki Robotics produced some of the first commercial Industrial robot arm products (licensing Unimation technology in the 1960s) and remains a major Articulated robot supplier for Manufacturing. Its arms handle Robotic welding, Assembly, and Palletizing, and it co-developed the duAro dual-arm Cobot for Collaborative robot tasks. Kawasaki integrates its robots with its own Robot controller and Motion control software.

plain: A Japanese company supplying the sensors, cameras, and measuring tools that automated factories rely on.
snappy: A Japanese supplier of sensors, vision systems, and precision measurement instruments for factory automation.
detail: Keyence offers a broad catalog of factory sensing, including the Photoelectric sensor, Inductive Proximity Sensor, laser displacement gauges, and vision systems used for Quality inspection and part detection. Its Smart camera products guide robotic Pick and place and verify assembly, feeding results to the Programmable logic controller. Keyence competes head-to-head with Cognex in Machine vision and with SICK AG in sensing, and its measurement tools support Statistical process control on the line.

plain: Pinpointing the few most meaningful spots in an image, such as a person's joints or the corners of a box, so a machine can reason about shape and position.
snappy: Locating salient, semantically defined image points such as human joints, object corners, or part landmarks.
detail: Keypoint Detection predicts coordinates (often as heatmaps from a Convolutional neural network) for landmarks that define an object's structure, distinct from generic Feature extraction because the points are semantically labeled. It is the basis of Human pose estimation for Human-robot interaction and of object landmark detection that feeds Perspective-n-Point and 6D Pose Estimation for a grasp. On a Humanoid robot it supports imitation from human motion, and in Manufacturing it locates mating features for precise Pick and place; learned detectors like SuperPoint generalize it for SLAM correspondence.

plain: A way of describing an object to a robot by marking a few important points on it, like the rim of a mug or the handle of a tool, rather than its whole shape.
snappy: Encoding a manipulation goal as a small set of task-relevant landmark points on an object rather than its full pose or geometry.
detail: Instead of estimating a full 6D Pose Estimation for an object, a keypoint approach (popularized as kPAM) detects semantically meaningful points, such as the tip and heel of a shoe, and defines the task as moving those points to target locations. This makes manipulation robust to shape variation across object instances and pairs naturally with Imitation learning and language-conditioned manipulation. It is widely used in Manipulation pipelines where category-level Grasp planning must generalize beyond a single known model.

plain: A matching slot cut into a shaft and the part on it, holding a small bar so the two turn together without slipping.
snappy: A slot in a shaft and mating hub that seats a key to transmit torque between them.
detail: A Keyway is the rectangular groove machined into both a shaft and a surrounding hub; a metal key dropped into the aligned slots locks the two so they rotate together. It is the classic way to transmit mechanical torque from a motor shaft to a gear or pulley without relying on friction alone, and is common where a Gearbox output drives a Wheeled robot or a Gear Train. For heavier or sliding loads a Spline Shaft is preferred, while a Shaft Collar handles purely axial location.

plain: A series of rigid bars connected by movable joints that together form a moving machine.
snappy: An assembly of rigid links coupled by joints that constrains relative motion.
detail: Every robot manipulator is modeled as a Kinematic chain of rigid Link members joined by a Joint at each connection, and this structure is what Forward kinematics and Inverse kinematics compute over. A chain may be an Open kinematic chain like a Serial manipulator, or a Closed kinematic chain like a Stewart platform. The chain's geometry is commonly encoded with Denavit-Hartenberg parameters or described in a URDF file.

plain: A trick that splits the hard problem of posing a robot arm into two easier ones: first decide where the wrist sits, then decide which way the hand points.
snappy: Partitioning a manipulator's inverse kinematics into a position subproblem for the arm and an orientation subproblem at a spherical wrist.
detail: Kinematic Decoupling (wrist partitioning) exploits the Pieper Criterion: because a Spherical wrist places three axes through one point, the wrist center position depends only on the first three joints, so Inverse kinematics splits into solving arm reach first and then wrist orientation. This yields a Closed-form IK solution for the typical Six-axis robot and dramatically simplifies real-time control, calibration with Denavit-Hartenberg parameters, and singularity analysis (e.g., Wrist Singularity, Elbow Singularity). Manipulators lacking a spherical wrist forgo decoupling and rely on numerical solvers instead.

plain: Having more joints than the bare minimum needed for a task, giving the robot extra freedom to choose how it moves.
snappy: Having more degrees of freedom than the task strictly requires.
detail: A redundant manipulator, such as a seven-joint arm doing a six-Degrees of freedom task, has spare motion that lets it avoid obstacles, dodge a Kinematic singularity, or improve Manipulability while still hitting the target Pose. Those internal motions live in the Null space of the Jacobian matrix, and the Jacobian pseudoinverse exploits them for secondary objectives. Humanoid Whole-body control depends heavily on this extra freedom.

plain: A pose where a robot arm momentarily loses the ability to move smoothly in some direction and may need huge joint speeds.
snappy: A configuration where the Jacobian loses rank and end-effector motion degrades.
detail: At a singularity the Jacobian matrix drops rank, so some Task space directions become unreachable instantaneously and the Jacobian pseudoinverse demands near-infinite joint velocities. The classic case is a fully extended arm or an aligned Spherical wrist. Path planners and Inverse kinematics solvers actively steer around singularities, and the Manipulability measure falls to zero exactly at them, signalling the danger.

plain: The study of how things move, considering only the geometry of motion and ignoring the forces that cause it.
snappy: The geometric study of robot motion, relating joint positions to end-effector pose without regard to forces.
detail: Kinematics answers where the parts of a robot are and how they move geometrically: Forward kinematics maps joint angles to End-effector Pose, while Inverse kinematics goes the other way. It works over a Kinematic chain of each Joint and Link, often described with Denavit-Hartenberg parameters, and exposes pitfalls like a Kinematic singularity. It is distinct from Dynamics, which adds forces and torques into the picture.

plain: A code library that figures out where a robot arm's hand ends up and how its joints relate to motion.
snappy: A library for modeling and computing the kinematics and dynamics of robot joint chains, originally from the Orocos project.
detail: KDL represents a robot as a Kinematic chain of joints and links, then solves Forward kinematics, Inverse kinematics (via numerical and Jacobian-based solvers), and Inverse dynamics along that chain. It was long the default kinematics plugin inside MoveIt before faster analytic solvers became common, and it ships as part of the Orocos toolset. It is frequently compared with the Rigid Body Dynamics Library and Pinocchio for serial-manipulator work.

plain: Programming a robot by grabbing it and physically guiding its arm through the motions you want it to repeat.
snappy: Programming a manipulator by physically backdriving it through a task while recording the joint trajectory.
detail: Kinesthetic teaching, also called lead-through programming, has an operator physically move a Backdrivable actuator arm through a task while the controller records joint angles, often with Gravity Compensation active so the arm feels weightless. It is a hands-on alternative to a Teach pendant and to Offline programming, and is common on a Collaborative robot like the Franka Emika Panda or KUKA LBR iiwa. The recorded path can seed reusable Dynamic movement primitives or serve as Demonstration data for Learning from demonstration.

plain: Planning a robot's motion while obeying not just where it can go but how fast it can speed up, slow down, and turn at the same time.
snappy: Motion planning that simultaneously satisfies kinematic and dynamic limits on velocity, acceleration, and force.
detail: Kinodynamic planning searches the combined state-and-control space so that the resulting motion is physically executable, accounting for momentum, actuator torque limits, and the robot's Dynamics rather than treating it as a free-floating point. It matters for agile platforms such as a Drone, a Legged robot, or a fast Autonomous mobile robot, where ignoring inertia would yield infeasible commands. Sampling-based planning variants like a kinodynamic Rapidly-exploring random tree sample controls directly, while Trajectory optimization and Model predictive control take a continuous-optimization route to the same goal.

plain: A route planner for robots that can't stop or turn instantly, which grows its search by simulating how the robot actually moves under real controls.
snappy: An RRT that respects dynamics by forward-propagating control inputs through the robot's equations of motion rather than connecting states with straight geometric edges.
detail: Kinodynamic RRT extends the Rapidly-exploring random tree to Kinodynamic planning: instead of assuming any two nearby states can be joined by a straight line, it grows the tree by sampling control inputs and integrating the robot's dynamics forward, so every edge is a dynamically feasible Trajectory respecting velocity and acceleration limits. This is essential for car-like vehicles with a Nonholonomic constraint, drones, and other systems where geometric Motion planning would produce infeasible paths, and it is supported in OMPL. SST is a sparse, near-optimal successor that avoids needing a steering function.

plain: A company that makes lightweight robot arms used to help people with disabilities and for research.
snappy: Maker of lightweight assistive and research arms like the Jaco and Gen3.
detail: Kinova's Jaco is a lightweight assistive Manipulator that mounts on a wheelchair to let users with limited mobility grasp objects, while the Gen3 is a research-grade arm with a built-in vision module. Both are backdrivable, low-payload arms favored for safe Human-robot interaction and Compliance control studies, and ship with ROS drivers and Kinematics and Dynamics Library support. They are common research building blocks for Mobile manipulation when paired with a mobile base.

full: Karlsruhe Institute of Technology and Toyota Technological Institute
plain: One of the first big public datasets of car-mounted camera and laser-scanner recordings, used to test self-driving algorithms.
snappy: A pioneering autonomous-driving benchmark covering stereo, optical flow, visual odometry, and 3D object detection from a sensor-equipped car.
detail: KITTI established standardized tasks for 3D object detection, Visual odometry, Stereo matching, and Optical flow using synchronized camera and Velodyne LiDAR data. Though smaller than newer sets like nuScenes and the Waymo Open Dataset, it remains a reference for Lidar Point Cloud detectors such as PointPillars and PointNet. Many a Self-driving stack and SLAM paper still report KITTI numbers for comparability.

plain: A widely used public collection of real driving sensor recordings that researchers use to test self-driving perception and navigation algorithms.
snappy: A benchmark autonomous-driving dataset providing synchronized stereo, LiDAR, and GPS data with labels for odometry, detection, and stereo tasks.
detail: The KITTI Dataset records city, highway, and rural drives with a Velodyne LiDAR, a Stereo camera rig, and GPS/INS Ground truth, and publishes leaderboards for Visual odometry, 3D object detection, Stereo matching, and SLAM. It became the standard yardstick for Autonomous vehicle perception, where methods like PointNet and Semantic segmentation models report KITTI scores. Though now complemented by larger sets such as the nuScenes and Waymo Open Dataset, KITTI remains a default first benchmark for embodied driving perception.

plain: Gathering all the parts needed to build one product into a single tray or box so assembly can start without hunting for components.
snappy: Grouping all components for one assembly into a single kit or container ahead of the build station.
detail: Kitting pre-stages every part for an assembly into one container, so a Production line or robot cell receives a complete, sequenced set instead of pulling from scattered bins. Robotic kitting uses Pick and place with Bin picking and a Parallel-jaw gripper or Suction gripper to assemble kits from a Goods-to-person feed. It supports lean Line balancing and Part feeding, and the kit lists are released and tracked by the Warehouse management system or the Manufacturing execution system.

plain: A robot forming and pulling tight a knot in rope, thread, or surgical stitching.
snappy: Forming and tightening knots in rope, suture, or cord, requiring coordinated bimanual control of a deformable linear object.
detail: Knot Tying requires a robot to wrap, thread, and cinch a flexible strand whose shape constantly changes, making it a demanding case of Deformable Linear Object Manipulation. It almost always uses Bimanual manipulation with state tracking from a Depth camera or Visual servoing and policies learned via Imitation learning or a Diffusion policy. In Medical & Surgical robotics, suturing knots are a core Dexterous manipulation skill on systems like Intuitive Surgical platforms, and the same methods transfer to industrial Lacing and Cable Routing.

plain: A company developing self-driving long-haul trucks that can carry freight on highways without a human driver.
snappy: An autonomous-trucking company building a driverless system specialized for long-haul highway freight.
detail: Kodiak Robotics (Kodiak) focuses its Automated driving system on highway lanes, a constrained Operational design domain that simplifies Motion planning and Trajectory Prediction relative to dense urban Robotaxi operations. Its Self-driving truck stack fuses LiDAR, camera, and Radar via Sensor fusion and uses redundant Drive-by-wire actuation for Fail-operational behavior. It competes with Aurora and the trucking arm of Pony.ai in the freight Platooning and long-haul space.

full: Kinodynamic Planning by Interior-Exterior Cell Exploration
plain: A planning method that explores a robot's possible motions by pushing into the parts of the space it has barely visited yet.
snappy: A tree-based kinodynamic planner that biases tree growth toward sparsely explored cells using interior-exterior coverage estimates.
detail: KPIECE grows a search tree by projecting states into a low-dimensional grid and preferentially expanding from cells on the frontier of coverage, distinguishing interior (well-surrounded) from exterior cells to direct effort where the space is thin. This makes it effective for Kinodynamic planning of systems with drift and tight dynamics, where forward propagation rather than steering is required, such as planning motions for an Autonomous vehicle or an underactuated platform subject to a Nonholonomic constraint. As a form of Sampling-based planning it is distributed in OMPL alongside Kinodynamic RRT and the Probabilistic roadmap, but targets Motion planning problems where straight-line connections between states are not valid.
aliases: Kinodynamic Planning by Interior-Exterior Cell Exploration

plain: A German company famous for its orange factory robot arms used to build cars and other products.
snappy: German industrial-robot maker of articulated arms and complete automation cells.
detail: KUKA is a leading maker of the Industrial robot arm, recognizable by its orange Articulated robot models heavily used in automotive Manufacturing for Robotic welding and Assembly. It also produces the LBR iiwa, a torque-sensing Cobot for Collaborative robot work, plus complete Robot cell automation. KUKA programs its arms through a Teach pendant and its KRL language, prioritizing Repeatability and Payload capacity.

plain: A sensitive seven-joint robot arm from KUKA that measures the force in each joint, so it can do delicate assembly and work safely beside people.
snappy: KUKA's seven-axis torque-controlled collaborative arm designed for sensitive force-aware assembly tasks.
detail: The KUKA LBR iiwa is a Seven-axis robot from KUKA with a Joint Torque Sensor at each axis, enabling Cartesian impedance control and Hybrid position/force control for sensitive operations like Peg-in-hole and Connector Mating. As a Collaborative robot it supports Hand guiding and Power and force limiting under ISO/TS 15066, letting it share a Collaborative workspace without fences. It competes with the Franka Emika Panda and Universal Robots UR series as a research and light-assembly platform, and is programmed through KUKA Sunrise or ROS-Industrial drivers.

plain: A number that tells you how fast a drone motor spins for each volt you feed it, which helps match motors to propellers.
snappy: A motor's velocity constant in RPM per volt, used to balance the thrust-versus-efficiency trade when pairing motors and propellers.
detail: KV rating expresses how many unloaded RPM a Brushless DC motor turns per applied volt, so a high-KV motor spins a small Propeller fast for an agile FPV racing drone while a low-KV motor swings a large prop efficiently for endurance. It is inversely related to the motor's torque constant and is selected together with battery voltage, the Electronic speed controller, and prop pitch to hit a target Thrust-to-weight ratio. Mismatched KV either bogs the motor down or overheats it.

plain: A fast-adapting controller designed so that reacting quickly to changes does not make it twitchy or unstable.
snappy: Adaptive control that uses a low-pass filter to decouple fast parameter estimation from loop robustness, enabling rapid adaptation with guaranteed margins.
detail: The L1 architecture separates a fast estimator from the control law via a bandwidth-limiting low-pass filter, so adaptation speed can be raised without the high-frequency chatter and Phase margin loss that plague classic Model reference adaptive control. It has been demonstrated on agile UAV flight and Learned quadrotor control where rapid Disturbance rejection is needed but robustness cannot be sacrificed. It is a modern branch of Adaptive control with explicit Robust control guarantees.

plain: The number of human working hours a robot system takes over, which is the main money-saving reason a company buys it.
snappy: The volume of human-labor hours a robot deployment replaces, expressed as full-time-equivalent headcount and used as the primary automation business case.
detail: Labor Displacement is the headline metric in most automation purchase decisions: how many full-time-equivalent workers a deployment offsets, which feeds directly into Return on investment and Total cost of ownership calculations. It is especially salient in Manufacturing and Logistics & Warehouse settings where a Cobot or Autonomous mobile robot fleet absorbs repetitive Material handling and Palletizing tasks. The displacement case is strongest where a chronic Labor shortage exists, and buyers increasingly weigh it against the offsetting need for Workforce Reskilling so displaced staff move into supervision and maintenance roles.

plain: Not having enough people willing or available to do certain jobs, which is the main reason many businesses turn to robots.
snappy: A scarcity of available workers, cited as the primary demand driver pulling robots into warehouses and factories.
detail: A labor shortage reframes automation from a cost-cutting choice into a necessity: when shifts go unfilled, robots do the work that would otherwise not get done at all, which sharply improves Return on investment. It is the dominant narrative behind warehouse Goods-to-person systems, factory Machine tending, and the surge of interest in a general-purpose Humanoid robot. The same pressure underpins Reshoring, because companies will only bring production home if robots can cover the workers they cannot hire.

plain: Threading a flexible strand through a series of holes or loops in order, like lacing a shoe or routing wire through eyelets.
snappy: Sequentially threading a flexible strand through holes, eyelets, or loops, combining insertion with deformable-strand control.
detail: Lacing threads a cable, lace, or wire through an ordered set of holes or eyelets, combining Peg-in-hole-style insertion with the state tracking of Deformable Linear Object Manipulation. Each pass needs alignment via Visual servoing and gentle Compliance control or Force control so the strand feeds without snagging, and the changing shape usually demands Bimanual manipulation. A specialized Manufacturing wire-lacing and threading task, it shares perception and policy techniques with Cable Routing and Knot Tying.

plain: A way of programming factory controllers by drawing diagrams that look like rungs of a ladder, mimicking old electrical relay wiring.
snappy: A graphical PLC programming language whose rungs visually represent relay-circuit control logic.
detail: Ladder logic (or ladder diagram) is the oldest and most widely used of the languages defined by IEC 61131-3, designed so electricians familiar with relay panels could read a Programmable logic controller program at a glance. Each rung shows contacts and coils flowing left to right, expressing conditions like 'if guard closed AND start pressed, energize motor.' It coexists with Structured text and the Function block diagram, and is the default for discrete machine control, interlocks, and sequencing on a Production line.

plain: A method that derives a robot's motion equations from its energy of movement and its stored energy, instead of tracking every force directly.
snappy: Deriving the equations of motion from a system's kinetic and potential energy.
detail: Lagrangian (Euler-Lagrange) mechanics writes down a system's kinetic minus potential energy and differentiates it to produce the Equations of motion, automatically yielding the Mass matrix and Coriolis and centrifugal forces without bookkeeping every internal constraint force. It is the textbook route to Rigid body dynamics for a Kinematic chain. For real-time computation engineers usually prefer the recursive Newton-Euler dynamics, which gives the same answer faster.

plain: A distinctive, easily recognized feature in the environment that a robot uses to figure out where it is.
snappy: A distinctive, re-observable environment feature used as a reference for localization and mapping.
detail: A landmark is a stable, recognizable feature, a corner, a sign, a tree, that a robot can spot repeatedly and use to fix its position. In SLAM and Visual SLAM the robot stores landmarks in its Map and uses Data association to recognize them again, refining its Localization through a Kalman filter or factor graph. Re-seeing a previously mapped landmark enables Loop closure, which corrects accumulated Drift in the trajectory; landmarks are detected via Feature extraction.

plain: Spotting the painted lines on a road from a camera so the vehicle knows where its lane is.
snappy: Detecting and localizing road lane markings from camera imagery to define drivable lane boundaries.
detail: Lane detection finds the painted lane lines and their geometry so a vehicle can stay centered, change lanes, or follow the road. It is the perception behind Lane keeping assist and a Highway pilot, and its output can be fused with an HD map or a Lane graph for robustness when markings are faded. In a Mobility stack it works alongside Traffic sign recognition and Free space detection, often built on a Convolutional neural network and projected into a Bird's-eye view.

plain: A map that connects road lanes together like a network, showing which lane leads to which, so a car knows where it can go.
snappy: A graph representation of lane segments and their connectivity used for routing, behavior prediction, and planning.
detail: A lane graph encodes nodes and edges for lane centerlines, successors, and neighbors, giving the planner a structured road model that constrains where the ego vehicle and other agents can travel. It is usually part of an HD map (the Lanelet format is one encoding) and is consumed by route planning, behavior prediction, and motion planning. Both nuScenes and the Waymo Open Dataset ship lane-graph map layers, and mapless driving aims to infer this connectivity live instead of relying on a prebuilt road graph.

plain: A system that gently steers the car to keep it centered in its lane if it starts to drift.
snappy: A driver-assistance feature that applies steering corrections to keep the vehicle centered within its detected lane.
detail: Lane keeping assist (LKA) uses a camera and lane detection to find lane markings, then commands small steering inputs through drive-by-wire to hold the vehicle in its lane. As an SAE Level 1 to 2 advanced driver-assistance systems feature, it combines with adaptive cruise control to deliver a highway pilot experience. It typically works with a driver monitoring system so the driver stays engaged, and degrades gracefully when lane markings vanish.

plain: A small map building block that describes one stretch of a driving lane and how it connects to others.
snappy: A map primitive representing an atomic drivable lane segment with its boundaries, connectivity, and traffic rules.
detail: A Lanelet (popularized by the open Lanelet2 format) encodes a lane segment's left and right bounds plus links to predecessor, successor, and adjacent lanes, forming a routable Lane graph inside an HD map. The Self-driving stack uses lanelets for Route planning and to constrain Behavior planning to legal paths, and Map-relative localization positions the Ego vehicle within them. They sit alongside Occupancy grid representations, encoding rules rather than raw geometry.

plain: A robot arm that does what you tell it in plain words, like 'put the red block in the bowl.'
snappy: Manipulation where a natural-language instruction conditions the policy's behavior on the requested task.
detail: Language-conditioned manipulation lets a user steer a robot arm with text or speech, so the same network performs many jobs based on the words it receives, a language-driven Goal-conditioned policy. It is the interface exposed by a Vision-language-action model such as RT-2 and OpenVLA, trained on language-labeled Demonstration data. Strong language grounding supports Zero-shot generalization to new instructions and is a defining feature of a modern Generalist policy.

plain: The final short trip that brings a package or meal from a local hub directly to the customer's door, a job some robots are now built to do.
snappy: The final leg of delivery to the end customer, a target market for sidewalk robots and delivery drones.
detail: Last-mile delivery is the most expensive and labor-intensive segment of logistics, which makes it a prime automation target. On the ground a Sidewalk delivery robot or wheeled Delivery robot navigates pavements using Localization and Obstacle avoidance, while in the air Drone delivery handles rural or congested routes, often requiring BVLOS operations approval. Both rely on a Remote operation center for human oversight, and economics hinge on cost per drop versus a human courier.

plain: Letting each sensor figure out what it sees on its own first, then merging those separate answers into one decision.
snappy: A fusion strategy that combines per-modality detections or tracks after each sensor pipeline runs independently.
detail: In Late Fusion (also called Decision-level fusion) a camera, an Automotive radar, and a LiDAR each produce their own detections, which are then associated and merged, often via the Hungarian Algorithm or a Kalman filter tracker. It is modular and fault-tolerant because a Sensor dropout in one modality degrades gracefully, but it discards cross-modal cues that Early Fusion preserves. It is a common backbone for Multi-object tracking and Object-Level Fusion in a Self-driving stack.

plain: The short delay between something happening and the machine reacting to it.
snappy: The time gap between an input event and the system producing its response.
detail: In robotics, latency in the Perception-action loop directly limits how fast and stable a robot can be: a humanoid running Balance control or a Self-driving car braking for a Pedestrian detection event both need end-to-end delay measured in milliseconds. Sources of delay include Sensor latency, network hops, and inference time on the Onboard compute, which is why high-stakes loops favor Edge computing over Cloud robotics. It is closely related to Control rate and Bandwidth, and excessive latency degrades Real-time computing guarantees.

plain: A compressed inner map a model uses to summarize what it sees or does, with fewer numbers than the raw data.
snappy: A lower-dimensional learned feature space encoding observations or actions in a compact, structured form.
detail: A latent space is the product of Representation learning: high-dimensional Camera frames or motor commands are squeezed into a small vector that captures the essentials for control. ACT and Diffusion policy plan actions partly in such spaces, and a Variational autoencoder explicitly learns one. Compressing observations into a latent space improves Sample efficiency and lets a Policy generalize, since nearby points correspond to similar situations or motions.

plain: A planner that builds routes only from a fixed menu of pre-computed drivable motion snippets that respect how the vehicle can actually move.
snappy: A search planner over a precomputed lattice of feasible motion primitives that respect vehicle kinematics.
detail: A Lattice Planner discretizes the state space into a regular State lattice and connects nodes only with precomputed, dynamically feasible Motion primitive segments, so every path it produces already satisfies the platform's Nonholonomic constraint. Searching this lattice with A* search or its anytime variants yields drivable routes for an Autonomous vehicle or planetary rover, unlike a grid path that may require post hoc smoothing. It is a structured alternative to sampling planners such as RRT* and is frequently paired with a Lattice and Spline Optimization refinement step.

plain: A script that starts up many robot programs at once with the right settings, instead of you typing each command by hand.
snappy: A declarative script (roslaunch or ros2 launch) describing which nodes, parameters, and arguments to start together as one system.
detail: A Launch File brings up a whole robot system in one command, specifying each Node to start, its Namespace and Remapping, and the parameter values to load onto the Parameter Server. In ROS 2 launch files are usually written in Python and can conditionally include other launch files, set up a robot_state_publisher, or start a simulator like Gazebo. For example, one launch file might start a camera driver, an AMCL localizer, and the Nav2 stack together.

plain: An outdoor robot that mows the grass on its own, staying inside a yard you have marked out for it.
snappy: An autonomous outdoor Service robot that mows grass within a bounded area, kept inside by a perimeter wire or satellite-based geofence.
detail: A lawn-mowing robot is an outdoor cousin of the Cleaning robot, traditionally confined by a buried boundary wire and more recently by RTK GNSS so it knows its position to centimeters. It runs a Coverage path planning routine — often a Lawnmower survey pattern — across the yard while Obstacle detection and a Bumper Sensor handle toys, pets, and trees. As a battery-powered Service robotics product, it returns autonomously for Wireless charging and increasingly uses Geofencing instead of physical wires to define the mow zone.

plain: A flight path made of parallel back-and-forth lines, like mowing a lawn, so a drone photographs every part of an area evenly.
snappy: A boustrophedon flight pattern of parallel, evenly spaced sweeps that gives uniform image overlap across a survey area.
detail: The lawnmower survey pattern is the default route for mapping missions, generated by Coverage Path Planning so that successive passes maintain the photogrammetric overlap needed for Aerial photogrammetry. A Ground control station plans the lines from the camera's field of view and target Ground sample distance, then uploads them as a Waypoint sequence to the autopilot. It is the workhorse trajectory behind producing a clean Orthomosaic or Digital surface model, and fixed-wing mappers from Wingtra rely on it for large-area coverage.

plain: A route planner that first builds a network of possible connections assuming everything is clear, and only checks for obstacles along the specific path it picks.
snappy: A roadmap planner that builds and searches a Probabilistic roadmap without collision-checking edges, validating only the edges on a candidate shortest path and removing any that are blocked.
detail: Lazy PRM cuts the dominant cost of a Probabilistic roadmap, which is Collision detection on every edge, by assuming all edges are free, running a graph search such as A* search for the shortest path, then checking only that path's edges and re-searching if any are invalid. This lazy-evaluation idea also underpins BIT* and other modern Sampling-based planning methods, and it is offered in OMPL for high-dimensional arm Motion planning. The tradeoff is repeated re-searches when many candidate edges turn out to be blocked.

plain: A fast messaging system that lets the programs on a robot share data with very little delay.
snappy: A low-latency publish-subscribe messaging and serialization library designed for tightly coupled real-time robotic systems.
detail: LCM uses UDP multicast to broadcast typed messages with minimal overhead, making it popular where Latency and Jitter matter, such as DARPA Robotics Challenge humanoids and autonomous-vehicle stacks. It serves a similar role to ROS topics and DDS but trades features for simplicity and speed, and it pairs with tools that record a log for Deterministic Replay. Its compact wire format competes with Protocol Buffers for compact message marshalling.

plain: A threaded rod that turns rotary motion from a motor into straight-line pushing or pulling.
snappy: A threaded power screw that converts rotational motion into linear motion via sliding thread contact.
detail: A Lead screw uses sliding threads to drive a nut along a straight path, giving a simple, low-cost, often self-locking Linear actuator for a Prismatic joint. The sliding contact creates friction and wear, so where high efficiency or speed matters engineers switch to a Ball screw. It commonly runs on a Linear guide and is turned by a Stepper motor or Servomotor.

plain: A robot team setup where one robot leads and the others simply keep a set distance and angle behind it.
snappy: A multi-robot control scheme in which follower robots maintain prescribed positions relative to a designated leader.
detail: Leader-follower control, also called convoying, is the simplest route to Formation control: each follower holds a fixed offset from a leader using relative Localization, so the human or autonomous leader's path is implicitly shared. It appears in vehicle Platooning, autonomous convoying for Defense & Security, and Mobility applications where a robot trails a person. The scheme is easy to implement under Decentralized control but has a clear weakness, the leader is a Single point of failure, motivating distributed Consensus algorithm variants with no fixed leader.

plain: Controlling a robot by moving a smaller hand-held copy of it, with the robot mimicking your movements.
snappy: Teleoperation where an operator-manipulated leader device commands a kinematically matched follower robot to replicate its motion.
detail: In leader-follower teleoperation the operator moves a leader arm and a matching follower robot tracks it joint-for-joint, the scheme behind ALOHA and Mobile ALOHA data collection and most Surgical robot consoles. When forces are reflected back it becomes Bilateral teleoperation; without that it is position-only. The captured leader-follower trajectories are a prime source of Demonstration data for Imitation learning and a Vision-language-action model, making it foundational to modern manipulation training.

plain: An open-source, low-cost robotic hand that researchers can 3D-print and build to study how robots grasp and manipulate.
snappy: An open-source, low-cost anthropomorphic hand designed to make dexterous manipulation research accessible.
detail: The LEAP Hand is an open-source, 3D-printable Anthropomorphic hand built around inexpensive Dynamixel servos, lowering the cost barrier that platforms like the Allegro Hand and Shadow Dexterous Hand pose for Dexterous manipulation research. Its open design makes it a common testbed for Reinforcement learning policies trained with Sim-to-real transfer and for In-hand manipulation experiments. It can be instrumented with a DIGIT tactile sensor for Contact-rich manipulation.

plain: A neural network trained to predict exactly how a robot's motors really respond, so a robot taught in simulation behaves the same way in the real world.
snappy: A neural network capturing real actuator dynamics to close the sim-to-real gap in learned control.
detail: A Learned Actuator Model fits a small Neural network to measured motor data so a simulator reproduces the true torque produced for a given commanded torque, current, and joint state, capturing effects like Friction Compensation residuals, Reflected Inertia, and latency that idealized models miss. Inserting this network into the loop during Massively parallel reinforcement learning is a cornerstone technique for Sim-to-real transfer of Learned locomotion on a quadruped or Humanoid robot, popularized by the actuator-network work behind the ANYmal and MIT Cheetah Actuator. It is trained from logs of real Torque Control Mode commands and outcomes.

plain: Letting a robot figure out how to pick up objects by learning from lots of examples instead of being given a hand-written formula for each shape.
snappy: Predicting where and how to grip an object directly from sensor data and learned models, rather than from analytic contact geometry.
detail: Learned grasping trains a model to output a Grasp pose or Grasp planning proposal from a Depth camera image or Point cloud, sidestepping the brittle analytic Force closure and Grasp matrix computations used in classical Grasping. It underpins reliable Bin picking and Pick and place in Logistics & Warehouse settings, often paired with a Parallel-jaw gripper or Suction gripper, and is commonly trained with Synthetic data plus Domain randomization. Systems like those at Amazon Robotics use it to handle the long tail of novel items in an Unstructured environment.

plain: Teaching a walking robot how to move by letting it practice millions of times in a computer simulation rather than hand-coding every step.
snappy: Walking, trotting, or running gaits acquired by training a control policy with reinforcement learning, typically in simulation before transfer to hardware.
detail: Learned locomotion replaces hand-tuned gait controllers with a Policy trained by Reinforcement learning, often a Neural network that maps Proprioception to joint targets at high Control rate. It powers modern Legged locomotion on a Quadruped robot or Humanoid robot, with training accelerated by Massively parallel simulation and made robust through Domain randomization and Sim-to-real transfer. Boston Dynamics, ANYbotics, and Unitree controllers increasingly rely on it to handle Terrain adaptation that Zero moment point methods struggle with.

plain: Using a trained neural network, rather than hand-written formulas, to decide how to spin a drone's motors to fly it.
snappy: Replacing hand-tuned UAV control loops with a neural-network policy that maps state directly to motor commands.
detail: Learned quadrotor control trains a Neural network policy, often via Reinforcement learning in massively parallel simulation, to map drone state to rotor thrust, supplanting cascaded PID and Model predictive control. The robotics challenge is Sim-to-real transfer: closing the Reality gap with Domain randomization so the policy survives unmodeled effects like Downwash and Wind disturbance rejection. This approach powered champion-level Autonomous drone racing and is attractive for agile flight where classical controllers struggle to exploit the full Thrust-to-weight ratio.

plain: Teaching a robot a skill by showing it how, instead of writing code line by line.
snappy: A paradigm where a robot acquires skills from human-provided demonstrations rather than from hand-coded programs or trial-and-error.
detail: Learning from demonstration captures example trajectories, often via Teleoperation, Hand guiding, or kinesthetic teaching, then fits a model that reproduces and generalizes the behavior. It underpins Imitation learning and Behavioral cloning and is the data engine behind a modern Vision-language-action model, where large Demonstration data sets teach manipulation Skills. On a factory cobot an operator can guide the arm through a Pick and place once, and the robot replays a smoothed Trajectory, sidestepping explicit programming.

plain: Control where the rules for moving the machine are learned from data and experience instead of being worked out by hand from physics.
snappy: Control policies obtained by training on data, rather than derived analytically from a dynamics model.
detail: Learning-based control trains a Policy (often a Neural network) via Reinforcement learning, Imitation learning, or System identification, and is how a Quadruped robot like Spot or ANYmal acquires Learned locomotion that is hard to hand-derive with Nonlinear control. Policies are typically trained in Massively parallel simulation (e.g. Isaac Lab) with Domain randomization, then crossed over via Sim-to-real transfer. It is increasingly fused with model-based methods like Model predictive control and Adaptive control, and extends to a Vision-language-action model for manipulation.

plain: Moving by stepping on legs instead of rolling on wheels.
snappy: Locomotion using discrete intermittent foot contacts with the ground rather than continuous wheels or tracks.
detail: Legged locomotion trades the efficiency of Wheeled locomotion for the ability to cross rough, broken, or stepped terrain by choosing where to plant each foot. It demands Foothold selection, careful Balance control, and a chosen Gait, and powers platforms from a Bipedal robot to a Quadruped robot. Modern systems increasingly use Learned locomotion trained in Isaac Sim and transferred via Sim-to-real to handle Terrain adaptation.

plain: Any robot that walks on legs instead of rolling on wheels or tracks.
snappy: A robot that locomotes using articulated legs, enabling travel over terrain impassable to wheels.
detail: Legged robots include the Bipedal robot, Quadruped robot, and Hexapod robot, and they trade mechanical and control complexity for the ability to step over gaps and climb stairs via Legged locomotion. Control relies on Foothold selection, the Support polygon, Whole-body control, and concepts like Zero moment point and Center of mass tracking. Modern legged platforms increasingly use Reinforcement learning with Sim-to-real transfer for Learned locomotion across Terrain adaptation.

plain: Moving in a way that makes it easy for people watching to guess what the robot is about to do.
snappy: A property of robot motion that lets an observer rapidly and confidently infer the robot's intended goal.
detail: Legibility is distinct from mere predictability: a legible Trajectory may exaggerate its early commitment so a human reads the goal sooner, for instance a Mobile manipulator clearly reaching toward one of several objects, or a Collaborative robot signaling which way it will move in a shared cell. It is a key output of Intent communication and underpins safe Joint action and Human-robot interaction. Legible motion is often generated within Motion planning by adding a cost term that rewards goal-revealing paths, trading a little Trajectory optimization efficiency for clarity.

plain: The way a camera lens bends straight lines into curves, especially near the edges of the picture.
snappy: Geometric warping of the image introduced by real lens optics, predominantly radial barrel or pincushion plus tangential components.
detail: Lens Distortion, mostly radial distortion seen as barrel distortion in wide-angle lenses, displaces pixels from their ideal perspective positions and must be modeled and removed before any precise geometry. Camera calibration estimates the distortion coefficients alongside the Camera intrinsics so images can be undistorted and Image rectification can enforce clean Epipolar Geometry for Stereo matching. Uncorrected distortion biases Perspective-n-Point pose and corrupts measurements in machine-vision metrology and Visual odometry.

plain: An open-source toolkit and shared library of real robot recordings that helps people train robots using machine learning.
snappy: Hugging Face's open-source library and dataset hub for real-world robot learning, models, and reproducible training pipelines.
detail: LeRobot standardizes datasets, model checkpoints, and training code for Imitation learning and Reinforcement learning on physical robots, lowering the barrier to reproducing policies like a Diffusion policy or ACT controller. It hosts Demonstration data collected via Teleoperation rigs such as ALOHA and supports affordable arms, connecting to Vision-language-action model research and Robot foundation model efforts. By sharing data and weights openly, it addresses Robot data scarcity the way large image datasets did for vision.

plain: A self-driving system that fully drives itself within certain conditions, with no human backup needed.
snappy: High driving automation where the system performs the entire dynamic driving task within its operational design domain without expecting human fallback.
detail: At Level 4 automation (L4) on the SAE levels of driving automation, the Automated driving system handles everything inside its Operational design domain and resolves failures itself by reaching a Minimal risk condition, so no Fallback-ready human is required. A driverless Robotaxi from Waymo or an Autonomous shuttle on a fixed route are canonical L4 deployments, typically Geofencing-bounded. Outside the ODD the vehicle simply will not engage, distinguishing it from the unbounded Level 5 automation.

plain: A self-driving system that can drive anywhere a person could, in any condition, with no human help.
snappy: Full driving automation that performs the dynamic driving task under all conditions a human driver could manage, with no operational design domain limits.
detail: Level 5 automation (L5) is the top of the SAE levels of driving automation: there is no Operational design domain restriction, so the Automated driving system handles any road, weather, and traffic a person could. No production vehicle has achieved it; today's driverless services like Waymo and Cruise are Level 4 automation, geofenced and weather-limited. L5 would eliminate the steering wheel entirely and remove any notion of a Takeover request or human Fallback.

plain: A graded scale describing how much a machine can do on its own versus how much a human must step in.
snappy: A graded scale classifying how much a system operates without human input, from full manual control to full self-direction.
detail: Levels of autonomy formalize the spectrum of Autonomy so engineers and regulators can talk about partial versus full self-direction precisely. The best-known example is the SAE levels of driving automation (Level 0 to Level 5), where an Automated driving system progresses from driver assistance up to Level 4 automation and Level 5 automation. Similar graded scales describe a Drone or an Autonomous mobile robot, with human roles spanning Teleoperation, Supervised autonomy, and Shared autonomy.

plain: A high-quality driving simulator that lets self-driving software companies test their cars in lifelike virtual worlds.
snappy: A high-fidelity, game-engine-based autonomous-driving simulator built to integrate tightly with the Autoware and Apollo stacks.
detail: The LGSVL Simulator (SVL Simulator) provides sensor-accurate LiDAR, camera, and Radar models and a bridge to ROS and ROS 2, letting teams run their real Self-driving stack against simulated traffic. It consumes OpenDRIVE road networks and OpenSCENARIO sequences for Scenario-based testing, much like the CARLA Simulator. It was widely paired with Autoware and Apollo for Hardware-in-the-loop simulation before development wound down.

plain: A sensor that fires invisible laser pulses and times how long they take to bounce back, building a precise 3D picture of the surroundings.
snappy: A ranging sensor that measures distance to surfaces by timing reflected laser pulses, producing dense 3D depth data.
detail: LiDAR is a cornerstone of Mobility and autonomous vehicle Perception, emitting many laser beams and computing distance from time-of-flight to build a Point cloud of the scene. It comes in Mechanical LiDAR, Solid-state LiDAR, Flash LiDAR, and FMCW LiDAR variants, and its output feeds Localization, Mapping, and SLAM as well as Camera-lidar fusion. Compared with Radar it offers far finer spatial detail but struggles in heavy fog or rain.

plain: A technique that uses a spinning laser scanner to figure out, in real time, how a vehicle is moving and to build a map as it goes.
snappy: A real-time lidar SLAM method that splits low-drift odometry from slower background map-building for accurate motion estimation.
detail: Lidar Odometry and Mapping (LOAM) extracts edge and planar features from each Lidar Point Cloud and registers consecutive scans for fast Odometry, while a lower-rate thread refines the Map. It pioneered the two-thread design later extended by LIO-SAM and FAST-LIO, which add Inertial measurement unit fusion. LOAM remains a foundational SLAM approach for Localization in a Self-driving stack and field robots, often benchmarked on KITTI.

plain: The collection of thousands of 3D dots a laser scanner produces, each marking where a beam bounced off something around the vehicle.
snappy: The set of 3D range returns produced by a LiDAR, sampling the surfaces of the scene as a sparse cloud of points.
detail: A Lidar Point Cloud is the raw geometric output a LiDAR feeds into a Self-driving stack, where it drives Ground segmentation, 3D object detection, and Point cloud registration for localization. Networks such as PointPillars and PointNet consume it directly, and it is the data type combined with imagery in Camera-lidar fusion. Each return also carries an Intensity Return value, and a Mechanical Spinning Lidar generates a fresh sweep many times per second.

plain: Working out exactly where a laser scanner sits relative to a camera so their views can be overlaid precisely.
snappy: Estimating the rigid 6-DoF transform between a LiDAR and a camera so 3D points project correctly onto image pixels.
detail: LiDAR-Camera Calibration solves for the extrinsic transform between a LiDAR and a Camera so that each Point cloud point lands on the correct image pixel, enabling Camera-lidar fusion for colored point clouds and 3D object detection. It typically aligns shared features, such as a planar target or checkerboard edges seen in both the image and the LiDAR Intensity Return, refining the Special Euclidean group SE(3) pose. Accurate extrinsics, together with Temporal Calibration, are prerequisites for reliable Sensor fusion on a Self-driving car.

plain: Figuring out exactly where a laser scanner sits relative to a camera so their data can be lined up in one shared 3D frame.
snappy: Estimating the rigid 6-DoF transform between a lidar and a camera so points project correctly onto the image.
detail: Lidar-Camera Extrinsic Calibration solves for the rotation and translation (a Homogeneous transformation matrix) relating the LiDAR frame to the Camera frame, often by matching a Checkerboard Calibration target or planar features seen by both. Combined with the camera's intrinsics, it lets 3D points overlay pixels for Camera-lidar fusion in detectors like BEVFusion and for coloring a Point cloud. Mobility and Manufacturing robots depend on it; even small errors blur the projection, so it is paired with Temporal Calibration to align timestamps as well.

plain: The mathematical space of tiny rotation changes, where each spin is written as a small three-by-three pattern that turns into an actual rotation when you let it run.
snappy: The tangent space of the rotation group SO(3): the set of 3x3 skew-symmetric matrices that map to angular velocity and exponentiate to rotation matrices.
detail: The Lie Algebra so(3) is the linearization of the Special orthogonal group SO(3) at the identity; its skew-symmetric matrices correspond to angular-velocity vectors, and the matrix exponential carries them back to a Rotation matrix. This structure underpins how robots integrate gyroscope readings, interpolate orientations alongside the Quaternion and Axis-angle representation, and linearize attitude error in state estimation such as the Extended Kalman filter. It generalizes to the Special Euclidean group SE(3) for full pose, where the Adjoint Representation and Screw theory describe rigid motion, and it is foundational to the Product of Exponentials Formula.

plain: A robot program that follows a defined startup and shutdown sequence so the system can bring it online in a predictable order.
snappy: A managed ROS 2 node with explicit unconfigured, inactive, active, and finalized states and transitions like configure, activate, and shutdown.
detail: A Lifecycle Node, also called a managed node, exposes a state machine so an orchestrator can configure it (allocate resources), activate it (start publishing), deactivate it, and clean it up in a controlled sequence. This determinism is valuable for safety-relevant systems where you must guarantee, say, that a Controller Manager and its sensors are fully configured before motion is allowed. A Launch File or supervisor drives these transitions, and the pattern is built on top of the same rclcpp and rclpy machinery as an ordinary Node.

plain: A robot that keeps picking up new skills over time without forgetting the ones it already knew.
snappy: Continually acquiring new skills and knowledge over a deployment lifetime while retaining previously learned ones.
detail: Lifelong learning, or continual learning, is what a Service robot in a changing home needs as it meets new objects and chores after deployment, building on Online adaptation. Its central obstacle is Catastrophic forgetting, where training on new tasks erases old skills, so methods use replay or regularization to protect prior knowledge. It is closely tied to Transfer learning and Meta-learning and is a stepping stone toward a robust Generalist policy.

plain: Continuously routing a whole fleet of robots that keep getting new pickup-and-delivery jobs, replanning on the fly as tasks arrive instead of solving one fixed problem.
snappy: A continual formulation of multi-agent path finding (also called MAPD) where agents are repeatedly assigned new goals and must be re-routed online as tasks stream in.
detail: Lifelong MAPF (Lifelong Multi-Agent Path Finding, or multi-agent pickup and delivery, MAPD) drops the assumption that every robot has a single fixed goal: instead robots continuously receive new tasks and the system must jointly handle Task allocation and ongoing Replanning so the fleet keeps flowing. It is the formulation behind real Logistics & Warehouse robot fleets and typically relies on fast solvers like PIBT rather than the one-shot optimal Conflict-Based Search. It feeds a fleet-level Traffic Management System that resolves congestion across the floor.

plain: A flying-taxi design that uses one set of upward-facing rotors just for taking off and landing vertically, and a completely separate forward propeller and wings for normal flight, so no part has to do both jobs.
snappy: An eVTOL configuration with dedicated vertical-lift rotors for takeoff and landing plus a separate fixed propulsion system and fixed wing for forward cruise.
