snappy: Medtronic's modular robotic-assisted surgery (RAS) system competing with Intuitive Surgical's da Vinci.
detail: The Medtronic Hugo RAS system uses separate arm carts and an open surgeon console to perform minimally invasive surgery, with each arm pivoting about a remote center of motion at the body wall. Like other surgical robot platforms it provides teleoperation with motion scaling and integrates cloud-based case recording. Hugo is a primary challenger to Intuitive Surgical in the soft-tissue robotic surgery market.

plain: A tiny sensor with microscopic moving parts etched onto a silicon chip, small and cheap enough to put almost anywhere.
snappy: A microfabricated inertial, pressure, or motion sensor built from tiny mechanical structures on a silicon chip.
detail: MEMS sensors use micron-scale mechanical elements fabricated like integrated circuits, making them small, low-power, and inexpensive. Most modern Accelerometer, Gyroscope, and Magnetometer parts are MEMS, which is why an Inertial measurement unit can fit inside a phone or a small Drone. The trade-off is higher Sensor noise and Sensor drift than larger industrial units, handled through Calibration and Sensor fusion.

plain: A 3D shape built from many tiny flat triangles, used to give a robot or object its visible form or its physical boundary.
snappy: A polygon (typically triangle) surface defining an object's visual appearance or its collision geometry.
detail: A mesh approximates a curved or complex surface with flat polygons; a detailed visual mesh is used for Photorealistic rendering, while a simplified collision mesh is used for fast Collision detection. Robot models in URDF, SDF, or USD link to mesh files for each Link, and planners load the collision mesh to check the Configuration space for obstacles. Overly dense collision meshes are a common cause of slow Motion planning, so engineers often hand-simplify them.

plain: A simulation error where two solid objects sink into or pass through each other instead of bumping.
snappy: A simulation artifact where collision geometries overlap or pass through one another instead of resolving contact.
detail: Mesh penetration (or tunneling) happens when a Physics engine fails to catch a collision in time, often because a fast body moves more than its thickness within one Simulation Timestep. It degrades the realism of Contact dynamics and Grasping, since a Parallel-jaw gripper may clip through an object rather than hold it. Fixes include Continuous Collision Detection, finer timesteps, convex collision shapes via Convex Decomposition, and contact-margin tuning in engines like PhysX or Bullet.

plain: A simple file that lists exactly what fields a piece of robot data contains, like a form template the data must fill in.
snappy: A typed schema (a .msg file) specifying the named, typed fields of a ROS topic message.
detail: A Message Definition declares the structure of data sent over a Topic, for example a Pose with position and orientation fields or a sensor reading with a timestamp. The build system uses these .msg files (and their service and action counterparts) to generate language-specific structs and classes for rclcpp and rclpy, a process governed by an Interface Definition Language. Standardized message packages let unrelated nodes interoperate, which is why a camera driver and a perception node agree on the same image message.

plain: When a piece of data a robot sends between its programs gets lost on the way, leaving the receiver with stale or missing information.
snappy: Lost middleware messages that leave downstream nodes with stale, missing, or out-of-order data.
detail: Message drop occurs when a Publish-subscribe channel in middleware like ROS 2, DDS, or LCM cannot deliver every message, often under high load, network congestion, or a misconfigured Quality of Service profile. The effect can range from harmless to dangerous: a dropped command can stall a control loop, while lost sensor frames degrade State estimation and Sensor fusion. Engineers tune QoS reliability, buffer depth, and bandwidth, and use tools like Foxglove Studio or rqt to detect Sensor dropout.

plain: Teaching a robot how to learn, so it can pick up brand-new tasks far faster than starting from scratch.
snappy: Learning an adaptation procedure or initialization from many tasks so new tasks can be mastered with very little data.
detail: Meta-learning, or learning to learn, trains across a distribution of tasks so that a robot adapts to an unseen one in a handful of trials, the basis of Few-shot learning. In robotics it can tune a manipulation Policy to a new object or a new terrain almost instantly, complementing Transfer learning and Online adaptation. It is often combined with Reinforcement learning and Representation learning to extract reusable structure across tasks.

plain: A simulated collection of fifty different robot-arm tasks designed to test whether one learning system can handle many tasks or quickly pick up new ones.
snappy: A benchmark suite of 50 simulated manipulation tasks for multi-task and meta-reinforcement-learning evaluation.
detail: Meta-World offers 50 distinct table-top manipulation tasks sharing one Sawyer-style arm, structured so researchers can measure Multitask learning and Meta-learning rather than single-task skill. Built on the MuJoCo physics engine, it benchmarks Reinforcement learning algorithms on generalization to held-out tasks, complementing manipulation suites like RLBench, robosuite, and ManiSkill. Its task taxonomy makes it a standard testbed for studying Transfer learning and Sample efficiency in embodied control.

plain: A very small flying robot, ranging from insect-sized to something you can hold in one hand.
snappy: A class of extremely small UAVs spanning insect-scale flyers up to handheld aircraft, defined by tight size, weight, and power limits.
detail: Micro air vehicles push aerodynamics and electronics into a regime where every gram matters, overlapping with the Insect-scale flying robot and Nano drone categories. Their limited payload forces lightweight Onboard compute and reliance on an Optical flow sensor or Visual-inertial odometry rather than heavy LiDAR for state estimation. MAV research drives advances in Flapping-wing drone designs and agile flight, and benchmark efforts such as the EuRoC MAV Dataset were collected to study perception and control at this scale.

plain: The tell-tale flutter a radar picks up from a target's small moving parts, like a drone's spinning blades or a walking person's swinging arms.
snappy: The time-frequency radar pattern produced by a target's internal micro-motions, used to classify what the target is.
detail: Beyond bulk Doppler Velocity Estimation, rotating or oscillating parts impose additional frequency modulations on a Radar return; the resulting Micro-Doppler Signature acts as a fingerprint distinguishing a Drone's propellers from a bird's wingbeats or a pedestrian's gait. Defense & Security systems use it for Counter-UAS classification and Mobility perception for vulnerable-road-user recognition, often pairing the spectrogram with a Convolutional neural network. It complements automotive radar tracking where a raw Bounding box alone cannot tell object classes apart.

plain: A small, highly automated warehouse placed close to where customers live so robots can fill online orders for fast local delivery.
snappy: A compact, robot-automated warehouse sited near demand to enable rapid order fulfillment, often for groceries.
detail: A micro-fulfillment center (MFC, or micro fulfillment) packs warehouse automation into a small footprint, often bolted onto the back of a store or a dense urban site, to enable same-hour delivery. It typically runs a Goods-to-person or Automated storage and retrieval system layout where robots present inventory to pickers, maximizing Pick rate in minimal space. The MFC is the upstream half of fast Last-mile delivery and lives or dies on its Return on investment versus a conventional store backroom.

plain: A slimmed-down version of robot software that runs on tiny, cheap chips instead of a full computer.
snappy: A ROS 2 stack for resource-constrained microcontrollers, bringing nodes and topics onto bare-metal devices.
detail: Micro-ROS ports ROS 2 concepts, nodes, the Publish-subscribe model, and DDS messaging, onto a Microcontroller running a Real-time operating system, so a sensor or motor board becomes a first-class participant in the robot's graph. It lets low-level Embedded system components publish directly to a Topic without a bridge PC. Typical uses include reading an Encoder, driving a Servomotor, or running a tight Real-time control loop close to the hardware.

plain: A tiny, cheap computer-on-a-chip that runs one dedicated job, like driving a motor or reading a sensor.
snappy: A small embedded processor with onboard memory and I/O that runs low-level motor and sensor firmware.
detail: A microcontroller (MCU) handles the deterministic, low-level layer of a robot: closing a PID controller loop, generating Pulse-width modulation for a Brushless DC motor, and reading an Encoder or Inertial measurement unit. It typically runs a Real-time operating system or bare-metal firmware as part of a larger Embedded system, reporting up to higher-level Onboard compute. Projects like Micro-ROS bring ROS 2 messaging down to the MCU so it integrates cleanly with the rest of the stack.

plain: A cluster of several microphones working together so a device can tell which direction a sound is coming from and focus on it.
snappy: Multiple spatially separated microphones whose combined signals enable sound-source localization and beamforming.
detail: A microphone array uses time differences between several mics to localize sound and to beamform — amplifying speech from one direction while suppressing noise — a key Sensing modality for a Service robot and Human-robot interaction. It supports voice command pickup on a consumer Service & Consumer platform and can feed Situational awareness alongside the Camera. Array geometry and Sampling rate set its angular resolution.

plain: A robot smaller than a grain of rice, sometimes tiny enough to travel inside the body.
snappy: A sub-millimeter robot, often powered and steered externally, used for tasks like targeted drug delivery or microscale manipulation.
detail: Microrobots are too small to carry an onboard motor or battery, so they are usually driven by external magnetic, acoustic, or chemical fields rather than a conventional actuator. Medical concepts envision a nanorobot navigating the bloodstream for targeted drug delivery, while larger microscale units perform manipulation under a microscope. The field draws on bio-inspired robot locomotion (swimming locomotion at low Reynolds number), soft robotics materials, and precise localization, and remains largely Research/Frontier work alongside Medical & Surgical applications.

plain: A depth-sensing camera from Microsoft that judges distance by timing how long flashes of invisible light take to bounce back.
snappy: Microsoft's time-of-flight Depth camera, successor to the original Kinect, widely used for robotics perception and human tracking.
detail: The Microsoft Azure Kinect uses a Time-of-flight sensor to produce a high-quality Depth map plus a wide-angle color Camera and a built-in Inertial measurement unit, making it a popular research Depth camera for Human pose estimation, semantic mapping, and Mobile manipulation. Its accurate depth at close range suits indoor Service robot and tabletop manipulation tasks, feeding Point cloud pipelines and 3D object detection. Like other ToF devices it struggles with sunlight and reflective surfaces, so outdoor robots favor Stereo camera or LiDAR instead.

plain: A gripper covered in tiny hooks that catch on the rough bumps of a surface, letting a robot cling to rock or rough walls.
snappy: A gripper using arrays of small spines that snag surface asperities to grip rough, hard surfaces.
detail: A microspine gripper carries hundreds of tiny independently sprung spines that individually hook onto micro-bumps and pits in a rough surface, distributing load so a robot can anchor to rock, concrete, or asteroid regolith. It enables a Climbing robot and is studied at NASA JPL for Free-flying space robot anchoring and surface sampling, where suction or Magnetic adhesion would fail. It is a non-smooth-surface alternative to Gecko-inspired adhesion.

plain: Hooking onto a rough surface with hundreds of tiny barbs, like how a climbing shoe catches on rock.
snappy: A climbing grip that uses dense arrays of small spines to snag micro-scale asperities on rough surfaces such as rock and concrete.
detail: Each compliant spine independently catches a tiny bump, and a large array shares the load so a Climbing robot can hold onto cliff faces, lava tubes, or asteroid regolith. NASA has flown and tested microspine grippers for anchoring and sampling on rocky low-gravity surfaces, where it pairs naturally with a Free-flying space robot or a Planetary rover. Microspine gripping needs surface roughness and so is the opposite of Gecko-inspired adhesion, and it joins Electroadhesion and Vortex adhesion as a non-magnetic option in Climbing locomotion.

plain: Smoothing a stepper motor's jerky steps into many tiny in-between positions by carefully blending the current in its coils.
snappy: Driving a stepper with sinusoidally apportioned phase currents to subdivide each full step.
detail: Microstepping commands the two phases of a Stepper motor with shaped, quadrature currents so the rotor settles at intermediate angles between full steps, greatly reducing vibration and acoustic noise and increasing apparent resolution. It is standard in a Microcontroller-driven stepper drive for a 3D printer, Manufacturing positioner, or Service & Consumer device, though torque per microstep falls and true accuracy is still bounded by Cogging torque and load. It trades the open-loop simplicity of a stepper against the smoothness usually associated with Field-oriented control of a Brushless DC motor.

plain: Plumbing software that lets the many separate programs running a robot talk to each other.
snappy: A communication layer that routes messages, services, and data between a robot's software components.
detail: Middleware sits between the operating system and application code, handling discovery, serialization, and transport so a perception program can hand data to a planner without either knowing where the other runs. ROS and ROS 2 are the dominant robotics middleware; ROS 2 builds its transport on the DDS standard. Communication typically follows a Publish-subscribe pattern over a Topic, with a Node for each process.

plain: How far a self-driving car typically drives on its own before a human has to step in, used as a rough progress score.
snappy: The average distance driven autonomously between human takeovers, a common headline metric of self-driving maturity.
detail: Miles per intervention (MPI), also called the disengagement rate, divides autonomous distance by the number of times a safety driver or remote operator had to intervene. It is widely cited but easy to game, since the figure depends heavily on the operational design domain, the definition of a disengagement, and how aggressively interventions are counted. It relates closely to interventions per mile and is reported in regulatory filings, though teams increasingly favor richer scenario-based testing over this single number.

plain: An open design for a compact, force-sensitive robot-leg motor module that made fast, agile legged robots affordable for researchers.
snappy: MIT's open proprioceptive quasi-direct-drive actuator module that catalyzed low-cost dynamic legged-locomotion research.
detail: The Mini Cheetah Actuator pairs a large-diameter Brushless DC motor with a low-ratio (around 6:1) planetary Gear reduction so the motor's torque can be sensed and modulated through the gears, making it a Proprioceptive Actuator with excellent Backdrivability and low Reflected Inertia. Developed at MIT for the MIT Cheetah family, the open module design let labs worldwide build affordable Quadruped robot platforms capable of jumping and backflips. It is commonly driven by a Moteus Controller or ODrive running Field-oriented control in Torque Control Mode.

plain: A safe stopped or parked state a self-driving car reaches when it can no longer keep driving safely.
snappy: A stable, reduced-risk state (such as pulling over and stopping) that an automated vehicle achieves when it cannot continue the driving task.
detail: When an Automated driving system hits an Edge case, leaves its Operational design domain, or suffers a fault, the Fallback maneuver brings it to a Minimal risk condition (MRC), for example easing to the shoulder and engaging hazards. Reaching an MRC autonomously is what lets Level 4 automation operate without a human, and the minimal risk maneuver itself is a safety-critical behavior built to Functional safety standards. It is the embodied safety net that Redundancy and Fail-operational design exist to guarantee.

plain: The safe action a self-driving car takes when something goes wrong, such as slowing down and pulling over to a safe spot before stopping.
snappy: A controlled fallback maneuver that brings the vehicle to a safe stopped state when the automated system can no longer continue driving.
detail: Defined in SAE and ISO automated-driving standards, an MRM is the action that achieves a Minimal risk condition after the Dynamic driving task can no longer be performed, for example when a sensor fails or the car exits its Operational design domain. Unlike a human Takeover request, it assumes no driver will respond, so the Automated driving system itself must execute a safe stop, often pulling to the shoulder. It is a key Fallback behavior for a Robotaxi and is closely tied to Fail-operational system design and the overall Safety case.

plain: A smooth flight path for a drone, designed so its motion never jerks abruptly, letting it fly fast and agile without losing control.
snappy: A polynomial trajectory that minimizes the fourth derivative of position to produce smooth, aggressive flight.
detail: A Minimum-snap trajectory fits piecewise polynomials between waypoints while minimizing snap, the fourth time-derivative of position, which for a multirotor maps directly to commanded motor accelerations and keeps the motion gentle on the Flight controller. This formulation, central to agile quadcopter flight research, lets a Drone thread tight gaps at high speed because the smooth high-order derivatives avoid saturating the rotors. It is a specialized form of Trajectory optimization and is often followed by Trajectory tracking control; minimum-jerk variants apply the same idea to robot arms.

full: Mobile Industry Processor Interface Camera Serial Interface
plain: A high-speed connection that pipes raw video straight from a robot's camera into its main vision chip.
snappy: A high-bandwidth serial interface (CSI-2) that streams raw image sensor data directly to a processor's image pipeline.
detail: MIPI CSI carries uncompressed pixel data over differential lanes from a CMOS Image Sensor into the image signal processor of a System on a chip, giving the low Latency a robot needs for Visual servoing or Object detection. It is the standard camera attach point on modules like NVIDIA Jetson and Qualcomm Robotics RB5, feeding frames into a Vision Processing Unit or GPU for onboard perception. Unlike USB cameras it bypasses general buses, leaving PCIe and Ethernet free for storage and networking.

plain: A four-legged robot from MIT known for running fast and doing backflips.
snappy: MIT's quadruped research robot line known for backflips and agile dynamic legged locomotion.
detail: The MIT Cheetah and its smaller Mini Cheetah use low-cost, backdrivable quasi-direct drive actuators to achieve high-bandwidth force control for explosive quadrupedal locomotion. The platform demonstrated the first quadruped backflip and is a popular base for model predictive control and reinforcement learning locomotion research, with its actuator design widely copied. It anchors much of the legged robot dynamic-control literature.

plain: A company that makes factory robot arms, sold under the MELFA brand, for assembling and moving parts.
snappy: Maker of MELFA industrial arms for assembly, material handling, and machine tending.
detail: The MELFA line spans the SCARA robot and Six-axis robot configurations and is tightly integrated with Mitsubishi's own Programmable logic controller and servo ecosystem for full-cell automation. The arms are common in electronics assembly and Machine tending, where deterministic timing and high Repeatability matter. They connect over CC-Link and other Industrial Ethernet fieldbuses to coordinate with the rest of the Production line.

plain: A robot stacking boxes of many different sizes into one neat, stable pallet.
snappy: Robotic stacking of varied case sizes into a single dense, stable pallet, often arranged store-aisle ready.
detail: Mixed-Case Palletizing (rainbow palletizing) is far harder than single-SKU stacking because the robot must solve a real-time 3D packing problem, balancing stability, density, and crush rules across boxes of different dimensions and weights. It depends on accurate vision, motion planning, and a robust Palletizing robot or Cobot palletizer with the right End-of-arm tooling. Denser pallets raise Throughput per Square Foot in the trailer and warehouse and reduce downstream handling. The task is the inverse of Depalletizing and is closely related to Truck Unloading in a distribution center's outbound flow.

plain: A way of working together where the person and the robot each take the lead at different moments, depending on who is better placed to act.
snappy: An interaction style in which human and robot fluidly trade task leadership as the situation and respective capabilities change.
detail: In mixed-initiative interaction neither party is permanently in charge; control passes back and forth opportunistically, unlike fixed master-slave Teleoperation. A Mobile manipulator helping in a home might let the user point out a target, then take initiative to plan the Grasp, then hand a decision back. It builds on Shared control, Shared autonomy, and Adjustable autonomy, and depends on good Intent communication, Legibility, and Joint action so each side understands when the other is leading. From the robotics angle it requires the robot to model the human partner, linking it to Theory of mind.

plain: The text file format that tells the MuJoCo simulator what a robot and its world are made of.
snappy: MuJoCo's native XML model format defining bodies, joints, actuators, and contact physics.
detail: MJCF describes a kinematic tree of bodies and the Physics engine settings MuJoCo needs for fast contact-rich simulation, making it the counterpart of URDF for ROS or SDF for Gazebo. Researchers favor MJCF for Reinforcement learning because MuJoCo's solver handles Contact dynamics efficiently across many parallel environments. Converters exist to bring a URDF robot model into MJCF for Sim-to-real experiments.

plain: An affordable wheeled robot with two arms that a person can puppeteer to teach it household chores by demonstration.
snappy: A low-cost mobile bimanual teleoperation rig used to collect imitation-learning demonstrations for whole-body household manipulation.
detail: Mobile ALOHA (Stanford, 2024) mounts the bimanual ALOHA leader-follower Teleoperation setup on a wheeled base, letting an operator demonstrate whole-body household tasks like cooking and wiping for Imitation learning. The collected demonstrations train policies such as the Action chunking transformer (ACT) and Diffusion policy for Bimanual manipulation. Its low cost and open hardware made it influential for Mobile manipulation data collection, and the resulting datasets feed Robot foundation model efforts; it is hardware-only with no built-in AI, contrasting with end-to-end models like Helix.

plain: A Danish company that makes self-driving carts which safely move materials around factories alongside people.
snappy: A Danish maker of collaborative autonomous mobile robots for internal logistics and material transport.
detail: Mobile Industrial Robots (MiR) builds a collaborative Autonomous mobile robot line that moves carts, totes, and pallets between stations without fixed guide paths, using onboard LiDAR and SLAM for Navigation and Collision avoidance. Designed for safe operation near people, the robots comply with ISO 3691-4 for driverless industrial trucks and are managed by fleet software, often interoperating via VDA 5050. Owned by Teradyne alongside Universal Robots, MiR competes with OTTO Motors and Geek+ in internal Material handling.

plain: Putting a robot arm on a moving base so it can drive around and pick things up anywhere it goes.
snappy: Combining a mobile base with an arm to manipulate objects across a large workspace.
detail: Mobile manipulation fuses navigation and Manipulation so a Mobile manipulator can drive to a shelf, localize, and then grasp an item, extending the reach of an arm far beyond a fixed Robot cell. It requires combining a Navigation stack and Localization for the base with Motion planning and Grasp planning for the arm, ideally through Whole-body control that treats base and arm as one system. Use cases include warehouse Goods-to-person picking, a Humanoid robot doing household tasks, and an Autonomous mobile robot servicing factory machines.

plain: A robot that combines a driving base with a robot arm, so it can move to a spot and then pick things up there.
snappy: A mobile base carrying a manipulator arm, combining navigation with grasping for navigate-and-fetch tasks.
detail: A mobile manipulator fuses an Autonomous mobile robot base with an Industrial robot arm or Cobot, enabling Mobile manipulation: the robot navigates to a workstation, then performs Grasping and Pick and place there. Coordinating the base and arm together is a Whole-body control problem, often planned with MoveIt and Nav2. It is used in Logistics & Warehouse order fulfillment and flexible Manufacturing where fixed cells are too rigid.

plain: A survey car packed with lasers, cameras, and precise GPS that drives roads to create the ultra-detailed maps self-driving cars rely on.
snappy: A survey vehicle integrating lidar, cameras, and GNSS/INS to capture georeferenced data for building high-definition maps.
detail: An MMS fuses a LiDAR scanner, calibrated cameras, and a GNSS/INS Integration unit to produce a georeferenced Lidar Point Cloud and imagery from which a High-Definition Map is constructed. Precise positioning typically uses RTK GNSS or Post-Processed Kinematic correction, while a Mechanical LiDAR or Solid-state LiDAR captures dense geometry. The output supports Semantic segmentation and feature extraction for lane lines and signs, and the same point clouds enable later Localization via Scan Matching.

plain: A company that makes the camera-and-chip systems many cars use to see the road and assist the driver.
snappy: Intel-affiliated maker of ADAS and self-driving vision chips (the EyeQ family).
detail: Mobileye supplies the EyeQ system-on-chip and Computer vision software behind much of the world's Advanced driver-assistance systems, from Lane keeping assist to Automatic emergency braking. It is also building a full Self-driving stack and championed the Responsibility-sensitive safety formal model for Autonomous vehicle decision-making. Its camera-centric Object detection and Pedestrian detection pipelines ship in millions of production cars.

plain: A specialized chip and software, widely used in cars, that processes camera images to help vehicles see and assist the driver.
snappy: A vision system-on-chip family with bundled perception software powering camera-based ADAS and autonomy.
detail: Mobileye EyeQ is a System on a chip purpose-built to run camera Perception efficiently, performing Object detection, Lane detection, Traffic sign recognition, and Free space detection for Advanced driver-assistance systems and higher Levels of autonomy. Deployed across millions of Mobility vehicles, it emphasizes a camera-first approach to perception with optional Sensor fusion. As a vertically integrated hardware-plus-software product it competes with platforms like NVIDIA DRIVE and the vision-only philosophy behind the Tesla Occupancy Network.

plain: A simple, decades-old way for industrial devices to talk to each other over a wire, still common because it is easy and cheap.
snappy: A simple, openly published legacy serial and TCP protocol for industrial device communication.
detail: Modbus is one of the oldest and most ubiquitous Fieldbus protocols, prized for its simplicity: a master polls registers and coils on slave devices over RS-485 (Modbus RTU) or Ethernet (Modbus TCP). It is common between a Programmable logic controller, a Remote terminal unit, sensors, a Variable frequency drive, and SCADA systems, especially in older or cost-sensitive installations. It lacks the speed and Determinism of EtherCAT or PROFINET, but its openness keeps it in wide use across Industrial automation.

plain: When an operator thinks a machine is in one setting but it is actually in another, so their actions have the wrong effect.
snappy: An operator's incorrect mental model of which automation mode is currently active, leading to inappropriate or unexpected control inputs.
detail: Mode confusion (also called automation surprise) is a classic human-factors failure where the interface does not make the active state obvious. In an Autonomous vehicle a driver may believe Adaptive cruise control is steering when only longitudinal control is engaged, or in aviation a pilot may misjudge what the Autopilot will do next. It motivates clear Human-machine interface design, strong Intent communication, and Legibility so the active mode is unambiguous, and it interacts with the Handoff problem during a Takeover request.

plain: A controller that looks a few seconds into the future, plans the best sequence of moves, does only the first one, then re-plans on the next step.
snappy: Control that solves a constrained optimization over a rolling prediction horizon each cycle and applies only the first command.
detail: MPC repeatedly solves a Trajectory optimization problem using a model of the Dynamics, naturally respecting limits like joint torque or Collision avoidance, which is why it is also called receding horizon control. It is central to modern Balance control and Whole-body control on a Humanoid robot, and to path-following on an Autonomous vehicle via Trajectory tracking. It demands fast Real-time control because the optimization must finish inside the Control rate, and it shares the cost-minimizing spirit of the Linear quadratic regulator and Optimal control.

plain: Storing a neural network's numbers with fewer digits so it takes up less memory and runs faster on a small robot chip.
snappy: Reducing the numerical precision of a network's weights and activations (e.g. FP32 to INT8) to shrink memory and accelerate edge inference.
detail: Model Quantization converts a network's high-precision weights to lower-bit formats such as INT8, trading a small accuracy loss for large gains in speed and memory on resource-constrained robots. It is essential for running a Diffusion policy or Vision-language-action model on Onboard compute like NVIDIA Jetson or a Google Coral Edge TPU, and tools such as TensorRT perform it during deployment. On a Service robot or Delivery robot doing Edge computing, quantization is what lets a heavy perception model fit inside the Latency and Thermal Throttling limits of the embedded hardware.

plain: A controller that automatically adjusts its own settings on the fly so the robot behaves like a chosen ideal model, even as conditions change.
snappy: Adaptive control that tunes parameters online so the closed-loop plant tracks the response of a specified reference model.
detail: MRAC defines a desired Reference model, measures the gap between the plant and that model, and uses an adaptation law (often gradient or Lyapunov-based) to update gains until the plant matches it, handling slowly varying or uncertain parameters. It is a core Adaptive control method used when a manipulator's payload changes or a drone's mass shifts, where fixed-gain Feedback control would degrade. It relies on Lyapunov stability for its adaptation guarantees and contrasts with the filtered, robustness-preserving L1 adaptive control.

plain: A learning approach where the robot first builds an internal model of how the world works, then uses it to plan good actions.
snappy: RL that learns a predictive world model and uses it to plan or generate training data.
detail: Model-based reinforcement learning learns a World model of environment dynamics and exploits it to plan, imagine rollouts, or generate synthetic experience, typically boosting Sample efficiency over Model-free reinforcement learning. This matters in robotics where real-world trials are slow and risky, so an accurate dynamics model lets a Robot rehearse internally before acting. Its quality hinges on the learned model, and errors there echo the Reality gap seen in Sim-to-real transfer.

plain: A learning approach where the robot improves purely from trial-and-error reward, without ever building a model of how the world works.
snappy: RL that learns a policy or value function directly from experience without modeling environment dynamics.
detail: Model-free reinforcement learning skips learning a World model and instead optimizes a Policy or Value function straight from observed Reward, as in Q-learning, Soft actor-critic, and Proximal policy optimization. It is simpler and avoids model-bias, but generally needs far more interaction, hurting Sample efficiency compared with Model-based reinforcement learning. In robotics it dominates learned Legged locomotion, where Massively parallel simulation supplies the enormous sample counts it requires.

plain: Building a self-driving system as separate stages, each handling one job like seeing, predicting, or planning.
snappy: An autonomy architecture decomposed into distinct perception, prediction, planning, and control modules with defined interfaces.
detail: The Modular pipeline is the dominant Self-driving stack design: Perception and Sensor fusion feed an explicit object list and Occupancy grid, prediction forecasts agents, then Behavior planning and Motion planning hand a trajectory to control. Each stage is separately testable and traceable, which suits Functional safety and ISO 26262, the key advantage over an End-to-end driving model. Waymo and Aurora favor this approach for its interpretability when diagnosing a Disengagement.

plain: A robot built from many small, interchangeable building blocks that can be rearranged into different shapes.
snappy: A robot composed of standardized modules that can be connected, swapped, or reconfigured to change its capabilities or form.
detail: Modular robots trade a fixed body for a kit of repeated units, each carrying its own actuator, sensor, and computer. Self-reconfigurable variants can rearrange their own modules to switch between a Snake robot, a Legged robot, or a rolling Wheeled robot for different terrain. Research platforms emphasize morphological computation and exploit changing morphology and degrees of freedom, and they are common testbeds for swarm robotics and emergent behavior, distinguishing them from a monolithic Industrial robot arm.

plain: A company making electric tractors that can drive themselves around farms and vineyards.
snappy: Maker of electric, driver-optional autonomous tractors aimed at vineyards and specialty farming.
detail: Monarch Tractor builds a battery-electric tractor with a driver-optional autonomous vehicle stack that lets it perform repetitive vineyard tasks like spraying and mowing without an operator. It uses cameras and a perception stack for row-following and obstacle detection, plus data logging for precision-agriculture analytics. It targets the agricultural labor shortage and competes with retrofit autonomy on conventional diesel tractors.

plain: A structure where the outer shell itself carries the loads instead of an internal frame.
snappy: A construction in which the external skin bears primary structural loads rather than a separate frame.
detail: In a Monocoque the outer skin is the structure, eliminating a separate internal frame to save weight, a strategy borrowed from aerospace and motorsport and valued where mass matters, as in a Space robot or a racing-style Chassis. It contrasts with the Endoskeleton approach and frequently uses Carbon fiber composite to maximize stiffness-to-weight, improving the Payload-to-weight ratio. Skin damage in a monocoque is structurally significant, unlike a cosmetic cover.

plain: A robot with a single springy leg that gets around by hopping like a pogo stick.
snappy: A single-legged robot that achieves dynamic balance and locomotion through repeated hopping.
detail: A Monopod robot is the simplest dynamically stable Legged robot, demonstrating that balance can be a control problem rather than a static one, famously formalized by the Raibert hopper control laws that decouple hopping height, forward speed, and body attitude. Its behavior is captured by the Spring-loaded inverted pendulum model and a clear Flight phase between ground contacts, making it a classic testbed for Legged locomotion and Push recovery research. Insights from the hopping monopod scaled directly into multi-legged platforms like the Quadruped robot and Bipedal robot.

plain: A way for a robot to guess where it is by scattering many candidate positions and keeping the ones that best match what its sensors see.
snappy: A particle-filter localization method that represents the robot's pose belief as a cloud of weighted samples updated by motion and sensing.
detail: Monte Carlo localization (MCL) applies a Particle filter to the Localization problem: each particle is a hypothesized Pose, motion commands push the cloud forward (akin to Dead reckoning), and each new Lidar scan reweights particles by how well they match the Occupancy grid map. Resampling concentrates particles on likely poses. MCL is robust to the multi-modal uncertainty that trips up a plain Kalman filter, which is why its adaptive variant AMCL is the default localizer in the ROS Navigation stack.

plain: The surprising observation that things any toddler does easily, like walking or picking up a toy, are extremely hard for robots, while abstract reasoning like chess is comparatively easy.
snappy: The principle that high-level reasoning needs little computation but low-level sensorimotor skills require enormous computation, making perception and motion the hard part of robotics.
detail: Named for Hans Moravec, the paradox explains why Manipulation and Locomotion lagged behind symbolic AI for decades: tasks like Grasping a soft object or Bipedal locomotion over rough ground demand exquisite Perception and control. It motivates today's emphasis on Imitation learning, Reinforcement learning, and large-scale Simulation to acquire the Dexterity humans take for granted. The paradox is often cited to temper expectations for a Generalist robot and to explain why a Contact-rich manipulation task remains a frontier problem.

plain: Letting a robot's body shape do some of the 'thinking', so the control software has to do less.
snappy: Offloading part of a robot's control and computation onto its physical body design, so mechanics handle work the controller otherwise would.
detail: Morphological computation says intelligence is partly embodied: clever Morphology can stabilize motion or simplify grasping with little active control. The classic example is Passive dynamic walking, where a well-tuned leg geometry produces a natural gait downhill with no motors, improving Energy efficiency. It is a guiding principle of Soft robotics and Bio-inspired robotics, where a Compliant mechanism or Series elastic actuator absorbs disturbances that a rigid robot would have to compute away.

plain: A robot's physical shape and how its parts are put together.
snappy: The physical form of a robot, the number, type, and arrangement of its links, joints, and limbs.
detail: Morphology covers whether a robot is a Quadruped robot, a Humanoid robot, or a wheeled platform, and how its Link and Joint elements connect, captured formally in a URDF or by Denavit-Hartenberg parameters. Form shapes function: morphology fixes the Workspace, the Degrees of freedom, and which gaits or grasps are possible. The idea that body design can do computational work for the controller is Morphological computation, and choosing morphology to match a task is central to Bio-inspired robotics.

plain: A small electronic board, made by mjbots, that mounts on a robot motor to control it precisely.
snappy: Compact CAN-FD brushless servo controller from mjbots designed to mount directly on legged-robot actuators.
detail: The Moteus Controller is a small Brushless DC Motor Controller that integrates Field-oriented control, an absolute Magnetic Encoder, and a CAN FD interface so it can be bolted directly onto an actuator, minimizing wiring on a Quadruped robot or Humanoid robot. It exposes a clean Torque Control Mode with feedforward, enabling the high-bandwidth force control that a Proprioceptive Actuator needs. Moteus is the controller of choice for mjbots' own quadrupeds and a popular alternative to ODrive for Quasi-direct drive joints.

plain: The smearing in a photo that happens when the camera or the scene moves while the shutter is open.
snappy: Image degradation in which moving scene content or camera motion smears intensity across pixels during the exposure interval.
detail: Motion Blur occurs when relative motion during exposure spreads a point's light over many pixels, degrading the corners that Feature extraction and Feature matching depend on and thus weakening Visual odometry and Visual SLAM. Fast robots and drones fight it with shorter exposures, a Global shutter sensor, image stabilization, or by switching to an Event camera that has no exposure window. Deblurring networks and IMU-aided correction can also recover sharpness for downstream Perception.

plain: A room rigged with special cameras that track a drone's exact position and orientation, used to study flight in a lab.
snappy: An external camera system that tracks reflective markers to deliver sub-millimeter pose of a drone for indoor experiments.
detail: Motion capture localization uses a Motion Capture System such as Vicon or OptiTrack to provide ground-truth Pose at high rate, removing the need for onboard SLAM during research flights. It is the standard testbed for aggressive maneuvers and Learned quadrotor control, letting researchers close the loop on Trajectory tracking before attempting GPS-denied navigation in the wild. Because the rig supplies near-perfect state, it serves as both a controller benchmark and a source of Ground truth for evaluating Visual-inertial odometry.

plain: A setup of external cameras that tracks reflective markers in a room to measure exactly where objects and robots are, down to millimeters.
snappy: An external optical tracking system using multiple calibrated cameras and reflective markers to provide millimeter-accurate ground-truth pose at high rate.
detail: A Motion Capture System such as Vicon or OptiTrack triangulates retro-reflective markers seen by ringed infrared cameras to deliver sub-millimeter Pose at hundreds of hertz, serving as the Ground truth reference for robotics labs. Researchers use it to benchmark a Visual SLAM or Visual-inertial odometry estimator and to provide Motion capture localization for indoor drone control. It also captures human demonstration trajectories for Imitation learning and Humanoid robot retargeting.

plain: Fixing the smear in a moving sensor's scan so a single sweep doesn't get stretched or warped while the robot is driving.
snappy: Correcting the distortion in a rolling sensor sweep caused by platform motion during the time it takes to capture one frame.
detail: A spinning LiDAR collects points over tens of milliseconds, so while the robot moves the Point cloud becomes skewed; Motion Compensation (lidar deskewing) re-projects each point to a common timestamp using ego-motion from an Inertial measurement unit, Wheel odometry, or Visual-inertial odometry. It is essential before Iterative closest point registration, Scan Matching, and Object detection in fast Mobility platforms. The same principle addresses Rolling shutter distortion in cameras, and accurate Time synchronization across sensors is a prerequisite.

plain: The system that coordinates several motors at once so a machine's many axes move together smoothly and in sync.
snappy: Coordinated regulation of position, velocity, and acceleration across multiple motorized axes.
detail: Motion control sits above per-axis Servo control, generating coordinated, jerk-limited profiles so a Cartesian robot, SCARA robot, or CNC machine moves its axes in concert, often over a Fieldbus like EtherCAT. It handles Time parameterization and synchronization of Trajectory tracking, run by a Motion controller and ultimately the Robot controller. It overlaps with Computer numerical control in machine tools and is the practical glue between Motion planning and the motors.

plain: A device that coordinates the precise, synchronized movement of several motors in a machine or robot.
snappy: A controller that plans and coordinates multi-axis servo and stepper motion in machinery.
detail: A motion controller generates coordinated position, velocity, and acceleration commands for multiple axes, handling tasks like interpolation, cam profiles, and electronic gearing that a generic Programmable logic controller may not. It drives a Servomotor or stepper through amplifiers, closing the loop with feedback from an Encoder, and underpins Motion control on machine tools, packaging lines, and an Industrial robot arm. Tight synchronization across axes typically demands a deterministic Industrial Ethernet link such as EtherCAT.

plain: Teaching a robot to move like a recorded example, such as a person's walk captured on camera, by training it to reproduce that reference motion.
snappy: Training a controller to reproduce captured reference motions, often requiring retargeting from a human or animal source onto the robot's body.
detail: Motion imitation drives a controller to track a reference trajectory, typically from a Motion Capture System, and usually requires Motion retargeting to map the source skeleton onto the robot's differing kinematics and mass. It is the standard route to natural, agile Humanoid robot and Quadruped robot skills, exemplified by DeepMimic, and feeds Sim-to-Real Locomotion pipelines. It contrasts with style-based methods like Adversarial Motion Priors and connects to Imitation learning more broadly.

plain: Working out how a robot should move from where it is to where it needs to be without bumping into anything.
snappy: Computing a feasible, collision-free trajectory through Configuration space from a start state to a goal.
detail: Motion planning generalizes Path planning by accounting for the robot's geometry, joint limits, and often its Dynamics, producing a sequence of configurations a manipulator or mobile base can actually execute. A typical pipeline uses a Global planner to find a coarse route and a Local planner to refine it against nearby obstacles, with Collision checking validating each candidate. Frameworks such as MoveIt and OMPL implement Sampling-based planning algorithms like Rapidly-exploring random tree and Probabilistic roadmap, while Trajectory optimization smooths the result before Time parameterization assigns speeds.

plain: A small, ready-made piece of movement that can be strung together with others to build up complicated actions.
snappy: A reusable parameterized action segment that serves as a building block for composing longer motions.
detail: A Motion primitive is a precomputed or learned chunk of movement, such as a short arc, a grasp approach, or a stepping motion, that a planner concatenates rather than solving every move from scratch. Driving robots build a State lattice from a library of kinematically feasible motion primitives so that Path planning becomes a graph search over drivable segments. In manipulation, a manipulation primitive like pushing or inserting is composed by a Task and motion planning layer, and learned motion primitives also underpin a Skill primitive in many imitation-learning systems.

plain: The planned recipe of speeds and accelerations a moving axis follows from where it starts to where it stops.
snappy: The planned position, velocity, and acceleration curve an axis follows over a single move.
detail: A motion profile is computed by the Motion controller and handed to a Servo drive so the axis reaches its target smoothly within time and acceleration limits. The classic trapezoidal shape ramps velocity up, cruises, then ramps down; an S-curve acceleration variant rounds the corners to cut shock. Profiles feed Trajectory generation for an Industrial robot arm and are closely tied to Time parameterization and Following error budgets.

plain: The electronics that decide how much power to send a motor and when, so it moves the way the robot wants.
snappy: Electronics that regulate motor current and commutation to execute a commanded motion.
detail: A motor controller (motor driver, or ESC for a drone) sits between the robot's computer and the motor, switching power transistors to set current, voltage, and Commutation so the motor produces the demanded torque or speed. It typically uses Pulse-width modulation to vary power and, for a Brushless DC motor, runs Field-oriented control with feedback from an Encoder or Hall effect sensor. It is the electronic half of the Servomotor and the Servo control loop closed by a PID controller.

plain: A number telling you how much turning force a motor produces for each unit of electrical current you feed it.
snappy: The proportionality constant (Kt) relating motor phase current to produced output torque.
detail: The Motor Torque Constant, written Kt, lets a controller convert a desired torque into a commanded current, which is the foundation of Torque Control Mode and of any Proprioceptive Actuator that senses force through current. Kt is numerically tied to the Back-EMF Constant in SI units, since a motor that is a good torque producer is equally a good generator. Knowing Kt accurately is essential for the current-based force estimation used in a Mini Cheetah Actuator and for sizing a Brushless DC motor against required Peak torque.

plain: A cautious way to drive a delayed robot: make a small move, wait to see the result, then move again.
snappy: A teleoperation tactic under large communication delay of issuing small incremental commands and pausing for feedback before the next.
detail: The move-and-wait strategy is how human operators cope with long round-trip Latency, as on a Planetary rover or deep-space arm where each command's result takes seconds or minutes to confirm. It is safe but painfully slow, which motivates a Predictive display, supervisory autonomy, and Bilateral teleoperation to recover responsiveness. It marks the practical limit of direct Teleoperation as delay grows, pushing systems toward Supervised autonomy and onboard Collision avoidance instead.

plain: A widely used free software package that figures out how to move a robot arm without hitting anything.
snappy: The de facto ROS motion-planning framework for manipulator arms, bundling planning, kinematics, and collision checking.
detail: MoveIt is the standard manipulation stack in the ROS ecosystem (now MoveIt 2 on ROS 2), wiring together Inverse kinematics solvers, Collision checking, and Trajectory optimization. It delegates the actual planning to sampling-based algorithms from OMPL and executes the result through ros2_control. A typical use is an Industrial robot arm doing Pick and place: MoveIt plans a collision-free Trajectory from the current Pose to a Grasp pose.

plain: The standard software for planning how a robot arm should move from one pose to another without hitting anything, built for the newer robot software framework.
snappy: The ROS 2 motion-planning framework for manipulator trajectory generation, collision checking, and execution.
detail: MoveIt 2 ports the MoveIt stack to ROS 2, orchestrating Inverse kinematics, sampling-based planners via OMPL, collision checking through the Flexible Collision Library, and trajectory Time parameterization for an Industrial robot arm. It consumes a robot's URDF and Xacro description, integrates with ros2_control for execution, and underpins perception-guided Manipulation tasks like Bin picking and Pick and place. Widely used with ROS-Industrial drivers, it is the default open-source path from a Grasp pose to a safe, collision-free arm Trajectory.

plain: A planning method that imagines thousands of slightly random future action sequences, then blends the good ones into the next move.
snappy: Sampling-based MPC that rolls out many noisy action sequences and weights them by an information-theoretic cost to form the control update.
detail: MPPI sidesteps gradients entirely: it samples large batches of noisy control rollouts through a (often learned or simulator) model, exponentially weights each by its cost, and takes the weighted average as the next command, fitting naturally on a GPU. Because it needs no derivatives it handles non-smooth costs and Contact-rich manipulation that trip up Convex MPC, and is widely paired with Model-based reinforcement learning and Learning-based control on off-road Autonomous vehicle and Mobile manipulation platforms. It is a stochastic cousin of Model predictive control and Trajectory optimization.

plain: A lightweight messaging system where devices publish data to a central hub and other systems subscribe to whatever data they care about.
snappy: A lightweight publish-subscribe messaging protocol widely used for IIoT telemetry from devices to the cloud.
detail: MQTT uses a tiny publish-subscribe model where edge devices send messages to a broker and consumers subscribe to topics, making it efficient over constrained or intermittent links. In factories it ships sensor and machine telemetry from the floor to cloud analytics, complementing deterministic protocols like OPC UA used closer to control. It is a backbone of the Industrial Internet of Things, and the Sparkplug B specification standardizes its topics and payloads so that data is self-describing rather than vendor-specific.

plain: A control design method that builds a controller proven to keep working even when the robot's true behaviour differs from the model in specific known ways.
snappy: Robust-control synthesis using the structured singular value (mu) to guarantee performance against structured model uncertainty.
detail: Mu-synthesis (often via D-K iteration) designs a controller that maximizes the structured singular value margin, guaranteeing both stability and performance across a defined set of structured uncertainties such as parameter ranges and unmodeled dynamics. It is the high-assurance end of Robust control, used where Loop shaping and a hand-checked Phase margin are insufficient, for instance in precision Servo control with variable payloads or flexible structures. It generalizes H-infinity design and complements uncertainty-tolerant schemes like L1 adaptive control.

plain: A company that makes smart brains for robots so they can pick, stack, and sort items without being programmed for each one.
snappy: Maker of intelligent robot controllers for piece-picking, palletizing, and bin handling.
detail: Mujin's controller combines real-time Motion planning with Machine vision so an arm can compute grasps and collision-free paths on the fly, reducing the per-part teaching that traditional automation needs. It is widely used for Bin picking, Palletizing, and Depalletizing in logistics, where mixed and unknown items defeat fixed programs. The controller pairs Grasp planning with Trajectory generation across many robot brands rather than locking to one Industrial robot arm vendor.

plain: A fast physics simulator that is especially good at modeling robots touching and gripping things, widely used in research.
snappy: A fast physics engine specializing in contact-rich rigid-body dynamics for robotics and learning research.
detail: MuJoCo's solver computes Contact dynamics and Rigid body dynamics efficiently enough to run many simulations in parallel, making it a favorite for Reinforcement learning and Sim-to-real research. Robots are described in MJCF, analogous to URDF or SDF, and the engine now ships free and open-source. It competes with PyBullet, Drake, and the Physics engine inside Gazebo, and underlies much Learned locomotion work.

plain: A free toolkit that runs the MuJoCo physics engine on a graphics card to train robot controllers quickly across many simulated robots at once.
snappy: An open GPU-accelerated suite of MuJoCo environments, built on MuJoCo XLA, for scalable reinforcement-learning policy training.
detail: MuJoCo Playground is an open collection of robot environments built on MuJoCo XLA (MJX), the JAX-based GPU port of MuJoCo, enabling Massively parallel reinforcement learning for Legged locomotion, manipulation, and Dexterous manipulation tasks. It brings GPU-Accelerated Simulation to the widely used MuJoCo physics engine, supporting fast Sim-to-real workflows with Domain randomization. It serves as an open alternative to Isaac Gym and the Genesis Simulator, and is commonly paired with Gymnasium-style training loops.

plain: A version of a popular robot physics simulator rewritten so thousands of copies can run at once on a graphics card.
snappy: A JAX/XLA reimplementation of MuJoCo (MJX) that runs the engine on GPU/TPU for massively parallel, batched simulation.
detail: MJX re-expresses MuJoCo's contact dynamics in JAX so it compiles through XLA to GPUs and TPUs, enabling thousands of parallel environments for Massively parallel reinforcement learning and policy search. It underpins MuJoCo Playground and competes with Brax, Genesis, and Isaac Lab as a training backend for Legged locomotion and Manipulation, while keeping MuJoCo's accurate Contact dynamics. Because it is differentiable-friendly, it also supports Differentiable Simulation workflows and rapid Sim-to-real iteration on robots like a Quadruped robot.

plain: Working out routes for a whole fleet of robots in the same building so they all reach their destinations without bumping into each other.
snappy: Planning collision-free paths for many robots that share one workspace so that none collide in space or time while reaching their goals.
detail: Multi-agent path finding (MAPF) assigns each robot a goal and computes time-indexed paths over a shared graph or Occupancy grid map such that no two agents occupy the same cell at the same step. Algorithms like Conflict-Based Search and prioritized planning scale to the hundreds of Autonomous mobile robot units in a goods-to-person Logistics & Warehouse, and tie directly into Fleet management and Multi-robot system coordination. It contrasts with reactive schemes like Optimal Reciprocal Collision Avoidance, which avoid collisions locally without a global joint plan.

plain: A laser scanner that, for each pulse it sends, can report several echoes from partly see-through things like dust, foliage, or rain.
snappy: A LiDAR that records multiple returns per emitted pulse, capturing surfaces behind partial occluders such as foliage or precipitation.
detail: Multi-Echo LiDAR records the first, last, and sometimes intermediate echoes of a single pulse, so a beam that clips a leaf can still report the ground behind it, producing a richer Point cloud through partial occluders. This dual-return capability is valuable in Agriculture for canopy mapping and in Mobility for seeing through dust, rain, and thin obstacles. The extra returns, combined with the Intensity Return, help Ground segmentation distinguish vegetation from solid surfaces.

plain: Following many moving things at the same time while never mixing up which is which.
snappy: Tracking multiple objects simultaneously while preserving a consistent identity for each.
detail: Multi-object tracking, often abbreviated MOT, extends Object tracking to crowded scenes where cars, cyclists, and pedestrians all move at once and must keep stable IDs frame to frame. The dominant tracking-by-detection approach runs Object detection each frame and then solves Data association to stitch detections into tracks, frequently using a Kalman filter to predict where each track will move. In a self-driving stack it produces the labeled, persistent obstacles that Behavior prediction and motion planning rely on, and it is benchmarked on datasets like nuScenes.

plain: A group of robots that work together as a team to get a job done.
snappy: A collection of two or more robots that coordinate their actions toward shared or complementary goals.
detail: A multi-robot system pools sensing, computation, and physical reach across many machines so the team can cover more ground or lift more than any single unit. In a warehouse a Fleet of Autonomous mobile robots split picking routes under a Fleet management layer, often communicating over a Publish-subscribe network and resolving conflicting paths with Multi-agent path finding. The approach spans from tightly choreographed Swarm robotics to loosely coupled cooperatives, and the resulting team can show Emergent behavior that no individual robot was programmed to perform.

plain: Building a detailed 3D model of a scene by combining many overlapping photos taken from different known viewpoints.
snappy: Dense 3D reconstruction that fuses per-pixel depth estimated from many calibrated, overlapping images into a consistent surface or point cloud.
detail: Multi-View Stereo (MVS) takes images with known camera poses (often from Structure from motion plus Bundle adjustment) and computes dense correspondences across views to recover a Point cloud or Mesh, extending two-view Stereo matching to many cameras using Epipolar Geometry. It produces the dense geometry that sparse Visual SLAM does not, and is widely used for Space and inspection 3D reconstruction, Aerial photogrammetry, and digital-twin capture. Modern neural variants overlap with NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting, but classic MVS remains the calibrated, metric workhorse behind detailed surface models.

plain: A positioning mistake that happens when satellite signals bounce off buildings or the ground before reaching the receiver, making the location reading wrong.
snappy: GNSS positioning error caused by satellite signals arriving via reflected paths off nearby surfaces in addition to the direct line-of-sight.
detail: Multipath Error arises when a Global Navigation Satellite System signal reflects off buildings, vehicles, or terrain and reaches the antenna alongside the direct path, biasing the pseudorange and corrupting the fix. It is the dominant urban-canyon error source that degrades RTK GNSS and Precise Point Positioning, and it cannot be removed by differential corrections the way atmospheric errors can. Robots mitigate it with antenna design, signal-quality weighting, and tight GNSS/INS Integration so an Inertial measurement unit carries the solution through reflective environments.

plain: A tracking method that, when it is unsure which new sensor blip belongs to which object, keeps several possible explanations alive until later data makes the answer clear.
snappy: A multi-target tracker that maintains and prunes multiple data-association hypotheses across frames, deferring hard assignment decisions.
detail: Multiple Hypothesis Tracking (MHT) addresses the core Data association problem in Multi-object tracking by branching a tree of possible measurement-to-track assignments and carrying them forward, scoring each hypothesis and pruning low-probability branches rather than committing immediately the way a greedy SORT or Hungarian Algorithm step does. Each track is typically propagated with a Kalman filter, and MHT excels in dense, ambiguous, or cluttered scenes. In Defense & Security and Mobility it tracks many vehicles or contacts from Radar or LiDAR, trading higher Onboard compute cost for robustness to missed and false detections.

plain: A drone held up by several spinning propellers, usually four, that can hover in place and take off straight up.
snappy: A drone lifted and controlled by several fixed-pitch rotors (commonly four), enabling hover and vertical takeoff.
detail: A multirotor controls attitude and position by varying the speeds of its rotors, typically arranged as a Quadcopter, Hexacopter, or Octocopter, with each motor driven by an Electronic speed controller. It hovers precisely but has limited Endurance compared with a Fixed-wing drone, so it suits Aerial cinematography, inspection, and Last-mile delivery. A Flight controller stabilizes it using an Inertial measurement unit, and vendors like DJI and Skydio dominate the consumer and prosumer market.

plain: Training one robot model to do many different jobs at once so it shares what it learns between them.
snappy: Training a single model jointly on multiple tasks so shared structure improves performance and data efficiency on each.
detail: In robotics, multitask learning lets one network learn picking, inserting, and wiping together, so features useful for one task help another and overall Sample efficiency improves. It underpins any Generalist policy and large systems like RT-1 and RT-X trained across diverse Demonstration data. It is closely tied to Transfer learning and Representation learning, and must guard against negative transfer where unrelated tasks interfere.

plain: Briefly turning off a safety sensor on purpose so an approved item, like a pallet, can pass through without stopping the machine.
snappy: The automatic, controlled suspension of a protective device for a valid reason such as material transport through its sensing field.
detail: Muting temporarily and automatically disables a presence-sensing device like a Light curtain or Safety scanner so a pallet can pass on a conveyor without triggering a Protective stop, while still detecting a person. It uses additional muting sensors arranged so that only the expected object profile and timing can suspend protection; incorrect sequencing immediately ends muting. Muting must be designed to preserve the Performance Level required by ISO 13849, and is distinct from Blanking, which permanently ignores fixed beams rather than suspending the whole device.

plain: A heavy-duty gearbox that lets big industrial robot arms move accurately while carrying large loads.
snappy: High-rigidity, high-ratio cycloidal precision reducer that dominates the base and shoulder joints of industrial robot arms.
detail: The Nabtesco RV Reducer is a two-stage Cycloidal drive combining a spur-gear input stage with a cycloidal output stage, giving exceptional torsional rigidity, shock resistance, and very low Gear Backlash under heavy load. It is the de facto standard for the high-torque base, shoulder, and elbow joints of large Industrial robot arm products, complementing the Harmonic drive used in lighter wrist axes. Each reducer typically pairs with a Permanent magnet synchronous motor and a Servo drive for closed-loop Position control.

plain: A French company that builds small robots that drive through fields and pull weeds by themselves.
snappy: French maker of autonomous field-weeding robots, including the Oz and Dino platforms.
detail: Naio Technologies builds agricultural robots such as the small Oz and the larger straddling Dino that autonomously weed vegetable rows using mechanical tools rather than chemicals. The machines navigate crop rows with RTK GNSS and camera-based row-following, a form of natural feature navigation. They are a European counterpart to laser weeders like Carbon Robotics in the field robotics market.

plain: A naming prefix that groups a robot's programs and data channels so several robots can run side by side without their names clashing.
snappy: A hierarchical prefix that scopes node, topic, parameter, and service names within a ROS graph.
detail: A Namespace prepends a path-like prefix to names so that, for example, two robots can each have a 'scan' Topic that resolve to '/robot1/scan' and '/robot2/scan' without collision. It works together with Remapping to organize a multi-robot system or to nest a subsystem cleanly, and it also scopes the names used by tf2 frames and the Parameter Server. Namespaces are usually assigned in a Launch File and applied by rclcpp or rclpy when a Node starts.

plain: A tiny flying robot light enough to fit in your palm, used for flying indoors or scouting small spaces.
snappy: A sub-100-gram aerial robot, typically a tiny multirotor, sized for indoor flight and short-range reconnaissance.
detail: A Nano drone is a palm-sized aerial robot, usually a miniature Quadcopter under 100 grams, whose small mass makes it safe to fly near people indoors but leaves almost no margin for battery, sensors, or Onboard compute. Strict size, weight, and power limits push research toward efficient Optical flow sensor navigation, lightweight state estimation, and tiny processors, making it a popular Research/Frontier and Defense & Security platform such as the Crazyflie. It sits at the small end of the Micro air vehicle spectrum, above the Insect-scale flying robot but below a typical Multirotor drone.

plain: Letting a warehouse robot find its way by recognizing the building's existing walls and racks instead of following tape or markers on the floor.
snappy: Infrastructure-free AGV navigation that localizes by matching live laser scans to existing environment features.
detail: Natural feature navigation, also called contour or free navigation, lets a vehicle localize against the building's permanent geometry using Scan Matching against a stored Map, removing the need for floor tape or reflectors. It builds on Localization and SLAM and is the basis of flexible Autonomous mobile robot deployments that reroute instantly when a layout changes. Compared with Magnetic tape guidance it cuts commissioning cost, while still relying on Traffic management to coordinate the wider fleet.

plain: The standard free software, built on the popular ROS robot platform, that gives a wheeled robot a complete sense-where-am-I-and-drive-there ability.
snappy: The ROS 2 navigation framework that orchestrates planners, controllers, costmaps, and recovery behaviors through a behavior tree.
detail: Nav2 is the production-grade Navigation stack for ROS 2, replacing the original move_base. It uses a Behavior tree to sequence a Global planner (for example Dijkstra's algorithm or A* search), a Local planner / controller such as the Dynamic Window Approach or Timed Elastic Band, a Cost map with an Inflation layer, and AMCL for Localization, plus recovery actions when the robot gets stuck. It is the default autonomy brain for countless Autonomous mobile robot and Service robot deployments built on ros2_control.

plain: Working out a route from where a robot is to where it needs to go, and then following it.
snappy: Deciding and following a collision-free path from a start to a goal in an environment.
detail: Navigation combines Localization (knowing where you are), Mapping, Path planning, and obstacle handling so a robot can travel safely. In practice it is delivered by a Navigation stack such as Nav2, which fuses a Global planner, a Local planner, a Cost map, and Collision avoidance. It is the core competence of an Autonomous mobile robot, a Delivery robot, and a Self-driving car alike, and depends on continuous Obstacle detection.

plain: The full bundle of software that lets a robot figure out where it is, decide a route, and actually drive there without hitting things.
snappy: The integrated software pipeline that maps, localizes, plans, and drives a mobile robot from point A to point B.
detail: A navigation stack ties together Mapping, Localization (often AMCL), a Global planner and Local planner, a Cost map with its Inflation layer, and recovery behaviors into one autonomy pipeline. It is the backbone of Logistics & Warehouse and Service & Consumer robots: a Differential drive Autonomous mobile robot uses it to follow Waypoint navigation goals while doing live Obstacle avoidance. The canonical modern implementation is Nav2, the ROS 2 successor to the original ROS Navigation stack.

plain: Imaging fields from the air to color-code how healthy and green the plants are, using light the human eye cannot see.
snappy: Producing crop-health maps from a vegetation index computed from red and near-infrared bands of drone multispectral imagery.
detail: NDVI mapping flies a Precision agriculture drone carrying a multispectral Camera, then computes the vegetation index per pixel to highlight stressed or vigorous crop zones. The index layer is georeferenced onto an Orthomosaic built by Aerial photogrammetry, with detail set by Ground sample distance, so agronomists can target irrigation or spraying. It is a staple Agriculture workflow, often flown the same mission that gathers the 3D reconstruction of the field.

plain: A gripper that grabs soft or porous materials by poking thin needles into them at angles, then pulling out to release.
snappy: A gripper that holds porous or fabric materials by driving angled retractable needles into them.
detail: A needle gripper (pin gripper) penetrates a porous or fibrous workpiece with several thin needles set at opposing angles, mechanically interlocking with the material so it can lift items that have no graspable rim and that a Suction gripper cannot seal against. It is the tool of choice for textiles, carbon-fiber preforms, foam, and insulation in apparel and composite handling. As specialized End-of-arm tooling it serves Pick and place where a Parallel-jaw gripper would crush or slip on limp material.

plain: A hole, ditch, or drop-off in the ground that a robot must spot and avoid, which is harder to see than a solid object sticking up.
snappy: A downward terrain hazard such as a ditch, cliff, or hole that perception must detect and avoid, in contrast to positive (raised) obstacles.
detail: Negative obstacles (ditch detection) are notoriously hard because a hole returns few or no sensor points, so a LiDAR or Depth camera may see only empty space until the edge is close. Off-road Unmanned ground vehicle and Planetary rover navigation use Ground segmentation, Elevation Map, and range-shadow analysis to flag them, and a Cliff Sensor handles the indoor analog for a Cleaning robot. They are a core difficulty in Obstacle detection for Field robotics and feed the Cost map used by the Local planner.

plain: When something a robot learned for one job actually makes it worse at another job.
snappy: A phenomenon where knowledge transferred from a source task degrades rather than improves performance on a target task.
detail: Negative transfer is the dark side of Transfer learning and Multitask learning: a grasping prior tuned on rigid boxes can hurt a policy that must do Deformable object manipulation, because the source bias misleads the target. It is a major risk when training a Cross-embodiment dataset where a wheeled robot's locomotion data confuses a Legged robot, and it underlies the Plasticity-stability dilemma. Mitigations include task-conditioning, gating, and careful curation in a Robot foundation model so unrelated skills do not interfere.

plain: A way of capturing a real scene with a few photos so a computer can then generate a realistic image of it from any angle you choose.
snappy: A neural network that encodes a scene's color and density as a continuous volume, letting you render photorealistic novel views from arbitrary camera poses.
detail: A NeRF trains a small neural network to predict color and opacity at every point in space, so a robot can render the scene from viewpoints it never directly photographed. In robotics it is used for dense 3D reconstruction and Photorealistic rendering of cluttered environments, feeding Sensor simulation pipelines and closing the Reality gap for Sim-to-real transfer. Capture requires accurate Camera intrinsics and poses, often recovered by Structure from motion or Visual SLAM, and the result complements Point cloud maps where smooth, view-dependent appearance matters. Rendering is slower than Gaussian splatting, which is why many embodied systems now prefer the latter for real-time use.

plain: Catching a fixed-wing drone by deliberately flying it into a big net so it can land without a runway.
snappy: Recovering a runway-less fixed-wing UAV by guiding it into a capture net that arrests its flight.
detail: Net recovery brings a Fixed-wing drone home by flying it into a tensioned net, arresting the aircraft without landing gear or a runway, which makes it the usual partner to Catapult launch on ships and in the field. Accurate terminal guidance, often aided by RTK GNSS or vision, is needed to hit the net, and the technique is widespread in Defense & Security UAS operations. It is one alternative to the vertical landing of a Hybrid VTOL or a Precision landing onto a pad.

plain: A learned way to boil an entire image down to one compact fingerprint, so a robot can tell whether two pictures show the same location.
snappy: A trainable global image descriptor that aggregates local CNN features into a compact vector for place recognition.
detail: NetVLAD adds a differentiable feature-aggregation layer on top of a Convolutional neural network so the whole network can be trained end-to-end to produce a single descriptor robust to viewpoint and illumination changes, improving on hand-crafted bag-of-words approaches like DBoW2. It is a leading Place recognition method, supplying loop-closure candidates that become a Loop Closure Constraint in Visual SLAM and GraphSLAM back-ends. For a Mobility robot revisiting a route, NetVLAD enables global Localization and drift correction in Visual odometry; modern variants build on DINOv2 features for stronger generalization.

plain: A brain-inspired computer model that lets a robot learn skills from examples instead of being hand-programmed, by adjusting many internal numbers.
snappy: A trainable model that maps a robot's sensor inputs to actions or predictions, with its internal weights learned from data.
detail: A neural network is the workhorse function approximator behind nearly every learned robot Policy, used to represent a Value function in Reinforcement learning, a perception model in Computer vision, or a control law in Learning-based control. Specialized variants dominate different jobs: a Convolutional neural network for images, a Transformer for sequences and a Robot foundation model. On robots it typically runs on Onboard compute such as an NVIDIA Jetson, where size constraints motivate Policy distillation.

plain: A way for a robot to build a detailed 3D model of a real space from ordinary camera photos, which it can then view from new angles it never actually photographed.
