detail: RoboCasa builds on the robosuite stack and the MuJoCo physics engine, assembling thousands of generative assets into procedurally varied kitchen scenes so a Mobile manipulator or Humanoid robot can practice tasks like opening drawers, operating appliances, and tidying counters. It is a form of Generative simulation: AI-authored objects and layouts produce massive Synthetic data sets for Imitation learning and for fine-tuning a Diffusion policy or a Vision-language-action model. The diversity of scenes targets Sim-to-real transfer and broad Generalization, addressing Robot data scarcity by cheaply expanding the training distribution beyond what teleoperated Demonstration data alone could cover.

plain: A robot AI from DeepMind that can control different robot arms and gets better over time by generating and learning from its own new attempts.
snappy: A self-improving, multi-embodiment manipulation agent that bootstraps new skills by generating its own training data.
detail: RoboCat, from DeepMind, is a Generalist robot agent that controls multiple manipulator embodiments and improves itself: after fine-tuning on a handful of demonstrations of a new task, it deploys to gather more data, then retrains on that self-generated data to consolidate the skill. This self-improvement loop is a form of Cross-embodiment learning and showcases the Robot foundation model paradigm seen in Gato, RT-X, and Octo policy. It targets sample-efficient acquisition of new Manipulation tasks across hardware.

plain: A method that takes an existing image-and-text AI and adds a small control module so it can become a robot that follows instructions.
snappy: A manipulation policy built by adding lightweight action heads to the pretrained Flamingo vision-language model, fine-tuned on imitation data.
detail: RoboFlamingo (2023) adapts the open Flamingo vision-language model into a Language-conditioned manipulation policy by freezing most of the backbone and training lightweight policy heads plus a recurrent module on Imitation learning demonstrations. It is an efficient route to a Vision-language-action model that reuses web-scale pretraining, evaluated on benchmarks like CALVIN for long-horizon tasks. The approach parallels the Robotics Transformer line (RT-2, OpenVLA) but emphasizes parameter-efficient fine-tuning rather than full retraining of a Foundation model.

plain: A research toolkit for teaching robots tasks by showing them recordings of the task being done, plus the datasets to do it.
snappy: A framework and dataset suite for studying learning from demonstration, standardizing offline imitation-learning algorithms and benchmarks.
detail: robomimic packages curated Demonstration data and reference implementations of Behavior cloning and Offline reinforcement learning so results on Learning from demonstration are comparable across papers. It runs on robosuite/MuJoCo tasks and supplies the datasets and baselines that later methods such as Diffusion policy were measured against, supporting Manipulation research. Its careful study of how demonstration quality and algorithm choice affect performance made it a standard reference for Imitation learning practitioners.

plain: A flexible toolkit of simulated robot-arm tasks used by researchers to train and compare robot learning methods.
snappy: A modular MuJoCo-based simulation framework and benchmark suite for standardized robot manipulation tasks.
detail: robosuite provides configurable arms, grippers, controllers, and tasks (lifting, stacking, Peg-in-hole, door opening) on top of the MuJoCo Physics engine, giving a common API for Reinforcement learning and Imitation learning research. It is the simulation substrate for the robomimic demonstration-learning suite and pairs with datasets used to train a Diffusion policy or Behavior cloning agent. As a Manipulation benchmark it sits alongside ManiSkill and the broader BEHAVIOR Benchmark for comparing policies before Sim-to-real transfer.

plain: A machine that can sense its surroundings, decide what to do, and physically move or act on its own.
snappy: A programmable machine that senses, computes, and acts physically in the world.
detail: A robot couples three capabilities in one body: Sensing the world through a Sensor, computing a decision, and Actuation to move. The classic Sense-plan-act loop runs continuously, whether the machine is an Industrial robot arm welding car panels, an Autonomous mobile robot ferrying totes in a warehouse, or a Humanoid robot. The field that studies and builds these machines is Robotics.

plain: A tune-up procedure that measures a robot's real shape and corrects its internal model so it reaches programmed points accurately.
snappy: A procedure aligning a robot's kinematic model to its true geometry to improve absolute accuracy.
detail: Robot calibration (or mastering) measures the true link lengths and joint offsets and updates the Denavit-Hartenberg parameters used in Forward kinematics and Inverse kinematics, turning good Repeatability into good Accuracy. It is essential before Offline programming can be trusted, since the simulated and physical robot must agree. Kinematic calibration typically uses a laser tracker or a Motion Capture System, and joint mastering re-zeros each Encoder to a known reference pose.

plain: The fenced or marked-off work area that contains a robot and everything it needs to do its job safely.
snappy: A bounded workspace housing a robot, its tooling, fixtures, and safety guarding.
detail: A robot cell groups the arm, its Robot controller, Fixturing, conveyors, and End-of-arm tooling inside a defined boundary protected by Machine guarding, a Light curtain, or a Safety scanner that triggers a Protective stop when breached. Cell layout sets reach, Cycle time, and operator access, and is typically engineered by a Robot integrator. A traditional cell is fully fenced, whereas a Cobot cell relying on Power and force limiting or Speed and separation monitoring can omit the fence under ISO 10218 and ISO/TS 15066.

plain: The computer cabinet that runs an industrial robot, deciding how each joint moves and executing its program.
snappy: A dedicated controller cabinet that executes an industrial robot's motion programs and drives its joint servos.
detail: The Robot controller houses the processor, motor drives, and safety circuits that turn programmed commands into coordinated arm motion, computing Inverse kinematics and Trajectory profiles for each Servomotor in real time. Operators write and edit programs through a Teach pendant connected to the controller, which also handles I/O with Fixturing and End-of-arm tooling. Major vendors such as FANUC, KUKA, and ABB Robotics each ship proprietary controllers, and the unit enforces Emergency stop and Protective stop logic inside the Robot cell.

plain: A safety feature that senses when a robot has hit something and stops it fast to limit damage.
snappy: Monitoring motor torque or current to detect an unexpected collision and trigger an immediate stop.
detail: Robot crash detection compares measured joint torque against the value predicted by the arm's Inverse dynamics model; a sustained mismatch signals an impact and triggers a Protective stop. It needs no extra Force/torque sensor because it reads existing Servo drive current, and it is foundational to a Cobot's Power and force limiting safety mode. Unlike Self-collision avoidance, which is preventive geometry, crash detection is reactive and pairs with an Andon alert and a Drive fault log so the Robot controller can flag the event for the operator.

plain: The problem that there is far less real robot motion data available than there is text or images, making it hard to train powerful robot models.
snappy: The shortage of large, diverse real-world robot interaction datasets relative to the web-scale text and image corpora used elsewhere in AI.
detail: Robot data scarcity is the central bottleneck for a Robot foundation model: collecting contact-rich teleoperated demonstrations is slow and costly compared with scraping the web. Responses include pooling a Cross-embodiment dataset such as Open X-Embodiment, scaling cheap Sim-to-real data via Domain randomization, and building a Data flywheel through Fleet learning. It is why the Scaling hypothesis is harder to test in robotics than in language, and it drives interest in Self-supervised learning from unlabeled video.

plain: A way of measuring how heavily a country or industry uses robots by counting how many robots there are for every 10,000 human workers.
snappy: An industry benchmark expressing installed robots per 10,000 manufacturing employees.
detail: Robot density (robots per 10,000 workers) is the headline figure the IFR publishes each year to compare automation intensity across countries, with South Korea, Singapore, and Germany historically leading. It signals how far Industrial robotics has penetrated a manufacturing base and is often read against a national Labor shortage and Reshoring trends. A rising density reflects falling Total cost of ownership for an Industrial robot arm and growing comfort with Collaborative robot installations on the floor.

plain: The study of the moral questions raised by how robots are designed, used, and allowed to act.
snappy: The field examining the moral and societal implications of designing and deploying robots.
detail: Robot ethics, or roboethics, asks who is responsible when robots cause harm, how autonomy should be bounded, and what limits society should place on robotic systems. It engages directly with an Autonomous weapon and the meaningful-human-control debate, with the labor effects of Automation, and with thought experiments like the Trolley problem in self-driving. It also revisits classic ideas such as the Three Laws of Robotics and connects to Trust and Explainability.

plain: A single large AI model, trained on huge amounts of robot data, that can serve as the brain for many different robots and tasks.
snappy: A large pretrained model used as a general-purpose backbone for robot perception and control.
detail: A robot foundation model is trained on broad, often cross-robot datasets (such as Open X-Embodiment) to produce a reusable control or perception backbone that adapts to many tasks with little extra data. A Vision-language-action model like RT-2 or OpenVLA is a prominent example, enabling Generalization and even Zero-shot generalization across new objects and embodiments via Cross-embodiment learning. Such models are reshaping how a Humanoid robot and Generalist robot are programmed, replacing per-task engineering with fine-tuning.

plain: Free software that gives robot programmers ready-made building blocks so they don't have to write everything from scratch.
snappy: An open-source middleware framework that structures robot software into communicating components with standardized messaging and tooling.
detail: Robot Operating System is not an operating system but a Middleware layer: programs run as a Node, exchange data over a Topic via Publish-subscribe, and share a common message and Transform tree convention. It bundles drivers, the Navigation stack, visualization in RViz, and bridges to MoveIt for arms and Gazebo for simulation, which is why most research and many products build on ROS or its successor ROS 2. Its package ecosystem makes a Hardware abstraction layer and reuse across robots practical.

plain: A powered turntable or fixture that tilts and spins the part while the robot works on it, so hard-to-reach spots become easy.
snappy: A motorized fixture that rotates and tilts a workpiece in coordinated motion with the robot.
detail: A robot positioner adds one or more external axes that the robot controller drives in coordinated motion, presenting the joint to an Arc welding robot at the ideal angle for a continuous, downhand weld. Treated as extra degrees of freedom alongside the arm, it expands the effective Workspace much as a Seventh axis does, and its frame is tied into the Work object frame. Headstock-tailstock and tilt-rotate styles are common in Robotic welding cells.

plain: Software that creates a virtual robot and world so you can test ideas on a computer before risking real hardware.
snappy: Software modeling a robot's physics, sensors, and environment so behavior can be developed and tested virtually.
detail: A robot simulator couples a Physics engine for rigid- and Soft-body simulation with Sensor simulation and rendering so a full control stack can run against a virtual world. It is the foundation for safe development, large-scale Synthetic data generation, and Reinforcement learning before Sim-to-real transfer bridges the Reality gap. Widely used examples include Gazebo, MuJoCo, Isaac Sim, PyBullet, Webots, and CoppeliaSim, many supporting Headless simulation and Parallel simulation.

plain: A specific arm pose where the robot momentarily loses a way to move smoothly, so it can lurch or refuse to continue.
snappy: An arm configuration where the Jacobian loses rank, making joint motion ill-defined and commanded joint speeds spike.
detail: At a robot singularity the Jacobian matrix becomes rank-deficient, so achieving a small Cartesian motion can demand near-infinite joint velocity, and the controller faults or the arm stutters. The classic case on a Six-axis robot is the Wrist Singularity, when two wrist axes align; Shoulder Singularity and Elbow Singularity are the others. Path planners and the Robot controller avoid singularities by reshaping the Trajectory, switching to Damped Least Squares Inverse kinematics, or routing the Tool center point around the degenerate region of the Spherical wrist.

plain: A set of web-page code libraries that let a normal browser talk to a robot and show its data and 3D models.
snappy: A suite of JavaScript libraries (roslibjs, ros3djs) that bridge web browsers to ROS for building web-based robot interfaces.
detail: Robot Web Tools connect a browser to a ROS system through the rosbridge WebSocket protocol, with roslibjs subscribing to a Topic and publishing commands and ros3djs rendering 3D scenes and a Transform tree. They make it easy to build a remote Human-machine interface or dashboard for Teleoperation and monitoring without native software. They are commonly used to put a lightweight control panel in front of a robot exposed via rosbridge.

plain: The cluster of small joints at the end of a robot arm that aims and tilts whatever tool is attached, like a human wrist orienting the hand.
snappy: The set of joints near the tip of a manipulator that controls the orientation of the end-effector.
detail: The robot wrist is the distal group of joints, typically the last three on a Six-axis robot, that sets End-effector orientation while the larger arm joints set position. A Spherical wrist whose three axes intersect at a point keeps Inverse kinematics tractable but introduces a Kinematic singularity when two axes align. The wrist carries the Tool flange and any Tool changer, and its design directly affects payload, reach, and Dexterity in both Manufacturing arms and Humanoid robot limbs.

plain: A robot program that takes the robot's joint angles and its physical description and works out where every part of the robot is in space.
snappy: A ROS node that reads joint states and the URDF to compute and broadcast each link's coordinate frame transform.
detail: robot_state_publisher subscribes to joint positions and, using the kinematic tree defined in the robot's URDF, computes the Transform of every Link relative to its parent and publishes them to tf2. This gives the rest of the system, including RViz, MoveIt, and planners, an up-to-date picture of where the robot's body is. It handles the moving joints, while a separate static publisher handles fixed offsets such as a sensor mount.

plain: A self-driving taxi you can hail with an app that arrives and drives you with no human driver.
snappy: A driverless passenger vehicle operated commercially as an on-demand ride-hailing service.
detail: A robotaxi is a Self-driving car deployed as a paid service, requiring Level 4 automation reliability inside a mapped operational design domain plus fleet management and remote operation center oversight. Operators like Waymo and Zoox add rider pickup logic, autonomous docking at curbs, and a minimal risk condition fallback when the Automated driving system cannot continue. Beyond the car itself, the business depends on uptime, fleet routing, and Mobility regulation, distinguishing it from a privately owned self-driving vehicle.

plain: A robot that smooths rough edges off freshly made parts by grinding or filing them with a spinning tool.
snappy: A robot removing burrs and excess material from parts using rotary abrasive or cutting tools.
detail: Robotic deburring presses a rotary tool against an edge while regulating contact via Force control or a Remote center of compliance so the tool follows surface variation without gouging. It overlaps Robotic Grinding and finishing, and the path is typically generated by Offline programming from CAD against the Work object frame. Because contact forces feed back into the arm, deburring is a textbook Compliant manipulation problem and may use a Force/torque sensor at the Tool flange.

plain: Using a robot to remove material from a part with a spinning abrasive wheel or belt, controlling how hard it presses.
snappy: Force-controlled robotic material removal using abrasive wheels or belts to remove stock, weld beads, or flash.
detail: Robotic Grinding has an Industrial robot arm drive an abrasive wheel or belt as End-of-arm tooling against a workpiece while regulating contact through Force control or Admittance control, since material removal rate depends directly on applied pressure. A Force/torque sensor closes the loop so the system maintains target force as the wheel wears and part geometry changes, often paired with Robotic deburring of edges and weld cleanup after Robotic welding. It is the heavy-stock-removal stage that precedes the finer Robotic Sanding and Robotic Polishing steps, and benefits from accurate Robot calibration and stiff Six-axis robot platforms to resist grinding reaction loads.

plain: A robot hand with several fingers that can grip and handle objects much like a person's hand.
snappy: A multi-fingered end effector that emulates the dexterity of a human hand for manipulation.
detail: A Robotic hand is a multi-fingered End-effector designed for far more versatility than a simple Gripper, enabling Dexterous manipulation and In-hand manipulation rather than just opening and closing. Designs include the Anthropomorphic hand and the Tendon-driven hand, often paired with Tactile sensor arrays for Slip detection and fine Grip force control. Robotic hands are central to Humanoid robot platforms such as Tesla Optimus and Figure AI, where one effector must handle tools and objects built for people.

plain: Using a robot to spray paint or coating onto parts, usually inside a sealed booth to contain the fumes.
snappy: Robot-applied atomized spray coating, performed by a paint robot in an explosion-proof booth to ensure uniform film and worker safety.
detail: Robotic Painting uses a dedicated Painting robot, typically a hollow-wrist Six-axis robot rated for hazardous atmospheres, to atomize and spray coating with consistent film thickness across complex geometry such as car bodies and appliances. Paths are usually built with Offline programming and rely on accurate Robot calibration plus a defined Tool center point so spray distance and overlap stay uniform, while Conveyor tracking lets the robot paint parts moving continuously down a Production line. It is the finishing stage after surface preparation by Robotic Sanding, and the explosion-proof booth, interlocked through a Safety PLC, keeps the flammable solvent environment isolated from operators.

plain: Using a robot to rub a part's surface with fine abrasives until it becomes smooth and glossy.
snappy: Robot-applied abrasive finishing that smooths and brings a workpiece surface to a high gloss under controlled contact force.
detail: In Robotic Polishing, an Industrial robot arm holds either the workpiece or a polishing pad as End-of-arm tooling and presses it against the surface with regulated contact, typically using Force control or Compliance control so the tool follows curved geometry without gouging. A Force/torque sensor or a Remote center of compliance lets the system hold consistent pressure across automotive trim, faucets, or medical implants where a uniform finish matters. It sits at the end of a finishing sequence after Robotic Grinding and Robotic Sanding, and like those it relies on accurate Robot calibration and a well-defined Tool center point to keep the abrasive path on the part.

plain: Using a robot to smooth a surface with sandpaper, usually to prepare it before paint or coating is applied.
snappy: Automated abrasive surface preparation, typically performed before painting or coating to ensure adhesion and finish quality.
detail: In Robotic Sanding, an Industrial robot arm sweeps an orbital or belt sander held as End-of-arm tooling across a surface, using Force control or Compliance control to keep even pressure over contours and avoid burn-through on thin material. It commonly precedes Robotic Painting on automotive panels and aerospace composites, where consistent surface roughness drives coating adhesion, and follows coarser Robotic Grinding when stock removal is needed first. Repeatable coverage depends on accurate path programming, often via Offline programming, plus reliable Robot calibration and a defined Tool center point so every pass overlaps correctly.

plain: A robot that automatically drives screws into parts and tightens them to exactly the right firmness.
snappy: Automated insertion and torque-controlled tightening of threaded fasteners by a robot.
detail: Robotic screwdriving feeds a fastener to a powered spindle on the End-of-arm tooling, then drives and tightens it while monitoring torque-versus-angle to verify the joint, a close relative of Threaded Fastener Insertion and Peg-in-hole assembly. Finding the hole reliably often uses a Spiral search or Force control to settle the screw before run-down. It is a common task for a Cobot in electronics Assembly and benefits from Compliance to absorb misalignment.

plain: A flexible touch-sensitive covering, like artificial skin, spread across a robot so it can feel contact anywhere on its body.
snappy: A flexible, large-area sensor sheet that gives a robot distributed touch sensing across its body.
detail: Robotic skin, or e-skin, distributes many tactile sensing elements over a robot's surfaces so contact can be felt across the whole body rather than only at a fingertip. It extends the idea of a single Tactile sensor to large, conformable coverage, supporting safe Human-robot interaction and Whole-body control. On a Humanoid robot it enables gentle Collision detection and grasping with the forearm, often built from a Capacitive sensor or piezoresistive array.

plain: A robot control method that renders a few simulated camera views of a scene, then uses those pictures to decide exactly how the arm should move.
snappy: A multi-view transformer (RVT) that re-renders the point cloud into several virtual camera images and predicts manipulation actions from them, replacing expensive voxel grids.
detail: RVT projects the captured Point cloud into a small set of orthographic virtual views, runs a Transformer over those images, and back-projects predictions to a 6-DoF action, achieving the accuracy of voxel methods like Perceiver-Actor while training and running much faster. It performs language-conditioned manipulation from Demonstration data and is evaluated on RLBench. As a multi-view spatial-action policy it sits alongside Transporter Networks in the manipulation-from-images lineage.

plain: Using a robot arm to weld metal parts together automatically instead of having a person hold the torch.
snappy: Automated arc, spot, or laser welding performed by a programmed industrial robot.
detail: A welding robot carries a torch or weld gun as its End-of-arm tooling and follows taught or planned seams with the Repeatability needed for consistent welds, far steadier than a human across a long shift. Arc-welding cells often add Conveyor tracking, seam-tracking Machine vision, and Fixturing to hold parts square, while spot welding dominates automotive body shops. It is one of the oldest and densest uses of the Six-axis robot, with FANUC, KUKA, and Yaskawa supplying most of the installed base, all governed by ISO 10218 safety rules.

plain: The branch of engineering that designs, builds, and runs robots.
snappy: The engineering discipline of designing, building, programming, and operating robots.
detail: Robotics spans mechanical design, Actuation, Sensing, control, and software, drawing heavily on Kinematics, Dynamics, and Control theory. It overlaps with Mechatronics and Cybernetics, and increasingly with machine learning for Perception and decision-making. A working Robot is the product of robotics integrating an End-effector, a Robot controller, and a Perception-action loop into one system.

plain: A family of robot AI models built on the transformer design that read camera images and instructions and output the next robot action.
snappy: The RT model family of transformer architectures mapping image and language inputs to tokenized robot actions, scaled across large multi-robot datasets.
detail: The Robotics Transformer family (Google) includes RT-1, RT-2, and RT-X, transformer policies that take camera frames and a language instruction and emit actions via Action Tokenization. RT-1 trained on large real-robot logs, RT-2 co-fine-tuned a web-scale vision-language model to become a Vision-language-action model, and RT-X trained on the Open X-Embodiment Cross-embodiment dataset to study positive transfer across robots. The line established the Robot foundation model paradigm later extended by OpenVLA, Octo, Pi-Zero, and the Robotic View Transformer.

plain: A business model where a company rents the use of robots on a subscription instead of buying the hardware outright.
snappy: Delivering robot capability on a recurring subscription rather than as a one-time capital purchase.
detail: Robotics-as-a-service (RaaS) bundles hardware, software, maintenance, and updates into a recurring fee, lowering the upfront barrier and shifting risk to the provider. Warehouse operators rent an Autonomous mobile robot fleet from vendors like Locus Robotics under RaaS, with Fleet management and updates handled remotely. The model leans on Cloud robotics and a Service-level agreement, and it reshapes the Return on investment and Total cost of ownership calculation versus outright purchase.

plain: A company that makes grippers and sensors designed to clip onto collaborative robots so they can pick things up.
snappy: A vendor of plug-and-play cobot grippers, force-torque sensors, and palletizing kits for collaborative robots.
detail: Robotiq supplies End-of-arm tooling built specifically for the Cobot market, including adaptive Parallel-jaw gripper and Suction gripper modules, a wrist-mounted Force/torque sensor, and turnkey Palletizing kits. Its hardware mounts on the Tool flange of a Universal Robots arm and similar Collaborative robot platforms with software plug-ins that avoid deep PLC integration. Robotiq competes with Schunk, OnRobot, and ATI Industrial Automation in the cobot-tooling segment, emphasizing fast deployment for Pick and place and machine-tending jobs.

plain: A widely used commercial robot hand, often a two-finger clamp, that adapts its grip to objects and bolts onto collaborative arms.
snappy: A family of industrial adaptive parallel-jaw and three-finger grippers designed for collaborative robots.
detail: Robotiq grippers, including the well-known 2F-85 Parallel-jaw gripper and a three-finger adaptive model, are plug-and-play End-of-arm tooling sold for a Cobot or Collaborative robot such as the Universal Robots UR series. Their fingers self-adapt to part shape and the grip force is programmable, easing deployment for Pick and place, Machine tending, and Bin picking. Robotiq also supplies a Force/torque sensor for Force control, positioning it alongside vendors like Schunk gripper and OnRobot.

plain: A Korean company that makes the smart motors and the small TurtleBot kits hobbyists and students learn robotics on.
snappy: Korean maker of Dynamixel smart servo actuators and the TurtleBot research/education kit line.
detail: Robotis is best known for the Dynamixel servomotor, a networked smart actuator with a built-in encoder and motor controller that exposes position control, velocity control, and torque control over a serial bus. Dynamixels power countless research arms, hexapod robot legs, and humanoid robot joints, and Robotis co-developed the TurtleBot reference platform built on ROS. The modules are a staple of robotics education.

plain: A way of getting robots where a company pays a monthly fee to use them instead of buying them upfront.
snappy: A subscription model in which a customer rents robots and their software for a recurring fee rather than purchasing the hardware outright.
detail: Robots-as-a-Service (RaaS) shifts a deployment from a large Capital Expenditure to a predictable Operating Expenditure, lowering the barrier to a first Pilot deployment and shortening the time to a positive Return on investment. The provider typically bundles the hardware, Fleet management software, Field Service, and a Service-level agreement into one monthly price tied to Utilization Rate or output. The model is common for Autonomous mobile robot fleets and Goods-to-person systems, where the vendor retains ownership and handles Predictive maintenance and Spare Parts Inventory. See the closely related catalog term Robotics-as-a-service.

plain: A controller deliberately designed to keep working even when the engineer's model of the machine is somewhat wrong or unexpected forces push on it.
snappy: Control synthesized to guarantee stability and performance across a bounded set of model uncertainties and disturbances.
detail: Robust control (including H-infinity design) optimizes worst-case performance over an uncertainty set rather than a single nominal model, trading peak performance for guaranteed margins. It is the conservative counterpart to Adaptive control and a hardening layer over a Linear quadratic regulator or Linear quadratic Gaussian, which can be fragile. Robotics uses it for reliable Disturbance rejection and Trajectory tracking when contact forces, friction, or unmodeled flexibility are bounded but uncertain, and it is verified with tools like Lyapunov stability.

plain: A robot's ability to keep working well even when conditions are messy, noisy, or not exactly what it expected.
snappy: The ability to maintain acceptable performance despite noise, disturbances, modeling error, and uncertainty.
detail: Robustness measures how gracefully a system tolerates the unexpected, from Sensor noise and Disturbance rejection to a Long-tail scenario the designer never anticipated. In control it is delivered by Robust control and Sliding mode control; in autonomy it shows up as Fault tolerance, Graceful degradation, and a Fallback behavior. It is closely tied to handling Uncertainty, and is a central concern when moving a policy from Simulation across the Reality gap in Sim-to-real transfer.

plain: A six-wheel suspension with hinged arms but no springs that keeps every wheel on the ground while crawling over big rocks.
snappy: A passive springless six-wheel suspension that distributes load and keeps all wheels grounded over rough, uneven terrain.
detail: The Rocker-Bogie Suspension is the signature drivetrain of NASA Mars rovers, letting a Planetary rover such as Perseverance climb obstacles roughly a wheel-diameter tall without tipping. Its pivoting linkage has no springs, so it averages terrain across all six wheels at low speed, maximizing traction and stability over boulders. It is a defining Space mobility mechanism, paired with steered corner wheels and careful Foothold selection style path choice on hazardous ground.

plain: An American company whose Allen-Bradley controllers run much of North American manufacturing.
snappy: Maker of Allen-Bradley PLCs and the Studio 5000 control platform for industrial automation.
detail: Rockwell Automation produces the Allen-Bradley Programmable logic controller families (ControlLogix, CompactLogix) programmed in Studio 5000 using Ladder logic, plus the Kinetix Servo drive line. Its controllers communicate over EtherNet/IP and the CIP Safety protocol, and the FactoryTalk suite extends into Manufacturing execution system territory. Dominant in North American Discrete automation, Rockwell competes with Siemens, Beckhoff, and Bosch Rexroth, and integrates robotic cells via standard fieldbus links to the Robot controller.

plain: A type of screw mechanism that turns spinning into pushing, using many small threaded rollers to carry very heavy loads in a compact size.
snappy: A linear actuator drive using planetary threaded rollers between screw and nut for high load capacity and long life.
detail: A Roller Screw (planetary or satellite type) replaces the recirculating balls of a Ball screw with multiple threaded rollers that spread the load over far more contact points, giving higher force capacity, stiffness, and shock tolerance in a compact envelope. This makes it the linear element of choice in high-force electric actuators - electric presses, Electrohydrostatic Actuator units, and the legs of some heavy Humanoid robot designs - where it converts a Brushless DC motor's rotation into powerful Linear actuator thrust. It outperforms a Lead screw or Ball screw on duty cycle and life under heavy load.

plain: A camera that records the image one row at a time from top to bottom, which can warp things that move quickly while it scans.
snappy: A camera readout mode that exposes rows sequentially, causing skew or wobble on fast-moving scenes.
detail: A rolling shutter reads out pixel rows one after another, so different parts of the frame are captured at slightly different times, bending or shearing fast-moving objects and complicating Visual SLAM. It is cheaper and common in consumer sensors, the opposite trade-off to a Global shutter. Robotics pipelines either compensate for the row timing in Visual-inertial odometry or choose a global-shutter Camera for demanding Perception.

plain: The skew or wobble you see when a camera reads its image one row at a time while something moves quickly past it.
snappy: Geometric image distortion caused by a sensor reading out rows sequentially rather than capturing the whole frame at once.
detail: A Rolling shutter sensor exposes image rows at slightly different instants, so fast relative motion of the Ego vehicle or a passing object bends straight lines and shifts apparent positions, corrupting feature geometry. This degrades Visual odometry, Structure from motion, and any 3D object detection that assumes a single capture time, which is why a Global shutter or explicit rolling-shutter modeling is preferred. The effect must be accounted for in Sensor Calibration and Motion Compensation for an Automated driving system.

plain: A free, widely used software toolkit that gives roboticists ready-made building blocks so they don't have to write every robot program from scratch.
snappy: An open-source middleware framework that structures robot software as nodes exchanging messages over topics, services, and actions.
detail: Despite its name ROS is not an operating system but Middleware plus tooling: each program is a Node, data flows over a Topic via Publish-subscribe, and request-response uses a Service while long jobs use an Action. The ecosystem includes RViz for visualization, the tf transform library, rosbag for logging, Gazebo for simulation, and MoveIt and Nav2 stacks. Its successor ROS 2 addresses real-time and multi-robot needs.

plain: The modern, rebuilt version of the popular robot software toolkit, designed to be reliable enough for real products and fleets.
snappy: A ground-up redesign of ROS built on DDS for real-time, secure, multi-robot, production-grade systems.
detail: ROS 2 keeps the familiar Node, Topic, Service, and Action concepts of ROS but replaces the old central master with the DDS discovery and transport standard, adding configurable quality-of-service, security, and Real-time support. It underpins production stacks like Nav2 and ros2_control, records data with rosbag2, and runs on microcontrollers via Micro-ROS. Simulators such as Gazebo and Isaac Sim integrate directly with ROS 2.

plain: A swappable connector that lets ROS 2 use different underlying networking software without changing the robot's program code.
snappy: The abstraction layer (rmw) that lets ROS 2 plug in different DDS vendor implementations behind a common API.
detail: The ROS Middleware Interface, or rmw, decouples ROS 2 client libraries from the specific transport that carries messages, so the same Node code works whether the backend is Fast DDS, Cyclone DDS, or Zenoh. It exposes the publish-subscribe and service primitives that rclcpp and rclpy build on, and it is where a Quality of Service policy is ultimately enforced. Choosing the rmw implementation tunes a robot's latency, discovery behavior, and resource use without touching application code.

plain: An open-source project that adapts the popular robot software framework for use with factory robot arms and automation equipment.
snappy: An open-source project (ROS-I) extending ROS and ROS 2 with drivers, libraries, and standards for industrial robot arms and automation.
detail: ROS-Industrial brings the ROS ecosystem to factory hardware by providing vendor drivers for an Industrial robot arm (FANUC, ABB Robotics, Universal Robots and others), plus calibration and process tools, so plants can use open Motion planning. It integrates tightly with MoveIt and MoveIt 2 for trajectory generation and with Offline programming workflows, bridging open software to PLC and Fieldbus shop-floor systems. The consortium maintains interfaces that let an Industrial robotics cell run perception-guided Pick and place and Robotic welding through ROS.

plain: A standard framework that lets robot control software talk to many different motors and sensors the same way.
snappy: The ROS 2 framework standardizing hardware interfaces and managing real-time controllers and their lifecycles.
detail: ros2_control (the successor to ros_control) defines a hardware-interface abstraction so a Controller, such as a Trajectory tracking or Position control loop, runs unchanged whether driving a simulated or real Actuator. It loads and switches controllers at runtime and runs them on a Real-time control loop. In practice MoveIt plans a path and hands the resulting trajectory to a ros2_control joint-trajectory controller, which commands each Servomotor through its Device driver.

plain: A recorder that captures everything a robot's programs are saying so you can play it back later to debug or build datasets.
snappy: A tool and file format for recording and replaying robot message streams across topics.
detail: A rosbag captures every message on selected topics with timestamps so engineers can replay a run offline, reproduce a bug, or harvest sensor data for training, much like a Log replay for the whole system. In ROS 2 it is called rosbag2 and stores data in the MCAP container, viewable in tools like RViz or Foxglove. Recorded bags feed Demonstration data pipelines and regression tests against a rosbag of real driving.

plain: The ROS 2 tool that records everything a robot's programs are saying to each other so it can be played back later.
snappy: The ROS 2 framework for recording topic, service, and action data to disk and replaying it deterministically.
detail: rosbag2 captures messages flowing over selected topics into a storage file (often using the MCAP format) and can replay them later as if the robot were live, which is the backbone of debugging, dataset collection, and Deterministic Replay. A recorded bag can drive perception or localization nodes offline, or feed PlotJuggler for time-series analysis. It is the ROS 2 successor to the original rosbag and respects each topic's recorded Quality of Service on playback.

plain: A piece of software that lets a web browser talk to a robot's internal messaging system over a standard web connection.
snappy: A WebSocket server (rosbridge_suite) that exposes ROS and ROS 2 topics, services, and actions as JSON so browser and non-ROS clients can interact with them.
detail: rosbridge translates between the binary ROS message bus and a JSON-over-WebSocket protocol, which is what front-end libraries such as Robot Web Tools build on to render live telemetry and send commands from a browser. It pairs naturally with Foxglove and RViz-style dashboards and is a common backbone for Teleoperation interfaces and remote monitoring of an Autonomous mobile robot. Because it bridges into the Node and Topic graph, anything published on a robot's Publish-subscribe network can be surfaced to a web Human-machine interface without native ROS bindings.

plain: A tool that automatically downloads and installs the outside software a robot package needs in order to build and run.
snappy: The ROS command-line tool that resolves a package's declared system dependencies and installs them via the OS package manager.
detail: rosdep reads the dependency keys a package lists in its manifest and maps them to the correct apt, pip, or other operating-system packages, then installs them so the workspace will build. It is run before a colcon build to satisfy non-ROS libraries that packages built with ament or catkin require, such as Eigen or OpenCV. This frees developers from manually tracking which third-party libraries a Node needs.

plain: A grid of numbers that records only how a body is turned, with no information about where it is.
snappy: An orthogonal 3x3 matrix describing a body's orientation relative to a frame.
detail: A rotation matrix has columns that are mutually perpendicular unit vectors, so it rotates without stretching, and its inverse is just its transpose. It forms the rotational core of a Homogeneous transformation matrix and is one of several interchangeable orientation encodings alongside the Quaternion, Euler angles, and Axis-angle representation. The set of all valid 3D rotation matrices is the Special orthogonal group SO(3).

plain: Choosing which roads to take to get from where you are to where you want to go, like a navigation app picking a route.
snappy: Selecting the high-level road sequence from origin to destination, typically over a road network or lane graph.
detail: Route planning is the strategic, map-level layer of a self-driving stack, running graph search such as Dijkstra's algorithm or A* search over a lane graph or HD map to produce the road sequence. It feeds the chosen corridor down to behavior planning and the local planner, which handle tactical and geometric decisions. Unlike motion planning, route planning operates on minutes-to-miles scales and is closely related to mission planning for delivery and a self-driving truck.

plain: A collection of point-and-click windows for inspecting what a robot's software is doing, like graphs of its programs and plots of its data.
snappy: A Qt-based plugin framework of GUI tools (rqt_graph, rqt_plot) for introspecting and debugging ROS systems.
detail: rqt hosts dockable plugins that visualize a running ROS system: rqt_graph draws the live Node and Topic connections, rqt_plot charts numeric topic values over time, and other plugins edit the Parameter Server or view logs. It complements RViz, which shows 3D state, by focusing on the software graph and time-series data. For deeper signal analysis many developers move to PlotJuggler, but rqt remains the quick first stop for seeing whether nodes are connected as expected.

plain: An improved version of the random-tree planner that keeps rearranging its connections as it goes so the route it finds gets shorter and shorter.
snappy: An asymptotically optimal RRT variant that rewires nearby branches to converge toward the lowest-cost path.
detail: RRT* augments the Rapidly-exploring random tree with a rewiring step: whenever a new sample is added, nearby nodes are reconnected through it if that lowers their cost, so the path quality improves toward optimal as samples accumulate. The trade-off is more computation per sample, so practitioners run it under a time budget and accept the best path found. Like plain RRT it is part of Sampling-based planning, lives in OMPL and MoveIt, and its solutions are typically post-processed with Path smoothing and Trajectory optimization before execution.

plain: A planning method that grows two branching search structures, one from the start and one from the goal, until they meet, so a robot can find a route quickly.
snappy: A bidirectional variant of RRT that grows two trees, one from the start and one from the goal, and greedily extends them toward each other until they connect.
detail: RRT-Connect speeds up Rapidly-exploring random tree planning by alternately growing a tree from the start and from the goal and using a greedy 'connect' step that repeatedly extends one tree toward the other tree's newest node. It is a workhorse Sampling-based planning algorithm for arm Motion planning in Configuration space, shipping in OMPL and used heavily inside MoveIt, though like base RRT it finds a feasible path rather than an optimal one and typically needs Path smoothing afterward. It still relies on a Collision detection check at each extension.

plain: A wiring standard that lets many devices share one long, noise-resistant cable to talk over big distances in a factory or vehicle.
snappy: A differential, multidrop serial standard supporting long cable runs and many nodes in electrically noisy environments.
detail: RS-485 transmits data as the voltage difference between two wires, which cancels electrical noise and supports cable runs of hundreds of meters with dozens of nodes, far beyond what UART or the I2C Bus can reach. It is the physical layer beneath fieldbuses like Modbus and PROFIBUS, connecting distributed sensors, drives, and a Programmable logic controller across a Production line or a large Mobility platform. Because it is half-duplex and multidrop, nodes take turns transmitting, and a Real-time control protocol manages who speaks when.

plain: An early large robot brain that learned many tabletop tasks by studying a huge amount of recorded robot practice.
snappy: A Transformer-based robot manipulation policy trained at scale on large, diverse real-robot demonstration data.
detail: RT-1 tokenizes camera images and language instructions and uses a Transformer to output discretized arm and base actions, demonstrating that scaling Demonstration data improves Multitask learning and generalization. It is a precursor to RT-2 and RT-X and an early Robot foundation model for manipulation. RT-1 helped establish the recipe of language-conditioned, large-scale Imitation learning that later Vision-language-action model systems extended.

plain: A robot brain built on a web-trained vision-and-language model, so it can use general world knowledge to follow instructions.
snappy: A vision-language-action model that fine-tunes a web-pretrained vision-language model to output robot actions.
detail: RT-2 is a Vision-language-action model: it takes an internet-scale vision-language model and co-trains it on robot Demonstration data so that broad semantic knowledge transfers into control, giving stronger Zero-shot generalization than RT-1. Because it reasons over language and images, it can act on novel objects and instructions described in words, a form of Language-conditioned manipulation. It is a flagship example of a Robot foundation model and a step toward a Generalist policy.

plain: A single robot brain trained on demonstrations pooled from many different robots so it works across hardware.
snappy: A generalist manipulation policy trained on the Open X-Embodiment dataset to operate across many robot embodiments.
detail: RT-X scales the RT-1 and RT-2 recipe to the pooled Open X-Embodiment corpus, showing that training on many robots' Demonstration data yields positive Transfer learning and better skills than single-robot training, the essence of Cross-embodiment learning. The result is a Generalist policy that runs on diverse arms with minimal adaptation. RT-X is a leading example of a Robot foundation model and informs open efforts like OpenVLA.

plain: Open-source software that lets a robot with a depth camera build and remember a 3D map of large spaces, recognizing places it has seen before without slowing down.
snappy: A graph-based RGB-D and stereo SLAM library with memory management and appearance-based loop closure for large-scale mapping.
detail: RTAB-Map fuses color and depth (from a Depth camera or Stereo camera) into a graph SLAM back-end, detecting Loop closure with a bag-of-words Place recognition front-end similar to DBoW2 and inserting each match as a Loop Closure Constraint. Its key feature is a memory-management scheme that keeps real-time performance over very large maps by paging older nodes out of the working set. Packaged for ROS, it produces dense Point cloud and Occupancy grid maps for the Navigation stack on Service and Mobility robots, complementing laser mappers like Cartographer.

full: Real-Time Kinematic Global Navigation Satellite System
plain: An upgraded satellite-positioning system that gives a drone centimeter-accurate location by comparing its signals with a fixed nearby reference station in real time.
snappy: Carrier-phase GNSS that uses real-time corrections from a base station to achieve centimeter-level drone positioning.
detail: RTK GNSS resolves the carrier-phase ambiguity of satellite signals using corrections streamed from a base station over a Telemetry radio or network link, sharpening a standard Global Navigation Satellite System fix from meters to centimeters. On a Precision agriculture drone or mapping platform it provides accurate geotags for Aerial photogrammetry, removing the need for many Ground control points. It is the real-time sibling of Post-Processed Kinematic correction and is supported by PX4 and ArduPilot flight stacks.

plain: A way of using satellite signals plus a nearby fixed reference station to pinpoint where something is to within a few centimeters, far more precisely than ordinary navigation.
snappy: Carrier-phase satellite positioning that uses corrections from a fixed base station to achieve centimeter-level accuracy in real time.
detail: RTK positioning improves on raw GNSS positioning and GPS by measuring the phase of the satellite carrier wave and applying corrections broadcast from a ground reference station, cutting error from meters to centimeters. Self-driving cars, an agricultural robot, and a precision agriculture drone all rely on it for lane-level or row-level accuracy. It is typically fused with an inertial measurement unit through sensor fusion to bridge brief signal gaps and support dead reckoning in GPS-denied navigation.

plain: A free software tool that smoothly speeds up and slows down a robot's motion so it never jerks or lurches, even when its goal changes mid-move.
snappy: An open-source library for instantaneous, jerk-limited online trajectory generation that can react to new targets within a single control cycle.
detail: Ruckig computes a time-optimal Jerk-limited trajectory that respects velocity, acceleration, and jerk limits, and it can recompute the profile every control step when the target moves. It is the modern successor to the Reflexxes library and is widely used inside Motion control and Trajectory generation pipelines, including the time parameterization stage in MoveIt 2. Compared with a precomputed Polynomial Trajectory or an S-Curve Motion Profile, Ruckig's strength is reacting online to changing setpoints without restarting the motion.

plain: Moving fast enough on legs that there are moments when no foot is touching the ground.
snappy: A fast legged gait featuring a flight phase in which all feet are simultaneously off the ground.
detail: Running differs from walking by its airborne flight phase, which gives a low Duty factor and demands strong Dynamic stability and energy storage, often modelled with the Spring-loaded inverted pendulum. Achieving stable running is a benchmark for a Bipedal robot and a Quadruped robot alike, with the four-legged version being the Gallop. It stresses actuators, the Ground reaction force, and Balance control far more than steady walking does.

plain: How long a robot can keep working before its battery dies or it needs refueling.
snappy: The duration a robot can operate on a single charge or fuel load before it must recharge, refuel, or swap power sources.
detail: Runtime is set by how much energy the robot stores against how fast it drains it, so it depends on Energy density, the Power budget of the motors and Onboard compute, and the workload. A warehouse Autonomous mobile robot might quote four hours of runtime, while a Humanoid robot like Tesla Optimus or one from Figure AI is often power-hungry enough that runtime is a headline limitation. Designers extend it with a Hot-swappable battery, opportunistic Wireless charging, or by switching to Tethered power when continuous operation matters more than mobility; State of charge is the live readout of how much runtime remains.

plain: A simple, trusted watchdog that lets a smart but unproven controller drive a robot, but instantly takes over if it is about to do something unsafe.
snappy: A monitoring architecture in which a verified safety controller overrides a complex or learned controller whenever the latter would violate safety constraints.
detail: Runtime assurance (RTA, also called a safety monitor) wraps an unverified high-performance Policy in a simple, certifiable shield, often a Simplex-style switch backed by a Control barrier function or Safety envelope. It lets a learned controller fly a Drone or steer an Autonomous vehicle while a trusted layer guarantees a Minimal Risk Maneuver if limits are approached. RTA is a key enabler for Corrigibility, Value alignment, and Scalable oversight in deployment, and it complements offline Verification and validation by catching the cases that escaped Distribution shift testing.

plain: A 3D viewer that shows you what a robot is sensing and thinking, drawing its sensors, body, and surroundings on screen.
snappy: The ROS 3D visualization tool for rendering sensor data, robot state, frames, and planning results.
detail: RViz subscribes to topics and renders them in 3D: a LiDAR point cloud, a Camera image, the robot model from its URDF, coordinate frames from tf, and planned paths from MoveIt or Nav2. It is the everyday window for debugging a robot's perception and Localization, complementing offline tools like Foxglove and rosbag. ROS 2 ships rviz2.

plain: A gentle way of speeding up and slowing down that eases into and out of motion instead of jolting, reducing wear and wobble.
snappy: A jerk-limited velocity ramp that smooths the start and end of a move to reduce mechanical shock.
detail: S-curve acceleration shapes the Motion profile so the rate of change of acceleration (jerk) stays bounded, producing an S-shaped velocity curve instead of the abrupt corners of a trapezoidal profile. Limiting jerk reduces vibration, Backlash slap, and Following error in a Servo drive, which matters for tall payloads on a Palletizing robot or fragile parts. It overlaps conceptually with a Jerk-limited trajectory and with Input shaping for residual-vibration suppression.

plain: A way of speeding a machine up and slowing it down gradually rather than abruptly, so motion is smooth and gentle on the hardware.
snappy: A jerk-limited velocity profile that ramps acceleration smoothly to reduce vibration and mechanical stress.
detail: Where a basic trapezoidal velocity profile changes acceleration instantly (infinite jerk), an S-Curve Motion Profile limits the rate of change of acceleration, rounding the corners so the drive excites less Resonance and the payload does not whip. Motion controllers use it for the point-to-point moves of an Industrial robot arm, Cartesian robot, and warehouse Linear actuator, trading slightly longer move times for less wear and more accurate settling. Libraries such as Ruckig generate these jerk-limited profiles online during Trajectory generation.

plain: A way of speeding up and slowing down a machine gently, easing into and out of acceleration so the motion is smooth instead of abrupt.
snappy: A jerk-limited velocity profile that ramps acceleration smoothly, producing S-shaped speed curves during start and stop.
detail: An S-Curve Velocity Profile bounds the rate of change of acceleration (jerk) so a machine ramps acceleration up and down smoothly rather than switching it on instantly like a Bang-bang control profile. It is standard in Manufacturing motion control for an Industrial robot arm or CNC machine, reducing vibration, mechanical wear, and residual oscillation when following a Motion profile. Libraries such as Ruckig compute these online during Time parameterization, and the result is closely related to a Jerk-limited trajectory used to protect drivetrains and payloads.

plain: A six-step scale, from no automation to fully self-driving, that ranks how much a car can drive itself.
snappy: The SAE J3016 taxonomy classifying driving automation into six levels, L0 through L5, by who performs the driving task and when.
detail: The SAE levels of driving automation define L0-L2 as driver-supervised (the realm of Advanced driver-assistance systems), L3 as conditional automation requiring a Takeover request, and L4-L5 as systems performing the full Dynamic driving task without a human Fallback. Level 4 automation works inside a bounded Operational design domain while Level 5 automation has none. The standard, SAE J3016, is the shared vocabulary regulators and companies like Mobileye and Aurora use to describe an Automated driving system.

plain: A drive function that reliably engages an external mechanical brake to hold a load that could otherwise fall.
snappy: A drive Safety Function that safely commands and monitors an external mechanical brake for holding an axis.
detail: Safe Brake Control (SBC) is a safe drive function in IEC 61800-5-2 that drives a holding brake in a way that meets a required Performance Level, typically used with Safe Torque Off on suspended or gravity-loaded axes where removing torque alone would let the load drop. Because Safe Torque Off does not brake the motor, SBC provides the missing mechanical holding force; the two are frequently specified together. The drive monitors brake feedback to maintain Diagnostic Coverage and may combine with Safe Brake Test routines as a form of Proof Test.

plain: A drive function that allows a motor to turn only one way, blocking motion in the dangerous direction.
snappy: A monitored drive Safety Function that permits motion only in a defined safe direction and trips a stop otherwise.
detail: Safe Direction (SDI) is a safe drive function from IEC 61800-5-2 that constrains the sign of motion: if the Servo drive detects movement in the prohibited direction it commands a Stop Category 1 or Stop Category 0. It complements Safely Limited Speed and Safely Limited Position, and is useful where an operator can safely be near an axis as long as it only moves away from them, such as feeding stock into a machine. Its integrity is verified against a target Performance Level under ISO 13849.

plain: A drive function that holds a motor still and resists being pushed, using only the force needed to keep it in place.
snappy: A drive Safety Function that holds a motor at a monitored standstill, applying just enough torque to keep position and tripping if it moves.
detail: Safe Operating Stop (SOS) is one of the safe drive functions defined in IEC 61800-5-2 and used alongside Safe Torque Off, Safely Limited Speed, and Safely Limited Position. Unlike a Stop Category 0 that removes power, SOS keeps the Servo drive energized so the motor actively resists external forces and holds its position, which matters for a vertical axis that would otherwise drop. It lets an operator approach a held axis safely during setup, and is monitored to a Performance Level set by the machine's Risk assessment.

plain: A built-in motor feature that makes a motor unable to produce any turning force, without having to switch off all the power.
snappy: A drive safety function that removes the torque-producing energy to a motor, preventing motion without disconnecting the entire power supply.
detail: Safe Torque Off (STO) is the most common drive-level safety function: it interrupts the gating signals to the power stage so the motor cannot generate torque, while keeping logic and feedback powered for fast restart. Defined in IEC 61800-5-2, STO is the building block for a category-0 Safety-rated stop and is often how an Emergency stop or Safety-rated monitored stop is implemented on a Variable frequency drive or Servomotor. It is certified to a Safety Integrity Level and a Performance Level.

plain: Dividing the area around a robot into zones so it slows down or stops when a person steps too close.
snappy: Defining layered warning and protective zones around a robot that trigger speed reduction or a safety-rated stop on intrusion.
detail: Safe Workspace Zoning configures a Safety scanner or Light curtain to define a warning field that slows the robot and a protective field that commands a Safety-rated monitored stop when crossed, the practical basis of Speed and separation monitoring. The zones are switched by a Safety PLC according to the robot's task, and the design must meet the Performance Level required by ISO 13849. In a warehouse, an Automated guided vehicle or Autonomous mobile robot uses zoning so a worker entering the cell triggers a Protective stop rather than a collision.

plain: A drive function that stops a moving axis before it can travel past a position defined as safe.
snappy: A monitored drive Safety Function that prevents an axis from exceeding a defined safe position envelope.
detail: Safely Limited Position (SLP) is a safe drive function in IEC 61800-5-2 that creates electronic safe limits without mechanical hard stops, so an axis cannot intrude into an operator zone. It is often combined with Safely Limited Speed and Safe Direction, and its monitoring depends on redundant position feedback to achieve the Performance Level demanded by the Risk assessment. In robot cells it underpins Safe Workspace Zoning and Safety-Rated Soft Axis Limiting, keeping a manipulator out of a region a person may occupy.

plain: A drive function that guarantees a motor never spins faster than a safe limit, even if the normal control fails.
snappy: A monitored drive Safety Function that trips a stop if motor speed exceeds a defined safe threshold.
detail: Safely Limited Speed (SLS) is a safe drive function from IEC 61800-5-2 that lets a machine keep moving slowly while an operator is present, instead of fully stopping; if the Servo drive detects speed above the limit it commands a Stop Category 1 or Stop Category 0. It relies on redundant feedback and Diagnostic Coverage to reach its target Performance Level, and pairs naturally with Safe Operating Stop, Safe Direction, and Safely Limited Position. A common use is jogging a robot during teach mode with an Enabling Device while SLS caps the speed.

plain: Designing and operating robots so they do not hurt people or damage their surroundings.
snappy: The practice of designing and operating robots to prevent harm to people, property, and environment.
detail: Safety in robotics combines hardware, software, and procedures to keep humans out of harm's way, governed by standards such as ISO 10218 and ISO/TS 15066 for collaborative work. Practical mechanisms include an Emergency stop, a Light curtain, Speed and separation monitoring, and Power and force limiting on a Cobot. It connects to Functional safety and Risk assessment, and to safety-rated hardware like a Safety PLC and Safe Torque Off circuits.

plain: A documented, structured argument that explains why a self-driving system is safe enough to be trusted on real roads.
snappy: A structured, evidence-backed argument that a system is acceptably safe for its intended operation and environment.
detail: A safety case marshals claims, arguments, and evidence, from scenario-based testing, simulation, field data, and analyses like SOTIF and responsibility-sensitive safety, to justify that an automated driving system is acceptably safe within its operational design domain. It draws on functional safety standards such as ISO 26262 and ASIL allocations, and is also used for defense and aerospace systems. The case must address residual risk from the long-tail scenario space and define the minimal risk condition fallback.

plain: A trained human who sits in a self-driving test car ready to grab the wheel instantly if the computer makes a mistake.
snappy: A trained human operator who supervises an automated test vehicle and is prepared to intervene at any moment.
detail: A safety driver oversees a self-driving car during testing and development, monitoring the self-driving stack and performing a disengagement or intervention whenever the system errs or behaves unsafely. Their interventions are logged and aggregated into metrics like interventions per mile and miles per intervention that track maturity. As confidence grows, operators move from an in-vehicle safety driver toward a remote operation center and eventually fully driverless service.

plain: A soft contact strip on a moving part that stops the motion the instant a person or object presses against it.
snappy: A deformable pressure-sensitive contact strip that triggers a stop when compressed by a person or obstruction.
detail: A Safety Edge is a trip device mounted on the leading edge of a moving part such as an automatic door, a Scissor Lift Mechanism, or a powered gate; deforming it signals a Safety Relay or Safety PLC to command a stop. It provides a last-line protective response where guarding cannot fully prevent contact, complementing presence-sensing devices like a Safety Mat or Light curtain. Its placement and the machine's Trip Distance must ensure motion ceases before the person is harmed, to the Performance Level set by ISO 13849.

plain: An invisible buffer of space the self-driving car keeps clear around itself so it always has room to stop or steer away safely.
snappy: The region of space and motion around a vehicle kept clear, with response rules, to guarantee a collision can always be avoided.
detail: The safety envelope defines the longitudinal and lateral clearances the ego vehicle must preserve given current speeds, formalized by models like responsibility-sensitive safety. Behavior planning, the local planner, and trajectory optimization are constrained to keep all road agents outside this envelope, monitoring time to collision continuously. If the envelope is about to be violated, the system triggers automatic emergency braking or a minimal risk condition fallback.

plain: A specific job a machine's safety system performs, like cutting power, whose failure could directly put someone in danger.
snappy: A defined control-system function whose correct operation reduces risk and whose failure can immediately increase risk to persons.
detail: A Safety Function is the basic unit of Functional safety: examples include an Emergency stop circuit, a Light curtain that triggers a Protective stop, or a drive holding Safe Torque Off. Each one is assigned a target reliability such as a Performance Level under ISO 13849 or a Safety Integrity Level under IEC 62061, and is implemented on dedicated hardware like a Safety PLC or Safety Relay. The Risk assessment from ISO 12100 determines which safety functions a machine needs and how robust each must be.

plain: A grade, from one to four, that says how dependable a safety function must be at preventing a dangerous failure.
snappy: A discrete rating (SIL 1-4) from IEC 61508 quantifying the probability that a safety function fails to perform on demand.
detail: Safety Integrity Level (SIL) is the risk-reduction measure of IEC 61508 and its process-industry derivatives, with SIL 4 being the most demanding. It quantifies the tolerable probability of dangerous failure of a safety function, such as a Safe Torque Off channel or an Emergency stop circuit, and is implemented on a Safety PLC. SIL is roughly cross-mapped to the Performance Level scale of ISO 13849 and to the ASIL scale of ISO 26262 in automotive work.

plain: A pressure-sensitive floor mat that detects when a person steps on it and triggers a machine to stop.
snappy: A pressure-sensitive floor mat that detects personnel presence in a hazard zone and commands a protective stop.
detail: A Safety Mat is a presence-sensing protective device: stepping on it closes a sensing layer that a Safety Relay or Safety PLC interprets as an intrusion, commanding a Protective stop. It is a classic area-guarding alternative to a Light curtain or Safety scanner where a defined floor zone must stay clear, and it is sized using the Trip Distance calculation so the machine halts before the person reaches the hazard. Mats are evaluated to a Performance Level per ISO 13849 based on the Risk assessment.

plain: Making sure a self-driving feature is safe not just when parts break, but when the system simply cannot cope with a tricky situation it was never designed for.
snappy: An assurance discipline (ISO 21448) addressing risks from functional or performance limitations and foreseeable misuse, even with no hardware fault.
detail: Safety of the intended functionality (SOTIF), standardized as ISO 21448, complements ISO 26262: where functional safety covers component faults, SOTIF covers limitations of perception and decision-making, such as a camera misreading a sign or behavior prediction failing on a novel agent. It is especially relevant to neural network and machine-learning components whose failure modes are statistical, overlapping with AI assurance concerns. SOTIF analysis drives scenario-based testing to shrink the unknown-unsafe region of the long-tail scenario space.

plain: A special factory computer, built and certified to a high standard, that watches over machines and shuts them down safely if something goes wrong.
snappy: A programmable logic controller certified to execute safety-rated control functions such as emergency stops, interlocks, and guard monitoring.
detail: A Safety PLC is a hardened version of a standard Programmable logic controller, with redundant internal channels and self-diagnostics certified to functional-safety standards like IEC 61508 and ISO 13849 (up to a given Performance Level). It runs the safety logic for an Emergency stop, a Light curtain, an Interlock, or a Safe Torque Off drive function while a normal PLC handles ordinary sequencing. In a robot cell, a Safety PLC typically commands a Safety-rated monitored stop or a Protective stop when a guard opens, and is wired to Machine guarding and a Safety scanner.

plain: A specialized hardwired electrical device that watches safety inputs like an e-stop and reliably switches a machine's power off.
snappy: A hardwired, fault-monitored relay device that evaluates safety inputs and switches safety outputs for simple Safety Functions.
detail: A Safety Relay implements a single Safety Function in dedicated hardware, monitoring devices such as an Emergency stop button, a Light curtain, or an interlocked guard and de-energizing outputs when triggered. It uses internally redundant, force-guided contacts and self-checking to achieve a Category 3 Architecture or Category 4 Architecture per ISO 13849. For more complex logic combining many inputs and functions, integrators step up to a programmable Safety PLC, but the simple, certifiable Safety Relay remains common on individual circuits.

plain: A spinning laser that watches an area on the floor and stops the machine if someone steps into a marked zone.
snappy: A safety laser scanner that monitors configurable two-dimensional protective and warning fields, triggering stops or slowdowns on intrusion.
detail: A Safety scanner (safety laser scanner) sweeps a horizontal plane to define warning and protective zones on the floor, commonly used to guard a Robot cell or to enable Speed and separation monitoring around an Autonomous mobile robot. As electro-sensitive protective equipment under IEC 61496, its zone breach triggers a Safety-rated stop via a Safety PLC at the required Performance Level. On an AMR or AGV the scanner shapes its protective field to vehicle speed, and unlike a Light curtain it covers an area rather than a plane.

plain: A sensitive covering on a robot that feels when something is near or touching it so it can stop.
snappy: A capacitive or tactile robot covering that detects proximity or contact across the body surface to trigger slowdown or stop.
detail: Safety Skin wraps a robot in a Capacitive sensor or tactile-sensor layer so it can sense an approaching hand before impact and halt, extending Pre-Collision Sensing across the whole structure rather than at a single Force/torque sensor. On a Humanoid robot or Cobot it enables gentle Power and force limiting behavior and supports Speed and separation monitoring without external fences. Unlike a discrete Safety Mat or Light curtain, the skin moves with the arm, giving continuous coverage useful for compliance with ISO/TS 15066.

plain: A robot setting that brings the machine to a complete, watched standstill the moment a person steps into its working area, then lets it resume once they leave.
snappy: A collaborative operation mode that holds the robot stationary with power on, monitored by a safety-rated function, while a person is in the shared workspace.
detail: Safety-rated monitored stop (SRMS) keeps the robot motionless but powered while an operator is present in the Collaborative workspace, resuming automatically when they leave without needing a manual reset. It is one of the four collaboration modes in ISO 10218 and is often realized with a Safe Torque Off function plus position monitoring at the required Performance Level. Triggering is typically by a Light curtain or Safety scanner, and it differs from a full Emergency stop because power and program state are retained.

plain: Software walls that keep a robot arm inside an allowed area, enforced reliably enough to count as a safety feature.
snappy: Safety-rated software boundaries that confine a robot's motion to a defined Cartesian or joint workspace volume.
detail: Safety-Rated Soft Axis Limiting uses certified monitoring in the Robot controller to enforce virtual walls in joint space or Cartesian space, stopping the robot if it tries to leave its allowed volume without physical fences. It is typically paired with Safely Limited Position and Safely Limited Speed functions and triggers a Safe Torque Off or Safety-rated stop on violation, meeting the Performance Level set by ISO 13849. On a Cobot, soft axis limiting shrinks the space a Pressure Distribution Sensor must validate by keeping the arm away from people-occupied zones.

plain: A set of standard ways to bring a machine to a safe halt, ranging from cutting power instantly to braking smoothly first.
snappy: Defined stop functions (categories 0, 1, and 2 per IEC 60204-1) that bring a machine to a halt in a safe, controlled manner.
detail: Safety-rated stop refers to the IEC 60204-1 stop categories: category 0 removes power immediately (an uncontrolled coast or brake), category 1 brakes under power then removes it, and category 2 is a controlled stop with power maintained. An Emergency stop usually maps to category 0 or 1, while a Safety-rated monitored stop is a category-2-style stationary state. The chosen category is realized through functions like Safe Torque Off on a Variable frequency drive and validated to a Performance Level.

plain: A company that makes wind-powered robotic sailboats that gather ocean data and watch the seas for long stretches with no crew.
snappy: Maker of autonomous wind-powered surface vehicles for ocean data collection and maritime surveillance.
detail: Saildrone builds an Unmanned surface vehicle that harvests wind for propulsion and solar power for electronics, enabling Persistent autonomy on missions lasting months at sea. The vehicles carry science and surveillance payloads, navigating via GPS and satellite links with onboard Obstacle avoidance for collision regulations compliance. They serve ocean research and maritime domain awareness, competing in the same uncrewed-marine niche as the Wave glider while complementing underwater Autonomous underwater vehicle fleets.

plain: How quickly a robot can learn a skill from only a few tries instead of needing millions of attempts.
snappy: A measure of how few environment interactions a learning algorithm needs to reach a target level of performance.
detail: Sample efficiency is critical in robotics because real-world trials are slow, costly, and risky for hardware, unlike a Gym environment that can run millions of episodes cheaply. Off-policy learning and Model-based reinforcement learning improve it by reusing past data, while Sim-to-real transfer and Massively parallel simulation sidestep the problem by gathering cheap experience first. Methods like Demonstration data and Few-shot learning boost it by starting from expert behavior rather than random exploration.

plain: Small, unwanted variations in the timing between a controller's repeated measurements and updates, which can make a robot's motion less smooth and stable.
snappy: Variation in the period of a control loop's sampling instants that degrades tracking accuracy and stability margins.
detail: A controller assumes a fixed Sampling rate, but operating-system scheduling, bus contention, or interrupt load can make the actual interval wander, which is sampling jitter. It erodes the Phase margin of a feedback loop and worsens Trajectory tracking, which is why robots use a Real-time operating system, PREEMPT_RT, or deterministic fieldbuses like EtherCAT to bound it. Sampling jitter is distinct from but related to Latency, Clock skew, and the broader notion of Jitter in distributed control.

plain: How many times per second a sensor takes a fresh reading.
snappy: The frequency, in Hz, at which a sensor produces new measurements.
detail: Sampling rate is how often a sensor delivers data — e.g. a Camera at 30 Hz, an Inertial measurement unit at 1000 Hz, or a spinning LiDAR at 10 Hz. It must be high enough to capture the dynamics a Control loop or Perception pipeline needs, and mismatched rates force resampling during Sensor fusion. Together with Sensor latency it governs how fresh the data driving Localization and State estimation actually is.

plain: A family of planning methods that explore by trying out random positions rather than checking every possible position in a fixed grid.
snappy: Planning that probes Configuration space with random samples instead of exhaustively discretizing it.
