In Task and motion planning, high-level skills are chained while a Motion planning layer fills in collision-free Trajectory details for each.

plain: Stringing together small robot behaviors so each one finishes in a state where the next one can start.
snappy: Sequencing primitive skills such that each skill's termination set lies inside the next skill's initiation set.
detail: Skill chaining composes entries from a Skill library into a Long-horizon task, ensuring the end Pose and conditions of one Skill satisfy the preconditions of the next, avoiding brittle handoffs. It is a practical mechanism behind Subgoal decomposition and the Option framework in Hierarchical reinforcement learning, and shows up in Task and motion planning for assembly. A failure here, where one skill leaves the robot outside the next skill's start region, is a common source of Compounding error.

plain: Letting a robot invent its own collection of distinct, reusable behaviors by exploring on its own, without anyone telling it what task to perform.
snappy: Unsupervised learning of a set of diverse, distinguishable skills without task reward, typically by maximizing the mutual information between skills and visited states.
detail: Methods like DIAYN reward an agent for reaching states that make its current Skill identifiable, producing a library of distinct behaviors before any task is specified, which can then be composed under the Options Framework. This Unsupervised skill discovery is driven by Intrinsic motivation rather than an external Reward function and helps with exploration in Sparse reward problems. The discovered behaviors feed Hierarchical reinforcement learning and Skill chaining, and the approach is closely tied to Novelty search and Quality diversity.

plain: A robot's stored collection of learned behaviors it can pick from and combine to do bigger jobs.
snappy: A reusable repertoire of learned or programmed behaviors that a robot composes to accomplish higher-level tasks.
detail: A skill library stores parameterized behaviors, each a Skill or Motion primitive, that a planner selects and sequences via Skill chaining or a Hierarchical task network. It is central to Task and motion planning and to long-horizon manufacturing work, where a robot might compose 'pick', 'insert', and 'screw' from the library. Growing the library over time relates to Lifelong learning and Skill Discovery, while a Foundation model can propose which skill to invoke for a Long-horizon task.

plain: The share of all the different products in a catalog that a picking robot can reliably handle.
snappy: The fraction of a catalog's distinct items (SKUs) a picking robot can grasp and handle reliably enough for production.
detail: SKU Coverage is the make-or-break spec for an Each Picking robot: a vision and grasping stack might handle rigid boxed goods easily but struggle with bags, blister packs, or deformable items, leaving a long tail uncovered. Items outside coverage fall to manual stations and drive the Exception Handling rate, which in turn worsens the Operator-to-Robot Ratio and Cost per Pick. Expanding coverage relies on better Grasp Detection, a more capable gripper, and Fleet learning that accumulates grasp experience across a Fleet. High SKU Coverage is what lets an operator raise the overall Automation Rate of a fulfillment center.

plain: A US company that makes drones smart enough to fly themselves around obstacles without a pilot steering them.
snappy: American maker of autonomous obstacle-avoiding drones used for infrastructure inspection, public safety, and defence.
detail: Skydio differentiates on autonomy: its aircraft run onboard Visual SLAM and Obstacle avoidance across an array of cameras, letting the Drone navigate cluttered environments and track subjects without manual piloting. This makes it well suited to bridge and powerline inspection and to defence reconnaissance, including BVLOS operations under appropriate waivers. As a US-headquartered alternative to DJI, it features prominently in procurement that restricts foreign-made unmanned aircraft system hardware.

plain: A robot building a map of an unknown place while figuring out where it is on that same map at the same time.
snappy: Simultaneously constructing a map of an unknown environment and tracking the robot's pose within it.
detail: SLAM solves the chicken-and-egg problem of needing a map to localize and needing a pose to map, doing both online from incoming sensor data. Implementations range from filter-based (Extended Kalman filter, Particle filter) to optimization-based using a Factor graph with Bundle adjustment, and they depend on Loop closure to bound Drift. It is the core of indoor robot navigation, with camera-driven variants called Visual SLAM and lidar variants built on Point cloud registration.

plain: A large ring-shaped bearing that lets a heavy robot base turn smoothly.
snappy: A large-diameter ring bearing that supports and rotates a heavy robot base or turret.
detail: A Slew bearing (or slewing ring) is a big-diameter Bearing carrying the combined load and overturning moment at the base of a heavy Serial manipulator, crane, or turntable, allowing the whole structure to rotate about a vertical axis. Its large diameter gives high moment stiffness, supporting the first Revolute joint of a large Industrial robot arm. Internal or external gear teeth often integrate it with the base Gearbox drive.

plain: A big, strong rotating bearing-and-gear unit that slowly swings heavy things like a robot arm base or a solar panel around in a circle.
snappy: A worm-driven large-diameter slewing bearing providing high-torque azimuth rotation.
detail: A Slewing Drive integrates a large-diameter Slew bearing with an enclosed Worm Drive so a single compact unit supports axial, radial, and tilting loads while rotating them under high torque, typically for azimuth (yaw) motion. Its self-locking worm holds heavy loads without continuous power, suiting Manufacturing turntables, the base joint of large arms, and Space solar-tracking and antenna pointing mechanisms. It delivers far higher Holding torque at the output than a comparable Planetary Gearbox stage.

plain: A linkage that turns the round-and-round spin of a wheel into a back-and-forth sliding motion, like a piston in an engine.
snappy: A four-link mechanism converting rotary crank motion into linear reciprocation of a slider, or vice versa.
detail: The Slider-Crank Mechanism converts a motor's rotation into straight-line reciprocation, driving pick-and-place strokes, pumps, and the legs of some hopping or walking machines. As a member of the Linkage family closely related to the Four-bar linkage, its output velocity varies nonlinearly with crank angle, a profile designers exploit for quick-return strokes. It is one alternative to a Rack and Pinion or Lead screw when converting rotary actuation into reciprocating linear motion.

plain: A control method that pushes a machine toward a fixed pattern of motion and then flips its commands on and off very fast to hold it on that pattern, even when something tries to knock it off course.
snappy: Robust nonlinear control that forces the state onto a designed sliding surface via high-frequency switching, then keeps it there.
detail: SMC defines a sliding surface in the state space and uses discontinuous switching to reach and stay on it, giving strong Disturbance rejection and insensitivity to matched uncertainty, a form of Robust control. Its main drawback is chattering, the rapid switching that can excite an Actuator, often softened with boundary layers. It is a type of Nonlinear control applied to Robotic hand grip force, Servomotor regulation, and underwater or aerial vehicles, and its design leans on Lyapunov stability.

plain: Noticing when a held object is starting to slip so the robot can squeeze a little harder.
snappy: Sensing the onset of an object sliding within the grasp so grip force can be increased in time.
detail: Slip detection senses incipient sliding between fingers and object, letting a robot tighten its grip just enough to hold without crushing. It typically relies on a Tactile sensor or Vision-based tactile sensor that detects micro-vibrations or shear at the Contact points, much as human skin does. Detected slip feeds directly into Grip force control and is essential for safe Manipulation of delicate or unknown objects with a Robotic hand during a Precision grasp.

plain: A sliding electrical contact that lets power and signals pass to a part that spins around forever without twisting the wires.
snappy: A rotary electrical joint using brushes on conductive rings to pass power or data across a continuously rotating interface.
detail: A Slip Ring lets a continuously rotating sensor head, such as a Mechanical LiDAR or a camera Gimbal, receive power and return data without a Cable Carrier eventually winding up and snapping. It removes the wrap limit that fixed Cable Routing imposes, which is why any unlimited-rotation axis relies on one rather than a coiled harness or an Absolute encoder cable that would otherwise twist. Wear of the brush contacts limits life and adds electrical noise, so signal-only versions sometimes use optical or capacitive rotary joints instead.

plain: Deciding where to store each product in a warehouse so that workers and robots walk or travel the shortest distance when picking orders.
snappy: The process of assigning SKUs to storage locations to minimize pick travel, handling effort, and replenishment cost.
detail: Slotting Optimization places fast-moving SKUs in the most accessible locations and groups items frequently ordered together, directly improving Pick rate and overall Throughput. It is a core input to a Warehouse management system and to Goods-to-person workflows served by a Goods-to-person robot or Autonomous mobile robot, where good slotting cuts the travel that dominates Cost per Pick. Unlike Cross-Docking, which avoids storage entirely, slotting governs how long-dwell inventory is arranged, and is periodically re-optimized as demand patterns shift across the SKU Coverage of the facility.

plain: A ROS tool for laying out a robot's job as a set of steps it moves between, like a recipe with branches.
snappy: A ROS Python library for building hierarchical, nested state machines that coordinate task-level robot behavior.
detail: SMACH lets developers define states and transitions in Python and nest them into a hierarchy, making it a classic way to encode the Finite state machine logic behind a manipulation or Navigation routine. It integrates with the ROS Action Server interface so each state can call long-running tasks like Pick and place. Newer projects increasingly favor a Behavior tree via BehaviorTree.CPP for better reactivity, but SMACH remains common in research Task planning.

plain: A camera with a built-in computer, so it captures and analyzes images by itself without a separate PC.
snappy: A self-contained vision device that captures and processes images onboard, outputting decisions rather than raw video.
detail: A smart camera packages the sensor, lighting interface, processor, and Machine vision software in one housing, so it can inspect a part and output a pass/fail or position result directly to a Programmable logic controller without an external Industrial PC. This makes it a cost-effective drop-in for Quality inspection, code reading, or simple Vision-guided robotics on a single station of a Production line. It trades the raw processing power of a PC-based system for simplicity, compactness, and faster deployment in a Robot cell.

plain: A highly automated, connected plant where machines, sensors, and software share data to run and improve production in real time.
snappy: A digitally connected, data-driven plant where automation, sensing, and analytics optimize production continuously.
detail: A smart factory networks its machines, Robot cell equipment, and sensors through the Industrial Internet of Things so a Manufacturing execution system and analytics can optimize flow, quality, and uptime in real time. It leans on Predictive maintenance, Condition monitoring, and often a Digital twin to simulate and improve the Production line before changing it physically. The concept is the operational core of Industry 4.0 and pushes toward Lights-out manufacturing where the line runs with minimal human presence.

plain: A method for slashing the time it takes to switch a machine from making one product to making another, ideally to under ten minutes.
snappy: A changeover-reduction method that converts internal setup steps to external ones to enable small, fast production runs.
detail: SMED separates 'internal' setup work that requires the machine stopped from 'external' work that can be prepared while it still runs, then converts as much as possible to external and streamlines the rest. Shorter changeovers shrink Cycle time and support Line balancing against the Takt time, lifting Overall equipment effectiveness. On automated cells, quick-change Tool changer hardware and a Robotiq or Schunk gripper swap let an Industrial robot arm switch jobs in minutes, and the recipe lives in the Manufacturing execution system.

plain: A control trick for systems with a long delay: it uses a model to predict where things are heading so the controller doesn't overreact to stale information.
snappy: A dead-time compensator that uses a plant model to predict the delay-free output, letting a controller be tuned as if no transport delay existed.
detail: A Smith predictor wraps a PID controller around an internal model that estimates the response without delay, then subtracts the model's predicted-but-delayed output so the loop effectively controls the undelayed plant. It tames transport-delay-dominated loops such as conveyor thermal processes, networked Teleoperation suffering Latency, and Tension control in web handling, where naive feedback would oscillate. Its effectiveness depends on model accuracy, so it is often combined with Disturbance rejection or Robust control safeguards.

plain: A small, free robot-control model designed to run cheaply on ordinary hardware while still letting a robot follow visual and spoken instructions.
snappy: A compact open Vision-language-action model trained on community-contributed data for affordable robot deployment.
detail: SmolVLA is a deliberately small Vision-language-action model released through the LeRobot ecosystem and trained largely on community-collected Demonstration data rather than proprietary fleets, lowering the barrier to running a learned Policy on low-cost arms. Where heavyweight models like OpenVLA and Pi-Zero demand server-class GPUs, SmolVLA targets Onboard compute so a hobbyist Manipulator can do Pick and place via Imitation learning. Its emphasis on Sample efficiency and accessible hardware makes it a common starting point for teaching a Generalist policy on a budget.

plain: Moving like a snake by rippling a long, jointed body, which lets a robot wriggle through pipes, rubble, and other tight gaps where wheels or legs can't fit.
snappy: Limbless movement produced by propagating body undulations or other gait patterns, letting a long, slender robot thread through confined and cluttered spaces.
detail: A Snake robot chains many actuated segments and propagates waves along its body, using ground or wall contact to push itself forward, sideways, or to climb. Because it has no wheels or legs, it excels at search-and-inspection inside pipes, collapsed structures, and other Unstructured environment settings, a frequent Research/Frontier and Bio-inspired robotics topic. Snake locomotion is a form of Continuum structure control closely related to the Continuum robot, and planning its many degrees of freedom draws on Gait design and Whole-body control techniques.

plain: A long, thin robot made of many joined segments that wriggles and slithers like a real snake to reach into tight spaces.
snappy: A slender, hyper-redundant robot of many serial segments that locomotes and reaches via snake-like body undulation.
detail: A snake robot has many Degrees of freedom along a thin body, giving Kinematic redundancy that lets it slither, climb pipes, and thread through rubble using Snake locomotion. Its serpentine form suits Research/Frontier search-and-rescue and, as a steerable snake-arm, Medical & Surgical access to hard-to-reach anatomy, overlapping with the Continuum robot family. Controlling so many joints is a Whole-body control challenge solved with coordinated gait waves.

plain: An assembly step where a part is pushed until a flexible tab clicks past a lip and locks it in place.
snappy: Seating a part past an interference click feature, requiring a controlled overshoot of insertion force before settling.
detail: Snap-fit insertion is a Contact-rich manipulation task with a characteristic force signature: force rises as the snap deflects, peaks, then drops sharply at the click, which a Force/torque sensor can monitor to confirm seating. It demands Force control or Impedance control rather than pure position, since rigid position commands risk part damage or a failed latch. It is a standard skill benchmarked on the NIST assembly task boards alongside Peg-in-hole and connector mating, and is related to Threaded Fastener Insertion.

plain: A way for a robot to move politely among people by treating nearby pedestrians like magnets that gently push it away while its goal pulls it forward.
snappy: A pedestrian-aware navigation model representing goals and people as attractive and repulsive forces summed into a motion command.
detail: The Social Force Model treats the robot and surrounding pedestrians as particles driven by a fictitious attractive force toward the goal and repulsive forces away from people and walls, with the net force shaping velocity. Originally a model of crowd dynamics, it is adopted in Service & Consumer robotics so a Delivery robot or Telepresence robot moves in a socially acceptable way, respecting Proxemics. It is closely related to the Potential field method and is often compared against velocity-based schemes like the Reciprocal Velocity Obstacle for crowd navigation and Human-robot interaction.

plain: A model that predicts how people walk by treating their goals and the others around them as pushes and pulls, like magnets.
snappy: A pedestrian-motion model representing goal attraction and inter-agent or obstacle repulsion as virtual forces.
detail: The Social Forces Model (Social Force Model) computes a pedestrian's acceleration from an attractive force toward their goal plus repulsive forces from other people and obstacles, producing plausible crowd flow. In autonomy it serves as an interpretable prior for Trajectory Prediction and Behavior prediction of a Vulnerable road user, and as agent behavior inside a Driving simulator. It is conceptually related to the Potential field method used in robot Motion planning and complements the car-following Intelligent Driver Model.

plain: A robot built mainly to interact with people in a natural, social way rather than to do heavy physical work.
snappy: A robot designed to engage humans through social cues such as speech, gaze, gesture, and expressive behavior.
detail: A social robot prioritizes communication and rapport over manipulation force or payload, using Gesture recognition, Affective computing, and expressive motion to feel approachable. Examples range from a tabletop companion to a Humanoid robot receptionist, all governed by Proxemics and Human-robot interaction principles. Designers manage the Uncanny valley and Anthropomorphism so expectations match capability, and many social robots overlap with Socially assistive robotics when their goal is coaching, education, or companionship.

plain: Robots that help people through encouragement, conversation, and coaching rather than by physically touching or lifting them.
snappy: A subfield in which robots aid users primarily through social interaction, such as motivation and coaching, rather than physical contact.
detail: Socially assistive robotics (SAR) sits between Social robot work and Assistive technology, helping with rehabilitation exercises, eldercare engagement, or autism therapy by motivating rather than manipulating. A SAR system tracks adherence and adapts encouragement using Affective computing and Human pose estimation, while respecting Proxemics. It builds on Human-robot interaction and Theory of mind so the robot can tailor coaching, and it is deliberately distinct from a physically Powered prosthesis or an Exoskeleton that provides direct bodily assistance.

plain: A rechargeable battery that stores energy using sodium, a cheap and abundant material instead of scarcer lithium.
snappy: A rechargeable cell chemistry using sodium ions as charge carriers, offering low cost and good cold-temperature behavior.
detail: A Sodium-Ion Battery shuttles sodium ions between electrodes much like a Lithium-ion battery but uses earth-abundant sodium, lowering cost and improving cold-weather and safety behavior at the price of lower Energy density. For a robot this can suit cost-sensitive or fixed Mobility platforms where weight matters less, sitting alongside chemistries like Lithium iron phosphate battery and Nickel-Metal Hydride Battery in the design trade space. Like any pack it needs a Battery management system, and its Battery Cycle Life and State of charge are tracked by methods such as Coulomb Counting.

plain: Free software that lets a computer act as the conductor for a chain of fast factory motors and sensors over a special cable.
snappy: An open-source EtherCAT master stack that drives real-time fieldbus networks of motor drives and I/O.
detail: SOEM implements the controller side of the EtherCAT Fieldbus, cyclically exchanging commands and feedback with EtherCAT slaves such as a Servo drive or remote I/O over a deterministic network. It typically runs on a PREEMPT_RT Linux kernel to hold the microsecond timing that Real-time control demands, and is common in Manufacturing cells coordinating many axes via the CiA 402 Drive Profile. It pairs with safety extensions like FSoE for Safe Torque Off over the same wire.

plain: An efficient robot-learning method for smooth, continuous control that deliberately keeps trying varied actions so it explores well.
snappy: An off-policy, entropy-maximizing actor-critic algorithm for continuous control.
detail: Soft actor-critic (SAC) augments the standard Reward objective with an entropy bonus that encourages the Policy to stay stochastic, improving Exploration vs exploitation and stability for continuous-action robotics. As Off-policy learning it reuses past experience from a replay buffer, giving it better Sample efficiency than on-policy Proximal policy optimization. It is an Actor-critic method well suited to Manipulation and continuous-control tasks where data is expensive to collect.

plain: A squishy robot hand that bends and wraps around objects instead of squeezing them hard.
snappy: A gripper made of deformable materials that passively conforms gently around an object.
detail: A Soft gripper is built from flexible elastomers or inflatable chambers so its fingers deform to match an object's shape, distributing contact and reducing the risk of damage. It is a product of Soft robotics and exhibits inherent Compliance, making it ideal for fragile or variable items, for example fruit harvesting in Agriculture or handling soft consumer goods. Related approaches include the Underactuated gripper and the Jamming gripper, and many designs use a Pneumatic actuator or Dielectric elastomer actuator to drive the bending.

plain: A timing requirement where being a little late now and then just lowers quality, rather than causing a disaster.
snappy: A timing regime where occasional missed deadlines degrade performance or quality but do not violate correctness or safety.
detail: In a soft real-time task, like streaming a camera feed to a Service robot's planner, a dropped frame or late update hurts smoothness but is tolerable, unlike hard real-time motor control where a missed deadline is a failure. The distinction guides which work runs under a Real-time operating system or PREEMPT_RT and which can run best-effort. Designers still bound timing variability via Jitter limits and budget against Worst-case execution time, even when the deadline is soft.

plain: A robot made of bendy, squishy materials instead of hard metal parts, so it can squeeze, stretch, and grip gently.
snappy: A robot built from compliant, deformable materials rather than rigid links, deriving motion from material flexibility.
detail: A soft robot exploits material Compliance and Morphological computation, often actuated by a Pneumatic artificial muscle, Dielectric elastomer actuator, or Shape memory alloy actuator, so safety and gentle contact come from the body itself. This Soft robotics approach yields a Soft gripper that conforms to fragile objects and Medical & Surgical devices that move atop delicate tissue. Modeling deformation requires Soft-body simulation rather than Rigid body dynamics, an active Research/Frontier area.

plain: Robots made of bendy, squishy materials instead of hard metal parts.
snappy: A field building robots from compliant, deformable materials that bend and conform rather than from rigid links and joints.
detail: Soft robotics replaces rigid links with elastomers, fabrics, and fluidic chambers, giving inherent Compliance that makes a Soft robot safe around people and good at conforming grasps. A Soft gripper or Jamming gripper can pick fragile produce without precise pose, and medical tools use a Continuum robot to snake through anatomy. The trade-off is harder modeling and control, since the body has near-infinite degrees of freedom, which motivates exploiting Morphological computation and Bio-inspired robotics principles.

plain: A robot hand with squishy air-filled fingers, food-safe and gentle enough to pick up delicate or oddly shaped items.
snappy: A food-grade soft pneumatic fingered gripper for handling delicate, variable-shape items.
detail: The Soft Robotics mGrip is a modular Soft gripper whose food-grade pneumatic fingers inflate to wrap gently around fragile or irregular items like produce and baked goods, where a rigid Parallel-jaw gripper would crush or miss them. Built on Soft robotics principles, its Compliance lets one tool handle a wide variety of shapes without precise Grasp planning. It is used in food handling and Logistics & Warehouse picking, alongside compliant designs like the Fin Ray gripper.

plain: A robot body made of bendy, squishy materials like rubber or silicone instead of hard metal parts, so it can deform and squeeze into tight spaces.
snappy: A robot body built primarily from flexible, deformable materials that achieve motion through continuous bending rather than rigid links and joints.
detail: A soft robotics structure is the deformable body at the heart of Soft robotics, typically molded from elastomers and driven by a Pneumatic artificial muscle, Dielectric elastomer actuator, or Shape memory alloy actuator. Because the body itself bends, it relies on Morphological computation and high Mechanical compliance rather than precise Joint angles, and a Soft gripper built this way safely conforms to fragile objects. Such structures overlap with the Continuum structure family and are widely explored for Medical & Surgical endoscopes and search-and-rescue Microrobot designs.

plain: Simulating objects that bend, stretch, or squish instead of staying perfectly rigid, like cloth or rubber.
snappy: Numerically modeling deformable bodies such as cloth, tissue, cables, and compliant grippers under contact and force.
detail: Unlike Rigid body dynamics, soft-body simulation tracks objects that change shape, which is essential for a Soft gripper, a Soft robot, or surgical tools interacting with tissue in a Surgical robot. It is computationally heavier than rigid simulation, so frameworks such as MuJoCo and NVIDIA Isaac add it selectively. It is widely used in Synthetic data pipelines and Sim-to-real transfer for deformable-object manipulation like folding cloth.

plain: The company behind Pepper and NAO, friendly humanoid robots used for greeting people, teaching, and research.
snappy: Maker of the Pepper and NAO social humanoid robots.
detail: Originally Aldebaran, SoftBank Robotics produced NAO, a small programmable Humanoid robot widely used in education and Human-robot interaction research, and Pepper, a wheeled Social robot built to read emotion and greet customers. NAO became a standard research and RoboCup platform with full Bipedal locomotion in a compact body. Both robots emphasize Affective computing and expressive Gesture recognition over heavy-duty manipulation.

plain: Testing a robot's control program against a simulated version of the robot, with no physical machine involved.
snappy: Running the real autopilot or control software against a simulator instead of physical hardware to validate behavior.
detail: In SITL the unmodified flight or control code, such as PX4 or ArduPilot, runs on a workstation while a simulator like Gazebo Sim provides fake sensor data and accepts actuator commands. It lets developers test Waypoint navigation, failsafes, and mission logic safely before moving to Hardware-in-the-Loop testing and real flight. In Defense & Security and drone work it is the standard first rung for validating an Autopilot against scenarios like GNSS jamming.

plain: Running a drone's real control software against a pretend, simulated drone on a computer so you can test it safely before any actual flight.
snappy: Executing unmodified autopilot firmware against a simulated physics model and sensors, with no flight hardware in the loop.
detail: Software-in-the-loop simulation runs the actual autopilot code, such as PX4 or ArduPilot, connected to a Physics engine like Gazebo that models the airframe dynamics and synthetic sensors. It lets developers validate mission logic, tune a PID controller, and exercise MAVLink commands long before risking real hardware, catching bugs that could otherwise cause a Flyaway. SITL is the cheaper, faster counterpart to Hardware-in-the-loop simulation and a staple of any UAV continuous-integration workflow.

plain: A robot that runs on electricity made by its own solar panels, so it can keep working in sunlight without plugging in.
snappy: A robot that draws operating or charging energy from onboard photovoltaic panels to extend autonomy without external power.
detail: A Solar-Powered Robot converts sunlight into electricity through panels that trickle-charge its Battery Pack, extending Endurance and enabling Persistent autonomy where Charging Infrastructure is absent. The harvested current is usually modest and intermittent, so it supplements rather than fully powers the platform; designers pair it with careful Power budget management and sometimes Energy Harvesting. It is common in Agriculture for a field robot patrolling crops and in Space for a Planetary rover, which may combine panels with a Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generator when sunlight is scarce.

plain: A next-generation battery that uses a solid material instead of liquid inside, promising more energy in a smaller, safer package.
snappy: A cell using a solid electrolyte instead of liquid, targeting higher energy density and improved safety over conventional lithium-ion.
detail: A Solid-State Battery (SSB) replaces the flammable liquid electrolyte of a Lithium-ion battery with a solid one, which can suppress fire risk and may enable higher Energy density and faster charging. For robotics this could raise the Endurance and Payload-to-weight ratio of a Humanoid robot or extend the Runtime of a mobility platform without growing the Battery Pack. The technology is still maturing toward production scale, so most fielded robots remain on conventional lithium or a Lithium iron phosphate battery, but SSB is a closely watched frontier for Power density.

plain: A laser-scanning sensor that aims its beam electronically instead of by physically spinning, making it smaller and more rugged.
snappy: A LiDAR that steers its beam with no rotating mechanical assembly, using optical-phased-array, MEMS, or flash techniques.
detail: Solid-state LiDAR replaces the spinning optics of Mechanical LiDAR with beam steering that has few or no moving parts, improving durability and lowering cost for high-volume Mobility programs and the Autonomous vehicle market. Some designs use a MEMS sensor mirror to scan, while Flash LiDAR illuminates the whole scene at once. Like all LiDAR it produces a Point cloud consumed by Perception and Sensor fusion.

plain: A way of sensing distance and shapes by sending out sound pulses and timing how long their echoes take to return, the way a bat or dolphin does.
snappy: An acoustic ranging and imaging modality that measures echo time-of-flight to detect, range, and map objects, especially underwater where light and radio fail.
detail: Sonar is the primary perception modality for an Autonomous underwater vehicle and Remotely operated vehicle because water absorbs the light a Camera or LiDAR needs and blocks the radio of GPS, leaving sound as the practical long-range Sensor. Active sonar emits a pulse and times the echo for ranging and bathymetric Mapping, and multibeam or side-scan units build images for seabed survey, while the same Doppler effect that powers a Doppler Velocity Estimation log gives underwater speed-over-ground for Dead reckoning. In air, cheap single-beam variants overlap the role of an Ultrasonic sensor for obstacle detection, and sonar returns feed the vehicle's SLAM and Sensor fusion stack much as a Lidar Point Cloud does on land.

plain: A fast, lightweight way for a robot to keep following the same objects across video frames and give each a steady ID.
snappy: A real-time multi-object tracker that links per-frame detections into tracks using motion prediction plus simple box association.
detail: SORT performs Multi-object tracking by running a Kalman filter to predict each object's next Bounding box, then matching predictions to new Object detection outputs with the Hungarian Algorithm scored by Intersection over Union. Its popular extension DeepSORT adds an appearance embedding to survive occlusions and ID switches. Mobility robots and Defense & Security platforms use it downstream of detectors like YOLO for pedestrian and vehicle tracking, valued for running on modest Onboard compute while staying online and real-time.

plain: A high-speed machine that automatically routes packages off a conveyor into the correct chute or lane for their destination.
snappy: A high-throughput conveyor subsystem that diverts items to destinations using shoes, tilt-trays, or cross-belts under scanned control.
detail: A sortation system reads each item's barcode and mechanically diverts it, with sliding-shoe, tilt-tray, and cross-belt designs trading speed against gentleness for different product mixes. It typically receives a metered stream from an Accumulation conveyor and is sequenced by the Warehouse control system against orders held in the Warehouse management system. Sortation underpins Material handling at parcel hubs, where Throughput and accurate diverts directly set the facility's Cost per Pick.

plain: Making sure an automated system is safe even when nothing is broken but the technology simply cannot handle a situation well enough.
snappy: A safety discipline addressing hazards arising from performance limitations of intended functions, with no component fault present.
detail: SOTIF, standardized as ISO 21448, targets hazards that occur even when every part works correctly, such as a Perception system failing to recognize a pedestrian in glare or an unanticipated scenario at the edge of the Operational design domain. It complements ISO 26262 functional safety, which assumes a fault, by analyzing performance gaps, foreseeable misuse, and unknown-unsafe scenarios in an Autonomous vehicle. Engineers expand the safe set through Scenario-based testing and ODD refinement, and SOTIF analysis often pairs with STPA to find unsafe control actions.

plain: A clever switching pattern that tells a motor drive's electronic switches when to turn on and off so the motor runs smoothly and efficiently.
snappy: Inverter switching scheme that synthesizes the desired three-phase voltage vector while maximizing usable DC-bus voltage.
detail: Space Vector Modulation treats the inverter's eight possible switch states as vectors and times their combination to produce a rotating voltage, giving roughly 15% more usable bus voltage and lower harmonic distortion than naive Pulse-width modulation. It is the standard modulation layer underneath Field-oriented control in a modern Servo drive or Brushless DC Motor Controller. Smoother phase voltages mean less Torque Ripple and lower losses, which matters for the precise Position control of an Industrial robot arm and for efficient mobile-robot traction.

plain: A stock of replacement parts kept nearby so a broken robot can be fixed fast.
snappy: The stock of critical replacement components held on or near site to minimize robot downtime when parts fail.
detail: Spare Parts Inventory (critical spares) is a deliberate trade-off between holding cost and the downtime cost of waiting for a part, and it is sized using Mean time between failures and Mean time to repair data. Items like a Harmonic drive, a servo drive, a Brushless DC motor, or a gripper finger are stocked because their failure halts a Robot cell. Good Predictive maintenance and Remote Diagnostics let teams pre-position the right spares before a fault becomes a stoppage, protecting Uptime. The cost of holding spares is a line item in Operating Expenditure and is often bundled into a Robots-as-a-Service contract.

plain: A set of rules that make factory data sent over MQTT consistent and self-describing, so different systems can understand it without custom mapping.
snappy: An MQTT topic and payload specification that standardizes industrial data structure and state for IIoT systems.
detail: Sparkplug B defines a namespace, payload encoding (via Protocol Buffers), and birth/death state model on top of MQTT so that every device reports its data in a discoverable, typed way with known online/offline status. This removes the per-integration mapping work that plagues raw MQTT deployments, accelerating Industrial Internet of Things rollouts and Industry 4.0 analytics. Sparkplug data commonly lands in an OT historian and feeds dashboards and Predictive maintenance models across a fleet of machines.

plain: A learning setup where the robot only gets a reward on rare success, making it hard to figure out what early moves were helpful.
snappy: A reward signal that is nonzero only on infrequent success, making credit assignment and exploration difficult.
detail: A sparse reward gives feedback only when a task fully succeeds, so a Reinforcement learning agent may wander for a long time before ever seeing a positive Reward, worsening the Exploration vs exploitation tradeoff and hurting Sample efficiency. Robotics tasks like Peg-in-hole and goal-reaching are naturally sparse. Common remedies include Reward shaping, Curriculum learning, hindsight relabeling, and seeding behavior with Imitation learning to get the agent near success states.

plain: A learning problem where the robot only gets a hint that it succeeded very rarely, making it hard to figure out what worked.
snappy: A reinforcement learning setting in which informative reward feedback occurs only on rare success, yielding a difficult credit-assignment problem.
detail: In a sparse-reward task the agent sees a Reward only at goal completion, so random exploration almost never stumbles onto it, a problem acute for a Long-horizon task like Peg-in-hole. Standard remedies are Reward shaping, Hindsight experience replay, Curriculum learning, and Intrinsic motivation to densify the signal, plus demonstrations via Imitation learning to bootstrap. It is a defining challenge for Reinforcement learning on real robots, where the related Sparse reward concept and exploration efficiency dominate training cost.

plain: A single six-by-six table that captures both how heavy a robot part is and how hard it is to spin, so motion math can treat mass and rotation together.
snappy: A 6x6 matrix encoding a rigid body's mass, center-of-mass offset, and rotational inertia for use in spatial-vector dynamics.
detail: The Spatial Inertia Matrix combines a link's mass, first moment about its Center of mass, and Inertia tensor into one 6x6 operator that maps a spatial Twist to a spatial momentum (and acceleration to a Wrench) within Spatial Vector Algebra. It is the per-link building block consumed by the Recursive Newton-Euler Algorithm, the Composite Rigid Body Algorithm, and the Articulated Body Algorithm, and is transformed between frames using the Adjoint Representation. Accurate spatial inertias come from Inertial Parameter Identification and feed directly into the Mass matrix used for Whole-body control.

plain: Thinking about where things are, what shape they are, and how they relate in space, like figuring out whether a box will fit on a shelf.
snappy: Reasoning about positions, orientations, distances, and geometric relations among objects and the robot itself.
detail: Spatial reasoning underpins tasks from warehouse stacking to opening a drawer, answering questions like 'is the mug behind the bowl?' or 'can the gripper reach there?'. It draws on a Scene graph and Semantic mapping, feeds Motion planning and Grasp planning, and is increasingly handled by a Vision-language-action model that grounds language like 'left of' into 3D space. In Logistics & Warehouse settings it drives Palletizing and Bin picking layout decisions.

plain: A compact notation that stacks a body's straight-line motion and its spinning motion into a single six-number quantity, so robot math handles both at once.
snappy: A six-dimensional notation that unifies linear and angular velocity (motion vectors) and force and moment (force vectors) for concise rigid-body dynamics.
detail: Spatial Vector Algebra packs translational and rotational quantities into single 6D objects, so a body's velocity becomes a spatial Twist and the force on it becomes a spatial Wrench, with the Spatial Inertia Matrix mapping between them. This notation, central to the Featherstone Algorithm, lets the Recursive Newton-Euler Algorithm, Articulated Body Algorithm, and Composite Rigid Body Algorithm be written as short recursions over the Kinematic chain. It is closely related to Screw theory and the Adjoint Representation used to move twists and wrenches between frames on the Special Euclidean group SE(3).

plain: The mathematical collection of all the ways a rigid object can be moved and rotated in three-dimensional space.
snappy: The group of rigid-body poses combining 3D rotation and translation.
detail: SE(3) is the set of all rigid-body Pose values, each representable as a Homogeneous transformation matrix, and it pairs a rotation from the Special orthogonal group SO(3) with a translation. Treating poses as group elements lets robotics use clean tools like the matrix exponential, which is the basis of Screw theory and the product-of-exponentials kinematics formula. A Twist is the velocity that lives in the tangent space of SE(3).

plain: The mathematical collection of all the ways an object can be rotated, without any moving or stretching.
snappy: The group of 3D rotations underlying every orientation representation.
detail: SO(3) is the set of all valid 3x3 rotation matrices, and every orientation encoding, a Quaternion, Euler angles, or the Axis-angle representation, is just a different chart on it. It forms the rotational part of the Special Euclidean group SE(3). Because SO(3) curves rather than being flat, naive linear averaging of orientations fails and Gimbal lock appears in poor parameterizations, which is why robotics estimators work on the group directly.

plain: A safety rating, from a European drone risk method, that says how trustworthy and rigorously built a particular drone operation must be.
snappy: A SORA-derived risk tier (SAIL I-VI) that prescribes the operational safety objectives and robustness required for a UAS operation.
detail: The Specific Assurance and Integrity Level is the output of the Specific Operations Risk Assessment, combining residual ground and air risk into a single tier from I to VI that escalates the rigor of evidence an operator must provide. A higher SAIL demands stronger design assurance, testing, and procedures, such as more reliable Detect and avoid, a robust Flight Termination System, and verified failsafes against a Flyaway. It functions as the European analog to assurance levels in other Functional safety regimes and gates approval for complex Beyond visual line of sight operations.

plain: A middle tier of drone-flight rules for missions that are riskier than everyday hobby flying but not as risky as carrying passengers, so the operator must get permission or prove the flight is safe before flying.
snappy: The European medium-risk tier of drone operation that requires either a prior Operational Authorization or a risk-assessment-based approval before flying.
detail: Under the European drone framework an Unmanned aircraft system operation falls into one of three risk tiers, and the Specific Category sits between low-risk Open operations and high-risk Certified ones. Operators justify each mission with a Specific Operations Risk Assessment, which yields a Specific Assurance and Integrity Level setting how much rigor and evidence the operation demands; missions like Beyond visual line of sight inspection or urban delivery typically land here. The output is an Operational Authorization granting the flight under stated conditions such as a defined Ground Risk Buffer and mitigations like a Flight Termination System, and it is broadly analogous in purpose to the US Part 107 Waiver process.

plain: A step-by-step European safety method for proving a riskier drone flight, like one out of the pilot's sight, is safe enough to be allowed.
snappy: An EASA methodology that quantifies ground and air risk of a drone operation to justify authorization in the Specific Category.
detail: The Specific Operations Risk Assessment (SORA) is the structured framework operators use to win approval for higher-risk flights, especially Beyond visual line of sight missions that fall outside simple open-category rules. It scores ground risk and air risk, applies mitigations like a Ground Risk Buffer and Detect and avoid, and outputs a Specific Assurance and Integrity Level that sets the required robustness of the system. It is the European counterpart to FAA waiver processes and a gateway for scaling Drone delivery services such as Wing within UAS traffic management.

plain: A safety method that watches how close a person is and makes the robot slow down or stop before they can get too near.
snappy: A collaborative operation mode that maintains a protective separation distance, reducing robot speed or stopping it as a human approaches.
detail: Speed and separation monitoring (SSM) uses sensors such as a Safety scanner or 3D vision to track the distance between an operator and the robot, then commands a Safety-rated monitored stop if the protective separation distance is breached. Defined in ISO 10218 and detailed in ISO/TS 15066, it is common where a Collaborative robot must move fast yet still allow people in the Collaborative workspace. The separation distance accounts for robot stopping time, human approach speed, and sensor latency.

plain: A ball-and-socket joint that lets a part swivel freely in any rotational direction.
snappy: A three-rotation joint connecting two links at a single pivot point.
detail: A Spherical joint contributes three rotational Degrees of freedom at one point, functionally equivalent to three intersecting Revolute joint axes; it is the model for a Spherical wrist and the leg attachments of a Stewart platform. Because it concentrates three rotations at one location, it is common in Parallel manipulator limbs and in humanoid hip and shoulder analogues. Real hardware often approximates it with a Bearing-mounted ball-and-socket or a gimbaled cluster of revolute joints.

plain: A robot sealed inside a ball that rolls around by shifting its weight or spinning internal parts, with nothing sticking out.
snappy: A mobile robot enclosed in a rigid sphere that propels and steers by relocating internal mass or driving an internal mechanism.
detail: By shifting an internal pendulum or driving a hamster-wheel mechanism, a spherical robot rolls without any external moving parts, giving it a sealed shell that is naturally dust-, water-, and impact-resistant for harsh Terrain adaptation. Its rolling dynamics are governed by a Nonholonomic constraint, making Trajectory tracking and Motion planning nontrivial, and it shares the internal-mass balancing idea with the Ballbot and Two-wheeled inverted pendulum. Variants serve planetary exploration, surveillance, and amphibious tasks, complementing the Tumbling locomotion and Self-righting behaviors of other Bio-inspired robotics designs.

plain: A robot sealed inside a ball that rolls along by shifting its weight around inside the shell.
snappy: A robot enclosed in a rigid sphere that locomotes by displacing internal mass or driving an internal pendulum to roll the shell.
detail: A Spherical rolling robot, or ball robot, drives its outer shell by shifting an internal mass, pendulum, or reaction wheels so the whole sphere rolls, a sealed form that is dust-tight, waterproof, and self-righting after impacts. The dynamics are a Nonholonomic constraint problem closely related to the Two-wheeled inverted pendulum and Ballbot balancing families, demanding careful control of the internal actuator. Its rugged enclosure suits Space surface scouting and Defense & Security reconnaissance where a conventional Wheeled robot would jam or topple.

plain: A robot wrist built so its three turning axes all cross at one single point, letting the tool spin in any direction around that spot.
snappy: A three-axis wrist whose rotation axes intersect at a common point, decoupling end-effector orientation from position.
detail: In a spherical wrist the three final rotation axes meet at one point, which decouples orientation from position and yields a Closed-form IK solution, the reason most Industrial robot arm designs adopt it. The intersecting-axis geometry is also why the wrist suffers a Kinematic singularity when the inner and outer axes line up, causing loss of one Degrees of freedom and runaway joint velocities. The wrist sits behind the Tool flange on a Six-axis robot and is a defining feature of the standard Robot wrist used across Manufacturing.

plain: A trick where a robot presses a part down and slowly traces an expanding spiral until it feels the part drop into a hole.
snappy: A force-guided expanding-spiral motion used to locate a hole entrance during insertion under position uncertainty.
detail: Spiral search compensates for small misalignment in Peg-in-hole insertion: holding light downward Force control, the End-effector traces an outward spiral until the peg slips into the chamfer and seating is detected. It is a classic recovery strategy paired with Impedance control or a Remote center of compliance to absorb contact, and it directly addresses Wedging and jamming failures. The technique is heavily used in robotic Assembly and is a baseline on the NIST assembly task boards.

plain: Fine-tuning the few control points of a smooth curve so a robot's path is both gentle and stays well clear of obstacles.
snappy: Generating a trajectory by optimizing spline control points against smoothness, dynamic feasibility, and clearance objectives.
detail: Spline Optimization parameterizes a path with a small set of control points (often of a B-spline Trajectory) and adjusts them to minimize a cost that blends smoothness, dynamic limits, and distance from obstacles, frequently using gradients from a signed-distance field or ESDF. It is the refinement stage in many local planners, taking a coarse route from a Lattice Planner or sampling planner and shaping it into a smooth, executable Trajectory. Quadrotor systems including EGO-Planner and Space rover planners use it to balance Time parameterization against clearance.

plain: A shaft with lengthwise ridges, like teeth running along it, that let a part slide back and forth while still turning with the shaft.
snappy: A shaft with longitudinal ridges that transmit torque to a mating hub while allowing the hub to slide along the shaft's axis.
detail: A Spline Shaft carries multiple parallel ridges along its length that engage matching grooves in a hub, sharing the transmitted mechanical torque across many teeth rather than the single key of a Keyway. The defining feature is that the hub can translate axially while still transmitting rotation, which makes splines ideal in a telescoping arm, a Linear guide combined with rotary drive, or a Differential Gear assembly. Because the load is spread over many contacts, spline couplings handle high torque with low Backlash, supporting precise Motion control.

plain: A four-legged robot, roughly dog-sized, that walks around buildings and sites taking readings and pictures.
snappy: Boston Dynamics' commercial quadruped robot used for autonomous inspection and sensor data capture.
detail: Spot is a Quadruped robot from Boston Dynamics deployed across Field robotics tasks like plant inspection, construction monitoring, and Defense & Security patrols. It carries swappable payloads, uses onboard Perception and SLAM for Navigation, and supports Teach-and-repeat routes so operators can program inspection rounds. Spot's Quadrupedal locomotion lets it climb stairs and traverse rough terrain where a Wheeled robot would get stuck.

plain: A robot that joins sheet metal by squeezing two electrodes against it and passing a current to fuse a single spot.
snappy: A robot that fuses sheet metal at discrete points by pressing electrodes and passing weld current.
detail: A spot welding robot wields a heavy resistance-weld gun as its End-of-arm tooling, indexing across a car body to make hundreds of resistance welds, so it needs high Payload capacity and fast point-to-point moves with Zone blending. Gun pressure and weld current are controlled by a weld timer while the Industrial robot arm handles positioning relative to the Work object frame. It is the workhorse of automotive body shops and a defining application of Robotic welding.

plain: A simple model that pictures a running robot as a bouncing ball on a springy pogo-stick leg.
snappy: A reduced template model representing running and hopping as a point mass atop a massless springy leg that compresses and rebounds during stance.
detail: The spring-loaded inverted pendulum (SLIP) captures the essential bouncing dynamics of Running and Hopping with just a point Center of mass and an elastic leg, abstracting away joints and limbs. It guides controller design for a Legged robot by predicting how leg stiffness and touchdown angle set hopping height and speed, and motivates hardware like a Series elastic actuator. SLIP is the running analogue of the Linear inverted pendulum model used for walking.

plain: The simplest kind of gear: a flat wheel with straight teeth around its edge that meshes with another to pass along turning motion.
snappy: A cylindrical gear with straight teeth parallel to its axis, meshing with like gears on parallel shafts.
detail: The Spur Gear is the basic building block of a Gear Train, transmitting power between parallel shafts and setting the Gear Ratio by the relative tooth counts. It is simple and efficient but meshes one tooth pair abruptly, making it noisier and lower in load capacity than a Helical Gear, and it always carries some Gear Backlash. Spur stages are the planets and sun of a Planetary Gearbox and the pinion of a Rack and Pinion, making this the foundational gear most other Gear reduction stages build on.

plain: A route planner for robots with real motion limits that keeps only a thin set of the best branches, getting near-best routes without needing to solve how to steer exactly between two states.
snappy: A sparse kinodynamic sampling planner that achieves asymptotic near-optimality by pruning dominated nodes and propagating random controls, requiring no two-point steering function.
detail: SST (Stable Sparse RRT) tackles Kinodynamic planning for systems where you cannot analytically steer between two states: like Kinodynamic RRT it forward-propagates sampled controls, but it keeps only a sparse set of locally best 'witness' nodes, which both bounds memory and yields asymptotic near-optimality. This makes it attractive for underactuated and Nonholonomic constraint robots where a Rapidly-exploring random tree with a steering function is unavailable, and it is implemented in OMPL. Every propagated edge is validated by Collision detection.

plain: A system's tendency to settle back toward balance after being pushed, rather than wobbling out of control.
snappy: The property whereby a controlled system returns toward equilibrium after a disturbance instead of diverging.
detail: Stability is the first thing a control design must guarantee: an unstable loop amplifies small errors until the robot oscillates or saturates. Engineers prove it with tools like Lyapunov stability and tune for it by adjusting Gain and Damping. For a Humanoid robot, stability also has a physical meaning, keeping the Zero moment point inside the Support polygon so the machine does not topple, which Whole-body control and Balance control actively maintain.

plain: The very most twisting force a motor can make when it is fully stopped and not turning at all.
snappy: The maximum torque a motor produces at zero speed (locked rotor), before it can turn no further.
detail: Stall Torque is the locked-rotor point at the high-torque end of a motor's torque-speed curve, where speed is zero and current (and heating) is highest, defining the peak force available to break static loads free or hold against Stiction. It anchors actuator sizing alongside continuous Peak torque, the no-load speed, and the limits set by Thermal Derating, since sustained operation near stall risks Demagnetization. Designers in Mobility and Manufacturing compare a candidate motor's stall torque against worst-case joint loads and the Reflected Inertia it must accelerate.

plain: The part of a step when a foot is planted on the ground bearing weight.
snappy: The portion of the gait cycle during which a given foot is in contact with the ground and supporting the body.
detail: During stance phase the leg transmits the Ground reaction force that supports and propels the body, so it is when the robot can push, steer, and balance. Its length as a fraction of the Gait cycle is the Duty factor, and overlapping stance phases across legs define the Support polygon underpinning Static stability. It alternates with the Swing phase, when the same foot is lifted and repositioned.

plain: A company that makes a low-cost six-jointed robot arm aimed at small workshops.
snappy: Maker of the affordable RO1 six-axis cobot for small-shop automation.
detail: Standard Bots positions its RO1 as a low-cost Collaborative robot with a high Payload for its price class, targeting small manufacturers priced out of traditional automation. As a Cobot it supports Hand guiding and power and force limiting so it can share a collaborative workspace with people, and it is programmed through a no-code Teach pendant interface for Pick and place and Machine tending. The company emphasizes fast deployment and a low Total cost of ownership.

plain: A steering rule, made famous by a self-driving car race, that corrects both which way the front wheels point and how far the car has drifted off the path.
snappy: A lateral path-tracking law that sets steering from the front-axle heading error plus an arctangent term in the cross-track error, named for Stanford's DARPA Grand Challenge winner.
detail: The Stanley Controller, developed for Stanford's 'Stanley' vehicle that won the DARPA Grand Challenge, references tracking error at the front axle and combines a heading-alignment term with a nonlinear cross-track-error term scaled by speed, giving strong convergence back onto the reference Trajectory. It is a common alternative to Pure Pursuit for Ackermann steering self-driving cars and is often used inside a larger Self-driving stack. Both are geometric controllers that assume a Bicycle Model of the vehicle.

plain: A company that runs small six-wheeled robots that deliver food and packages along sidewalks.
snappy: Operator of small sidewalk robots delivering food and parcels on campuses and in towns.
detail: Starship operates fleets of the Sidewalk delivery robot for Last-mile delivery on university campuses and in suburbs, navigating pedestrian paths with cameras, Ultrasonic sensor arrays, and GPS-aided localization. The cooler-sized Delivery robot crosses streets autonomously but escalates to a human via Remote Assistance for tricky situations, an example of Supervised autonomy. It is one of the most-deployed examples of the autonomous Last-mile delivery category.

plain: Working out a robot's true situation, like where it is and how fast it is moving, from imperfect sensor readings.
snappy: Inferring a robot's hidden internal state (pose, velocity, and more) from noisy, incomplete sensor measurements.
detail: State estimation combines a motion model with sensor data to recover quantities the robot cannot measure directly, such as its Pose, velocity, or orientation. Classic tools include the Kalman filter and Particle filter, and the estimate usually carries an explicit Uncertainty. It underpins Localization, Odometry, and the feedback loops that make Closed-loop control possible.

plain: A way of steering a machine where the controller looks at the machine's complete internal condition and uses all of it to decide what to do next.
snappy: A control law that computes commands as a function of the full system state rather than just the measured output.
detail: State feedback multiplies the system's state vector by a gain matrix to produce a control command, the foundation of State-space control. Because the true state is often not directly measured, it is usually paired with State estimation from a Kalman filter, and the gains are chosen by Pole placement or by solving a Linear quadratic regulator. It underlies controllers from balancing a Bipedal robot to regulating a Servomotor.

plain: A grid of pre-built movement snippets that a car-like robot can search through, where every snippet is a motion the vehicle can really perform.
snappy: A search graph whose edges are precomputed, dynamically feasible motion primitives connecting discretized states.
detail: A State lattice discretizes the robot's state, including heading and sometimes velocity, and connects states only with a precomputed library of feasible Motion primitive segments, so any path found by Graph search is guaranteed drivable. This is a popular Global planner for Autonomous vehicle and rover navigation because it captures the Nonholonomic constraint of the platform up front, much like Hybrid A* but with an explicitly enumerated edge set. The lattice planner pairs with A* search or Dijkstra's algorithm over the lattice and was central to several DARPA Challenge vehicles.

plain: How much energy is left in a robot's battery, shown as a percentage like a phone's battery icon.
snappy: The remaining charge in a battery pack relative to its full capacity, expressed as a percentage.
detail: State of charge (SOC) is the battery's fuel gauge, estimated by the Battery management system from voltage, current integration, and cell models since it cannot be measured directly. A robot uses SOC against its Power budget to decide when to trigger Autonomous docking or a Hot-swappable battery swap before Endurance runs out. Accurate SOC is harder near the flat discharge curve of a Lithium iron phosphate battery, so the BMS fuses multiple signals.

plain: A score for how much life a battery has left compared to when it was brand new.
snappy: An estimate of an aging battery's remaining usable capacity and performance relative to its original rated specification.
detail: State of Health (SoH) tracks how a pack degrades over hundreds of charge cycles, falling as internal resistance rises and capacity fades; the Battery management system estimates it from voltage, temperature, and Coulomb Counting history. It tells a fleet when a pack's shrinking Battery Cycle Life will no longer cover a shift, informing Predictive maintenance and replacement scheduling for an Autonomous mobile robot or Automated guided vehicle. SoH is distinct from State of charge, which is the present fill level, and operators pair it with Depth of Discharge limits to slow degradation and hold down Total cost of ownership.

plain: Describing a system by tracking a set of internal numbers that capture its condition, and the rules for how they change over time.
snappy: Modeling and controlling a system through its internal state variables and their first-order evolution equations.
detail: State-space control represents a system as a vector of state variables, like positions and velocities, evolving by first-order differential equations, enabling multi-input multi-output design beyond single-loop methods. It is the foundation for State feedback, Pole placement, Optimal control like the Linear quadratic regulator, and estimators such as the Kalman filter that recover unmeasured states. Robotics uses it for State estimation and to control coupled multi-joint Dynamics that classical Control theory handles awkwardly.

plain: Being balanced even when standing completely still, like a table that will not tip over.
snappy: Balance that holds without any motion, achieved by keeping the projected center of mass inside the support polygon at all times.
detail: A statically stable robot will not topple if you stop it at any instant, because its Center of mass always projects inside the Support polygon formed by its ground contacts. This is the principle behind a Crawl gait, where a Quadruped robot keeps at least three feet down so the body stays supported. Static stability is simpler and safer than Dynamic stability but inherently slower, since the robot must always preserve a valid base of support.

plain: Cleaning up a 3D scan by deleting stray dots that sit far away from all their neighbors and are probably just noise.
snappy: A point-cloud filter that rejects points whose mean distance to their k nearest neighbors exceeds a statistical threshold.
detail: Statistical Outlier Removal computes, for each point, the average distance to its neighbors, then discards points lying beyond a chosen number of standard deviations from the global mean. It is a common cleanup stage in the Point Cloud Library, usually applied after Voxel Downsampling and before Euclidean Cluster Extraction or Point cloud registration. Mobility and Manufacturing robots use it to strip Sensor noise and spurious returns from LiDAR or Depth camera data so that downstream segmentation and Object detection see cleaner geometry.

plain: Using statistics and charts to watch a manufacturing process so you can spot it drifting toward defects before bad parts are made.
snappy: Monitoring process measurements with control charts to detect and correct variation before defects occur, abbreviated SPC.
detail: SPC plots measurements, dimensions, weights, temperatures, on control charts with statistically derived limits, distinguishing normal random variation from a genuine shift that signals the process is going out of control. Data often comes from automated Quality inspection and Machine vision gauging, and acting on SPC signals keeps the quality term of Overall equipment effectiveness high. It is a cornerstone of lean and Six Sigma practice and increasingly runs live on Industrial Internet of Things data inside a Smart factory.

plain: A leftover gap between where a system ends up and where it was supposed to be, even after it stops moving.
snappy: The residual offset between setpoint and actual value remaining after the response has fully settled.
detail: Steady-state error is the persistent component of the Error signal once all transients decay, caused by friction, gravity, or constant disturbances that a proportional Gain alone cannot fully cancel. The integral term of a PID controller exists precisely to drive it to zero by accumulating error over time, though that integral can suffer windup during Saturation, requiring Anti-windup. Feedforward control also reduces it by preempting known loads like gravity in a robot arm.

plain: A steering system where turning the wheel sends electronic signals to motors, with no mechanical shaft connecting the wheel to the tires.
snappy: Electronically actuated steering with no mechanical column linking the steering wheel to the road wheels, commanded by signals.
detail: Steer-by-Wire replaces the steering column with electric actuators and force-feedback, enabling variable steering ratios and clean command of steering by an Automated driving system. As a Drive-by-wire actuator it must be Fail-operational, with redundant power, sensing, and the Controller Area Network or FlexRay buses, and is governed by ISO 26262 functional safety. It pairs with Brake-by-wire to give an autonomy stack full control authority over the vehicle.

plain: A motor that moves in small, fixed steps, letting a machine position itself precisely without needing to check where it is.
snappy: A motor that rotates in discrete steps, enabling open-loop positioning without feedback.
detail: A stepper divides each rotation into many equal steps, so a Motor controller can command an exact angle simply by counting pulses, giving repeatable positioning in Open-loop control without an Encoder. This makes it popular in 3D printers, CNC machines, and Manufacturing automation where loads are predictable. Its weaknesses are limited high-speed torque and the risk of silently losing steps under overload, which a true Servomotor with feedback avoids.

plain: Keeping your balance by quickly stepping to a new spot to catch yourself, the way a person staggers a step when shoved.
snappy: A balance-recovery method in which a legged robot takes a reactive step to move its support base under its falling body.
detail: When a disturbance pushes a humanoid robot beyond what ankle and hip torques can correct, the controller commits to a recovery step, placing a foot to enlarge or relocate the Support polygon under the toppling Center of mass. The target foothold is computed from the Capture point, the spot where stepping arrests momentum, often expressed through the Divergent component of motion. It complements ankle and hip strategies in Push recovery and Balance control, realized by Footstep planning.

plain: A pair of side-by-side cameras that judge how far away things are, the way two eyes give people depth perception.
snappy: A two-lens camera that infers depth by measuring left-right disparity between matched image points.
detail: A stereo camera uses two lenses a known distance apart and computes Depth estimation from the horizontal shift, or disparity, between matching features in the left and right images via Stereo matching. Unlike a Depth camera using Structured light, it is passive and works outdoors in sunlight, making it popular for Mobility and Visual SLAM. Its output is typically a Depth map or Point cloud used for Obstacle detection.

plain: Working out distance by comparing the slightly different views from two side-by-side cameras, the way two eyes judge depth.
snappy: Finding corresponding points across a calibrated camera pair to compute per-pixel disparity and hence depth.
detail: Stereo matching searches for the same scene point in the left and right images of a Stereo camera; the horizontal shift between them, called disparity, is inversely proportional to distance and yields a Depth map. It depends on accurate Camera calibration and on Image rectification so corresponding points lie on the same image row. It is a standard source of Depth estimation for Mobility robots and a building block of 3D reconstruction.

plain: A moving platform supported by six adjustable legs that can tilt and shift it in any direction.
snappy: A six-actuator parallel mechanism providing full six-degree-of-freedom platform motion.
detail: The Stewart platform connects a base and a top plate with six length-adjustable legs, each ending in a Spherical joint, making it a stiff Closed kinematic chain with six Degrees of freedom. It is the archetypal Parallel manipulator, used in flight and driving simulators, precision positioning, and machine tools. Its Inverse kinematics is simple (per-leg length) while its Forward kinematics requires numerical solving.

plain: The math describing how a movable platform supported by six adjustable legs is positioned and tilted by changing each leg's length.
snappy: The kinematic equations relating the six leg lengths of a Gough-Stewart hexapod to the position and orientation of its moving platform.
detail: A Stewart platform connects a moving plate to a fixed base through six extensible legs, forming a closed kinematic chain whose Loop Closure Constraint makes its inverse problem easy but its forward problem hard. Given a desired platform pose, each leg length follows directly from geometry, so the Inverse kinematics has a clean closed-form solution; computing the platform pose from measured leg lengths (Forward kinematics) instead requires solving coupled polynomials with up to forty solutions. As a Parallel robot it offers high stiffness and payload, which is why it underpins flight simulators, six-axis machining heads, and precision positioning stages.

plain: The extra grip that keeps a part stuck still until you push hard enough to break it loose, which then makes very slow, fine movements jumpy.
snappy: Static friction that must be overcome before motion begins, causing a dead zone and stick-slip that degrades fine positioning.
detail: Stiction is the breakaway Static friction higher than the sliding friction that follows, so a joint sits motionless until the command exceeds it and then lurches, hurting low-speed Position control and Repeatability. It is a dominant error source in a Gearbox or Harmonic drive and is commonly countered with Friction Compensation, dither, or a Backdrivable actuator. Stiction interacts with Backlash and the Coulomb friction model and can trigger a Limit cycle near a setpoint.

plain: How strongly a part resists bending or stretching when force is applied; a stiff thing barely moves, a flexible thing gives easily.
snappy: The ratio of applied load to resulting elastic deflection in a structure, member, or joint.
detail: Stiffness is the inverse of Mechanical compliance: high stiffness means a Link, Joint, or Robot wrist deflects little under load, preserving Accuracy and Repeatability at the End-effector. A robot built from Carbon fiber composite achieves high stiffness at low mass, raising structural Bandwidth and the natural frequency of the arm. Controllers can also command apparent stiffness electronically through Impedance control, and a Variable stiffness actuator lets a robot switch between rigid and springy behavior for safe Human-robot interaction.

plain: A way for a group to coordinate by leaving marks or changes in their shared surroundings, the way ants follow trails left by other ants.
snappy: Indirect coordination in which agents influence one another by modifying a shared environment rather than communicating directly.
detail: Stigmergy is a foundational mechanism in Swarm robotics: robots deposit and sense environmental traces so the medium itself carries coordination signals, removing the need for explicit messaging. A classic example is pheromone-style trail laying during Foraging behavior, where a robot marks a path to a resource and others reinforce it, producing Self-organization without a central controller. It exemplifies Decentralized control and underpins much Collective intelligence, and warehouse Multi-robot system designs use virtual stigmergic markers in a shared Cost map to deconflict routes.

full: Stochastic Trajectory Optimization for Motion Planning
plain: A planning method that improves a robot's path by trying many small random tweaks and blending the ones that work out best, no calculus required.
snappy: A sampling-based stochastic optimizer that improves a trajectory by averaging noisy rollouts weighted by cost.
detail: STOMP perturbs the current trajectory with many noisy variations, evaluates each against a cost combining smoothness and obstacle clearance, and updates toward the lower-cost samples, so it needs no gradient and can handle non-differentiable costs. This gradient-free trait lets it escape local minima that can trap the gradient-based CHOMP, making the two complementary Trajectory optimization planners in MoveIt for robot arms. Like CHOMP it typically refines an initial guess from a Sampling-based planning method and respects joint limits before Time parameterization.

plain: An emergency stop that instantly cuts all power to the motors, letting the machine coast to a halt on its own.
snappy: An uncontrolled stop achieved by immediately removing power to machine actuators, per IEC 60204-1.
detail: Stop Category 0 is the most abrupt stop defined in IEC 60204-1: power to actuators is removed at once, so the machine decelerates uncontrolled by friction and inertia. It maps directly to the Safe Torque Off drive function and is the default behavior of a simple Emergency stop. Because coasting can be hazardous for high-inertia or vertical axes, designers often prefer a Stop Category 1 instead, or add Safe Brake Control; the choice follows from the Risk assessment.

plain: A safe stop that first brings the machine to rest in a controlled way, then cuts power once it has stopped.
snappy: A controlled stop with power maintained to decelerate the actuator, followed by power removal at standstill, per IEC 60204-1.
detail: Stop Category 1 keeps the Servo drive powered just long enough to brake the motor under control, then transitions to Safe Torque Off (a Stop Category 0 condition) once standstill is reached. It avoids the dangerous coasting of a Stop Category 0 while still ending in a de-energized, safe state, making it the usual choice for high-inertia or vertical axes. The controlled deceleration phase is itself monitored to a Performance Level, and may be combined with Safe Brake Control on gravity-loaded axes.

plain: A controlled stop that brings the machine to a standstill but keeps power on so it can hold position and restart quickly.
snappy: A controlled stop that decelerates the actuator and then keeps it energized at standstill, per IEC 60204-1.
detail: Stop Category 2 brings a machine to rest while keeping power applied, ending in a monitored standstill equivalent to the Safe Operating Stop drive function rather than a de-energized state like Stop Category 0 or Stop Category 1. It is used for productivity where frequent stop-and-go is needed, but because the drive stays live it requires reliable standstill monitoring with adequate Diagnostic Coverage.
