It is not permitted for an Emergency stop, which must end in a power-removed condition.

plain: A way of finding dangers in complex automated systems by looking at how the controllers might give the wrong commands.
snappy: A control-theoretic hazard analysis that identifies unsafe control actions and their causal scenarios in complex autonomous systems.
detail: STPA, built on the STAMP accident model, treats safety as a control problem and searches for unsafe control actions, for example a planner in an Autonomous vehicle commanding a lane change when a vehicle occupies the gap. Unlike the failure-enumeration of FMEA or Fault Tree Analysis, it captures hazards from interactions, software logic, and human-automation confusion, making it well suited to a Self-driving stack and SOTIF analysis. STPA results guide where to add a Control barrier function, a Minimal risk condition, or Runtime assurance monitors.

plain: A thin element that changes its electrical resistance when it is stretched or squeezed, letting a robot measure force.
snappy: A sensing element whose electrical resistance changes with mechanical deformation, used to measure force or strain.
detail: A strain gauge bonds to a structure and changes resistance as the material stretches under load; arranging several into a bridge circuit yields a sensitive force signal. It is the underlying transduction element inside a Load cell and most of a Force/torque sensor. Robots use strain gauges for Force control, Compliance sensing, and Condition monitoring, often paired with Calibration to convert resistance to engineering units.

plain: The thin, springy cup-shaped gear inside a high-precision robot reducer that flexes into shape to create huge gear reduction.
snappy: The thin-walled flexible toothed cup whose elastic deformation produces a strain-wave drive's reduction.
detail: The flexspline is the deforming element of a Harmonic drive: a thin steel cup with external teeth that the Wave Generator squeezes into an ellipse so a few teeth mesh with the rigid circular spline, yielding very high Gear reduction with near-zero Backlash. Its elastic compliance gives the strain-wave gear its characteristic torsional stiffness curve and is why such reducers dominate precision joints on a Humanoid robot or Industrial robot arm. Companies like Harmonic Drive LLC manufacture these alongside competing Cycloidal drive units.

plain: Building a 3D model of a place by combining many photos taken from different positions as the camera moves around.
snappy: Jointly recovering 3D scene geometry and camera poses from a set of 2D images taken from different viewpoints.
detail: Structure from motion, or SfM, takes overlapping images and simultaneously solves for where each photo was taken and where the 3D points lie, usually refined by Bundle adjustment. It relies on Feature extraction and Feature matching to find common points across views and on RANSAC to reject bad matches. It underpins 3D reconstruction and Aerial photogrammetry, and is the offline, multi-image cousin of online Visual odometry used in Space and Mobility surveying.

plain: A workspace engineered to be neat and predictable so a robot's job is much easier.
snappy: A controlled, well-known workspace where object positions, lighting, and layout are engineered to be predictable.
detail: In a structured environment such as a fixtured assembly station, parts arrive in known poses on a Conveyor tracking line, so a robot can rely on Open-loop control or simple Programming by teaching rather than rich Perception. This predictability underpins classic Industrial robotics and high Repeatability. Removing that structure forces the move toward Computer vision, Bin picking, and adaptive policies needed in an Unstructured environment.

plain: A way to measure 3D shape by shining a known pattern of light onto an object and watching how the pattern bends over its surface.
snappy: A depth-sensing method that projects a known light pattern and computes distance from its observed distortion.
detail: Structured light projects a precise pattern, such as stripes or a dot grid, and a Camera observes how the pattern deforms across surfaces to triangulate depth. It is one of the main technologies inside a Depth camera and supports detailed Pose estimation for Bin picking and Grasp planning. Because it relies on seeing its own projection, it works best indoors and is challenged outdoors where a Stereo camera or Time-of-flight sensor may be preferred.

plain: A text-based way of programming factory controllers that looks like a regular computer programming language with if-statements and loops.
snappy: A high-level, Pascal-like textual PLC programming language defined by IEC 61131-3.
detail: Structured text (the ST language) is one of the five languages in IEC 61131-3, favored for math, loops, and complex algorithms that would be cumbersome to draw as Ladder logic. It runs on a Programmable logic controller or a Programmable automation controller and is often mixed with a Function block diagram in the same project, with computation in ST and machine sequencing in ladder. Motion calculations, recipe handling, and data manipulation on an Industrial PC frequently use structured text for its readability and power.

plain: A robotic arm that guides a surgeon's tools to cut bone exactly right during joint-replacement surgery.
snappy: Stryker's haptically guided robotic arm for precise orthopedic bone cuts in joint replacement.
detail: The Stryker Mako is a surgeon-guided robotic arm used in hip and knee replacement: a preoperative CT builds a patient-specific plan, then the arm uses haptic feedback and a hard safety envelope to keep the cutting tool inside the planned bone boundary. Unlike teleoperated systems the surgeon physically moves the arm under impedance control while the robot enforces limits. It is a leading orthopedic surgical robot.

plain: A Swiss company that builds fast, very precise robotic arms used in factories.
snappy: Swiss maker of high-speed, high-precision six-axis industrial arms and fast tool-change systems.
detail: Stäubli's enclosed-design Industrial robot arm models are known for tight Repeatability and resistance to harsh environments, making them common in cleanroom and pharmaceutical assembly cells. The arms run a proprietary controller but are frequently integrated via ROS-Industrial for tasks like Pick and place and Machine tending. Stäubli also supplies quick-change Tool changer connectors that let one robot swap End-effector tooling mid-cycle.

plain: Splitting a long task into a few easier milestones the robot can aim for one at a time.
snappy: Breaking a long-horizon objective into intermediate subgoals that are individually easier to plan for and reach.
detail: Subgoal decomposition turns 'make coffee' into reachable waypoints like 'grasp mug', 'place under spout', 'press button', each a target for Motion planning or a learned Skill. It tames the Sparse reward problem in a Long-horizon task and underlies Hierarchical reinforcement learning, the Option framework, and Hierarchical task network planning. A Foundation model is increasingly used to propose the subgoal sequence from a natural-language command, which lower controllers then execute via Skill chaining.

plain: A way of layering a robot's behaviors so that more important ones can take over from less important ones.
snappy: A layered reactive control architecture in which higher-priority behavior layers can suppress or override the outputs of lower ones.
detail: Introduced by Rodney Brooks in 1986, the subsumption architecture stacks competence layers, with each layer a complete sensing-to-action loop; higher layers like wander or explore subsume lower ones like avoid-collision when they need control. Crucially there is no shared world model, making it the flagship of Behavior-based robotics and a pure form of Reactive control. Its limits in long-horizon tasks led designers toward the Hybrid architecture that bolts a planner on top of reactive layers.

plain: A way of storing what a robot expects to happen in the future so that if its goal or reward changes, it can quickly reuse what it already learned instead of starting over.
snappy: A value decomposition that factors expected future state features from the reward weights, enabling fast transfer of a policy across new reward functions.
detail: Successor features split the Value function into expected discounted future state-features times a reward-weight vector, so when only the Reward function changes, a previously learned policy can be re-evaluated almost instantly via generalized policy improvement. This makes them powerful for multi-task and Transfer learning settings in Reinforcement learning, such as a mobile robot that learned navigation features and must now optimize a new objective. They connect to Successor-style ideas in Hierarchical reinforcement learning and the Options Framework.

plain: A robot tool that grabs things by sucking onto them like a sink plunger.
snappy: An end effector that holds objects by pulling a vacuum through one or more suction cups.
detail: A Suction gripper uses vacuum, generated by a pump or venturi, to hold objects against rubber suction cups, requiring only one flat, sealable surface rather than two opposing faces. This makes it the dominant choice for Bin picking and Goods-to-person logistics work, where a single cup can pick a box, bag, or book. Compared with a Parallel-jaw gripper it grasps faster and handles flat items, but struggles with porous or curved objects; Grasp planning for suction predicts where a cup can form a reliable seal.

plain: A device that stores a little energy but can charge and release it extremely fast.
snappy: A high-power-density energy store that charges and discharges rapidly to buffer peak loads on robots.
detail: A supercapacitor (ultracapacitor) bridges battery and capacitor, offering very high Power density and millions of cycles but modest Energy density, so it buffers bursts rather than providing long Endurance. On a robot it smooths the current spikes a Lithium-ion battery dislikes, for instance absorbing regenerative braking energy or handling a peak motor load to ease the Power budget. It is often paired with a battery and managed alongside the Battery management system; pure-supercap robots are rare due to limited storage.

plain: A neural network that decides which detected points in one image correspond to points in another, even when many of them are ambiguous or missing.
snappy: A graph-neural-network feature matcher that reasons jointly about two sets of keypoints, using attention and optimal transport to produce robust correspondences.
detail: SuperGlue treats Feature matching as an attention-based reasoning problem over a graph of keypoints from two images, learning to assign matches and reject outliers via a differentiable optimal-transport layer. Paired with SuperPoint keypoints it dramatically improves correspondence quality for Visual odometry, Loop closure, and relocalization compared with nearest-neighbor matching plus RANSAC. Its successor LightGlue trades a little accuracy for the speed robots need on Onboard compute.

plain: An extra robotic arm a person wears that gives them more limbs than they were born with, helping them hold or reach things.
snappy: A wearable robotic limb that adds to, rather than replaces, a human's natural limbs, augmenting reach, grasp, or support.
detail: A supernumerary robotic limb (SRL) is a body-worn extra arm or leg that augments rather than restores capability, unlike a Powered prosthesis or an Exoskeleton that wraps an existing limb. Mounted at the waist or shoulder, it can brace a workpiece, hold a tool, or provide a third point of support, controlled by gestures, EMG, or a Brain-computer interface. Used in Manufacturing assembly and explored at the Research/Frontier, it raises Human-robot interaction and Proxemics challenges since the wearer must coordinate a limb they did not grow, often via shared Teleoperation-style control.

plain: A neural network that automatically finds the most distinctive spots in an image and describes them, so the same spots can be re-recognized in other pictures.
snappy: A self-supervised convolutional network that jointly detects interest points and computes their descriptors in a single forward pass.
detail: SuperPoint is a Convolutional neural network trained with Self-supervised learning via homographic adaptation to output both Keypoint Detection heatmaps and dense descriptors, replacing hand-crafted detectors like SIFT and ORB features. Its repeatable, learned keypoints feed Feature matching front-ends for Visual odometry and Visual SLAM, especially under viewpoint and lighting changes that defeat classical detectors. On a robot it commonly pairs with SuperGlue to produce robust correspondences for relocalization.

plain: A way for robots to plan a grip by approximating an object as a simple mathematical egg-or-box shape and then choosing where to hold that shape.
snappy: Grasp planning that fits superquadric shape primitives to sensed objects and reasons about grasps on the compact recovered geometry.
detail: Superquadric grasping fits parametric superquadric primitives (a family that spans boxes, spheres, and cylinders) to a Point cloud from a Depth camera, then plans contacts on the smooth recovered surface rather than raw, noisy points. The compact representation makes Grasp planning and Grasp quality metric evaluation tractable for multi-finger hands and supports Antipodal grasp generation on a Parallel-jaw gripper. It is a model-based alternative to learned Grasp Pose Detection, often paired with simulators like GraspIt! for analytic Force closure checks.

plain: A setup where the robot does the work on its own while a person watches and can take over if needed.
snappy: An operating mode where a robot acts autonomously while a human monitors and retains authority to intervene.
detail: Under supervised autonomy the machine executes tasks by itself, but a human supervisor stays in the loop to monitor, approve, or override, the Human-in-the-loop model used for an Autonomous weapon, a Self-driving truck with a Safety driver, or an inspection Drone. It is a midpoint on the Levels of autonomy between full Teleoperation and full Autonomy, and differs from Shared autonomy, where human and robot act simultaneously rather than the human supervising. Intervention is triggered by a Takeover request, a Disengagement, or a detected anomaly.

plain: The area on the ground enclosed by everything a robot is standing on, like the patch between its two feet.
snappy: The convex hull of a robot's ground contact points, defining the region for static balance.
detail: The support polygon (or base of support) is the convex region spanned by all current Contact point locations, such as the outlines of both feet plus the gap between them. For Static stability the Center of mass projection must stay inside it; for Dynamic walking the Zero moment point and Center of pressure must stay inside it instead. It shrinks to a line or point during single-support stance, which is why a Humanoid robot relies on the Capture point to plan recovery steps that re-establish a valid polygon.

plain: Using cameras to spot scratches, dents, or flaws on manufactured parts that a person might miss on a fast production line.
snappy: Machine-vision identification of surface anomalies such as scratches, dents, cracks, or contamination on parts.
detail: Surface Defect Detection applies Machine vision to flag deviations from a defect-free reference, ranging from classical thresholding and Edge Detection to deep Anomaly detection trained mostly on normal samples. Manufacturing cells use it for Quality inspection of welds, coatings, and machined surfaces, often with structured or raking illumination and a Smart camera. Because real defects are rare and varied, practitioners frame it as Out-of-Distribution Detection and guard against Domain Shift when lighting or part batches change, sometimes augmenting scarce examples with Synthetic data.

plain: A robot a surgeon controls to perform operations through very small incisions with great precision.
snappy: A teleoperated or assistive robotic system that lets a surgeon perform minimally invasive procedures with enhanced precision, dexterity, and tremor filtering.
detail: A surgical robot maps a surgeon's hand motions, captured at a console, onto small instruments inside the patient through teleoperation, scaling motion and removing tremor for fine dexterous manipulation. Systems such as those from Intuitive Surgical use a continuum robot or cable-driven mechanism wrist for tight workspaces and rely on haptics and force/torque sensor feedback. Newer work explores shared autonomy and visual servoing for sub-tasks, but the human surgeon stays in the loop under strict functional safety requirements.

plain: One of many simple robots that work together as a group, like a colony of ants, with no single robot in charge.
snappy: An agent in a multi-robot system where many simple, locally-interacting units produce coordinated collective behavior without central control.
detail: Swarm robots follow simple local rules so that useful group patterns appear as emergent behavior rather than from a master controller, a core idea in swarm robotics and bio-inspired robotics. Each unit senses only its neighbors, making the system robust to losing members, which suits a Drone swarm for area coverage or distributed search. The field overlaps with multi-agent path finding and multi-robot system coordination, and is studied for Defense & Security and exploration tasks where many cheap units beat one expensive Field robot.

plain: Using lots of cheap, simple robots that together behave like one smart group, without a boss telling each one what to do.
snappy: A field that builds collective capability from many simple robots following local rules, with no central controller.
detail: Swarm robotics takes inspiration from ants and bees: each robot senses only its neighbors and follows simple local rules, yet the group produces useful Emergent behavior such as coverage, foraging, or formation keeping. Because there is no single point of failure, a swarm degrades gracefully and scales well, which is why a Drone swarm is attractive for Defense & Security mapping. It is a decentralized special case of a Multi-robot system, and it leans heavily on Bio-inspired robotics for its coordination strategies.

plain: A drive system where each wheel can both spin and turn to point any direction, letting the robot move and rotate freely.
snappy: A drivetrain of independently steered and driven wheel modules enabling holonomic-like motion and in-place rotation.
detail: A Swerve Drive gives a mobile robot near-Holonomic motion by letting each corner module independently set both wheel speed and steering angle, so the chassis can translate any direction while rotating. Each module typically pairs a drive motor with a steering motor through a slewing gear and a Constant Velocity Joint or coaxial path, demanding tight coordination through the Navigation stack. It rivals the Mecanum wheel and Omnidirectional drive for agility but keeps the traction and payload advantages of standard rubber wheels.

plain: How an underwater robot moves through water, whether by spinning propellers, flapping fins, or wriggling its body like a fish.
snappy: Propelling a robot through water using fins, body undulation, propellers, or thrusters to generate thrust against the surrounding fluid.
detail: Swimming robots either use a Propeller and thrusters for efficient cruising or mimic fish with undulating bodies and fins for quiet, agile maneuvering in tight or sensitive habitats, a recurring Research/Frontier and Bio-inspired robotics theme. The platform is typically an Autonomous underwater vehicle or a Remotely operated vehicle, and control must contend with buoyancy, currents, and drag rather than ground contact, putting weight on Attitude and heading reference system data and Sensor fusion. Like Snake locomotion, fin-based swimming relies on propagating body waves, and station-keeping demands fine Thrust-to-weight ratio and Control allocation.

plain: The part of a step when a foot is lifted off the ground and moving forward to its next position.
snappy: The portion of the gait cycle during which a foot is off the ground and swinging forward to its next placement.
detail: In swing phase the leg carries no load and is free to reposition, so this is when Foothold selection chooses where the foot will next land. The shorter the swing relative to the Stance phase, the higher the Duty factor and the more statically stable the Gait. Coordinating swing and stance across legs through the Gait cycle is what produces a Trot, Crawl gait, or Gallop.

plain: A rugged, magnet-free electric motor that turns simply by energizing its coils in sequence to pull the iron rotor around.
snappy: A magnet-free motor producing torque by sequentially energizing stator phases to align a salient iron rotor.
detail: A Switched Reluctance Motor (SRM) has no rotor windings or magnets - just a salient iron rotor that is pulled toward whichever stator phase is energized, making it cheap, robust, and tolerant of high temperatures and faults. Its independence from rare-earth magnets and its fault tolerance attract interest for industrial traction and mobile-robot drives, though it requires a custom Motor controller and is prone to acoustic noise and Torque Ripple. Unlike a Brushless DC motor it cannot be demagnetized, sidestepping the Demagnetization risk entirely.

plain: The puzzle of how words or symbols inside a robot come to actually mean real things in the world, rather than just being meaningless tokens.
snappy: The problem of connecting an agent's internal abstract symbols to the real-world sensory and motor experiences they are meant to denote.
detail: The symbol grounding problem asks how a token like cup acquires meaning for a robot rather than remaining an empty symbol shuffled by rules; the answer must route through real Perception and the Perception-action loop. It is central to Embodied cognition and Developmental robotics, where meaning is bootstrapped from sensorimotor experience, and to Affordance theory, which grounds objects in what they let the robot do. The problem has resurfaced sharply with Vision-language-action model and Foundation model systems, which must bind language tokens to actual Grasping and Manipulation, and it is closely related to the broader Grounding challenge and the Frame problem.

plain: A company that builds high-speed robot systems to store and retrieve boxes of goods inside large warehouses.
snappy: Warehouse-automation firm whose autonomous case-handling robots travel a dense storage structure at high speed to build mixed pallets.
detail: Symbotic replaces conventional racking with a dense grid through which fast Autonomous mobile robot units retrieve and sequence individual cases, functioning as a software-driven Automated storage and retrieval system. The robots coordinate via Fleet management and Multi-agent path finding to feed automated Palletizing, raising warehouse Throughput and density. Major retailers such as Walmart deploy its systems to reconfigure distribution-centre Material handling.

plain: Fake-but-labeled training examples created by a computer instead of collected in the real world.
snappy: Simulator-generated, automatically labeled data used to train robot perception models and policies at scale.
detail: Because a Robot simulator already knows the exact position and identity of every object, it can emit perfectly labeled images, depth maps, and Point cloud data for free, sidestepping costly manual annotation and giving cheap Ground truth. Synthetic data is generated with Photorealistic rendering and Sensor simulation, then combined with Domain randomization to survive the Reality gap during Sim-to-real transfer. Pipelines built on NVIDIA Isaac and Isaac Sim produce millions of frames to pretrain Object detection and grasping networks.

plain: Measuring how a real robot actually behaves, like its true weight, friction, and motor strength, so the simulator can be made to match it.
snappy: Estimating a system's true dynamics parameters from data so models and simulators match real-world behavior.
detail: System identification fits parameters of a robot's Dynamics, such as link masses in the Inertia tensor, joint friction, motor constants, and Backlash, by exciting the hardware and observing its response. Accurate sys-ID shrinks the Reality gap so that a Policy trained in a Physics engine transfers cleanly, complementing Domain randomization rather than replacing it. It feeds Model predictive control and Computed torque control, and is a prerequisite for trustworthy Sim-to-real transfer of Learned locomotion.

plain: A specialist company that takes robots and other parts and assembles them into a complete working setup tailored to a customer's factory or warehouse.
snappy: A firm that designs, builds, installs, and commissions complete robotic cells and lines for end customers.
detail: A system integrator (often just 'integrator') is the bridge between a robot vendor and the factory floor: it selects the arm, designs the End-of-arm tooling, programs the Robot controller, and ensures the installation meets safety standards like ISO 10218 before handover. Integrators build the Robot cell around a process, wiring it to the plant's Programmable logic controller and Manufacturing execution system. They are a large share of any Total cost of ownership, and the same role for mobile fleets is sometimes called a Robot integrator.

plain: A single chip that packs a robot's whole computer onto one piece of silicon.
snappy: An integrated chip combining CPU, GPU, memory controllers, and accelerators on one die for compact robot compute.
detail: A System on a chip (SoC) lets a robot's Onboard compute fit in a small, low-power package by merging a CPU with a Graphics processing unit and often an AI accelerator or DSP. The NVIDIA Jetson modules are SoC-based and serve as the compute core for many a Humanoid robot, drone Flight controller, and Autonomous mobile robot. Choosing an SoC trades raw performance against the robot's Power budget and Thermal management constraints.

plain: A brand of lightweight electric motors originally made for drones that engineers now use to build agile robot legs.
snappy: Maker of high-torque-density brushless gimbal and drone motors widely repurposed for quasi-direct-drive legged robots.
detail: T-Motor (Tiger Motor) builds outrunner Brushless DC motor designs with large diameters and many poles, giving high Torque density at low speed - exactly what a Quasi-direct drive leg actuator needs. Researchers pair T-Motor antigravity-series motors with a low-ratio gearbox and an ODrive or Moteus Controller to build cheap, backdrivable joints for a Quadruped robot or Humanoid robot. The combination delivers the proprioceptive force sensing and Backdrivability that dynamic legged-locomotion control demands.

plain: A device that measures how fast a spinning shaft is turning, usually reported in revolutions per minute.
snappy: A sensor that measures the rotational speed of a shaft, typically in RPM, for velocity feedback in a motor control loop.
detail: A Tachometer closes the inner velocity loop of a Servo control system, supplying the speed feedback a Cascade control scheme regulates beneath a position loop. Classic analog DC tachogenerators output a voltage proportional to speed, while modern drives derive the same signal by differentiating an Incremental encoder or reading a Hall effect sensor, and some Brushless DC motor controllers infer it from Back-EMF in Sensorless Commutation. It is distinct from a Tachometer's positional cousins like the Resolver: a tach reports rate, not angle, and is essential wherever a DC motor or Stepper motor must hold a commanded RPM.

plain: Figuring out exactly how an object is positioned in a robot's grip purely from the feel of touching it, even when cameras can't see it.
snappy: Estimating an object's pose from a sequence of tactile contact measurements rather than vision.
detail: Tactile pose estimation infers an object's Pose by fusing successive Contact point readings from a Tactile sensor, often a Vision-based tactile sensor like GelSight, into a probabilistic estimate, useful when the part is occluded inside the gripper. It supports precise insertion such as Peg-in-hole and complements visual Pose estimation when In-hand manipulation shifts the object. Filters and Factor graph formulations track the evolving estimate as the fingers explore the surface.

plain: Teaching an AI to make sense of the signals from a robot's sense of touch by learning compact summaries of what different contacts feel like.
snappy: Learning embeddings from raw touch-sensor signals to capture contact state for downstream contact-rich manipulation.
detail: Tactile Representation Learning trains encoders, often via Self-supervised learning or Contrastive Predictive Coding, to compress raw signals from a Tactile sensor such as GelSight, DIGIT, or BioTac into features useful for Contact-rich manipulation. The learned embeddings support Slip detection, Tactile pose estimation, and control, feeding a Visuomotor Policy or a Tactile-Reactive Control loop. It is central to Dexterous manipulation on hands like the Shadow Hand and Allegro Hand, where vision alone cannot resolve fine contact during In-hand manipulation.

plain: A robot's ability to feel physical contact, pressure, and surface texture through touch, much like a human fingertip.
snappy: Sensing contact, pressure, slip, and texture at a robot's surfaces through touch.
detail: Tactile sensing gives a robot local contact information that Vision cannot see, such as how hard it is gripping or whether an object is slipping. A Robotic hand uses a Tactile sensor array on its fingertips to enable Grip force control and Slip detection during Dexterous manipulation. Newer approaches use a Vision-based tactile sensor that watches a soft pad deform, feeding Contact-rich manipulation and Tactile servoing controllers.

plain: A sensor that lets a robot feel touch, pressure, or texture where it contacts an object.
snappy: A sensor that detects contact, pressure distribution, or texture on a robot's surface.
detail: A tactile sensor gives a robot a sense of touch at the contact interface, reporting where, how hard, and sometimes how an object presses. It is central to Dexterous manipulation and In-hand manipulation, supporting Slip detection, Grip force control, and Tactile servoing. Implementations range from a Capacitive sensor array to a Vision-based tactile sensor, and large coverings form a Robotic skin on a Humanoid robot.

plain: Letting a robot adjust its grip moment-by-moment based on what its fingertip sensors feel touching the object.
snappy: Closing the control loop on tactile (often vision-based) sensor feedback for in-hand control.
detail: Tactile servoing makes the touch signal the feedback in a Control loop, the touch analogue of Visual servoing, so a robot continuously regulates contact location, force, or slip to keep an object correctly seated in the hand. It typically reads a Vision-based tactile sensor or other Tactile sensor and is the workhorse for In-hand manipulation, Slip detection, and Dexterous manipulation. By complementing Grip force control and Compliant manipulation, it lets a Robotic hand handle delicate or unmodeled objects that pure vision and Pose estimation cannot fully resolve.

plain: Letting a robot adjust its grip and movements moment-to-moment based on what it feels through touch sensors, like a person tightening their grasp when something slips.
snappy: Closed-loop control that uses real-time touch-sensor feedback to regulate contact forces and react to slip during manipulation.
detail: Tactile-Reactive Control (tactile servoing) closes a fast feedback loop on signals from a Tactile sensor, adjusting grip and motion in response to Slip detection, contact location, and force, analogous to Visual servoing but using touch. It enables Contact-rich manipulation tasks like Peg-in-hole insertion, cable handling, and stable Grasping under disturbance, often combined with Force control or Impedance control. Sensors such as GelSight, DIGIT, and TacTip provide the high-bandwidth input, and learned variants pair it with Tactile Representation Learning for Dexterous manipulation.

plain: A soft fingertip sensor that tracks tiny pins inside a rubber skin with a camera to sense touch, copying how human skin works.
snappy: A biomimetic optical tactile sensor that tracks the motion of internal marker pins beneath a compliant skin.
detail: TacTip is a Vision-based tactile sensor whose camera tracks an array of white-tipped pins embedded in a soft skin, mimicking the dermal papillae of human fingertips; pin displacement encodes contact shape and shear. As a Visuotactile sensing device it supports Tactile servoing, edge following, and Slip detection, and integrates onto a Tendon-driven hand or other Robotic hand. Its biomimetic structure makes it a touchstone in Tactile sensing research alongside GelSight.

plain: A fixed-wing flying robot that sits upright on its tail to take off straight up, then pitches over to fly forward like a plane.
snappy: A fixed-wing VTOL aircraft that takes off and lands resting on its tail, then pitches to horizontal for cruise.
detail: A Tail-sitter drone is a Tailsitter VTOL aircraft that takes off and lands vertically while balanced on its tail, then rotates its entire airframe ninety degrees to cruise as a Fixed-wing drone, avoiding the heavy tilting mechanism of a Tilt-rotor drone. The hover-to-cruise Transition flight maneuver is aerodynamically demanding because the wing passes through stall, requiring robust attitude tracking and Control allocation. As a Hybrid VTOL form it appeals to Defense & Security and Research/Frontier programs seeking long endurance from a small, mechanically simple launch-anywhere platform.

plain: An aircraft that stands upright on its tail to take off and land like a rocket, then tips over to fly forward on its wings like a normal plane.
snappy: A VTOL aircraft that sits vertically on its tail for takeoff and landing, then pitches the entire airframe roughly 90 degrees into horizontal winged cruise.
detail: A Tailsitter is the simplest Hybrid VTOL concept because the whole vehicle rotates rather than tilting any rotors or wings, so a single propulsion set serves both hover and cruise, unlike a Quadplane that carries separate lift motors. The tricky part is Transition flight: the Flight controller must manage a large attitude swing where control authority shifts from thrust to aerodynamic surfaces, demanding careful Wind disturbance rejection. Used in Defense & Security for compact launch-anywhere reconnaissance, it competes with the Tilt-rotor drone and Lift-Plus-Cruise layouts; see also the related Tail-sitter drone.

plain: A clear prompt telling the human driver to put their hands back on the wheel and take over driving from the automated system.
snappy: A multimodal prompt issued by a conditional-automation system asking the human to resume manual control within a time budget.
detail: A takeover request (TOR) is central to SAE Level 3 driving: when a highway pilot reaches the edge of its operational design domain, it alerts the driver via audio, visual, and haptic cues to resume control. The driver monitoring system verifies the driver is ready, and if no handover occurs within the time budget the vehicle executes a fallback to a minimal risk condition. TOR timing and clarity are key safety case arguments for any Level 3 system.

plain: The rhythm a production line must hit to exactly meet customer demand, like a metronome pace for making things.
snappy: The available production time divided by customer demand, setting the required pace per unit.
detail: Takt time is computed as available working time divided by units demanded, so if customers need 480 units in an 8-hour shift, each unit must finish every minute. It sets the target rhythm that each station on a Production line and every Robot cell must meet, and the actual Cycle time of each operation must stay below takt to keep up. Balancing stations to takt is central to lean manufacturing and to hitting the performance term in Overall equipment effectiveness.

plain: A specific job you want a robot to do, like move a box from here to there.
snappy: A defined objective or job a robot is meant to accomplish, often decomposed into sub-goals and primitive actions.
detail: A task is the unit of work a robot is assigned, from a single Pick and place to a multi-step assembly; it is what Task planning sequences and what a Skill or Motion primitive executes. Tasks set the success criteria against which a Benchmark or Reward is judged. In Task and motion planning a symbolic task plan (what to do and in what order) is interleaved with geometric Motion planning (how to move there) so the abstract goal becomes a feasible Trajectory.

plain: Deciding which robot in a team should do which job so the whole team gets the most done.
snappy: The assignment of tasks to robots in a multi-robot team so as to optimize a team-level performance objective.
detail: Multi-Robot Task Allocation (MRTA) is the problem of matching robots to tasks under constraints of capability, location, and timing, and it sits at the heart of warehouse and defense Multi-robot system operations. Solutions range from centralized optimal assignment via the Hungarian Algorithm to fully Decentralized control schemes, most notably Market-based coordination where robots bid for jobs. It interacts tightly with Multi-agent path finding (who goes where without collisions) and Foraging behavior, and a Fleet management system performs continuous MRTA as new orders arrive.

plain: Planning both the big sequence of steps a robot should do and the exact arm-and-body movements for each step, at the same time, so the plan actually works.
snappy: Jointly solving the discrete what-to-do (symbolic task) and the continuous how-to-move (collision-free geometry) so that each action is physically executable.
detail: Task and motion planning (TAMP) closes the gap between Task planning (often in PDDL) and Motion planning: a symbolic step like 'put cup in cupboard' is only valid if a collision-free Inverse kinematics and Grasp planning solution exists, so TAMP interleaves the two layers and backtracks when geometry fails. It is essential for Manipulation by a Humanoid robot or Manufacturing arm rearranging cluttered objects, where Collision checking constrains which symbolic plans are even reachable. TAMP solvers couple a Sampling-based planning motion layer with a symbolic search.

plain: Deciding the ordered list of big steps a robot should take, like 'open door, then pick up box, then carry it out', to reach its objective.
snappy: High-level sequencing of discrete, symbolic actions whose preconditions and effects chain together to achieve a stated goal.
detail: Task planning (symbolic planning) reasons over discrete states and Action operators with preconditions and effects, searching for a sequence that transforms the start state into the goal, often specified in PDDL. For a Humanoid robot or Manufacturing arm, a planner might output 'grasp tool, move to fixture, insert part' before any geometry is considered. Because a symbolic step like 'place the cup' may have no collision-free Motion planning solution, task planning is increasingly fused with low-level motion in Task and motion planning. Modern systems also pair it with a Behavior tree or Foundation model for execution.

plain: A way to make a robot pursue several goals at once by ranking them, so a lower-ranked goal is only chased using motion left over by the higher ones.
snappy: A redundancy-resolution scheme that executes lower-priority tasks within the null space of higher-priority tasks so the important goal is never disturbed.
detail: Task priority control projects each secondary objective into the Null space of the higher-ranked task's Jacobian matrix, so a Humanoid robot can, for example, keep its hand on a target (top priority) while using leftover freedom to dodge a joint limit or stay balanced. It relies on Kinematic redundancy and uses a Jacobian pseudoinverse or Weighted Pseudoinverse at each layer, and it is a core building block of Whole-body control and Operational space control. The hierarchy keeps the critical Task space goal exact while gracefully sacrificing lower-priority goals near a Kinematic singularity.

plain: The everyday description of where a robot's hand is and how it is angled, rather than the settings of its individual joints.
snappy: The Cartesian space of end-effector position and orientation, as opposed to joint angles.
detail: Task space (or operational space) describes a goal in terms a person cares about, such as 'move the gripper to this Pose above the part,' rather than in terms of individual joint values. It is the natural setting for Operational space control and for Inverse kinematics, which converts a task-space target back into Joint space. The Jacobian matrix is the bridge that relates velocities in task space to velocities in joint space.

plain: A measure of how heavy and sluggish a robot's hand feels when you push it in a given direction, accounting for the whole arm behind it.
snappy: The apparent inertia of the end-effector in operational space, formed by projecting the joint-space mass matrix through the Jacobian.
detail: The Task-Space Inertia Matrix (the Lambda matrix) expresses how much inertia an applied Wrench at the End-effector actually encounters, computed by projecting the joint-space Mass matrix through the Jacobian matrix and inverting. It is the central quantity in the Operational Space Formulation and in Operational space control, letting a controller decouple Cartesian directions and command consistent end-effector accelerations regardless of arm configuration. Its conditioning degrades near a Kinematic singularity, which is why robust schemes pair it with Damped Least Squares or operate on the Manipulability ellipsoid.

plain: One single touch-sensing point in a grid of them, like a pixel but for feeling pressure instead of seeing light.
snappy: An individual sensing element in a tactile sensor array, the touch analogue of a pixel.
detail: A taxel (tactile element) is the smallest unit of a Tactile sensor array; many taxels tiled across a fingertip or a patch of Robotic skin form a spatial pressure map, the touch counterpart of a camera pixel. Taxel density and dynamic range set the resolution available for Slip detection, Contact estimation, and Tactile pose estimation. The term applies across technologies including a Capacitive Tactile Array and the marker grids of a Vision-based tactile sensor.

plain: A handheld controller with buttons and a screen used to move an industrial robot by hand and write its program.
snappy: A handheld terminal for jogging, teaching points, and editing programs on an industrial robot.
detail: An operator uses the Teach pendant to jog the arm to physical positions, record those waypoints, and step through a program before running it at speed, a workflow known as Programming by teaching. It connects to the Robot controller and includes a deadman switch plus an Emergency stop button required by ISO 10218. On a Six-axis robot doing Robotic welding or Machine tending, the technician teaches each path point on the pendant rather than coding coordinates by hand.

plain: First train an expert robot brain that is allowed to cheat by seeing hidden information, then copy its skills into a second brain that only uses the robot's real onboard sensors.
snappy: Distilling a privileged teacher policy, trained with full simulator state, into a student policy that runs from onboard sensors alone.
detail: Teacher-Student Distillation is the dominant recipe for robust learned locomotion on a Quadruped robot or Humanoid robot. A teacher is trained quickly with Reinforcement learning using Privileged learning inputs (terrain height, contact states, true friction); a student network is then trained by Policy distillation to reproduce the teacher's actions using only a proprioceptive history available on hardware. This two-stage approach, related to Asymmetric Actor-Critic, sidesteps the partial-observability problem and is a backbone of modern Sim-to-real transfer and Rapid motor adaptation pipelines.

plain: Training one robot brain that can secretly see everything, then teaching a second brain to copy it using only the sensors the real robot will actually have.
snappy: A two-stage scheme that first trains a teacher with privileged simulator information, then distills its behavior into a student policy that uses only deployable sensor inputs.
detail: The teacher learns easily because Privileged learning gives it ground-truth terrain, contact, and friction; the student then learns to reproduce the teacher's actions from realistic, partial observations such as proprioception and camera feeds. This Policy distillation is now the dominant recipe for deployable Legged locomotion, underpinning systems like Rapid motor adaptation and many controllers trained in Isaac Gym before Sim-to-real transfer. By decoupling what is easy to learn from what is available at runtime, it sidesteps the hard credit-assignment problem of training directly on deployable inputs with Reinforcement learning.

plain: A Taiwanese maker of robot arms that come with a built-in camera so they can see what they're doing.
snappy: Taiwanese cobot maker with integrated vision, owned by electronics giant Quanta.
detail: Techman Robot (the TM Robot) distinguishes its Collaborative robot arms with a built-in Smart camera, so Vision-guided robotics tasks like Pick and place and Quality inspection need no separate vision system. Owned by Quanta, it leverages electronics-manufacturing scale and integrates Machine vision directly into its programming flow. Like other cobots it supports Hand guiding and safe Human-robot interaction under ISO/TS 15066.

plain: A numbered scale, typically one to nine, that rates how far a technology has come from a lab idea to something proven in real use.
snappy: A 1-to-9 maturity scale rating how far a technology has progressed from basic concept to flight- or field-proven operation.
detail: Technology readiness level (TRL), originated by NASA and adopted by DARPA and ISO 16290, anchors program decisions: a Planetary rover subsystem might be TRL 4 in the lab but must reach TRL 8 or 9 before a mission. In robotics it frames the Valley of death between a working prototype and a deployable product, and it pairs with Verification and validation evidence. Defense and Space programs use it to gate funding and to compare the maturity of competing actuator or sensor designs.

plain: A company that makes thermal cameras and rugged ground robots like PackBot that handle bombs and scout dangerous areas.
snappy: Maker of unmanned ground robots like PackBot for explosive-ordnance disposal and reconnaissance.
detail: Through its acquisition of iRobot's defense unit and Endeavor Robotics, Teledyne FLIR makes the PackBot, a tracked Unmanned ground vehicle used for EOD (explosive-ordnance disposal) and reconnaissance via Teleoperation. The Tracked robot uses Articulated tracks to climb stairs and rubble, and FLIR's core Thermal camera technology equips many of these platforms with a Thermal imaging payload. Operators control it from a safe standoff using a ground control station.

plain: A two-way radio that lets a drone report its status to the ground and receive commands while flying.
snappy: A bidirectional, relatively low-bandwidth data link carrying flight status and commands between a UAV and its ground station.
detail: A telemetry radio carries the MAVLink stream between an aircraft and its Ground control station, sending battery, attitude and position data down while uploading waypoints and mode changes up. It is distinct from the high-rate Radio control link used for stick inputs and the one-way Video transmitter; it prioritizes range and reliability over bandwidth. Telemetry links can be a target for GNSS jamming and are a key dependency for Beyond visual line of sight operations.

plain: Controlling a robot from a distance, with a person moving the controls while the machine does the physical work somewhere else.
snappy: Human-driven remote control of a robot, where an operator's inputs map to the robot's motion in real time.
detail: Teleoperation puts a human directly in command of a robot over a link, used heavily by the Surgical robot (the operator drives a manipulator from a console) and by a Remote operation center supervising a Robotaxi. It is also the workhorse for collecting Demonstration data: an operator teleoperates an arm and the recorded trajectories feed Imitation learning and Behavioral cloning. Latency and feedback quality are critical, which connects teleoperation closely to Haptics and Human-in-the-loop control.

plain: A remote-control setup where the operator not only moves the robot but also feels the forces the robot encounters, like resistance when it touches something.
snappy: Two-way master-slave teleoperation that reflects the remote contact forces back to the operator's controller for haptic feedback.
detail: In bilateral control the operator's master device commands the follower robot while the forces it experiences are fed back, closing a force loop so the human feels contact, a property quantified as Teleoperation transparency. It builds on Teleoperation and Haptic feedback and must contend with communication Latency, which can destabilize the loop; remedies include passivity-based designs and the Wave variable method. It is central to Surgical robot systems and remote handling in Defense, and relates to Leader-follower teleoperation and Bilateral teleoperation.

plain: A control room where human operators can remotely drive or help robots that get stuck.
snappy: A staffed facility where remote operators monitor a fleet and take control of, or assist, robots that cannot proceed autonomously.
detail: A Teleoperation Center (teleop center) is the human backstop for large autonomous fleets, where operators receive escalations through Exception Handling and respond with Remote Driving or higher-level Remote Assistance such as approving a path. Its design must contend with Latency and Teleoperation transparency, and a Predictive display can mask network delay during direct Remote Driving. The key economic metric is the Operator-to-Robot Ratio, since fewer operators per robot lowers Cost per Mile and Cost per Pick. Functionally it is the same concept as a Remote operation center and is the scaffolding that lets Robotaxi services run Driver-Out Operations while a low Recovery Rate is improved.

plain: How accurately a remote operator can feel and see what the robot is really experiencing, as if they were there.
snappy: A measure of how faithfully a teleoperation system conveys the remote environment's true forces, motions, and impedances to the operator.
detail: Teleoperation transparency captures whether the operator's hands feel the genuine remote impedance: perfect transparency means free motion feels free and hard contact feels hard. It is the central design goal of Bilateral teleoperation, traded off against stability because high Latency forces a more conservative, less transparent controller. Engineers improve it with Haptic feedback fidelity, a fast Force/torque sensor, and predictive techniques like a Predictive display, and it directly shapes how usable a Surgical robot or Space manipulator feels.

plain: Technology that lets a person feel as if they are somewhere else by seeing, hearing, and acting through a remote machine.
snappy: Remote embodiment that gives an operator a sense of being present at the robot's location.
detail: Telepresence extends Teleoperation by adding rich sensory feedback, including video, audio, and Haptics, so the operator feels present rather than just issuing commands. A Telepresence robot lets someone attend a meeting or inspect a site remotely, and the same idea underlies remote surgery and a Remote operation center for vehicles. It sits within Telerobotics and complements Shared autonomy, where remote control blends with onboard Autonomy to cope with Latency.

plain: A wheeled stand topped with a screen and camera that lets a faraway person see, hear, and drive around a room as if they were there.
snappy: A mobile remote-presence platform — typically a screen and camera on a self-driving base — that a remote operator pilots to move through and interact with a physical space.
detail: A telepresence robot is a form of Telepresence built on a Differential-drive robot or similar mobile base, streaming two-way video so a remote user can navigate hallways and join conversations. It is a low-stakes flavor of Teleoperation: the operator issues high-level Waypoint navigation or direct driving commands while onboard Obstacle avoidance and Collision avoidance keep it from bumping into people. Common in hospitals for remote rounds and in offices for distributed teams, it overlaps with the Avatar robot concept and relies on a steady Radio control link or Wi-Fi for Human-robot interaction.

plain: The field of operating a robot from a distance while getting feedback, such as video or touch sensations, that lets the operator feel almost present at the robot's location.
snappy: The study and practice of remotely controlling robots with sensory feedback to the operator, spanning teleoperation, telepresence, and time-delayed control.
detail: Telerobotics encompasses Teleoperation and Telepresence but emphasizes the feedback channel, including Haptics that render contact forces back to the operator's hand. NASA uses it to drive planetary rovers despite long Latency, and a Surgical robot like those from Intuitive Surgical lets a surgeon operate through a console. When delay grows large, telerobotics blends into Supervised autonomy and Shared autonomy, where the robot handles fine motion locally while the human sets intent.

plain: Figuring out the exact time delay between two sensors so their measurements can be lined up correctly.
snappy: Estimating the unknown time offset between unsynchronized sensor streams so their data can be temporally aligned for fusion.
detail: Temporal Calibration recovers the latency or clock offset between sensors whose timestamps are not hardware-synchronized, for example the delay between an Inertial measurement unit and a Camera in a Visual-inertial odometry rig. Even a few milliseconds of misalignment corrupts Sensor fusion and SLAM accuracy when the platform moves fast, so toolboxes like Kalibr jointly estimate this offset along with extrinsics. It complements spatial Extrinsic calibration and Time synchronization, and is essential when combining a rolling-shutter Camera, LiDAR, and IMU.

plain: A learning method where a robot updates its guess about how good a situation is by comparing it to its guess about the very next situation, learning a little at every step.
snappy: Bootstrapped value learning that updates an estimate toward an immediate reward plus the discounted estimate of the successor state.
detail: Temporal Difference Learning (TD learning) sits between Monte Carlo methods and dynamic programming: it updates a Value function from the TD error, the difference between the current estimate and the reward-plus-next-estimate, without waiting for an episode to end. It is the engine inside Q-learning, Deep Q-Network, and the critics of every actor-critic method like Soft actor-critic. In robot Reinforcement learning, the TD error also drives Prioritized Experience Replay sampling and underlies the Markov decision process foundations of value-based control.

plain: Moving a robot's fingers or limbs by pulling cables that act like the tendons in a human hand.
snappy: Actuation that transmits force through tendon-like cables, common in dexterous robotic hands.
detail: Tendon-driven actuation mimics biology by running cables from remote motors to joints, so a compact Robotic hand or Anthropomorphic hand can have many fingers without bulky motors in each digit. Routing the actuators away from the moving parts lowers inertia and improves Backdrivability, but cable stretch, friction, and routing complicate control. It is a scaled-up form of Cable drive and is central to a Tendon-driven hand and Underactuation strategies for grasping.

plain: A robot hand whose fingers are pulled by cables connected to motors tucked away in the forearm.
snappy: A robotic hand actuated by cables routed like tendons from finger joints to motors placed remotely.
detail: A Tendon-driven hand moves its fingers with cables that run over pulleys to motors located in the palm or forearm, keeping the fingers themselves light and slender, an example of Tendon-driven actuation. This Cable-driven mechanism lets engineers pack many Degrees of freedom into an Anthropomorphic hand, but introduces friction, Backlash, and stretch that complicate Grip force control. It is the standard construction for dexterous Robotic hand designs used in research on In-hand manipulation and the Underactuated gripper.

plain: A robot whose joints are pulled by cables running from motors placed elsewhere, much like tendons moving fingers from muscles in the forearm.
snappy: A robot that actuates its joints remotely through tensioned cables or tendons, keeping heavy motors off the moving limb.
detail: A Tendon-driven robot relocates its actuators away from the joints they drive, routing force through tensioned cables so the moving structure stays light and low-inertia, a principle central to many a Tendon-driven hand and lightweight Humanoid robot limb. Because cables only pull, joints usually need antagonistic pairs or return springs, and friction in the routing (often via a Bowden Cable) complicates force control and backdrivability. The approach overlaps with Tendon-driven actuation and is prized in dexterous manipulation where compact, biomimetic fingers must remain Backdrivable and safe near humans.

plain: Moving by squeezing and stretching a springy ball made of rods held together by cables, so the whole shape rolls or steps.
snappy: Locomotion achieved by actuating the cables of a tensegrity structure to shift its center of mass and make the rod-and-cable network roll or punch forward.
detail: Built on a Tensegrity structure of rigid struts suspended in a network of tensioned cables, a Tensegrity robot deforms itself to topple over a face and roll, giving impact tolerance that protects payloads on landing. NASA's Super Ball Bot studied tensegrity rovers precisely because the structure can absorb a hard drop and then locomote, a robust alternative to a fragile Planetary rover. As a class of whole-body Locomotion it shares the deliberate-toppling logic of Tumbling locomotion while gaining built-in shock absorption through Compliance.

plain: A robot built from stiff rods that never touch, held in place by a web of tension cables, so the whole structure can squash and bounce.
snappy: A robot whose body is a tensegrity structure of compression rods suspended in a network of tensioned cables, deforming to roll or absorb impact.
detail: A Tensegrity robot embodies the tensegrity structure principle, where isolated rigid rods float in a continuous tension network, giving a body that is lightweight, compliant, and remarkably impact-tolerant, which is why NASA prototypes like the SUPERball are studied for planetary-lander Space missions. Locomotion uses Tensegrity locomotion, actuating cable lengths to shift the center of mass and tumble the structure, a control problem closely tied to Morphological computation. Its inherent Compliance lets it survive drops that would destroy a rigid Wheeled robot, at the cost of difficult modeling and precise control.

plain: A structure where stiff rods seem to float, held in place only by a web of tensioned cables so none of the rods actually touch each other.
snappy: A self-stabilizing structure of rigid compression struts held in equilibrium by a continuous network of tensioned cables.
detail: A tensegrity structure balances rigid struts in islands of compression suspended within a continuous net of cables in tension, giving a lightweight, deployable form that distributes loads and absorbs impact. A Tensegrity robot uses a Cable-driven mechanism to change cable lengths and roll or deform its whole frame, exhibiting strong Mechanical compliance and impact tolerance. NASA has studied tensegrity for Space landers that survive hard touchdowns and self-deploy, and the concept connects to Soft robotics and Bio-inspired structure research.

plain: Keeping a continuous strip of material pulled just tight enough as it winds through a machine, not too loose and not so tight it tears.
snappy: Closed-loop regulation of web tension across driven rollers in continuous material processing.
detail: Tension control uses a Load cell or dancer-arm feedback in a Feedback control loop that trims each driven roller's Servo drive, often layered on top of Electronic gearing between rolls. It is central to web handling for film, paper, and foil, where uneven tension causes wrinkles or breaks. The controller coordinates with Registration mark correction and uses Anti-windup on its integrators to handle splice and roll-change transients.

plain: A specialized chip that lets a robot run its AI brain quickly, doing the heavy number-crunching behind tasks like recognizing objects and deciding how to move.
snappy: A specialized accelerator built for the tensor and matrix math of neural-network inference, used as onboard compute to run a robot's perception and control models.
detail: A Tensor processing unit (TPU) is a class of AI accelerator optimized for the dense linear algebra of a Neural network, offering high throughput per watt that suits a robot's tight Power budget. On a humanoid robot it accelerates Computer vision and Vision-language-action model inference on Onboard compute, often integrated as a block within a System on a chip. Like other accelerators its capability is quoted in TOPS, and it competes with or complements the Graphics processing unit for Edge computing inference.

plain: Software from NVIDIA that rearranges a trained neural network so it runs as fast as possible on the robot's onboard chip.
snappy: NVIDIA's inference optimizer and runtime that compiles trained networks into low-latency engines for deployment on Jetson-class hardware.
detail: TensorRT takes a trained Neural network and applies layer fusion, kernel selection, and Model Quantization (such as INT8) to cut inference Latency on the robot's Onboard compute. It is the standard deployment path for perception and control networks on NVIDIA Jetson and inside the NVIDIA Isaac stack, where a Vision Transformer or Object detection model must run inside a tight Control Loop Frequency. Engineers profile against the target GPU System-on-Module to confirm the optimized engine meets the robot's real-time budget.

plain: A robot changing how it walks or drives to suit the ground it's on, picking careful footing on rocks or shifting its stance on a slope, instead of using one fixed motion.
snappy: Adjusting gait, foothold choice, stiffness, and posture in response to the ground underfoot so a robot can traverse uneven, soft, or unstructured surfaces.
detail: A Legged robot adapts by sensing the surface through Exteroception and Proprioception, then revising Foothold selection, Gait, and limb stiffness to stay stable on rubble, stairs, mud, or loose scree. Modern systems learn this behavior with Reinforcement learning and Sim-to-real transfer, training across many surfaces via Domain randomization so a Quadruped robot generalizes to ground it never saw. Crucial in Defense & Security and field deployments, terrain adaptation works alongside Balance control, Self-righting, and Tracked locomotion to keep a robot upright and moving on broken ground.

plain: Teaching a robot to walk by starting it on flat ground and only making the simulated terrain rougher once it succeeds.
snappy: A training schedule that progressively increases simulated terrain difficulty so a locomotion policy masters easy ground before facing hard ground.
detail: A terrain curriculum is a form of Curriculum learning in which a Legged robot graduates from flat floors to slopes, stairs, and rubble only as it succeeds, preventing the early collapse that happens if Reinforcement learning starts on impossible terrain. It is typically implemented inside Massively parallel reinforcement learning runs in Isaac Gym, generating game-inspired procedural obstacle fields, and it directly improves Terrain adaptation and the robustness needed for Sim-to-real transfer. The technique was central to landmark learned controllers behind Perceptive locomotion and Blind locomotion.

plain: Tesla's giant custom-built supercomputer made to train the artificial-intelligence systems that drive its cars, using huge amounts of video.
snappy: Tesla's purpose-built training supercomputer and custom silicon optimized for video-based neural networks behind its driving stack.
detail: Tesla Dojo (Dojo) was designed to train the large vision models behind Tesla Full Self-Driving on fleet video at scale, supporting the Tesla Occupancy Network and an End-to-end driving policy. It is training infrastructure, not Onboard compute, complementing the in-car NVIDIA DRIVE-class inference hardware. Its existence reflects the Scaling hypothesis applied to Vision-only autonomy and the data flywheel of a deployed fleet.

plain: Tesla's driver-assistance software that aims to let the car steer, brake, and navigate on its own using mainly cameras.
snappy: Tesla's vision-centric driver-assist suite pursuing end-to-end neural control of steering, braking, and navigation.
detail: Tesla Full Self-Driving (FSD, Tesla Autopilot) follows a Vision-only autonomy philosophy, leaning on the Tesla Occupancy Network and increasingly an End-to-end driving policy rather than HD map reliance. It is an Advanced driver-assistance systems product requiring a Safety driver and operating under SAE levels of driving automation Level 2 supervision. Its perception models are trained on fleet video using Tesla Dojo, contrasting with the LiDAR-and-HD-map Self-driving stack of Waymo.

plain: Tesla's camera-only system that builds a live 3D map of which spaces around the car are filled or empty, even for objects it has never seen.
snappy: A vision-only network predicting dense 3D volumetric occupancy of the scene for autonomous driving.
detail: The Tesla Occupancy Network fuses surround-camera video into a Bird's-eye view and predicts a dense Occupancy network volume, labeling each cell of 3D space as occupied or free regardless of object class. This lets the car react to arbitrary obstacles without relying on a fixed Object detection taxonomy, an alternative to lidar-centric stacks like BEVFusion and PointPillars. It underpins Tesla Full Self-Driving's vision-only autonomy, is related to Semantic Occupancy Prediction research, and depends on large fleets to cover the Long-tail scenario distribution.

plain: Tesla's human-shaped robot designed to do everyday physical jobs in factories and eventually homes.
snappy: Tesla's general-purpose Humanoid robot intended for factory and consumer tasks, sharing its self-driving AI stack.
detail: Tesla Optimus (the Tesla Bot) is a Bipedal robot Tesla is developing to handle repetitive Manufacturing work, leveraging the company's Computer vision and Vision-only autonomy expertise from its cars. It depends on Imitation learning from human demonstrations plus Sim-to-real transfer to learn Manipulation skills like Pick and place. Tesla frames it as a Generalist robot whose perception and learning pipeline overlaps heavily with its Autonomous vehicle program.

plain: A drone connected to the ground by a cable that supplies it with power so it can hover in one spot for hours or days.
snappy: A drone held aloft and powered through a physical ground tether, trading mobility for near-unlimited hover time.
detail: A tethered drone runs a thin cable to a ground power supply, so Tethered power removes the battery Endurance limit and lets a Multirotor drone hover persistently as an elevated sensor or relay mast. The tether also carries a secure data link, which helps in GPS-denied or jamming environments where wireless control is risky. It is used for Defense & Security overwatch, border surveillance, and communications, filling the gap between a free-flying Drone and a fixed tower; station-keeping still relies on the Flight controller and Inertial measurement unit.

plain: Running a robot off electricity sent through a cable instead of carrying its own batteries.
snappy: Powering a robot through a physical cable rather than from an onboard battery, trading mobility range for unlimited runtime.
detail: Tethered power eliminates the Runtime ceiling imposed by a Lithium-ion battery, letting a robot operate indefinitely as long as the cable is connected, at the cost of restricted reach and an entangling cable to manage. It is common on a Tethered drone used for persistent surveillance, on a Remotely operated vehicle exploring deep water, and on bomb-disposal Unmanned ground vehicle platforms in Defense & Security. The tether often carries data alongside current, and a DC-DC converter or Power distribution board at the robot end conditions the incoming voltage for its motors and Onboard compute.

plain: A bookkeeper that keeps track of where every part of a robot is relative to every other part, moment by moment.
snappy: A ROS library that maintains a time-stamped tree of coordinate-frame transforms across a robot.
detail: tf (and its successor tf2) stores the relationships between every Coordinate frame on a robot as a Transform tree, letting code ask where a sensor reading sits in the base or world frame at a given time. It applies Homogeneous transformation matrix math under the hood and is consumed by RViz, MoveIt, and Nav2. Correct tf is essential for Sensor fusion and Localization, since a bad transform silently corrupts every downstream Pose.

plain: A robot software library that keeps track of where every part of the robot and its sensors are relative to each other, even as they move over time.
snappy: The ROS library that maintains a time-stamped tree of coordinate frame transforms and answers queries between any two frames.
detail: tf2 buffers time-stamped transforms so any Node can ask where one Coordinate frame is relative to another at a given moment, interpolating as needed, which is essential because sensor data arrives with latency. It maintains the Transform tree that links the map, the robot base, each Link, and sensor frames, fed by robot_state_publisher and localization nodes like AMCL. Almost every perception, planning, and visualization tool, including RViz and Nav2, depends on a consistent tf2 tree.

plain: The ability to reason about what someone else is thinking, believing, or intending, so you can work with them better.
snappy: An agent's capacity to model another agent's beliefs, goals, and intentions in order to interact effectively.
detail: For an embodied robot, theory of mind means inferring a human partner's hidden intent from observed action, enabling smooth Joint action and Mixed-initiative interaction rather than reactive following. A Social robot that recognizes a person is searching for an object can offer help proactively; a Robotaxi that models a pedestrian's intended crossing path plans more politely. It underpins Intent communication and Legibility (the inverse problem of being read), draws on Behavior prediction and Trajectory Prediction, and remains a hard open challenge in Human-robot interaction.

plain: A camera that sees heat instead of visible light, so it can spot warm objects and people in total darkness.
snappy: A camera that images infrared heat radiation to see in darkness or detect temperature differences.
detail: A thermal camera, or infrared camera, forms an image from the heat radiated by objects rather than reflected visible light, letting a robot operate in darkness, smoke, or fog. In Defense & Security it supports Pedestrian detection and surveillance, and it is combined with a normal Camera through Sensor fusion to add warmth cues to Perception. It also drives Condition monitoring and Predictive maintenance by spotting overheating components.

plain: Backing off how hard a motor is allowed to push as it heats up, so its insides don't burn out.
snappy: Reducing the allowable continuous torque as motor winding temperature approaches its rated limit.
detail: Because motor heating scales with current squared, sustained high torque eventually pushes the windings toward their thermal limit, so the Motor controller applies Thermal Derating to cap demand before damage. It relies on a winding temperature estimate or sensor and ties into broader Thermal management and Thermal Throttling of the drive electronics; ignoring it risks Demagnetization of the rotor magnets. In a Humanoid robot or Mobility platform, derating sets the realistic continuous Peak torque budget versus the brief Stall Torque a joint can sustain.

plain: An infrared camera carried by a drone that sees heat instead of light, revealing warm objects, animals, or faults.
snappy: An onboard infrared camera that maps heat signatures for inspection, search-and-rescue, and surveillance.
detail: A thermal imaging payload detects emitted infrared rather than visible light, letting a drone find warm bodies in search-and-rescue, spot livestock at night, or locate failing electrical and irrigation components. It is typically mounted on a stabilized Gimbal and combined with a visible-light camera for dual feeds streamed via the Video transmitter or logged onboard. It complements NDVI mapping for crop scouting and pairs with GPS-denied navigation when satellite signals are unreliable.

plain: Keeping a robot from overheating by carrying its heat away from motors and chips.
snappy: The design of cooling and heat-dissipation paths that keep a robot's motors and compute within safe temperatures.
detail: Motors, a Graphics processing unit, and battery packs all generate heat, and without thermal management a robot will throttle its Onboard compute or shut down to protect itself. A Humanoid robot running high-torque actuators continuously must shed heat through fins, fans, or liquid cooling, which competes for mass within the Power budget. Thermal limits cap sustained Power density and effective Duty cycle, and a Battery management system monitors pack temperature to prevent thermal runaway.

plain: When a robot's chip gets too hot and automatically slows itself down to avoid damage.
snappy: Automatic reduction of clock speed or power when a processor or actuator exceeds its safe temperature, trading performance for protection.
detail: Thermal Throttling triggers when temperature sensors detect a die or coil approaching its limit, so the system reduces clock frequency, current, or duty cycle to shed heat, also called Thermal Derating. On a robot this can silently lower Onboard compute speed and break the assumed Control Loop Frequency, so a Vision-language-action model or perception network on NVIDIA Jetson may miss its Latency budget under load. Designers fight it with Thermal management, Liquid Cooling, and Model Quantization to keep the workload within the Power budget before throttling ever engages.

plain: A grid-based route finder that lets path segments cut across cells at any angle by checking whether two points can 'see' each other, giving shorter, more natural routes.
snappy: An any-angle variant of A* search that, during expansion, tries to reparent a node directly to its grandparent whenever line-of-sight permits, removing grid-aligned zig-zags.
detail: Theta* removes the artificial 8-direction restriction of grid A* search: when it expands a cell it checks whether the cell's parent has line-of-sight to the new cell, and if so connects them directly, yielding any-angle paths much closer to the true shortest route. It is widely used for ground-robot Path planning over an Occupancy grid and avoids the heavy Path smoothing that plain A* output usually needs. It is related to Field D* and Jump Point Search, which attack the same grid-suboptimality problem in different ways.

plain: A robot lining up a screw or bolt with a hole and turning it until it is tightened to the right firmness.
snappy: The contact-rich assembly task of aligning a threaded fastener with a hole and driving it to a target torque without cross-threading.
detail: Threaded Fastener Insertion (robotic screwdriving) requires aligning the fastener, finding the thread start, and applying controlled rotation while sensing reaction torque to avoid cross-threading and to detect seating. Robots use Force control or Hybrid position/force control with a Force/torque sensor, often a Spiral search to locate the hole, and Compliance control or a Remote center of compliance to absorb misalignment. It is a staple Manufacturing Assembly operation evaluated on the NIST assembly task boards, closely related to Connector Mating and Peg-in-hole.

plain: A famous set of fictional rules from science-fiction author Isaac Asimov meant to keep robots from harming people.
snappy: Isaac Asimov's fictional safety hierarchy (don't harm humans, obey orders, protect yourself) that popularized the idea of designed-in robot ethics.
detail: First stated in Asimov's 1942 story, the Three Laws are literary, not engineering, standards: they cannot be coded directly because terms like harm resist formal specification. Real safeguards instead come from standards such as ISO 10218 and ISO/TS 15066, mechanisms like an Emergency stop and Safe Torque Off, and broader Robot ethics debate around an Autonomous weapon. The laws remain a useful cultural touchstone when discussing Trust, Safety, and the limits of Autonomy.

plain: How much work a machine or system actually gets done in a given period, such as the number of items finished per hour.
snappy: The rate at which an automated system completes useful work, usually counted in units per hour.
detail: Throughput is the bottom-line output rate of an automation cell or warehouse, often quoted as units per hour (UPH) or a Pick rate in fulfillment. It depends on Cycle time, uptime, and how well stations are balanced; a single slow Industrial robot arm or a misfeeding Conveyor tracking station caps the whole line. In Logistics & Warehouse settings, fleets of Autonomous mobile robot units and Goods-to-person stations are sized to hit a target throughput, and the metric rolls up into Overall equipment effectiveness.

plain: How much work a warehouse gets done for each piece of floor space the robots take up.
snappy: A warehouse-automation metric normalizing output (picks or orders) by the floor area the system occupies.
detail: Throughput per Square Foot (or Throughput per Square Meter) captures why dense automation like Goods-to-person robots, a Shuttle system, or an Automated storage and retrieval system can justify high Capital Expenditure: they pack more Throughput into expensive real estate than manual shelving.
