detail: Unreal Engine (UE5) supplies the Photorealistic rendering and lighting that make camera-based perception testing realistic, which is why simulators like AirSim and the CARLA Simulator are built on it. Self-driving and Mobility teams use it to generate Synthetic data and exercise edge cases an Autonomous vehicle rarely sees on the road. In Research/Frontier work it underpins Sensor simulation and Domain randomization pipelines alongside NVIDIA Isaac Sim and the Unity Robotics Hub.

plain: A method that lets a robot keep a good running guess of things it cannot measure directly, like exactly where it is and how fast it is going, even when its movement curves and changes in complicated ways, by tracking a small set of carefully chosen example points.
snappy: A recursive estimator that propagates a deterministic set of sigma points through the system's true (possibly highly curved) motion and measurement models via the unscented transform to estimate state and covariance.
detail: The Unscented Kalman Filter avoids the linearization error of the Extended Kalman filter by passing sigma points through the true dynamics and measurement functions, then recovering the posterior mean and covariance. This often yields better State estimation accuracy for systems whose behavior is strongly curved, such as spacecraft attitude or Quaternion-based orientation tracking fused from an Inertial measurement unit. It sits alongside the classic Kalman filter and the Particle filter in the robotics estimation toolbox.

plain: A messy, unpredictable real-world setting that the robot cannot count on staying the same.
snappy: A workspace with uncontrolled layout, lighting, and contents that the robot must perceive and adapt to on the fly.
detail: An unstructured environment, like a home kitchen, a farm field, or a public road, defeats the assumptions of a Structured environment and demands strong Perception, SLAM, and Generalization. It is the natural home of Field robotics and Open world operation, where a Long-tail scenario can appear at any time. Coping with it drives interest in Learning from demonstration, a Foundation model, and Domain randomization to bridge the Reality gap from simulation to reality.

plain: The share of its scheduled working time that a robot is actually running and doing useful work rather than stopped or broken.
snappy: The fraction of scheduled time a deployed robot is operational and productive, also called availability.
detail: Uptime is the reliability KPI customers care about most, because a robot earning its keep only when running directly drives Return on investment. It is degraded by faults, maintenance, and integration stalls, and it is the metric most often guaranteed in a Service-level agreement. Uptime is closely linked to Mean time between failures and Mean time to repair, and it feeds the manufacturing measure Overall equipment effectiveness alongside speed and quality.

plain: A future transport system of small electric aircraft that fly people and cargo on short hops across and around cities.
snappy: Air taxi and cargo operations using electric vertical-takeoff aircraft to serve short intra- and inter-urban routes.
detail: Urban air mobility (UAM) envisions fleets of eVTOL aircraft carrying passengers and freight between rooftops and a Vertiport network, relieving ground congestion on short city routes. The aircraft typically use Distributed electric propulsion and depend on Detect and avoid, dense UAS traffic management, and Beyond visual line of sight autonomy to scale safely. The broader term advanced air mobility (AAM) extends the concept to regional and cargo flights, and it overlaps with Drone delivery infrastructure for Mobility.

plain: A text file that describes a robot's body to software: its parts, how they connect, and what they look like.
snappy: An XML format specifying a robot's links, joints, kinematics, visual meshes, and collision geometry.
detail: A URDF declares each Link and the Joint connecting them, encoding the Kinematics that MoveIt and tf use to compute Forward kinematics and Inverse kinematics. It is loaded by RViz to draw the robot and converted to SDF or MJCF for simulation in Gazebo or MuJoCo. Hand-writing long URDFs is tedious, so engineers generate them with Xacro macros.

plain: A flexible 3D file format, originally from film, used to assemble large detailed virtual scenes for robots.
snappy: An extensible, composable 3D scene description format (OpenUSD) used in Isaac Sim and digital twins.
detail: Created by Pixar and now open as OpenUSD, USD layers and references many assets into one scene, which suits the photorealistic, large-scale worlds of NVIDIA Isaac and Isaac Sim and the building of a Digital twin. It carries geometry, materials, physics, and sensors, playing the role for Isaac that SDF plays for Gazebo or MJCF for MuJoCo. USD scenes drive Photorealistic rendering and Synthetic data generation.

plain: How much of the time a robot is actually doing useful, paid work versus sitting idle.
snappy: The share of available time a deployed robot or fleet spends performing revenue-generating work.
detail: Utilization Rate (asset or fleet utilization) is the denominator-killer for unit economics: spreading fixed Capital Expenditure over more productive hours is what drives down Cost per Mile and Cost per Pick. It is distinct from Uptime (being available) because a robot can be up but idle waiting for orders, charging, or stuck in Depot Operations. Low utilization plagues early Pilot deployment projects and is a hallmark of Pilot purgatory. Operators raise it by smoothing demand, shortening Charging Infrastructure dwell with Opportunity Charging, and improving the Recovery Rate so robots spend less time waiting on human Exception Handling.

plain: A public collection of camera and motion recordings from very fast, aggressively flown drones, used to test navigation algorithms.
snappy: A benchmark dataset of high-speed FPV drone flights with ground-truth pose, used to evaluate visual-inertial odometry under aggressive motion.
detail: The UZH-FPV dataset captures camera, inertial measurement unit, and Motion Capture System ground-truth from a racing quad flown at high speed, deliberately inducing Motion Blur and large velocities that break naive estimators. It is a stress test for Visual-inertial odometry and Visual SLAM, exposing how methods degrade under the dynamics of Autonomous drone racing. For robotics researchers it complements gentler benchmarks like the EuRoC MAV Dataset by targeting the high-agility regime, and the AI overlap lies in training and evaluating learning-based state estimators.

plain: A small device that uses a blast of compressed air to create suction for a robot's suction cups, with no pump motor needed.
snappy: A compressed-air venturi device that generates vacuum for the cups on a suction gripper.
detail: A vacuum generator (Venturi or ejector) passes shop air through a nozzle to entrain and evacuate air, producing the suction a Suction gripper or vacuum End-of-arm tooling uses to lift parts. Because it has no moving parts and mounts at the gripper, it gives fast response for high-rate Pick and place, Depalletizing, and Case packing. A vacuum or pressure Proximity sensor confirms part presence, and air consumption is a real cost driver in a Robot cell.

plain: The dangerous gap between having a working prototype and turning it into a real product people can buy, where many projects run out of money and die.
snappy: The funding and commercialization gap between a demonstrated prototype and a reliably manufacturable, shipped product.
detail: The valley of death is where many robotics startups stall: a flashy demo at a low Technology readiness level needs years of hardening in Field reliability, manufacturing, and cost before it sells. Crossing it demands a defensible Bill of materials, repeatable production, and often Vertical integration to control cost and quality. It is as much a business and Total cost of ownership problem as a technical one, and the Pilot purgatory of stalled trials is one of its symptoms.

plain: Making sure an automatic system actually wants to do what its human designers and users intend, not just what they literally said.
snappy: The problem of ensuring an autonomous system's objectives faithfully reflect human intentions and values.
detail: For an embodied agent, value alignment means a Policy pursues the operator's true goal rather than a literal proxy, avoiding Reward hacking and the failure pattern named by Goodhart's law. A home Mobile manipulator should infer that tidying does not mean discarding valuables, which links alignment to Theory of mind, Inverse reinforcement learning, Preference learning, and Reinforcement learning from human feedback. It is complemented by Corrigibility and Scalable oversight, and enforced at runtime by a safety layer such as Runtime assurance.

plain: An estimate of how good a situation is for a robot, measured by how much reward it can expect to collect from there onward.
snappy: An estimate of expected cumulative future reward from a given state or state-action pair.
detail: A value function predicts the long-term Reward an agent can expect from a state (or from taking an action in a state), giving Reinforcement learning a way to compare options without simulating every outcome. State-action values are learned directly in Q-learning, while an Actor-critic architecture pairs a learned value critic with a Policy actor. Accurate value estimates are central within a Markov decision process and improve Sample efficiency by propagating credit across time.

plain: An electronic box that controls how fast an AC electric motor spins by changing the frequency of the power it sends.
snappy: A drive that controls AC motor speed and torque by varying the frequency and voltage of its output.
detail: A VFD (or variable speed drive) sits between the mains and an AC motor, synthesizing a variable-frequency output to smoothly control speed on pumps, fans, conveyors, and spindles. By matching motor speed to demand it saves energy and reduces mechanical stress versus running flat-out, a staple of Industrial automation energy efficiency. A VFD takes commands from a Programmable logic controller or Motion controller over a Fieldbus such as PROFINET or Modbus, and is distinct from a full servo drive used for precise positioning.

plain: A robot control method that changes how stiff or soft the arm feels from moment to moment, matching the firmness needed at each step of a task.
snappy: Impedance control whose stiffness and damping are modulated online to match the current task phase, often by a learned or scheduled policy.
detail: Variable impedance control (VIC) tunes the parameters of Impedance control during execution, for example stiffening to insert a peg precisely and softening to slide along a surface. In embodied robotics the modulation policy is frequently acquired through Reinforcement learning or Learning from demonstration, letting an arm like the Franka Emika Panda discover when to be rigid versus compliant for Contact-rich manipulation. It extends both Cartesian impedance control and Joint impedance control with time-varying gains, and is related to Gain scheduling.

plain: A motor-and-spring device that can be made stiff or springy on demand, like tensing or relaxing a muscle.
snappy: An actuator whose mechanical stiffness can be adjusted on the fly during operation.
detail: A variable stiffness actuator (VSA), also called a variable impedance actuator, uses an adjustable elastic element so a robot can be soft and safe during contact yet stiff and precise for fast, accurate motion. This tunability extends the fixed-spring idea of the Series elastic actuator and supports energy-efficient hopping and human-safe interaction in a Humanoid robot. It is a sophisticated Compliant actuator that mechanically realizes adjustable Impedance control.

plain: A propeller whose blade angle can be changed in flight, letting a drone change or even reverse its thrust faster than by changing motor speed.
snappy: A propeller with mechanically adjustable blade angle, enabling rapid thrust modulation and reverse thrust independent of RPM.
detail: A variable-pitch propeller (VPP) changes thrust by twisting its blades rather than by spinning faster, so it can modulate or reverse thrust much quicker than spooling a heavy Propeller up and down through the Electronic speed controller and Brushless DC motor. This bandwidth advantage benefits aggressive aerobatic and inverted flight and echoes the collective control in Cyclic and collective pitch. The trade is added mechanical complexity and weight versus a fixed-pitch rotor selected by KV rating.

plain: A model that squeezes a robot's camera images or sensor readings into a few meaningful numbers it can act on, then rebuilds them.
snappy: A generative model that compresses robot observations into a smooth latent distribution, enabling reconstruction and sampling of plausible states or actions.
detail: A VAE maps high-dimensional robot observations such as camera frames into a structured Latent space, a form of Representation learning that gives downstream control a compact state to act on. In robotics it is used to compress observations for a World model, to model the multimodal action distributions seen in human Demonstration data, and as a building block in skill-learning architectures like ACT. It belongs to the same generative family as the Diffusion model but trades sample sharpness for a smooth, samplable latent.

plain: A shared rulebook that lets warehouse robots from different makers all take orders from one central control system.
snappy: An open interface standard for commanding and monitoring AGVs and AMRs from a central master control system.
detail: VDA 5050 defines a vendor-neutral MQTT-based message protocol so a master controller can send orders, nodes, and actions to mobile robots and receive state back, regardless of manufacturer. In Logistics & Warehouse fleets it lets a single Fleet Management Software layer mix an Automated guided vehicle and an Autonomous mobile robot from different vendors. It complements broader coordination frameworks like Open-RMF and the MassRobotics AMR Interoperability Standard for true Interoperability.

plain: A company that makes self-driving forklifts and pallet movers for warehouses.
snappy: Maker of autonomous forklifts and pallet-moving robots for warehouse logistics.
detail: Vecna builds the Autonomous forklift and Autonomous Pallet Jack class of vehicles that move loaded pallets through distribution centers without a driver, governed by the ANSI/ITSDF B56.5 and ISO 3691-4 safety standards for driverless industrial trucks. Its Pivotal orchestration software handles Fleet management and Traffic management so mixed fleets and human-driven trucks share aisles safely. The robots use onboard LiDAR and a Navigation stack for localization in changing warehouse layouts.

plain: A reactive obstacle-dodging method that builds a circular chart of where obstacles are densest around the robot and steers toward the clearest gap.
snappy: A real-time obstacle-avoidance method that maps local sensor data into a polar density histogram and selects a low-density steering direction toward the goal.
detail: The Vector Field Histogram (VFH, and its successors VFH+ and VFH*) is a reactive Obstacle avoidance method that converts a local Occupancy grid into a one-dimensional polar histogram of obstacle density, then picks a steering direction through a sufficiently empty sector that best heads toward the goal. It improves on the simpler Potential field method by being less prone to local-minima trapping in cluttered scenes, and it competes with the Dynamic Window Approach as a local planner for mobile-robot navigation. It performs only local reactive steering, so it is normally paired with a global Path planning layer.

plain: A neural network that represents roads and other vehicles as connected lines rather than images, helping a self-driving car predict where everything will move.
snappy: A graph neural network that encodes HD-map lanes and agent histories as polyline vectors for hierarchical motion prediction.
detail: VectorNet replaces rasterized bird's-eye images with sparse polylines, encoding each map element and agent track as a subgraph, then a global interaction graph over them. This vectorized representation made Trajectory Prediction more efficient and accurate, and seeded follow-ups that pair it with attention. It consumes the Lane graph and HD map and is benchmarked on Argoverse and the Waymo Open Motion Dataset within a Self-driving stack.

plain: A way for cars to wirelessly talk to other cars, traffic lights, roadside equipment, and even pedestrians' phones to share what is happening around them.
snappy: Wireless communication linking a vehicle with other vehicles, infrastructure, pedestrians, and networks to share safety and traffic information.
detail: Vehicle-to-everything (V2X) is the umbrella for connected-vehicle messaging, encompassing vehicle-to-vehicle communication, vehicle-to-infrastructure communication, and pedestrian links. It lets the ego vehicle receive information beyond its own line of sight, enabling cooperative perception and earlier hazard awareness around blind corners. Implemented over DSRC or Cellular V2X, it augments onboard automotive radar and LiDAR rather than replacing them.

plain: Cars wirelessly talking with roadside equipment like traffic lights and signs to learn things like when a light will turn red.
snappy: Wireless communication between vehicles and roadside infrastructure such as traffic signals, signs, and work zones.
detail: Vehicle-to-infrastructure communication (V2I) is the roadside subset of vehicle-to-everything, letting a vehicle receive signal phase and timing, work-zone alerts, and lane-closure data from connected infrastructure. It supports cooperative perception and smoother behavior planning, for example slowing ahead of a red light it cannot yet see. V2I is essential for automated valet parking, where the garage infrastructure guides the car, and runs over DSRC or Cellular V2X.

plain: Cars wirelessly sending messages straight to each other, like 'I'm braking hard' or 'I'm in your blind spot.'
snappy: Direct wireless data exchange between nearby vehicles sharing position, speed, and intent for cooperative safety.
detail: Vehicle-to-vehicle communication (V2V) is the car-to-car subset of vehicle-to-everything, broadcasting basic safety messages with position, heading, and braking status to neighbors. It enables cooperative perception and platooning, where a self-driving truck convoy shares intent to close gaps safely, and warns of hazards a car's own sensors cannot yet see. Like the rest of V2X it runs over DSRC or Cellular V2X and complements automotive radar and a camera.

plain: Telling a robot joint or motor how fast to spin or move, and keeping it at that speed.
snappy: Closed-loop control that commands and regulates the speed of a joint, wheel, or actuator.
detail: Velocity control regulates rate rather than place, using an Encoder or Resolver to measure speed and a PID controller to hold the Setpoint despite load. It is the natural mode for the wheels of a Differential-drive robot, for Conveyor tracking, and as the inner stage of a Cascade control loop beneath Position control. With Torque control it forms the trio of Servo control modes a Servomotor and its Motor controller can run.

plain: The set of speeds and directions that would eventually crash the robot into a moving object, which the robot is told to avoid choosing.
snappy: The cone of velocities that would lead to a future collision with a moving obstacle, excluded during velocity selection.
detail: A Velocity obstacle reasons in velocity space rather than position space: given another agent's current velocity, it computes the set of the robot's own velocities that would cause a collision at some future time and constrains the planner to pick outside that set. This makes it well suited to dynamic environments with moving people or other robots, where static Obstacle avoidance is insufficient, and it underlies a reactive Local planner for an Autonomous mobile robot. Its multi-robot extension, Optimal Reciprocal Collision Avoidance, splits the avoidance effort between agents.

plain: A company that pioneered the spinning, multi-laser sensors mounted on self-driving cars to build a 3D map of their surroundings.
snappy: Pioneer of spinning multi-beam automotive LiDAR, whose HDL-64E defined the early self-driving sensor stack.
detail: Velodyne's HDL-64E spinning Mechanical LiDAR became the iconic rooftop sensor on most DARPA Grand Challenge and early Autonomous vehicle prototypes, producing a dense 360-degree Point cloud. Each unit stacks many laser-Photodetector pairs that rotate to sweep the scene, feeding downstream 3D object detection and SLAM. Its data format and 64-beam geometry are baked into benchmarks like the KITTI Dataset, though newer Solid-state LiDAR and digital competitors such as Ouster have since pressured its market position.

plain: Being stuck with one robot company because their machines, software, and parts only work with each other, making it expensive to switch.
snappy: Dependence on a single supplier's closed, proprietary robot ecosystem that raises the cost and difficulty of switching to alternatives.
detail: Vendor Lock-In arises when a buyer's robots, Fleet management software, chargers, and spare parts all come from one supplier's closed stack, so adding equipment from another vendor is impractical. In Logistics & Warehouse this is the central tension addressed by Interoperability efforts and open specs like VDA 5050 and the MassRobotics AMR Interoperability Standard, which let an Autonomous mobile robot from one maker share a site and Traffic management system with another. Lock-in inflates Total cost of ownership over a deployment's life and is one reason buyers value Right to Repair and open orchestration layers such as Open-RMF.

plain: A company whose 3D-camera systems let people work safely next to large factory robot arms by slowing or stopping them when someone gets close.
snappy: Maker of 3D safeguarding systems (FreeMove) enabling safe human-robot collaboration around standard industrial arms.
detail: Veo's FreeMove uses an array of depth sensors to monitor a workcell in 3D and implement Speed and separation monitoring, dynamically slowing or issuing a Safety-rated monitored stop on a full-size Industrial robot arm as a person approaches. This lets a non-collaborative high-payload arm operate safely in a collaborative workspace without caging, complementing standards like ISO/TS 15066. It is an alternative to redesigning a line around a low-payload Cobot.

plain: Two checks on a robot: confirming it was built correctly to its design, and confirming the design actually does the right job in the real world.
snappy: Verification confirms the system was built to spec; validation confirms it meets the real-world need.
detail: Verification and validation (V&V) answers two distinct questions: did we build the system right, and did we build the right system. For an Autonomous vehicle, verification checks the Self-driving stack against requirements, while validation uses Scenario-based testing, Closed-loop simulation, and Log replay to show safe behavior across the Long tail. V&V feeds a Safety case and aligns with functional-safety standards like ISO 26262 and the Safety of the intended functionality framework.

plain: A company building most of the parts and software of its product in-house rather than buying them from others.
snappy: A strategy of designing and producing a robot's hardware, software, and supporting stack internally rather than sourcing them externally.
detail: Vertical integration lets a robotics company control its own Actuator design, Motor controller, Onboard compute, and Self-driving stack, trading higher upfront cost for tighter performance and a leaner Bill of materials at scale. Tesla and Boston Dynamics exemplify it, designing custom Quasi-direct drive actuators rather than buying off-the-shelf. It can shorten Hardware-software co-design loops and improve Field reliability, but it raises capital needs and is a recurring factor in surviving the Valley of death.

plain: A tall enclosed cabinet that stores trays stacked vertically and automatically delivers the right tray down to a worker's reach.
snappy: An enclosed automated tray-storage unit that uses an extractor to deliver stored goods to an ergonomic operator pick window.
detail: A vertical lift module (VLM) packs trays densely up a column and uses an internal extractor to bring a requested tray to the access opening, recovering floor space and shortening walk time. As a compact Goods-to-person device it is a cousin of the Automated storage and retrieval system, and it is commonly paired with Pick-to-light guidance at the window to confirm picks. Its retrievals are directed by the Warehouse management system, and the ergonomic delivery height improves Pick rate while reducing operator strain.

plain: A small airport-like pad where electric air taxis take off and land vertically, with space to charge and board passengers.
snappy: Ground infrastructure with takeoff/landing pads, charging, and passenger handling for eVTOL air-taxi operations.
detail: A vertiport is the eVTOL equivalent of a heliport, providing one or more vertipads, fast charging, passenger flow, and air-traffic interfaces to enable Urban air mobility at scale. Siting and layout must account for downwash, noise, and the precise vertical approaches that Distributed electric propulsion aircraft fly, often using Autonomous docking-style precision guidance on final approach. A network of vertiports is the physical backbone of Mobility air-taxi service and connects to UAS traffic management for sequencing.

plain: A company that offers an online platform for building, setting up, and managing robots in one place.
snappy: Maker of a modular cloud platform for building, configuring, and managing robots.
detail: Viam provides a Cloud robotics platform where developers wire together hardware components, sensors, and Computer vision services through a modular config rather than writing low-level drivers, then deploy and monitor robots remotely. It offers a Hardware abstraction layer and Over-the-Air Update tooling so a Fleet of heterogeneous machines can be managed from a browser. It positions as a more app-developer-friendly alternative to assembling a stack purely from ROS packages.

plain: The onboard radio that beams a drone's live camera picture down to the pilot's video goggles.
snappy: An onboard transmitter that streams the live camera feed to FPV goggles, usually as a one-way low-latency video link.
detail: A video transmitter (VTX) sends the camera image to the pilot's goggles for First-person view flying, optimized for minimal latency rather than picture quality so the pilot can react in Rate mode. It is one of three independent links on an FPV racing drone alongside the Radio control link for stick inputs and the Telemetry radio for status. Analog and digital VTX systems trade latency against image clarity, and the link can be denied by GNSS jamming or RF interference.

plain: The way a person's attention naturally fades when they have to watch something reliable for a long time and almost nothing ever happens.
snappy: The measurable decline in sustained attention and detection performance during prolonged monitoring of a rarely-failing system.
detail: Vigilance decrement is a well-documented human-factors effect: detection rate drops within tens of minutes of monotonous monitoring. It is a primary mechanism behind the Out-of-the-loop performance problem and Automation complacency, relevant whenever a human performs Supervised autonomy over a Drone swarm, a Teleoperation Center screen wall, or a Safety driver watching an Autonomous vehicle. Countermeasures include attention-directing Human-machine interface alerts, rotating duty, and reducing the human's monitoring load through Adjustable autonomy.

plain: A soft robot that grows forward by turning itself inside-out from its tip, like an unrolling fire hose, snaking through tight gaps.
snappy: A soft growing robot that extends by everting pressurized tubing from its tip, lengthening without sliding against its surroundings.
detail: A Vine robot is a Soft robot that lengthens through eversion, unfurling new material from its tip under pneumatic pressure so the body never drags against the environment, letting it thread through rubble, pipes, or the human body. Steering is achieved by selectively lengthening one side, a form of Peristaltic locomotion control driven by a Pneumatic actuator, and it shares lineage with the Continuum robot family. Applications span search in Defense & Security collapse sites and atraumatic navigation for Medical & Surgical access where rigid tools cannot reach.

plain: A software system that lets a robot figure out where it is and how it is moving using just one ordinary camera combined with a small motion sensor.
snappy: An optimization-based monocular visual-inertial state estimator that fuses a single camera with an IMU to recover real-scale motion and pose.
detail: VINS-Mono, developed at HKUST, performs Visual-inertial odometry by tightly fusing tracked image features with Inertial measurement unit readings inside a sliding-window optimizer, recovering metric scale that a single camera alone cannot. It runs a separate Loop closure thread to correct accumulated drift, making it a popular Visual SLAM backbone for drones and other weight-constrained platforms where stereo rigs are too heavy. Like other modern back-ends it leans on nonlinear least-squares over a Factor graph, and its design heavily influenced later estimators such as VINS-Fusion.

plain: A method that watches human video and learns a sense of how close a scene is to a goal, which it then hands to a robot as a built-in reward signal for learning new tasks.
snappy: A goal-conditioned value pretraining method that yields a dense reward and embedding from action-free human video, usable for downstream control.
detail: VIP trains a goal-conditioned Value function on action-free human video so that distance in its embedding space behaves like a smooth, dense Reward function, turning a Sparse reward manipulation task into a tractable one. The learned embedding doubles as a visual Representation learning backbone, much like R3M and Masked Visual Pretraining, and the implicit reward supports Reinforcement learning and trajectory optimization for Manipulation. It is a Research/Frontier approach to extracting reward signals without robot data or human action labels.

plain: A method of moving a walking robot by imagining invisible springs and shock absorbers attached to it and computing the forces those imaginary parts would produce.
snappy: A control technique that generates joint torques by simulating virtual springs and dampers acting between the robot and its environment, then mapping their forces through the Jacobian transpose.
detail: Virtual model control (VMC) lets engineers specify intuitive behaviors, such as a virtual spring holding a Bipedal robot's torso upright, and converts those imagined forces into joint commands via Jacobian transpose control. It is conceptually a form of Impedance control applied at the whole-body level and is often paired with Centroidal dynamics reasoning or Ground reaction force control for Legged locomotion. VMC was a foundational idea behind early dynamic walkers and remains a clear way to encode Compliance control intentions.

plain: A map for finding the shortest route around obstacles by connecting the corners of obstacles with straight lines that do not pass through anything.
snappy: A roadmap whose nodes are obstacle vertices and whose edges are all mutually visible, collision-free straight segments.
detail: A Visibility Graph connects start, goal, and every obstacle vertex with straight edges wherever a clear line of sight exists, and because the shortest collision-free path among polygonal obstacles must touch obstacle corners, searching this graph with Dijkstra's algorithm or A* search yields the true shortest path. It is a classic Path planning method for polygonal Configuration space, contrasting with Voronoi Diagram Planning, which trades path length for maximum clearance. In practice it produces taut, hug-the-corner routes, so it is often followed by Path smoothing or clearance inflation for safety.

plain: Using cameras to let a robot see and understand what is around it.
snappy: The use of cameras and image processing to let a robot perceive its surroundings.
detail: Vision is the dominant sensing channel for most robots, turning Camera images into the spatial and semantic understanding that drives Perception. A mobile robot fuses Vision with Object detection and Semantic segmentation to recognize obstacles, while a manipulator uses Visual servoing to align its end-effector to a target. Vision underpins Visual SLAM and Visual odometry for navigation, and overlaps heavily with Computer vision and Machine vision in industry.

plain: A specialized low-power chip built to handle camera and image processing tasks quickly without draining much energy.
snappy: A low-power processor specialized for accelerating computer-vision and neural-inference pipelines on power-constrained robots.
detail: A Vision Processing Unit (VPU), such as Intel's Myriad, packs vector engines and hardware image blocks tuned for the convolution-heavy math of Computer vision, delivering Perception inference at a few watts. It suits a small Autonomous mobile robot, drone, or warehouse robot that must run Object detection or Depth estimation within a tight Power budget rather than carry a full GPU System-on-Module. As an Edge computing accelerator it performs Hardware Accelerator Offload alongside peers like the Hailo Accelerator and Google Coral Edge TPU, typically requiring Model Quantization to hit its efficiency targets.

plain: A way of letting an image-understanding model treat a picture like a sequence of small tiles and weigh how each tile relates to every other, instead of scanning it with sliding filters.
snappy: An image model that splits a picture into patch tokens and applies Transformer self-attention over them for visual recognition.
detail: The Vision Transformer (ViT) adapts the Transformer architecture from language to vision by embedding fixed-size image patches as tokens and processing them with global self-attention, an alternative to the local receptive fields of a Convolutional neural network. It underpins modern detectors and segmenters like DETR and the backbones in DINOv2, CLIP, and the Segment Anything Model. In robotics it provides the perception backbone for Foundation model policies and Vision-language-action model systems running on accelerators such as NVIDIA Jetson, where global context helps with cluttered Mobility and Manufacturing scenes.

plain: A touch sensor that works by filming a soft gel pad with a tiny camera and watching how the gel squishes against an object.
snappy: A tactile sensor that images a deformable gel surface with an internal camera to reconstruct contact geometry.
detail: A vision-based tactile sensor, such as GelSight, places a soft elastomer over an internal Camera and lights; when the gel presses an object, the camera captures fine surface shape and shear in high resolution. This dense data excels at Slip detection, Tactile servoing, and Contact-rich manipulation, far richer than a simple Capacitive sensor. It is a leading research direction for Dexterous manipulation on an Anthropomorphic hand.

plain: A robot that uses camera images to see where things are and adjust its movements to pick or place them accurately.
snappy: Using camera feedback to compute and correct a robot's position relative to parts in real time, abbreviated VGR.
detail: In VGR a Machine vision system locates a part's Pose and sends corrected coordinates to the Robot controller, letting the arm grasp items that are not precisely fixtured, the basis of Bin picking from a randomly filled tote. It tightly couples perception to motion through Hand-eye calibration so camera coordinates map onto the robot's frame, and at high update rates it becomes Visual servoing. VGR overlaps with AI through learned Object detection and Grasp planning, and it powers flexible Pick and place where rigid Fixturing is impractical.

plain: A robot following spoken or written directions like 'go down the hall and turn left at the kitchen' to reach a place it has never been.
snappy: The task of following free-form natural-language route instructions to navigate previously unseen 3D environments.
detail: Vision-Language Navigation requires an agent to ground a natural-language instruction in what its camera sees and to act, step by step, toward the described destination in an unseen building. It is an Embodied AI benchmark frequently run in simulators like Habitat, and modern approaches lean on a Foundation model or a Vision-language-action model to connect words, pixels, and actions. It overlaps with Semantic navigation and Instruction following, and a robot embodiment must additionally handle real Localization and Obstacle avoidance when the policy is deployed beyond simulation.

plain: A single AI model that looks at camera images, reads an instruction in plain language, and directly outputs the moves a robot should make.
snappy: A model that maps visual observations and natural-language instructions directly to robot actions.
detail: A vision-language-action model (VLA) fuses image understanding and language comprehension to output motor commands, enabling Language-conditioned manipulation where a Humanoid robot follows a spoken instruction. VLAs such as RT-2, OpenVLA, and the RT-X family are a type of Robot foundation model trained on large, cross-robot datasets like Open X-Embodiment to achieve broad Generalization. They form a learned Policy that replaces hand-engineered Perception and planning pipelines with end-to-end control.

plain: A single AI model for a self-driving car that takes in what the cameras see plus a written instruction, and directly outputs how to steer, brake, and accelerate.
snappy: A driving policy that maps camera images and natural-language prompts directly to vehicle control actions in one learned model.
detail: Adapting the manipulation-focused Vision-language-action model to the road, a Driving VLA fuses perception and reasoning so a single network can both explain a scene and produce trajectories, rather than relying on a Modular pipeline of separate perception and planning stages. It is a flavor of End-to-end driving that adds language conditioning, letting an operator or onboard Reasoning model issue intents like 'pull over after the bus.' Companies such as Wayve pursue this approach, training on logs from datasets like nuScenes and the Waymo Open Dataset.

plain: Trying to make a car drive itself using just cameras, without expensive laser scanners.
snappy: A self-driving approach that relies on cameras for perception, deliberately forgoing lidar and sometimes radar.
detail: Vision-only autonomy bets that cameras plus deep learning can recover depth and geometry well enough to drive, avoiding the cost of LiDAR, an approach championed by Tesla. It leans heavily on Depth estimation, an Occupancy network, and a Bird's-eye-view representation to reconstruct the scene from pixels alone, where lidar-based stacks get range directly. Critics argue it is brittle in glare and rare Edge case lighting, which is why some teams add 4D imaging radar for redundancy rather than going purely camera-only.

plain: A very large image-understanding model trained on huge amounts of data that gives robots ready-made, robust visual features without task-specific training.
snappy: A large pretrained vision backbone (e.g. DINOv2) supplying general-purpose, robust image features that robots reuse for perception across tasks.
detail: A Visual Foundation Model is a large network pretrained on massive image data, such as DINOv2, whose frozen features serve as a reusable Perception backbone for downstream robot tasks like Grasp Detection, Semantic segmentation, and Pose estimation without retraining from scratch. In embodied systems these features feed a Vision-language-action model or policy, improving Generalization and reducing the robot data scarcity problem. They pair with Open-vocabulary perception tools like Grounding DINO and Segment Anything Model to let a manipulator find objects it was never explicitly trained on.

plain: Flying a drone close enough that the operator can always see it directly with their own eyes.
snappy: Drone operation that keeps the aircraft within the pilot's unaided sight at all times.
detail: VLOS is the baseline assumption of most drone rules, including FAA Part 107, because the pilot can personally spot and avoid other aircraft and obstacles without onboard Detect and avoid. The pilot may still use an Autopilot for Waypoint navigation or Loiter, but must keep the craft within naked-eye view, optionally aided by a visual observer. Extending operations past this boundary becomes Beyond visual line of sight, which carries far stricter requirements.

plain: Figuring out how a robot has moved by watching how the scene shifts between one camera frame and the next.
snappy: Incremental motion estimation from tracking image features across consecutive camera frames.
detail: Visual odometry (VO) tracks features through successive Camera frames and recovers the Camera's incremental motion via Feature matching and geometry, a key input to Ego-motion estimation and Localization. Fusing it with an Inertial measurement unit yields more robust Visual-inertial odometry, and closing a loop turns it into Visual SLAM. It is widely used in Mobility and on drones where Wheel odometry is unavailable.

plain: Steering a robot continuously by watching live camera images, nudging it until what the camera sees matches the desired view of the target.
snappy: A closed-loop control technique that drives a robot's motion directly from visual feedback to reduce the error between current and desired image features or object pose.
detail: Visual servoing puts a camera inside the Control loop, computing motion commands so that observed image features (image-based) or an estimated target Pose (position-based) converge to a goal, correcting in real time as the scene changes. It depends on a calibrated camera and a Jacobian matrix relating feature motion to robot motion, and is commonly used for Peg-in-hole assembly, Conveyor tracking, and instrument alignment in a Surgical robot. Because it is feedback-driven it tolerates Calibration error and Backlash better than pure open-loop motion, complementing Hand-eye calibration and Pose estimation. In Manufacturing it enables Vision-guided robotics for high-precision insertion and alignment without rigid Fixturing.

plain: Mapping and self-positioning a robot using mainly its cameras instead of laser scanners.
snappy: SLAM that builds a map and tracks pose primarily from camera imagery rather than lidar.
detail: Visual SLAM (vSLAM) tracks features such as ORB features across Camera frames to estimate motion and reconstruct 3D structure, often jointly with a Bundle adjustment back end. It commonly fuses an IMU to become Visual-inertial odometry for robustness, and uses Place recognition for Loop closure. It powers low-cost navigation on drones and AR headsets where LiDAR is too heavy or expensive, though it struggles in textureless or poorly lit scenes.

plain: Tracking how a robot moves by combining what its cameras see with readings from its motion sensor.
snappy: Estimating motion by fusing camera imagery with inertial measurement unit data.
detail: Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) blends visual feature tracking with high-rate accelerometer and gyroscope data from an Inertial measurement unit, giving each sensor's strength: the camera fixes drift while the IMU bridges fast motion and blur. It is a form of Visual odometry tightly coupled through an Extended Kalman filter or a Factor graph, and it underlies tracking on drones and the foundation of many Visual SLAM systems. VIO is favored for GPS-denied navigation indoors and aboard a Quadcopter.

plain: A way for a walking robot to track where it is by combining what its cameras see, its motion sensor, and how its legs are moving.
snappy: State estimation for legged robots that fuses camera features, IMU data, and leg kinematics with contact constraints to reduce drift during walking.
detail: Visual-Inertial-Legged Odometry (VILO) augments Visual-inertial odometry with leg kinematics and Contact Estimation, treating a stance foot as a temporarily fixed point to bound velocity drift via factors similar to a Zero-Velocity Update. Fusing Ground reaction force and joint encoder data with the Inertial measurement unit and camera lets a Legged robot estimate its body pose even when vision is poor. It is an active research topic for the Humanoid robot and quadrupeds operating in GPS-denied navigation.

plain: A robot controller that looks at raw camera pictures and directly decides how to move its motors, without a separate step to identify objects first.
snappy: A learned policy mapping raw image observations end-to-end to low-level motor or end-effector commands.
detail: A Visuomotor Policy maps raw camera pixels directly to motor or End-effector commands, fusing Perception and control in one network rather than a Modular pipeline of detect-then-plan. Trained by Imitation learning (e.g., Behavior cloning, Diffusion policy) or Reinforcement learning, it powers Manipulation and Legged locomotion controllers and underlies modern Vision-language-action model action heads like those in Pi-Zero and Helix. Because it consumes high-dimensional images, it benefits from Representation learning and Domain randomization for robust Sim-to-real transfer.

plain: A way of giving robots a sense of touch by filming, with a tiny built-in camera, how a soft pad deforms when it presses on something.
snappy: Tactile sensing that images the deformation of an elastomer surface with an internal camera to recover contact geometry and force.
detail: Visuotactile sensing converts touch into a rich image stream by placing a camera behind a soft gel or marker membrane and watching it deform on contact, the principle behind GelSight, the DIGIT tactile sensor, and TacTip. Because the output is an image, it pairs naturally with a Convolutional neural network for Slip detection, Tactile pose estimation, and Contact-rich manipulation. It gives a Robotic hand dense, high-resolution touch where a sparse Taxel array would be coarse.

plain: A small, fast-reacting device that moves a short distance back and forth, like the part that pushes a loudspeaker cone.
snappy: A direct-drive electromagnetic actuator producing fast, precise, short-stroke linear motion.
detail: A voice coil actuator (VCM) drives a coil through a fixed magnetic field, producing force in direct proportion to current with essentially no gearing or friction, the hallmark of a Direct drive. Its very high Bandwidth and smooth, backlash-free motion suit hard-disk head positioning, camera autofocus, fine Force control, and active vibration isolation. The trade-off is a short stroke, so it excels at small, rapid, precise moves rather than large travel.

plain: A headset system that tells warehouse workers what to pick through spoken instructions, leaving their hands and eyes free.
snappy: A voice-directed picking system delivering spoken pick instructions and capturing verbal confirmations hands-free via headset.
detail: Voice picking streams text-to-speech commands to an operator's headset and uses speech recognition to capture spoken confirmations such as check digits, keeping hands and eyes on the product rather than a screen. It improves accuracy and Pick rate in cold-storage and full-case zones where a Pick-to-light display is impractical. The dialog is driven by the Warehouse management system, and many sites blend voice with light-directed methods or a Put wall to match each zone's product profile.

plain: Routing a robot along the lines that stay as far as possible from all surrounding obstacles, so it travels down the middle of open space.
snappy: Planning along the generalized Voronoi diagram (medial axis) to maximize clearance from obstacles.
detail: Voronoi Diagram Planning routes the robot along the medial axis, the set of points equidistant from the two nearest obstacles, which maximizes clearance and keeps the robot away from walls. The generalized Voronoi diagram forms a roadmap that is then searched with Dijkstra's algorithm or A* search, making it a complement to the Visibility Graph, which instead minimizes path length by hugging corners. It is widely used for an Autonomous mobile robot navigating cluttered indoor space, and is conceptually related to the Potential field method in how it favors safe, central routes.

plain: Sticking a robot to a surface by spinning a fan that sucks air out from underneath, creating suction without touching tightly.
snappy: Negative-pressure climbing adhesion produced by a spinning impeller that generates a low-pressure region to press the robot against a surface.
detail: Unlike a conventional Suction gripper that needs a tight seal, vortex adhesion tolerates rough or porous walls because the impeller maintains a pressure differential even with a leaky gap, letting a Climbing robot grip brick or concrete. The trade-off is continuous power draw, noise, and a high Cost of transport, so it is usually reserved for surfaces where Magnetic adhesion (no metal) and Gecko-inspired adhesion (too rough) both fail. It is one of several attachment options for Climbing locomotion, evaluated against Electroadhesion and Microspine gripping for a given surface.

plain: A dangerous condition where a fast-descending drone sinks into its own swirling downward air and suddenly loses lift.
snappy: A rotor aerodynamic condition during rapid vertical descent where recirculating tip vortices cause severe, unrecoverable thrust loss.
detail: Vortex ring state (VRS), or settling with power, occurs when a rotorcraft descends fast enough to fall into its own Downwash, so the rotor recirculates air in a ring and lift collapses even at high power. On a Multirotor drone it can cause sudden altitude loss and loss of control during steep descents, and recovery requires breaking the recirculation by gaining forward airspeed. It is the hazardous opposite of Ground effect and a known cause of drone crashes during aggressive Precision landing approaches.

plain: Shrinking a huge 3D scan into a smaller one by dividing space into little cubes and keeping just one point per cube.
snappy: A point-cloud reduction filter that replaces all points in each fixed 3D grid cell with a single representative point.
detail: Voxel Downsampling overlays a Voxel grid on a Point cloud and collapses the points inside each cell to their centroid, drastically cutting data volume while preserving overall shape. It is a standard preprocessing step in the Point Cloud Library before heavier operations like Iterative closest point registration or Euclidean Cluster Extraction. Mobility and Logistics & Warehouse robots apply it to LiDAR scans so that Object detection and mapping run within real-time budgets on limited compute.

plain: A way of carving up 3D space into a stack of equal-sized cubes, like 3D pixels.
snappy: A representation that discretizes 3D space into a regular lattice of cubic volume cells (voxels).
detail: A voxel grid divides space into uniform cubes, each of which can store occupancy, color, or a learned feature, giving a simple 3D analog of the 2D Occupancy grid. Robotics uses it to downsample a dense Point cloud before Iterative closest point, to build 3D maps, and inside an Occupancy network. The memory-efficient sparse counterpart for mapping is the OctoMap, which adapts cell size with an octree.

plain: A method where an AI reads an instruction and paints invisible 3D maps showing where the robot should go and where to avoid, then plans a motion through them.
snappy: A zero-shot manipulation method where an LLM and VLM compose 3D value maps of affordances and constraints that a motion planner optimizes trajectories through.
detail: VoxPoser (Stanford, 2023) uses a large language model together with a vision-language model to write code that fills voxel grids with attraction and repulsion values, producing 3D Affordance and constraint maps without task-specific training. A Trajectory optimization step then plans a Manipulation path that maximizes reward through the composed map, enabling Zero-shot generalization to new objects and instructions. It sits alongside Code as Policies in the LLM-as-planner family and is demonstrated on tabletop arms doing tasks like opening drawers or sweeping, complementing learned approaches like Diffusion policy.

plain: An aircraft that rises straight up and lands straight down, so it needs no runway.
snappy: Any aircraft that takes off and lands vertically rather than along a runway.
detail: Every Multirotor is technically a VTOL, but the term is most useful for aircraft that combine vertical lift with efficient forward flight, such as a Hybrid VTOL or a Tiltrotor. VTOL capability is the defining feature of the eVTOL air taxis pursued for Urban air mobility, which operate from a Vertiport rather than an airport. The contrast class is the Fixed-wing drone, which needs a runway or launcher but cruises far more efficiently.

plain: A drone that lifts off and lands straight up like a helicopter, then flies forward efficiently like an airplane.
snappy: An aircraft combining rotor-borne vertical takeoff and hover with efficient fixed-wing forward cruise.
detail: A VTOL drone, also called a Hybrid VTOL, gives the field-friendliness of a Multirotor drone (no runway) with the range of a Fixed-wing drone by transitioning between hover and wing-borne flight, sometimes using a Tiltrotor or Distributed electric propulsion layout. The same VTOL principle scales up to eVTOL air taxis in Urban air mobility, served by a Vertiport. It is valued for Logistics & Warehouse drone delivery and Defense & Security reconnaissance over long ranges.

plain: A person on the road without the protection of a vehicle body, such as someone walking or cycling.
snappy: An unprotected road participant, such as a pedestrian, cyclist, or motorcyclist, requiring heightened care from automated systems.
detail: VRUs are a priority class for an automated driving system because collisions with them carry severe outcomes, so perception must reliably handle pedestrian detection, prediction of erratic motion, and occlusion. Benchmarks like nuScenes and the Waymo Open Dataset label VRUs heavily, and responsibility-sensitive safety frameworks reserve extra margin around them. Handling a cyclist who suddenly enters the ego vehicle path is a canonical hard case for behavior prediction and collision avoidance.

plain: Official permission to fly a drone in a way the normal rules would forbid, like at night or far from the operator.
snappy: A regulatory exemption from specific standard drone-operation rules, granted by an aviation authority when the operator proves equivalent safety.
detail: A Waiver is the FAA's mechanism for permitting operations outside the default Part 107 small-drone rules, such as flying Beyond visual line of sight, over people, or at night. For commercial Drone delivery the Beyond visual line of sight waiver is the critical one, since routine package routes cannot rely on a Visual line of sight observer. Waivers are case-specific and contrast with the broader, scalable approval path of a Specific Operations Risk Assessment leading to an Operational Authorization, and they are a frequent bottleneck in clearing the Demo-to-Deployment Gap for aerial logistics.

plain: The real-time controller that coordinates a warehouse's conveyors, sorters, and robots so they all move material at the right moment.
snappy: A real-time execution layer coordinating conveyors, sorters, and automation equipment on the warehouse floor.
detail: A warehouse control system (WCS), sometimes called a warehouse execution system, takes order tasks from the Warehouse management system and drives the moment-to-moment behaviour of an Accumulation conveyor, a Sortation system, a Shuttle system, and lifts. It performs the diverts, metering, and sequencing that keep Throughput balanced and avoid jams, and increasingly does Traffic management for mobile-robot fleets on the floor. As a piece of Operational technology it speaks fieldbus and Industrial Ethernet protocols down to the PLCs running each conveyor segment.

plain: The software brain of a warehouse that tracks what inventory is where and tells workers and machines what to receive, store, and ship.
snappy: Software that directs inventory, receiving, putaway, storage, and order fulfilment across a warehouse.
detail: A warehouse management system (WMS) holds the inventory record and the order workload, deciding what to store where and which orders to release, then handing execution detail to the floor. It sits above the Warehouse control system, which sequences the physical Sortation system, conveyors, and any Goods-to-person robot fleet in real time. The WMS connects upward to Enterprise resource planning and uses Slotting Optimization to place fast movers near pick faces, directly shaping Pick rate and Cost per Pick.

plain: A simple countdown that quietly resets a machine into a safe state if its computer freezes or stops responding.
snappy: A hardware or software timer that triggers a safe action if it is not periodically reset, detecting compute or software hangs.
detail: A Watchdog timer is a core safety and reliability primitive in any Embedded system or Microcontroller running a robot: the software must "kick" the timer periodically, and if a hang or crash stops the kicks, the timer fires to force a reset or a Safety-rated stop. It is widely used in a Flight controller, a Robot controller, and a Real-time operating system to catch deadlocks and infinite loops. Watchdogs are a building block for Fail-safe behavior and contribute to the diagnostic coverage counted toward a Performance Level or Safety Integrity Level.

plain: A slow, steady legged gait where legs lift one after another in a wave from back to front, keeping the most legs on the ground for stability.
snappy: A slow legged gait lifting legs in a sequential back-to-front metachronal wave to maximize support-polygon size.
detail: The wave (metachronal) gait keeps the highest Duty factor of any Hexapod locomotion pattern, lifting only one leg at a time so the Support polygon stays large and Static stability is maximal, at the cost of speed. It anchors the slow end of the continuum whose fast end is the Tripod gait, with the Ripple gait in between, all parameterizable from a single Central pattern generator. Legged robots invoke the wave gait when crossing rough or sloped Terrain adaptation scenarios or carrying heavy Payload where margin against Toppling matters more than velocity.

plain: An oval-shaped hub that, as it spins, squeezes a flexible gear into a moving wave so a robot reducer can shrink fast spin into slow, strong motion.
snappy: The elliptical cam-and-bearing element that deforms a strain-wave gear's flexspline into mesh.
detail: The Wave Generator is the input member of a Harmonic drive: an elliptical cam wrapped by a thin ball bearing that pushes the Strain Wave Flexspline teeth into engagement with the circular spline at the ellipse's major axis. As the cam rotates, the contact zone sweeps around, advancing the output slowly to create the drive's high Gear Ratio. It is the moving heart of the zero-Backlash reducers used in precision Manufacturing and Humanoid robot joints made by suppliers such as Harmonic Drive LLC.

plain: A floating ocean robot that turns the up-and-down motion of waves into forward movement so it can travel for months without fuel.
snappy: A wave-powered unmanned surface vehicle that harvests energy from ocean swell for propulsion, enabling months-long persistent autonomy.
detail: A wave glider couples a surface float to a submerged wing rack tethered below it; as waves lift and drop the float, the wings convert that vertical heave into forward thrust, while solar panels power the electronics. As an Unmanned surface vehicle built for Persistent autonomy, it carries oceanographic sensors and maintains communications relays over voyages spanning thousands of kilometers. It competes with the Saildrone and the buoyancy-driven Underwater glider in long-endurance ocean monitoring, navigating via GPS and Waypoint navigation.

plain: A mathematical trick that lets a person safely control a faraway robot even when there is a delay in the connection, by reshaping the signals so the system never builds up runaway energy.
snappy: An encoding of velocity and force signals into power-carrying variables that keeps delayed bilateral teleoperation passive and therefore stable.
detail: Wave variables (also called the scattering transformation) combine velocity and force into a single 'wave' quantity so that the communication channel cannot inject energy into the loop, guaranteeing stability of Bilateral teleoperation regardless of how large the round-trip Latency grows. This makes them foundational to Passivity-based control of master-slave systems where a Teleoperation link spans seconds of delay, such as Earth-to-orbit Telerobotics for an Orbital servicing robot or long-distance Surgical robot work. The trade-off is reduced Teleoperation transparency: heavier wave-variable filtering trades crisp force feedback for guaranteed Stability, so designers tune it against the application's tolerance for sluggish Haptic feedback.

plain: A grid route planner that spreads numbers outward from the goal like a flood, then a robot just walks downhill in those numbers to reach the goal.
snappy: A grid planner that propagates a breadth-first cost wave outward from the goal cell, after which any start cell follows the descending gradient to the goal.
detail: The Wavefront Planner (also called the grassfire or brushfire algorithm) assigns the goal cell cost zero and floods increasing costs outward across a free-space Occupancy grid, equivalent to a uniform-cost Dijkstra's algorithm or a Breadth-first search from the goal; the robot then performs gradient descent on the resulting Cost map. It guarantees a path on the grid if one exists and underlies many simple Coverage Path Planning and Path planning systems. Its single-sweep, march-from-goal structure is the same idea that FMT* exploits in continuous space.

plain: Google's sister company that runs driverless taxis people can actually hail in some cities.
snappy: Alphabet's autonomous-vehicle company operating a commercial driverless robotaxi service.
detail: Waymo, Alphabet's self-driving unit, operates a commercial Robotaxi service using the Waymo Driver, a Self-driving stack built on LiDAR, Radar, Camera, and HD map data. It runs at Level 4 automation within a defined Operational design domain, publishing the Waymo Open Dataset to advance Autonomous vehicle research. Its sensor-rich, map-reliant approach contrasts with Tesla's Vision-only autonomy bet.

plain: A big set of real self-driving sensor data that Waymo shared publicly so researchers can build and compare autonomy algorithms.
snappy: A large-scale, high-resolution LiDAR-and-camera dataset released by Waymo for perception, prediction, and motion research.
detail: The Waymo Open Dataset (WOD) offers densely labeled 3D object detection and multi-object tracking data plus a separate motion and prediction split with a lane graph, captured across diverse cities and conditions. It is a heavily used benchmark for autonomy research, complementing nuScenes, and its size makes it valuable for training large perception and behavior prediction models. Vulnerable road user labels and long-tail scenes make it a stress test for real-world robustness.

plain: A very large set of real traffic recordings, released by the self-driving company Waymo, used to teach computers to predict how road users will move.
snappy: A large-scale, interaction-rich motion-forecasting dataset of mined real-world scenarios released by Waymo for trajectory prediction research.
detail: The Waymo Open Motion Dataset emphasizes interactive scenarios, providing object tracks, the Lane graph, and traffic-signal states for Trajectory Prediction and Behavior prediction. It is a standard benchmark alongside Argoverse and nuScenes, and complements the perception-focused Waymo Open Dataset. Released by Waymo, it stresses hard cases like an Unprotected left turn and Cut-in interactions relevant to any Self-driving stack.

plain: A marked spot along a planned route that a robot aims to pass through on its way to the final destination.
snappy: An intermediate target pose along a route that the robot is commanded to reach in sequence.
detail: A Waypoint breaks a long route into manageable segments, so instead of solving for the whole journey at once the robot performs Waypoint navigation, reaching each point before heading to the next. A warehouse Automated guided vehicle follows waypoints laid out along its aisles, while a Drone executes a mission as an ordered list of GPS waypoints. The Global planner typically outputs the waypoint sequence, and a Local planner or Trajectory tracking controller handles the motion between consecutive waypoints.

plain: Programming a drone to fly itself along a route by visiting a list of GPS map points in order.
snappy: Autonomous flight along a preset route of geographic coordinates managed by the Autopilot.
detail: An operator draws a series of waypoints in a Ground control station, and the Autopilot, fusing GPS with its Inertial measurement unit, flies between them at set speeds and altitudes, optionally triggering camera or sensor actions at each point. It is the backbone of repeatable Agriculture surveys, mapping, and inspection, and is configured identically in PX4 and ArduPilot via MAVLink. For smooth aggressive flight the path can be refined into a Minimum-snap trajectory rather than straight legs.

plain: Showing a robot a path by driving it by hand to each spot you want and recording those spots one by one.
snappy: Defining a robot path by jogging the arm to positions and recording each as a waypoint.
detail: Waypoint teaching uses a Teach pendant (or Hand guiding on a Cobot) to jog the robot to each Waypoint, capturing the Tool center point pose at every point relative to the Work object frame. The recorded points are then joined into a path the controller executes, optionally smoothed with Zone blending. It is the on-cell complement to Offline programming and remains the fastest method for short pick-and-place and Machine tending routines.

plain: A UK company building self-driving software that learns to drive directly from experience rather than from hand-written rules.
snappy: British autonomy startup developing end-to-end learned driving models that map sensor input straight to steering and pedal actions.
detail: Wayve pioneered an end-to-end driving approach in which a single neural network learns the full perception-to-control mapping, in contrast to the modular pipeline of a traditional self-driving stack with separate perception, prediction, and planning stages. The company favours camera-centric, vision-only autonomy and trains large driving foundation models, positioning its work alongside the vision-language-action model trend in embodied AI. Its systems are evaluated on disengagement and intervention metrics and tested through closed-loop simulation before fleet deployment in cities.

plain: A free, beginner-friendly robot simulator that comes with ready-made robots and simulated sensors out of the box.
snappy: An open-source robot simulator with bundled robot models, sensor emulation, and multi-language controllers.
detail: Webots ships a library of standard robots and sensors so users can prototype Navigation or Manipulation without authoring every model, and it offers a ROS and ROS 2 bridge. It occupies a middle ground between the lightweight PyBullet and the heavier Gazebo or Isaac Sim, and it is widely used in education and competitions. Like other simulators it relies on a Physics engine and supports Sensor simulation.

plain: An insertion failure where a peg jams at an angle, pressing hard against two spots on the hole's walls so it can move no further.
snappy: An insertion jamming failure where the peg locks against the hole walls at two contact points, preventing further motion.
detail: Wedging is a two-point jamming failure in Peg-in-hole insertion: the peg tilts and presses simultaneously against opposite hole walls so friction within the Friction cone resists any downward push, distinct from simple sticking. It is analyzed with the Coulomb friction model and avoided by keeping the insertion within the wedging-free force/moment region using Force control, a Remote center of compliance, or a Spiral search recovery. It is a key failure mode tracked on the NIST assembly task boards.

plain: A route finder that exaggerates how close it thinks it is to the goal so it rushes there faster, at the cost of maybe not finding the very shortest route.
snappy: A* search with the heuristic multiplied by a factor w > 1, trading a bounded loss of optimality for greatly reduced node expansions.
detail: Weighted A* inflates the Heuristic function of A* search by a weight w greater than one, which biases the search greedily toward the goal and expands far fewer nodes, returning a path guaranteed to be at most w times the optimal cost. This speed-for-quality tradeoff is the basis of the Anytime algorithm ARA*, which sweeps w downward over time. It is a staple of robot Path planning whenever an admissible-but-slow optimal A* search is too expensive for the available compute.

plain: A way of choosing among a robot's many possible joint motions that favors some joints over others to get a preferred, natural-looking move.
snappy: A Jacobian pseudoinverse with a weighting matrix that biases redundancy resolution toward low-cost or preferred joint motions.
detail: When an arm has Kinematic redundancy, infinitely many joint velocities produce the same Task space motion, and a weighted pseudoinverse picks the one that minimizes a weighted joint cost, for example penalizing motion of slow or near-limit joints. It generalizes the ordinary Jacobian pseudoinverse used in Resolved-Rate Motion Control and is often combined with Damped Least Squares to stay well-behaved near a Kinematic singularity. In Whole-body control of a Humanoid robot the weights encode joint inertia or limit proximity so the redundancy in the Null space resolves toward stable, energy-efficient postures.

plain: A robot arm that holds a welding torch or gun to join metal parts together automatically.
snappy: An articulated arm fitted with an arc or spot welding tool that performs automated Robotic welding along programmed paths.
detail: A Welding robot is the single most common Industrial robot arm application, dominating automotive body shops where a Spot welding robot fuses sheet panels and an Arc welding robot lays continuous beads. Path accuracy and Seam tracking matter intensely, so these cells combine precise trajectory tracking with through-arc or vision sensing to correct for part variation. The torch or gun mounts at the end-effector on the Robot wrist, and offline programming is used to generate weld paths before the cell is commissioned.

plain: Working out how far and which way a robot has moved by counting how much its wheels have turned.
snappy: Pose-change estimation derived from integrating wheel encoder counts and a kinematic model.
detail: Wheel odometry counts rotations from an Encoder on each wheel and applies the robot's drive geometry to estimate incremental Pose change, a form of Dead reckoning common on a Differential drive Autonomous mobile robot in Logistics & Warehouse. Wheel slip and uneven floors cause Sensor drift, so it is fused with an Inertial measurement unit and Visual odometry inside a Kalman filter for reliable State estimation. It is cheap, high-rate, and a backbone input to Localization and SLAM.

plain: When a robot's wheels spin or slide more than the robot actually moves, like tires spinning on ice, throwing off how far it thinks it has traveled.
snappy: The mismatch between commanded and actual wheel travel that degrades traction and corrupts wheel-based odometry.
detail: Quantified as a slip ratio, wheel slip arises when traction at the Contact point cannot support the demanded acceleration, so the wheel travels more (or less) than the ground, injecting drift into Wheel odometry and Dead reckoning. It is a primary error source for Differential-drive robot and Skid steering platforms and a key term in Terrain adaptation and planetary rover traction models, often estimated by fusing Inertial measurement unit data via an Extended Kalman filter. Mitigations include traction control, slip-aware Localization, and detecting it as an Anomaly detection signal feeding the Navigation stack.

plain: A robot that uses wheels with leg-like spokes, so it rolls fast on flat ground but can climb over obstacles like a walker.
snappy: A robot combining rotating wheels with leg-like spokes (whegs) to roll efficiently yet climb steps and obstacles.
detail: A Wheel-leg hybrid robot fuses the speed and simplicity of a Wheeled robot with the obstacle-clearing ability of a Legged robot, classically using Whegs, rotating spokes that grab and step over edges as the hub spins. It is a close cousin of the fully reconfigurable Wheeled-legged robot, and both target the efficiency-versus-mobility trade central to field locomotion. The form excels in Defense & Security and Space exploration where terrain alternates between smooth stretches and rubble, letting one drivetrain handle both without a Rocker-Bogie Suspension.

plain: A robot whose legs end in wheels, so it can roll smoothly on flat ground and step over obstacles when rolling will not work.
snappy: A hybrid mobile robot with wheels at the ends of articulated legs, switching between energy-efficient rolling and obstacle-clearing stepping.
detail: By combining the low Cost of transport of Wheeled locomotion with the obstacle-negotiation of Legged locomotion, a wheel-legged robot rolls on smooth ground then lifts and places its wheeled feet to climb stairs or cross gaps, demanding a Whole-body control stack that arbitrates both modes. ANYbotics' wheeled ANYmal and ETH's Ascento are canonical examples, and the design is closely related to the Wheel-leg hybrid robot and Wheeled-legged robot families plus Rocker-Bogie Suspension rovers. Control blends Footstep planning with rolling Trajectory tracking and active balance akin to a Two-wheeled inverted pendulum.

plain: Moving on rolling wheels, the efficient way to travel over smooth, flat ground.
snappy: Locomotion using rotating wheels for continuous, low-energy travel over relatively flat terrain.
detail: Wheeled locomotion offers a far lower Cost of transport than Legged locomotion on flat floors, which is why almost every Autonomous mobile robot and Automated guided vehicle in a warehouse rolls rather than walks. Steering schemes range from Differential drive and Skid steering to Ackermann steering and an Omnidirectional drive using a Mecanum wheel. Its weakness is steps and rough ground, which motivates the hybrid Wheeled-legged robot.

plain: A robot that gets around by rolling on wheels, best suited to smooth, flat floors.
snappy: A mobile robot driven by wheels, offering simple, efficient locomotion on flat or paved surfaces.
detail: Wheeled robots are the most common mobile form because Wheeled locomotion is energy-efficient and mechanically simple, powering most of Logistics & Warehouse and Service & Consumer robotics. Steering variants include the Differential-drive robot, Ackermann steering, Skid steering, and the holonomic Omnidirectional robot using a Mecanum wheel or Omni wheel. They underpin platforms from the Delivery robot to the Autonomous mobile robot, though they struggle where a Legged robot or Tracked robot excels.

plain: A robot that has wheels at the ends of its legs, so it can roll fast on smooth ground and step over obstacles when needed.
snappy: A hybrid platform with wheels mounted on articulated legs, combining rolling speed with legged obstacle-crossing agility.
detail: A wheeled-legged robot rolls efficiently like a Wheeled robot on flat ground but lifts and places its wheeled feet like a Legged robot to climb steps or cross gaps, using Whole-body control to manage Balance control. ANYbotics and ETH Zurich research platforms popularized the concept for inspection over mixed terrain. It blends low Cost of transport with Terrain adaptation, sitting between the Quadruped robot and the omnidirectional wheeled base.

plain: Spoked wheels with a few legs sticking out, blending the speed of rolling with the obstacle-climbing of legs.
snappy: Spoked wheel-leg hybrids whose protruding spokes combine wheeled cruising speed with legged step-climbing ability.
detail: Whegs (wheel-legs) let a small Field robot scramble over rubble and curbs that would stop a plain wheel, while still rolling efficiently on flat ground. As a form of Wheel-leg hybrid robot they avoid the control complexity of a fully Legged robot yet gain much of its terrain ability, popular in Defense & Security inspection platforms. The rotating spokes give a bouncy ride, so designers tune spoke count and phasing for Terrain adaptation, related to the broader Wheel-legged robot class.

plain: An artificial bristle, copied from a cat's whiskers, that lets a robot feel objects and air movement by sensing how much the bristle bends.
snappy: A biomimetic flexible filament that detects contact and airflow by measuring deflection or bending strain at its base.
detail: A Whisker Sensor is a Bio-inspired robotics approach to Tactile sensing for the region just beyond a robot's body, useful in the dark, in dust, or in tight gaps where a Camera or LiDAR fails. Deflection at the filament root is read by a Strain gauge, Hall effect sensor, or capacitive element, letting a Service robot or small Mobile robot do wall-following and gap detection much like a rodent, and sweeping arrays can reconstruct nearby surface contours. It complements rather than replaces a Tactile sensor on the fingertips, extending the Perception-action loop to graze-contact and Active perception for navigation in an Unstructured environment.

plain: Coordinating every joint of a robot at once so it can do a task and stay balanced at the same time.
snappy: A control framework that commands all of a robot's joints together to satisfy task goals and balance simultaneously.
detail: Whole-body control solves, every Control loop, an optimization that distributes a task, like reaching, across all joints while respecting balance, joint limits, and contact constraints. It relies on the robot's full Dynamics, often via Centroidal dynamics and Floating-base dynamics, and frequently sits beneath a Model predictive control planner.
