A Humanoid robot like Atlas uses WBC to step, push a door, and keep its Zero moment point stable all at once, exploiting Kinematic redundancy and the Null space.

plain: Figuring out how every joint of a free-standing robot should move so it can reach with its hands, point its head, and keep its balance all at the same time.
snappy: Solving a floating-base robot's joint motions to satisfy multiple simultaneous Cartesian, posture, and balance tasks.
detail: Whole-Body Inverse Kinematics generalizes single-chain Inverse kinematics to a Floating-base dynamics system, computing all joint and base motions that simultaneously satisfy hand-pose, foot-contact, gaze, and Center of mass objectives. Because tasks conflict, solvers exploit the Jacobian matrix Null space to layer them, and prioritization is commonly cast as Hierarchical Quadratic Programming or a stack-of-tasks. It is essential for Humanoid robot reaching and is closely tied to Whole-body control, the Operational Space Formulation, and balance metrics like the Zero moment point. Implementations appear in Pinocchio and MoveIt-style frameworks.

plain: When a robot uses its whole body at once - legs, trunk, and arms together - to move around and do tasks like pushing a door or carrying a load.
snappy: Coordinating legs, torso, and arms together as one system to move the robot while also reaching, bracing, or manipulating, rather than treating walking and arm motion separately.
detail: Instead of locomotion and arm control being separate modules, whole-body locomotion solves them jointly so a Humanoid robot can lean its torso to keep balance while an arm reaches, or brace a hand against a wall to push off. This is the basis of loco-manipulation, where carrying or opening doors changes the robot's own dynamics, and it is implemented with Whole-body control optimizers that respect the Zero moment point, the Support polygon, and joint Torque control limits. It generalizes Bipedal locomotion by folding manipulation, Centroidal dynamics, and Balance control into a single Trajectory optimization.

plain: The ability of a drone's controller to keep it steady and on course even when wind and gusts try to push it around.
snappy: Control techniques that estimate and counteract aerodynamic disturbances so a UAV holds its trajectory under wind and gusts.
detail: Wind disturbance rejection extends basic Feedback control with a disturbance observer that estimates the external force pushing on the airframe and feeds a correction forward, a form of Disturbance rejection critical for stable hover and Precision landing. Methods range from L1 adaptive control and Active disturbance rejection control to learned residual terms layered onto Learned quadrotor control. It matters most for delivery aircraft like Wing operating Beyond visual line of sight in real weather, and for any Multirotor drone fighting gusts near buildings.

plain: Alphabet's drone-delivery company, which lowers packages to your yard on a string from a hovering aircraft.
snappy: Alphabet's drone-delivery service operating hybrid VTOL aircraft that hover and lower packages by tether to the ground.
detail: Wing (Wing Aviation) is one of the leading Drone delivery operators, flying a Hybrid VTOL aircraft that cruises on wings for range then hovers to deposit cargo via a winch rather than landing. Its operations run Beyond visual line of sight under an integrated UAS traffic management framework and Part 107-style authorizations, competing with Zipline in last-mile logistics. The tethered-lowering approach avoids ground contact and Brownout landing risk while keeping the aircraft clear of people and obstacles.

plain: A company that makes drones which take off straight up like a helicopter but then fly forward on wings to map large areas of land.
snappy: A maker of tailsitter VTOL fixed-wing mapping drones aimed at surveying and large-area aerial data capture.
detail: Wingtra builds the WingtraOne, a Tailsitter that launches vertically then transitions to efficient fixed-wing cruise, combining the convenient takeoff of a Multirotor drone with the endurance of a Fixed-wing drone. Equipped with PPK or RTK GNSS and a survey camera, it flies a Lawnmower survey pattern to capture imagery for Aerial photogrammetry, producing an Orthomosaic and Digital surface model with minimal Ground control point reliance. It targets surveyors and Precision agriculture drone users who need to cover hundreds of hectares per flight.

plain: Recharging a robot's battery through the air, with no plug or metal contacts to connect.
snappy: Transferring power to a robot's battery without physical contacts, typically via inductive coupling.
detail: Wireless charging uses inductive coupling between a floor or wall pad and a coil on the robot, removing the exposed contacts and connector wear that complicate Autonomous docking. It suits a service robot and warehouse Autonomous mobile robot that dock frequently in dirty or wet environments, though it is less efficient and adds Thermal management load. The Battery management system still governs the charge profile and State of charge, and it competes with a Hot-swappable battery approach for minimizing downtime.

plain: A company building self-flying electric air taxis that carry passengers with no pilot on board.
snappy: A developer of autonomous, pilotless passenger eVTOL air taxis backed by Boeing for urban air mobility.
detail: Wisk Aero develops an autonomous eVTOL air taxi using Distributed electric propulsion and a Lift-Plus-Cruise configuration, distinguishing itself from rivals by removing the onboard pilot entirely. From a robotics view, the hard problems are the full Autonomy stack, Detect and avoid for sharing airspace, and a Remote operation center providing supervisory oversight under FAA rules. Its pilotless vision raises the certification bar relative to the piloted Joby Aviation, while both target Vertiport-to-Vertiport service in the Urban air mobility market.

plain: A testing trick where a hidden human secretly controls a robot while users believe it is acting on its own, so designers can study reactions before the smart software exists.
snappy: An HRI evaluation method in which an unseen operator teleoperates a robot that participants believe is fully autonomous.
detail: Wizard of Oz prototyping lets teams test interaction design for a Social robot or Service robot long before the autonomy is built, by having a hidden operator drive responses via Teleoperation. It is invaluable for studying Proxemics, Intent communication, and Affective computing reactions in realistic Human-robot interaction studies. The method controls for capability so researchers measure user response rather than algorithm quality, and it informs requirements for the eventual perception and Behavior planning stack.

plain: A way of describing the robot's moves in relation to the part it is working on, rather than in relation to the room or the floor.
snappy: A user-defined coordinate frame attached to a part or fixture that robot moves are expressed in.
detail: A work object frame is a Coordinate frame the robot controller maintains so taught positions follow the part if the fixture is relocated, expressed as a Homogeneous transformation matrix relative to the robot base. Programming an Industrial robot arm in the work object frame, rather than world coordinates, makes Offline programming and Robot calibration corrections portable. It works together with the Tool center point definition and is established during cell setup via Hand-eye calibration or three-point teaching.

plain: Retraining the people whose jobs a robot took over so they can run, fix, and oversee the robots instead.
snappy: The practice of retraining displaced staff to operate, maintain, and supervise deployed robots rather than perform the manual task the robot now does.
detail: Workforce Reskilling is the human counterpart to Labor Displacement: instead of cutting headcount, a plant retrains line workers to program a Teach pendant, monitor a Fleet, or service a Robot cell. In Manufacturing this often means moving operators into roles supervising a Cobot or running Fleet management software, and it materially changes the Total cost of ownership because trained in-house staff reduce reliance on a System integrator for every change. Successful reskilling is also a hedge against Vendor Lock-In, since staff who understand the stack can adapt or replace equipment more freely.

plain: All the places a robot's hand can physically reach.
snappy: The set of all poses a robot's end-effector can attain given its joint limits.
detail: A robot's reachable Workspace is bounded by its link lengths, Joint ranges, and overall Reach; the smaller Dexterous workspace is where the End-effector can reach with any orientation. The Workspace shape is determined by the robot's Kinematic chain and the type of Serial manipulator or Parallel manipulator architecture. Planners use the Workspace to verify a target Pose is attainable before solving Inverse kinematics.

plain: A very large pretrained model that can imagine and roll forward how the physical world will change, used to help robots plan and train.
snappy: A large pretrained generative model of physical-world dynamics, usable as a learned simulator or planning prior for robots.
detail: A world foundation model generalizes the per-task World model into a broadly pretrained system that predicts future video or state given actions, enabling rollout-based planning, Synthetic data generation, and Real-to-sim style training. It connects to Model-based reinforcement learning and to driving-focused variants like the Driving World Model, and is exemplified by efforts around NVIDIA Isaac and large video-prediction backbones. For Mobility, a WFM can hallucinate plausible traffic scenes to stress-test a planner.

plain: A robot's internal mental picture of its surroundings and how things move, which it uses to imagine what will happen before acting.
snappy: A learned or built internal representation of the environment and its dynamics that a robot uses to predict outcomes and plan.
detail: A world model lets a Robot forecast how the environment will respond to its actions, supporting planning without acting blindly in the real world. In Model-based reinforcement learning, the agent learns a world model and rolls it forward to evaluate candidate plans, improving Sample efficiency over Model-free reinforcement learning. World models are central to Embodied AI and increasingly to Generative simulation, where learned dynamics fill in for an expensive Physics engine.

plain: Building a robot's internal predictor of how the world will change before training it on any task, so it can later imagine outcomes and plan instead of trying everything for real.
snappy: Pretraining a predictive dynamics model from data, later used for planning or as a learned simulator for the policy.
detail: A World model is trained to predict future observations or latent states from current ones and actions; pretraining it on broad interaction or video data yields a learned simulator a robot can roll out internally for planning or Model-based reinforcement learning. Systems like Dreamer learn the policy entirely inside the imagined model, improving Sample efficiency for Mobility and Manipulation. It is closely tied to Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture and the predictive objectives of Contrastive Predictive Coding, and overlaps with the World foundation model concept.

plain: A gear setup where a screw turns a wheel, giving big speed reduction and locking in place so the load can't drive it backward.
snappy: A screw-and-wheel reducer giving high single-stage ratio and self-locking, non-backdrivable output.
detail: A Worm Drive meshes a helical screw (the worm) against a worm wheel to achieve a high Gear Ratio in one stage, and the steep helix angle makes it self-locking so the output holds position without an Electromagnetic Brake. This non-backdrivable, gravity-holding behavior suits Manufacturing positioners and Mobility steering, though it sacrifices efficiency and Backdrivability compared with a Planetary Gearbox or Cycloidal drive. It is the gearing element at the heart of a Slewing Drive.

plain: A screw that turns a toothed wheel, giving a large drop in speed and a big boost in strength while resisting being turned backward.
snappy: A screw-shaped worm meshing with a toothed wheel to deliver very high single-stage reduction with inherent self-locking against back-driving.
detail: Because the sliding screw contact resists reverse motion, a Worm Gear (also called a Worm Drive) provides self-locking that holds a load without power, useful for pan-tilt heads and lift axes that must stay put when de-energized. It offers a much higher Gear Ratio per stage than a comparable Spur Gear or Helical Gear, at the cost of efficiency and the elimination of Backdrivability. The high friction makes it a poor choice where a robot needs Force control through its Gear Train.

plain: The longest a computing task could ever possibly take to finish, used to make sure deadlines are always met.
snappy: An upper bound on a task's execution time, used to prove real-time schedulability under all conditions.
detail: WCET bounds how long a piece of code can run in the worst case, so engineers can guarantee a Control loop meets its deadline rather than just usually meeting it. Establishing it is essential for Real-time control and for safety arguments under Functional safety standards, and it underpins schedulability analysis on a Real-time operating system or PREEMPT_RT. Pessimistic WCET wastes compute, while underestimating it invites deadline overruns that show up as Jitter or, worse, a missed hard deadline.

plain: A single bundle describing both a push and a twist that a body applies, combined together.
snappy: A six-vector combining force and torque acting on a body.
detail: A wrench stacks three force and three torque components into one six-vector, the force-side dual of a Twist. A Force/torque sensor at the robot wrist measures the wrench during Force control, Impedance control, or a delicate Peg-in-hole insertion. The transpose of the Jacobian matrix maps an end-effector wrench into the joint torques needed to produce it, which is how arms render Cartesian forces.

plain: A pose where two of a robot wrist's rotating axes line up, so the wrist briefly loses one way it can turn.
snappy: A configuration of a spherical wrist where two of its rotation axes become collinear, dropping the rank of the Jacobian and losing an orientation freedom.
detail: On a Six-axis robot with a Spherical wrist, a wrist singularity occurs when the fourth and sixth axes align, so both rotate the tool about the same line and one orientation Degrees of freedom vanishes. At this Kinematic singularity the Jacobian matrix loses rank and the Inverse kinematics demands near-infinite joint speeds to follow a smooth path, causing erratic flips. Planners avoid it by reorienting the approach or by damping the solution with Damped Least Squares, and it is one of the three classic Robot singularity families alongside the Elbow Singularity and Shoulder Singularity.

plain: A shortcut language that lets engineers write a robot description once with reusable templates instead of repeating themselves.
snappy: A macro preprocessor that generates parameterized, reusable URDF (or SDF) robot descriptions.
detail: Xacro adds variables, math, conditionals, and macros to XML, so a six-legged robot's identical legs are written once and instantiated six times, then expanded into a flat URDF at build time. It dramatically cuts duplication in describing a Manipulator or Quadruped robot and is standard practice in ROS and ROS 2 workflows. The expanded URDF then feeds RViz, tf, MoveIt, and Gazebo.

plain: Software plumbing that lets the many programs running on a complex robot send messages to each other.
snappy: A middleware layer for asynchronous inter-process communication across the distributed software of a robot.
detail: YARP provides a Publish-subscribe and port-based messaging model that decouples sensing, control, and perception processes, playing a role similar to ROS or LCM. It is best known as the backbone of the iCub humanoid, where it carries data between vision, motor, and Whole-body control modules. Its device-driver abstraction lets the same Humanoid robot code run against simulated or real hardware.

plain: A Japanese company that makes Motoman factory robots and the motors and controllers that drive them.
snappy: Japanese maker of Motoman industrial robots, servomotors, and motion controllers.
detail: Yaskawa, through its Motoman brand, is one of the 'big four' Industrial robotics suppliers, building the Articulated robot for Robotic welding, painting, and Material handling. The company is also a dominant maker of the Servomotor and Variable frequency drive that power countless other machines, giving it deep Motion control expertise. Its robots use a dedicated Robot controller tuned for high-speed, high-Repeatability work on the Production line.

plain: A standard physical box of everyday items, like cans, mugs, and tools, that labs worldwide use so their grasping results can be fairly compared.
snappy: A standardized set of everyday physical objects with 3D models for benchmarking grasping and manipulation across labs.
detail: The YCB object set is a curated collection of common items (food cans, kitchenware, tools) shipped with high-quality 3D scans, letting different groups run the same Grasping experiments on identical hardware for reproducible comparison. It supports both physical trials and simulation, and underlies grasp Benchmark protocols and the YCB-Video pose dataset used to evaluate 6D Pose Estimation. It is a physical-object complement to simulated suites like RLBench and Meta-World.

plain: A method that lets a robot's camera spot and label every object in a picture in a single quick glance, fast enough to keep up with live video.
snappy: A single-stage real-time object detector that predicts bounding boxes and class labels for all objects in one forward pass of a neural network.
detail: YOLO reframes Object detection as a single regression over a grid, so unlike two-stage pipelines it does not run a separate region-proposal step. Built on a Convolutional neural network backbone, it emits many candidate Bounding box predictions per image that are pruned by confidence thresholds and overlap filtering scored with Intersection over Union. Its speed makes it the default perception front-end on resource-limited Onboard compute such as an NVIDIA Jetson, where a Mobile manipulation robot or Autonomous mobile robot needs to localize parts, pallets, or people at camera frame rate; accuracy is usually reported as Mean Average Precision on the COCO Dataset.

plain: A camera by Stereolabs that uses two lenses, like eyes, to judge distance and track a robot's motion.
snappy: Stereolabs stereo depth cameras providing 3D depth, point clouds, and visual odometry for robots.
detail: The ZED is a passive stereo camera that computes a depth map via stereo matching without an infrared projector, making it usable outdoors where a RealSense struggles. Its SDK provides built-in visual odometry and visual-inertial odometry plus a point cloud, feeding navigation and 3D reconstruction. ZED cameras are common on outdoor mobile robots and run well on NVIDIA Jetson onboard compute.

plain: A lightweight communication system that lets separate computer programs share data with each other very efficiently, even across networks.
snappy: A pub-sub and distributed-query protocol used as an alternative transport for ROS 2, optimized for low overhead across constrained and wide-area networks.
detail: Zenoh unifies publish-subscribe messaging, distributed storage, and remote queries in one protocol, and is increasingly adopted as a ROS 2 transport via the zenoh-bridge to replace or complement DDS implementations like Fast DDS and Cyclone DDS. Because it scales gracefully from tiny Microcontroller targets up to cloud links, it suits Multi-robot system fleets and Cloud robotics deployments where Publish-subscribe traffic must cross unreliable WANs. Robotics teams use it to stream Point cloud and Odometry topics off-robot without the LAN-centric assumptions of standard DDS discovery.

plain: The spot on the ground where a walking robot's tipping forces cancel out, used to tell whether it stays balanced.
snappy: The point on the ground where the net horizontal torque from foot reaction forces is zero.
detail: The zero moment point (ZMP) coincides with the Center of pressure during balanced contact, and a biped is dynamically balanced as long as its ZMP stays strictly inside the Support polygon. ZMP-based gait generation, often built on the Linear inverted pendulum model, drove early Humanoid robot walking and Bipedal locomotion controllers. It complements newer criteria like the Capture point and Centroidal dynamics that better handle Dynamic walking and recovery steps.

plain: A walking-robot method that keeps the robot balanced by making sure the spot where ground forces effectively act stays underneath its feet.
snappy: Gait control that keeps the Zero moment point inside the support polygon so contact forces remain valid and the biped does not tip.
detail: Zero moment point control plans body and foot motion so the Zero moment point stays within the Support polygon, guaranteeing the foot does not roll about its edge during Bipedal locomotion. It is commonly realized with Preview control over a Linear inverted pendulum model to track a desired ZMP trajectory, an approach popularized by Kajita. It contrasts with Capture point control and Centroidal momentum control, and underpins the classic flat-footed walking of early humanoid robots.

plain: A robot succeeding at a task it was never specifically trained on, with no extra practice.
snappy: Performing an unseen task or handling unseen objects with no task-specific training examples.
detail: Zero-shot generalization is a headline capability of a Vision-language-action model like RT-2, which can act on novel objects described in language thanks to web-scale priors. It is the strongest form of generalization, beyond Few-shot learning, and is the aspiration for any Generalist policy or Robot foundation model. In practice it leans on Transfer learning and rich Representation learning so that a Humanoid robot can attempt instructions outside its Demonstration data.

plain: A trick that corrects the slow buildup of error in a motion sensor by noticing when the device is briefly standing still and resetting its assumed speed to zero.
snappy: An estimator correction applied during detected stationary phases that constrains velocity to zero to bound inertial drift.
detail: A Zero-Velocity Update (ZUPT) exploits moments when a foot is planted or a device is stationary to inject a pseudo-measurement of zero velocity into the Kalman filter, sharply reducing the drift that an Inertial measurement unit accumulates through Dead reckoning. It pairs naturally with Contact Estimation in foot-mounted pedestrian and Humanoid robot navigation. ZUPT is heavily used in GPS-denied navigation for dismounted soldiers and indoor walkers.

plain: A well-known rule-of-thumb recipe for setting up a controller by first pushing it until it just starts to oscillate.
snappy: A classic heuristic for tuning PID gains derived from the onset of sustained oscillation.
detail: The Ziegler-Nichols method increases the proportional Gain until the loop oscillates steadily, records that ultimate gain and its period, then plugs them into a lookup table to set PID controller parameters. It is a fast starting point for Gain tuning on Manufacturing process loops and simple motor Servo control, though it tends to produce aggressive responses with noticeable Overshoot that often need manual refinement. It remains a textbook baseline against which modern model-based tuning is compared.

plain: A company that uses small autonomous aircraft to fly medicines and packages directly to people, dropping them by parachute or on a tether.
snappy: Drone-delivery operator flying fixed-wing and hybrid aircraft to deposit medical and retail payloads autonomously.
detail: Zipline built one of the first at-scale Drone delivery networks, originally flying blood and vaccines to clinics across Rwanda and Ghana using a catapult-launched Fixed-wing drone. Its newer platform adds a VTOL hover stage with a lowered delivery droid for precise Last-mile delivery to homes. Operations depend heavily on BVLOS operations approvals, Geofencing, and Detect and avoid systems to share airspace safely.

plain: Letting a robot cut the corner near a target point instead of stopping dead on it, so it keeps moving smoothly and faster.
snappy: Rounding a robot's path near a waypoint so it maintains speed instead of decelerating to a stop.
detail: Zone blending defines a tolerance radius around a Waypoint within which the controller fuses the incoming and outgoing segments, trading exact passage through the point for continuous speed and lower cycle time. The blend radius is tuned per point during Waypoint teaching and shapes the resulting Trajectory and Motion profile. It is essential for smooth Adhesive dispensing and Arc welding robot paths where stopping would leave a defect, and interacts with Following error and S-curve acceleration limits.

plain: Amazon's self-driving company building a custom, symmetrical vehicle with no steering wheel.
snappy: Amazon's autonomous-vehicle company building a purpose-built, bidirectional robotaxi.
detail: Zoox, owned by Amazon, designs a ground-up Robotaxi with no steering wheel, bidirectional driving, and four-wheel steering rather than retrofitting an existing car. Its purpose-built vehicle pairs a full Self-driving stack of LiDAR, Radar, and Camera with Level 4 automation inside a chosen Operational design domain. The clean-sheet design lets Zoox optimize the Chassis and sensor placement for the Autonomous vehicle task from the start.
